# ArtAttack code review, round 2 — full findings appendix


**901 findings, 56 groups, 56 source reports.**  Severity spread: 13 critical, 174 high, 421 medium, 293 low.


This is the appendix, not the argument. The README states a conclusion in a line; this
document holds the evidence behind it. Every finding from every group's authoritative
report is reproduced here in full and unedited — nothing merged, nothing dropped, nothing
compressed into a summary. Where a group had a verifier, the verified report is the one
reproduced and the reviewer's raw draft is discarded; the twenty cross-cutting sweeps had
no separate verifier, so their raw reports stand as written and are labelled as such. Each
group keeps its own preamble, its Themes, and its Rejected section, because what a
verifier threw out is often as informative as what survived; only the heading levels were
normalised, and each group heading now carries a one-line stamp giving its count, its
severity spread and the report it came from. Read it two ways: down the
[contents](#contents) when you want a module's whole story, or through the
[index by file](#index-by-file) when you have one path in your hand and want everything
anyone said about it. Headings nest group (`##`) > section (`###`) > finding (`####`), so
any editor's outline view will fold it.

# Index by file


Every tracked repository path that any finding names. **Subject of** lists the groups whose
finding is filed *against* that path, with its severities — this is the column that answers
"what is wrong with this file". **Also cited by** lists groups that quote the path as
evidence inside a finding filed elsewhere, which is where a file's second-order problems
show up. Paths are resolved against `git ls-files`; a bare filename in a finding is
resolved to its unique tracked path.

# Engine modules

<a id="g-core-objects"></a>

## core-objects — Object and state interfaces

*Group `core-objects` · 15 findings (3 high, 8 medium, 4 low) · source `review2/verified/core-objects.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened all seven assigned files in full and every line the reviewer cited, in
`engine/app/application.{h,cpp}`, `game/game_data.cpp`, `game/states/*.cpp`,
`game/objects/{player,projectile,projectile_*,level,weapon,debug_text}.*`,
`engine/render/{draw_object,animation_object,visual}.h`, `engine/ui/widget.h`,
`samples/minimal/`, all three `tests/*/CMakeLists.txt`, the vendored
`directxtk/SpriteBatch.h`, and `git show c6696af`. I also re-counted every claim
that carried a number.

The reviewer's structural reading is right and holds up: this group is three
interfaces at three levels of finish, and `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` in
`IGameObject::draw` is the single line that breaks `core`'s module contract, keeps
both non-math test targets from linking the engine, and forces a stranger's
`CMakeLists.txt` to `find_package(directxtk)` to compile a hello-world. Their line
numbers are almost all exact — 20 `draw(...) const override` sites across exactly 13
headers, `SpriteBatch.h:15-16` including `<d3d11_1.h>`, `application.h:131-134,159`,
`player.h:104`, `player.cpp:970-973`, `hello_state.cpp:53-55,62,68-70`,
`game_data.cpp:62-68`, `pause_menu.cpp:87-97`, `game_states.cpp:312` — all confirmed
as quoted.

What I threw out is mostly arithmetic and framing. Their `dx_` finding claims nine
accessors where there are twelve, says six of nine have no callers where seven of
twelve do, and asserts `set_dx()` has zero callers when `player.cpp:1033` calls it;
it also says the member "makes `Projectile` 32 bytes instead of 24", which is the
`MovingObject` subobject, not `Projectile`. Their `State::update(dt)` finding is
framed as an oversight — "the pass reached `IGameObject` and stopped" — when
`c6696af`'s own commit message argues the opposite in writing ("State::update()
stays argument-free… states can already reach dt through the application"); the
conflict with PHILOSOPHY:358 is real, the "they forgot" is not, and I re-graded it
and the twinned `draw()` finding from high to medium since neither is a live defect
and both are the same mechanical edit. The parallel-rendering docs finding needed
its argument repaired: PHILOSOPHY explicitly describes the destination and not the
current code (PHILOSOPHY.md:11-14), so "the code disagrees" is not by itself a
defect — the defect is that split-screen makes disjoint object slices unreachable at
the destination too. Smaller corrections: 42 `transition_to` sites, not 43;
`tests/math` *does* link `MattMath`, so ARCHITECTURE's `tests --> math` arrow is
satisfied and only the engine arrow is missing; the "everything the engine drags in"
phrase is in `tests/assets`, not `tests/core`; and three doc line citations were off
by a few lines.

What they missed, in the files they were given. First, `StateContext::state_` lives
in a *base* subobject of `Application`, and C++ destroys members before bases — so
the entire live state tree is destroyed *after* every service, including the
`AudioEngine` whose ordering `application.h:137-143` calls load-bearing, and after
`CoUninitialize()`. `application.h:113-114` promises the exact opposite in writing.
Second, ARCHITECTURE and PHILOSOPHY both say the shell owns a state *stack*;
`StateContext` is a one-slot holder with no push, no pop and no return channel, and
the one client has compensated with four nested `StateContext`s and three
heap-allocated enums used as out-parameters. Third, `MovingObject`'s dead surface is
much worse than reported: 13 of its 27 accessors have zero callers anywhere, and the
whole rotation triple is write-only — `set_rotation(0.0f)` once, never read, because
the rotation that is actually drawn is `DrawObject::draw_rotation_`. I added two
lower-severity items on the interface's own contract text.

### Themes

- The recent passes stopped at `IGameObject` and never reached `State`: `dt`, const
  `draw()`, a parameterised draw and forty lines of contract exist on one interface
  and none of them on the other, in the same folder.
- `engine/core` names a vendor type in a public signature. That one line is why
  `core` fails its own module contract, why two test targets refuse to link the
  engine, why the sample's build file must find DirectXTK, and why a second backend
  is a 20-site edit.
- Constness in this group is decorative where it is not compiler-enforced:
  `StateContext::update() const` drives every mutation in the program because
  `unique_ptr` launders constness.
- `MovingObject` is neither mechanism nor policy — it is shared state with ceremony.
  Half its API has no callers, its rotation is write-only, and its one override
  exists solely to widen access.
- Contract lives in comments where it has been written at all, and the two APIs in
  this group whose contracts are genuinely dangerous — `transition_to` destroying its
  caller, and a state tree that outlives every service — are the ones with none.
- The engine's own documents promise machinery this group does not supply: a state
  stack that is a single slot, and services that outlive the states, which they do
  not.

#### Move `SpriteBatch` out of the core interface: `engine/core` names a DirectXTK type in its public signature

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:4,41-42`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`core` may depend on `math` only)

**What:** The one interface every drawable implements takes a
`DirectX::SpriteBatch*`, so `engine/core` includes a DirectXTK header — and through
it `<d3d11_1.h>` — and every implementer's signature is written against one backend.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:1-4`, `:41-42`:

    #pragma once

    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"
    #include <SpriteBatch.h>
    ...
        virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
            const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;

`out/build/x64-debug/vcpkg_installed/x64-windows/include/directxtk/SpriteBatch.h:15-16`:

    #include <d3d11_1.h>
    #include <dxgi1_2.h>

`tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-5`:

    # The manifest loader reads a file and parses JSON, and that is all it does -
    # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units
    # directly rather than linking the engine and everything the engine drags in.

`samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:1-4` — the "dozen honest lines" a new project copies:

    # xaudio2redist first: directxtk's config references Microsoft::XAudio2Redist
    # but does not find it itself.
    find_package(xaudio2redist CONFIG REQUIRED)
    find_package(directxtk CONFIG REQUIRED)

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE.md:130-131 gives `core` exactly one permitted
dependency (`math`), and ARCHITECTURE.md:141 makes `core` "the only module everything
may lean on" — so this include is why every module in the engine transitively depends
on DirectXTK. Four consequences I verified in the tree:

1. A second backend or a headless renderer means editing 20
   `draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch*, const mattmath::Camera&) const override` declarations
   across exactly 13 headers (`engine/render/text_drop_shadow.h`,
   `engine/render/visual.h`, `engine/ui/widget.h`, and ten `game/objects/*.h`),
   inside a wider blast radius of 53 header lines and 49 source lines naming
   `DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch`.
2. `tests/assets` and `tests/core` both compile translation units directly rather
   than link `ArtAttackEngine`, and `tests/assets` states the reason above in the
   author's own words. `tests/math` links `MattMath` happily — the arrow that is
   missing is `tests --> engine` (ARCHITECTURE.md:35), and only that one.
3. PHILOSOPHY.md:445-447 promises "everything below the platform edge is testable
   headlessly", and `state.h` includes *nothing at all* — yet it cannot be tested by
   linking the library it ships in.
4. The sample's `CMakeLists.txt` — the file ARCHITECTURE.md:167 calls "a dozen honest
   lines" and the template a new project copies — has to `find_package(directxtk)`
   before it can compile a state that draws two strings, because linking the engine
   drags the SDK headers in.

Note the seam is wider than this one line: `engine/math/matt_math.h:5` also
`#include <d3d11.h>`, so `MattMath`, which ARCHITECTURE says depends on nothing,
already drags D3D. That belongs to the math group; it does not soften this one.

**Remedy:** Introduce the `draw_sprite(...)` renderer interface PHILOSOPHY.md:367-370
already specifies and change the signature to take it; the DirectXTK implementation
becomes one class in `engine/render/d3d11/`.

#### Rethink `MovingObject`: 27 virtual protected accessors and a vptr around twenty bytes, 13 of them dead

- **File:** `engine/core/moving_object.h:7-59`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 ("Inheritance and virtual dispatch are tools of last resort, not the default modelling grammar"), T1

**What:** An engine type that supplies no mechanism — it holds three fields and never
acts on them — is shaped as a polymorphic base with every accessor `virtual` and
`protected`, so it can only be consumed by inheritance. Half its API is unreachable
and its rotation is write-only.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/moving_object.h:17-19,50-57` (the protected block runs 27 declarations):

    protected:
        virtual const mattmath::Vector2F& velocity() const;
        virtual float velocity_x() const;
        ...
        virtual float rotation() const;
        virtual void set_rotation(float rotation);
        virtual void alter_rotation(float rotation);

    private:
        mattmath::Vector2F velocity_ = mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO;
        mattmath::Vector2F dx_ = mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO;
        float rotation_ = 0.0f;

Callers, counted by grepping `MovingObject::<name>(` across all of `engine/`,
`game/` and `samples/`. **13 of the 27 have none:** `alter_velocity`,
`unit_velocity`, `velocity_magnitude`, `velocity_angle`, `dx`, `alter_dx`,
`alter_dx_x`, `alter_dx_y`, `unit_dx`, `dx_magnitude`, `dx_angle`, `rotation`,
`alter_rotation`.

The rotation triple is write-only. Its only two touches in the tree are
`game/objects/projectile.cpp:20` (`MovingObject(velocity, rotation)`) and
`game/objects/player.cpp:1031`:

        MovingObject::set_rotation(0.0f);

Nothing reads `MovingObject::rotation()` — the rotation that is actually *drawn* is a
different member on a different base, `DrawObject::draw_rotation_`
(`engine/render/draw_object.h:23,29,39`), deliberately renamed to avoid the clash.

`game/objects/player.h:104` and `game/objects/player.cpp:970-973` — the only override
of any of the 27, in the whole codebase:

    const mattmath::Vector2F& velocity() const override;   // player.h:104, public section

    const Vector2F& Player::velocity() const
    {
        return MovingObject::velocity();
    }

**Why it matters:** `Vector2F` is `{float x; float y;}` (`matt_math.h:399-402`), so the
payload is 20 bytes and the `MovingObject` subobject is 32 with the vptr — 60%
overhead on a base of `Projectile` (`game/objects/projectile.h:18`), the class a paint
shooter instantiates in bulk. Nothing is gained for it: every call site in the game is
*qualified* (`MovingObject::set_velocity_x(...)`, `player.cpp:803`;
`MovingObject::set_dx_x(...)`, `projectile.cpp:268`), which suppresses virtual dispatch
entirely, and the single override is a forwarding no-op whose only purpose is to widen
`protected` to `public` for one external reader (`game/objects/debug_text.cpp:26`).
That override is the proof `protected` is the wrong access: the one real client spent
a vtable slot to get at its own velocity. The type is also not mechanism (T1) — it has
no `position`, so it can never integrate anything; the real motion step
(`rectangle_.offset(dx_x(), dx_y())`) lives in `Player` and in each of the five
`projectile_*.cpp` files instead. It is not on ARCHITECTURE.md:83's roster for `core`
("game loop, fixed-step timing, Scene, states, services, registries"), and its only
two users are game classes.

**Remedy:** Replace with a public value struct
(`struct Motion { Vector2F velocity; float rotation; };`) that `Player` and
`Projectile` hold as a member, dropping the 13 dead accessors and the vptr; if the
engine wants a motion mechanism in `core`, give it one that owns a position and
integrates it, and test it (T9's standing obligation).

#### Document or design away the state contract: `transition_to` destroys its caller and null-dereferences

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.h:10-18`, `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/The public face ("Every public engine header is documented: the contract, the intent"), T6

**What:** `state.h` and `state_context.h` carry zero prose between them while encoding
four load-bearing contracts: `transition_to` runs `~State()` on the state whose
`update()` is on the stack; `init()` must run before `update()`; `transition_to(nullptr)`
— and therefore `Application::run(nullptr)` — dereferences null; and `context()` may be
null.

**Evidence:**

The whole of `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`:

    void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
    {
        this->state_ = std::move(state);
        this->state_->set_context(this);
        this->state_->init();
    }

Line 23 destroys the outgoing state. Line 24 dereferences `state_` with no guard,
while `update()` and `draw()` (lines 5-20) both guard for exactly that. The public
entry point inherits it — `engine/app/application.cpp:187-189`:

    int Application::run(std::unique_ptr<State> first_state)
    {
        this->transition_to(std::move(first_state));

A representative caller, `game/states/main_menu.cpp:60-63`, calling it from inside the
very object line 23 destroys:

                this->play_wave(this->confirm_sound_);
                this->context()->transition_to(std::make_unique<MainMenuHome>(
                    this->main_menu_data()));
                return;

`engine/core/state_context.h` is 19 lines with no comment on any of it.

**Why it matters:** The self-destruction hazard was reported in the previous review
(`all-findings.md`, `ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp`, two graded high) and is unfixed —
the three lines are byte-identical after the move to `engine/`. What is new is the
context: the file now ships inside `ArtAttackEngine`, a static library
ARCHITECTURE.md:33-39 says a stranger's game links, and the same passes that gave
`i_game_object.h` forty lines of contract (`i_game_object.h:8-22,27-33,35-40,43-60`)
and `application.h` seventy (`application.h:26-29,54-70,104-114,137-143`) added
nothing here. I re-walked all 42 `transition_to` sites in `game/states/` (31 of them
`this->context()->transition_to(...)`): every one happens to touch no member after the
call, so nothing crashes today, and the two in `game/states/pause_menu.cpp:87-97` that
do not `return` survive only because the following clauses are `else if`. A stranger
writing `this->context()->transition_to(...); this->cleanup();` gets a heap
use-after-free with nothing in the header to warn them. Separately, `run(nullptr)` or
a moved-from `unique_ptr` gets an access violation rather than the named failure T6
requires.

**Remedy:** Make the transition deferred — park the incoming state in a `pending_`
member and swap it in inside `StateContext::update()` after `state_->update()` returns
— which removes the hazard instead of documenting it. Throw a named
`std::invalid_argument` for a null state. Document the `init()` ordering on the header
either way.

#### The state tree outlives every service: `state_` is in a base subobject, and members die before bases

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.h:17`, `engine/app/application.h:71,113-114,137-143`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("Construction and destruction order are designed")
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `Application` derives from `StateContext`, so the `unique_ptr<State>` that
owns the entire live game tree sits in a *base* subobject. C++ destroys a class's
members before its base classes, so every service the application owns — including the
`AudioEngine` whose ordering the header calls load-bearing — is destroyed *before* the
states that borrowed it, and after `CoUninitialize()` has already run.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/state_context.h:16-18`:

    private:
        std::unique_ptr<State> state_ = nullptr;
    };

`engine/app/application.h:71`:

    class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext

`engine/app/application.h:113-114`, on the service accessors:

        // Borrowed, every one: the Application owns them and outlives the states
        // it runs.

`engine/app/application.h:137-144`:

        // DECLARATION ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING BELOW THIS LINE.
        //
        // Members destruct in reverse declaration order. DirectXTK requires the
        // AudioEngine to outlive every WaveBank and SoundEffectInstance - their
        // destructors unregister themselves from it - and AudioResources owns the
        // SoundBanks that own those. So audio_engine_ is declared FIRST and dies
        // LAST.
        std::unique_ptr<DirectX::AudioEngine> audio_engine_ = nullptr;

`engine/app/application.cpp:21-31` — the destructor suspends audio and uninitialises
COM, and never resets the state:

    Application::~Application()
    {
        if (this->audio_engine_)
        {
            this->audio_engine_->Suspend();
        }
        if (this->com_initialized_)
        {
            CoUninitialize();
        }
    }

**Why it matters:** The ordering comment is correct about *members* and silent about
the one owner that is not a member. `audio_engine_` dies last among members; `state_`
dies after all of them. The header's "the Application owns them and outlives the
states it runs" is therefore false by construction, in the file that says it. Today
this is latent rather than live: I checked every destructor reachable from a state —
`~GameLevel`, `~GameMenu`, `~Level`, `~Player`, `~Weapon`, `~Projectile`, `~MenuPage`,
`~HelloState` are all implicit or `= default`, and game objects hold services and
sound effects as *non-owning pointers and handles* (`game/objects/weapon.h:54,62,67`),
never as `ComPtr` or owned `SoundEffectInstance`. The first state that owns a
`SoundEffectInstance`, a `ComPtr`, or anything that unregisters itself on destruction
— which is the ordinary thing for a game to do, and the thing the comment exists to
warn about — gets a use-after-free at shutdown with no diagnostic. A stranger reading
`application.h:113-114` has been told it cannot happen.

**Remedy:** Reset the state before the services die. Either give `~Application()` a
`this->transition_to(nullptr)`-equivalent as its first act (which needs the null case
fixed above), or hold the `StateContext` as a *member* declared last rather than as a
base, so it falls under the same reverse-declaration rule the comment already
documents. Then amend the comment to say which owner is being ordered against which.

#### Give `State::update()` a `dt` parameter: the shell still publishes frame time as a heap `float*`

- **File:** `engine/core/state.h:12`
- **Severity:** medium (reviewer: high)
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("Frame time is a parameter — `update(float dt)` — not shared state")

**What:** `State::update()` takes no `dt`, so the application shell still owns a
heap-allocated `float` and publishes a raw pointer to it as the only way a state can
learn the frame time.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/state.h:12-14`:

        virtual void update() = 0;
        virtual void draw() = 0;
        virtual void init() = 0;

`engine/app/application.h:131-134`, `:159`:

        // Seconds the last fixed step covered. A pointer because the objects that
        // read it are built once and outlive any particular frame; the value
        // behind it is rewritten every update.
        const float* dt() const;
        ...
        std::unique_ptr<float> dt_ = nullptr;

`samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:53-55`:

            // dt is a pointer because the objects reading it outlive any one
            // frame; the shell rewrites the value behind it every fixed step.
            const float dt = *this->app_->dt();

`game/game_data.cpp:62-68`:

    float* GameData::dt() const
    {
        // The shell hands out a const float* because nothing downstream should be
        // writing the frame's own timestep. The game's older signatures still take
        // a float*, so the cast lives here, in one place, rather than at each of
        // the several dozen call sites - and goes when those signatures do.
        return const_cast<float*>(this->application_->dt());
    }

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY.md:358 is one sentence long and this is its exact
subject. **This was a deliberate choice, not an omission** — `c6696af`'s commit
message says so in writing: "State::update() stays argument-free, like State::draw().
It is the shell-facing entry point, above the object graph rather than in it, and
states can already reach dt through the application." That rationale is precisely what
PHILOSOPHY.md:358 rules out, and the decision is recorded nowhere a reader of the
headers or the design docs would find it. The observable costs are real but not
severe: the shell keeps a `unique_ptr<float>` whose reallocation on device loss was
critical finding #9 (now harmless — I confirmed nothing in `game/` or `samples/`
stores the pointer any more; `Level` keeps `frame_dt_` as a value,
`game/objects/level.h:118-120`), the game has a standing `const_cast` on the engine's
read-only loan, and the *sample* — the file ARCHITECTURE.md:180-186 designates as the
anatomy a new project copies — teaches the pointer deref in a comment. Re-graded to
medium because there is no live defect and the fix is a mechanical edit of three state
hierarchies, not structural work.

**Remedy:** Change to `virtual void update(float dt) = 0;` and have
`StateContext::update(float dt)` forward `StepTimer::GetElapsedSeconds()`;
`Application::dt_`, `Application::dt()` and `GameData::dt()`'s `const_cast` then
delete themselves. Or amend PHILOSOPHY.md:358 to carve out the shell-facing entry
point — but pick one, in the same PR, as the preamble requires.

#### Make `State::draw()` `const` and parameterised: the const-draw wall has a hole at its top

- **File:** `engine/core/state.h:13`, `engine/core/state_context.h:13-14`
- **Severity:** medium (reviewer: high)
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering ("`draw()` is `const` all the way down and receives what it needs as parameters")

**What:** `State::draw()` is the only draw in the tree that is neither `const` nor
handed what it draws with, and `StateContext::draw() const` is a const that does not
mean anything, because `unique_ptr` does not propagate constness.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/state.h:12-13`:

        virtual void update() = 0;
        virtual void draw() = 0;

`engine/core/state_context.h:13-14`:

        void update() const;
        void draw() const;

`engine/core/state_context.cpp:13-20`:

    void StateContext::draw() const
    {
        if (this->state_ == nullptr)
        {
            return;
        }
        this->state_->draw();
    }

One level below, `game/objects/level.h:79-81` is already what the philosophy asks for:

    void draw(std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
        std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
        std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

**Why it matters:** `std::unique_ptr<T>::operator->() const` yields a non-const `T*`,
so a `const` member of `StateContext` calls a mutating `State::draw()` and the
compiler is content — and `StateContext::update() const` drives every mutation in the
program while declaring itself a read. IMPLEMENTED.md:70-72 records the value of the
const pass as being "fixed in the sense that survives someone editing the code". That
guarantee starts at `IGameObject` and stops one level below the root:
`GameLevel::draw()` (`game/states/game_states.cpp:312`) and `HelloState::draw()`
(`samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:62`) are both non-const, and both are the top
of the render tree. Because `draw()` also takes nothing, both have to go *find* the
renderer — `hello_state.cpp:68-70` fetches `device_resources()`,
`deferred_context(0)` and `sprite_batches()->at(0)` off the `Application` and
hand-rolls `FinishCommandList`/`ExecuteCommandList`/`Release`. That is the engine's
hello-world. Re-graded to medium alongside the `dt` finding: same interface, same
edit, no live defect — the `const` on `StateContext` is misleading rather than unsafe.

**Remedy:** `virtual void draw(Renderer& renderer) const = 0;` on `State` once the
renderer seam exists, and drop `const` from `StateContext::update` and `draw` now, so
the declarations stop claiming something the type cannot enforce.

#### The state "stack" is a single slot: the one client has grown four nested contexts to compensate

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.h:8-18`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy), ARCHITECTURE/`app` ("owns the state stack")
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** Both design documents say the shell owns a state *stack*. `StateContext` is a
one-slot holder: no push, no pop, no way to resume the state underneath, and no channel
for a finished state to report a result. The game has rebuilt all of that by hand.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/state_context.h:8-18` in full — one slot, one setter, no stack:

    class StateContext
    {
    public:
        virtual ~StateContext() = default;
        StateContext() = default;
        void update() const;
        void draw() const;
        void transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state);
    private:
        std::unique_ptr<State> state_ = nullptr;
    };

ARCHITECTURE.md:92-93 and :157-158, and PHILOSOPHY.md:331-333, all name a stack:

    │   └── app/                the application shell: window, device, services,
    │                           main loop, state stack

The workaround, `game/states/game_states.h:24,59-68` — four `StateContext`s inside the
state hierarchy, each paired with a heap-allocated enum used as an out-parameter:

    std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> menu_ = nullptr;
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> pause_menu_ = nullptr;
    std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuAction> pause_menu_action_ = nullptr;
    std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuData> pause_menu_data_ = nullptr;

    std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> results_menu_ = nullptr;
    std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuAction> results_menu_action_ = nullptr;
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> end_menu_ = nullptr;
    std::unique_ptr<EndMenuAction> end_menu_action_ = nullptr;

and the return channel in use, `game/states/pause_menu.cpp:81-82`:

            *this->pause_menu_data()->action() =
                PauseMenuAction::resume;

**Why it matters:** This is T1 read backwards. A pause menu that suspends gameplay and
resumes it is the canonical thing a state stack is for, and because the engine supplies
a one-slot holder, the game invented the mechanism itself: four nested contexts, a
`GameLevelState` enum to route between them, and three `unique_ptr<enum>` acting as
return values. Every one of those is machinery a second game would have to reinvent, and
`game/states/game_states.cpp` is where finding #18 ("Level is both the scene abstraction
and the paint-battle ruleset", still outstanding) already lives — this is part of what
makes it that big. A `unique_ptr` to an enumerator is also the loudest possible signal
that the interface has no way to say what it needs to say.

**Remedy:** Either give `StateContext` the stack the documents promise —
`push(unique_ptr<State>)` / `pop()`, with `update()`/`draw()` running the top and the
deferred swap from the `transition_to` finding making both safe — or amend
ARCHITECTURE.md:92-93,157 and PHILOSOPHY.md:332 to say "the current state" and accept
that suspend/resume is game-side policy. The four nested contexts are the evidence for
which of those is true.

---

#### Rename `IGameObject` to `GameObject`: it is the counter-example CONVENTIONS uses by name

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:23` (and the filename)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never ("`I`, `C`, `F`, `U` or any other type prefix")

**What:** The engine's most-implemented type keeps the `I` prefix that CONVENTIONS
forbids and quotes verbatim as its own illustration, and the file is named after the
prefixed spelling.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:23`:

        class IGameObject

`docs/design/CONVENTIONS.md:32-34`:

    - **No prefixes, ever.** Interfaces are just types — `GameObject`, not
      `IGameObject`; whether a type is abstract is visible in its header, not
      encoded in its name.

`docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:304,312,329` and `ARCHITECTURE.md:213` all name it
`GameObject`.

**Why it matters:** Four conventions passes have landed — `#pragma once`,
trailing-underscore members, enum and namespace renames, dropping `get_` — and each
touched more sites than this would. The prefix survived on the exact name the document
picked to explain the rule, which makes CONVENTIONS read as aspirational rather than
binding, and it is the first type a stranger meets. It has propagated:
`game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:7` and `game/objects/i_paintable_game_object.h:9`
copy it, and `engine/ui/widget.h:9` uses a different forbidden prefix (`MObject`,
alongside `MContainer`, `MWidget`, `MTexture`, `MText`, `MTextDropShadow`). The
mechanical cost is small — the 20 `override` sites already counted, plus the files that
name the type.

**Remedy:** Rename the class to `GameObject` and the file to
`engine/core/game_object.h` in one pass, and take the `I`- and `M`-prefixed
derivatives with it.

#### Delete `MovingObject::dx_`: a cached derived value under an off-allowlist name

- **File:** `engine/core/moving_object.h:34-48,56`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Variables and members ("The allowlist of short forms is small and closed: `dt`, `id`, `src`, `dst`, `min`, `max`")

**What:** Twelve of the type's 27 accessors serve a member called `dx` that holds
`velocity * dt` for the current frame — a value written and read back within one
update — and the name is both off the closed allowlist and the universal shorthand for
DirectX, in a header that transitively includes `d3d11.h`.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/moving_object.h:34-48` — twelve declarations, not nine:

        virtual const mattmath::Vector2F& dx() const;
        virtual float dx_x() const;
        virtual float dx_y() const;

        virtual void set_dx(const mattmath::Vector2F& dx);
        virtual void set_dx_x(float x);
        virtual void set_dx_y(float y);

        virtual void alter_dx(const mattmath::Vector2F& dx);
        virtual void alter_dx_x(float x);
        virtual void alter_dx_y(float y);

        virtual mattmath::Vector2F unit_dx() const;
        virtual float dx_magnitude() const;
        virtual float dx_angle() const;

Its entire lifetime, `game/objects/player.cpp:886-890`:

        MovingObject::set_dx_x(MovingObject::velocity_x() * dt);
        MovingObject::set_dx_y(MovingObject::velocity_y() * dt);

        this->rectangle_.offset(MovingObject::dx_x(),
            MovingObject::dx_y());

**Why it matters:** Seven of the twelve — `dx()`, `alter_dx()`, `alter_dx_x()`,
`alter_dx_y()`, `unit_dx()`, `dx_magnitude()`, `dx_angle()` — have zero callers
anywhere in `engine/`, `game/` or `samples/`. The live uses are the write-then-read
pair above, the same pair in `game/objects/projectile.cpp:268-269` read back in each of
the five `projectile_*.cpp` files at their `:37-40`, and one `set_dx(Vector2F::ZERO)`
in `Player`'s reset (`player.cpp:1033`) that exists only because a derived value is
being stored as state. Storing a per-frame derivative on the object is what makes the
`MovingObject` subobject 32 bytes instead of 24, and it means a reader of `engine/core`
has to guess whether `dx` is a delta, an x-component, or DirectX. CONVENTIONS.md:59-61
closes the abbreviation list precisely against this.

**Remedy:** Delete the member and all twelve accessors; compute the displacement into a
local at the two places it is produced, and pass it to the subclass step that consumes
it.

**What:** The core test target covers two header-only types and nothing else. `State`,

includes no headers at all.

**Evidence:**

`tests/core/CMakeLists.txt:3-15`:

#### Amend PHILOSOPHY's parallel-rendering clause: split-screen makes disjoint object slices unreachable

- **File:** `docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:371-372`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY preamble ("a change that fights a philosophy means either the change is wrong or the philosophy is, and if the philosophy is, this file is edited in the same PR")

**What:** PHILOSOPHY gives "render workers own disjoint slices of the scene" as half of
why parallel rendering is sound. `i_game_object.h` states in writing that the
parallelism axis is *views*, so every worker enters `draw()` on the same object — which
is not just what today's renderer does, it is what any split-screen renderer must do.

**Evidence:**

`docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:371-372`:

    - Parallel rendering is sound because drawing is a pure read; render workers
      own disjoint slices of the scene.

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15`:

        // draw() is const, and that is the whole contract that makes parallel
        // rendering sound. The render workers do not own disjoint slices of the
        // object list - the parallelism axis is *views*, so every worker enters
        // draw() on the SAME object at the same time. Under that fan-out the only
        // safe draw is a pure read, and const is how the compiler holds a new
        // object to it instead of a comment nobody reads.

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY explicitly describes the destination and not the current
code (PHILOSOPHY.md:11-14), so "today's renderer disagrees" is not on its own a defect
— `game/objects/level.cpp:536-554`, where each worker walks every object against its
own camera view, could in principle be the thing that changes. It is not, and that is
the point: split-screen is a headline feature named in PHILOSOPHY.md:289 and :381, and
whenever two views exist the same object is drawn twice concurrently, so disjoint
object slices are not reachable at the destination either. IMPLEMENTED.md:89-93 already
recorded the mismatch and nothing was amended, so the tie-breaker document and the
engine's most-read header now say opposite things about the one question that decides
whether `const draw()` is sufficient or merely helpful. A reader who trusts PHILOSOPHY
concludes a per-object scratch buffer is safe; under the real fan-out it is a data race.

**Remedy:** Amend PHILOSOPHY.md:371-372 to say the parallelism axis is views, that
every worker may enter `draw()` on the same object, and that the pure-read contract is
therefore load-bearing rather than convenient — the wording `i_game_object.h:10-15`
already has.

#### Include `<cmath>` in `moving_object.cpp`: `atan2` arrives only transitively

- **File:** `engine/core/moving_object.cpp:1-3,61-64,109-112`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (include order, "then standard library")

**What:** Two functions call unqualified global `atan2` in a translation unit that
includes no `<cmath>`; it compiles only because `engine/math/matt_math.h` happens to.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/moving_object.cpp:1-3` — the entire include section:

    #include "engine/core/moving_object.h"

    using namespace mattmath;

`engine/core/moving_object.cpp:61-64` (and identically `:109-112` for `dx_angle`):

    float MovingObject::velocity_angle() const
    {
        return atan2(this->velocity_.y, this->velocity_.x);
    }

`engine/math/matt_math.h:6` — the only reason it resolves:

    #include <cmath>

**Why it matters:** The name is found through two levels of transitive include and
through the global namespace rather than `std::`, so trimming `matt_math.h`'s includes
— which PHILOSOPHY.md:453-454 explicitly wants ("light headers, disciplined includes")
— breaks this file at a distance, and `using namespace mattmath;` on line 3 means any
future `mattmath::atan2` would silently win the overload. Graded low because both
functions are dead: `velocity_angle()` and `dx_angle()` are two of the 13 accessors
with no callers anywhere, so the only cost today is that the file stops compiling when
an unrelated header is cleaned up.

**Remedy:** Add `#include <cmath>` after the engine include and write `std::atan2` —
or delete both functions with the rest of the dead accessors.

#### Take `StateContext&` at construction: `set_context` is public and reseatable at any moment

- **File:** `engine/core/state.h:15-19`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("A non-owning pointer is a documented loan")

**What:** The back-pointer a `State` holds to its owner is settable by anyone through a
public method, is never validated, and is handed out as a mutable pointer from a
`const` accessor.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/state.h:15-19`:

        void set_context(StateContext* context);
    protected:
        StateContext* context() const;
    private:
        StateContext* context_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** `set_context` has exactly one caller in the tree
(`engine/core/state_context.cpp:24`) but is public API, so any code holding a `State*`
can point a live state at a different context — or at nothing — while its `update()`
runs. All 31 game call sites then write `this->context()->transition_to(...)` with no
null check (`game/states/main_menu.cpp:61`, `game/states/pause_menu.cpp:87`,
`game/states/game_states.cpp:82`, 28 more), so a null `context_` is an immediate crash.
I could not reach it: `transition_to` always sets the context before calling `init()`,
and no `init()` in `game/` or `samples/` calls `context()`. Returning a non-const
`StateContext*` from a `const` member is the smaller half of the same looseness, and
`State`'s user-declared destructor leaves the implicit copy constructor in place, so a
copied state silently shares the pointer.

**Remedy:** Pass the owning `StateContext&` to the `State` constructor and delete
`set_context`, or make it private with `StateContext` a friend. Delete the copy
operations while you are there.

#### `update(float dt)` collides with `AnimationObject::update(float dt)`: one declaration overrides two unrelated virtuals

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:34`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness), T5
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `IGameObject::update(float dt)` is public and pure virtual;
`AnimationObject::update(float dt)` is protected and virtual, with the identical
signature and an unrelated meaning (advance the animation frame). Every class that
inherits both gets a single `update(float dt) override` that silently overrides both
vtable slots and widens the protected one to public.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:34`:

        virtual void update(float dt) = 0;

`engine/render/animation_object.h:25-26`:

    protected:
        virtual void update(float dt);

`game/objects/player.h` / `game/objects/projectile_*.h` inherit both. The only thing
keeping the two apart is that every call is qualified — `game/objects/player.cpp:736`,
`projectile_ball.cpp:40`, `projectile_jet.cpp:40`, `projectile_mist.cpp:42`,
`projectile_spray.cpp:42`, `paint_tile.cpp:166`:

        AnimationObject::update(dt);

**Why it matters:** No live defect: I checked all six call sites and every one is
explicitly qualified, so the animation step is reached and nothing recurses. But the
guard is convention, not structure. One unqualified `update(dt)` added inside
`AnimationObject` or `SpriteSheetObject` — the natural way to write a frame advance in
its own base — dispatches virtually into `Player::update`, which calls
`AnimationObject::update` again: unbounded recursion, no warning, and `/W4` cannot see
it. The collision predates `c6696af` (both took no arguments before it) and survived
because the dt pass moved them in lockstep. Two engine interfaces owning the same verb
at the same signature for different jobs is also T4's problem before it is anyone
else's.

**Remedy:** Rename the animation one for what it does — `advance_animation(float dt)`
— which removes the collision and reads better at all six call sites.

#### `bounds()` is specified in world space, but `draw()` accepts any camera

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:43,61`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering ("Objects expose bounds; the scene culls")
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** The header fixes `bounds()` in world space while `draw()` takes whatever
camera the caller supplies, so an object's extent is meaningful only under one camera
and the interface neither says which nor lets the object say.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:38-43,61`:

        // A camera-less draw is just Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA,
        // which is the identity, so callers wanting screen space pass it.
        virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
            const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;
        // The object's drawn extent, in world space.
        ...
        virtual mattmath::RectangleF bounds() const = 0;

The `ui` module implements it in screen space — `engine/ui/widget.cpp:108-121,162,262,321`
report widget rectangles positioned against the resolution, e.g.
`samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:27-29` places text at `resolution * 0.5f`.
The only cull in the tree, `game/objects/level.cpp:536,545,554`, tests them against a
world-space view:

            if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))

**Why it matters:** Nothing is broken today because menus are drawn through the
viewport path and never reach that cull. But PHILOSOPHY.md:373-374 makes culling the
scene's job for *every* registered object, and the moment `Scene` culls uniformly, a
widget's screen-space rectangle gets intersected with a world-space camera view and
menus vanish or survive by accident. The header is the only place this could be stated
and it states the half that is false for a whole engine module. This is the same shape
as the note the header already carries — "an object cannot report itself invisible" —
and deserves the same treatment.

**Remedy:** Say in the comment that `bounds()` is in the space the object is drawn in,
and that an object drawn under a non-identity camera reports world space while a
screen-space object reports screen space — then have `Scene` cull the two sets against
different views, rather than assuming one.

---

### Rejected

- **"`set_dx()` has zero callers in the entire tree"** — false. `game/objects/player.cpp:1033`
  calls `MovingObject::set_dx(Vector2F::ZERO)`. Corrected in the surviving finding.
- **"Nine of the type's 27 accessors serve a member called `dx`"** — false; there are
  twelve (`moving_object.h:34-48`), and the reviewer's own evidence block quotes all
  twelve. Corrected.
- **"six of the nine have zero callers anywhere"** — false; seven of the twelve do.
  Corrected.
- **"Storing a per-frame derivative as object state is what makes `Projectile` 32 bytes
  instead of 24"** — false. 32 vs 24 is the `MovingObject` subobject; `Projectile` is far
  larger. Corrected to name the subobject.
- **"43 `transition_to` call sites in `game/states/`"** (and "45" in the reviewer's own
  summary) — 42: 17 in `game_states.cpp`, 21 in `main_menu.cpp`, 4 in `pause_menu.cpp`.
  31 of them go through `this->context()`. Corrected.
- **"`tests/core/CMakeLists.txt:3-5` says the same [as `tests/assets`]"** — it does not use
  the "everything the engine drags in" phrasing; it gives a shorter reason ("links neither
  the engine nor D3D - it includes the two headers directly"). Quote reattributed to
  `tests/assets`.
- **"ARCHITECTURE.md:35 draws `tests --> engine`; no test target links [anything]"** —
  `tests/math/CMakeLists.txt` links `MattMath`, satisfying line 36's arrow. Only the
  engine arrow is unsatisfied. Corrected.
- **"the `dt` pass reached `IGameObject::update(float)` and stopped one level above it"**
  as an oversight — rejected as framing. `c6696af`'s commit message argues explicitly that
  "State::update() stays argument-free… states can already reach dt through the
  application." The finding survives (the rationale is what PHILOSOPHY.md:358 forbids, and
  it is recorded nowhere a reader would look), re-graded high → medium.
- **"the document now contradicts the header… the header is right and the document is
  wrong"** — rejected as stated. PHILOSOPHY.md:11-14 says the file describes the
  destination and deliberately says nothing about the current codebase, so a description
  mismatch is not itself a defect. Finding survives with the repaired argument: split-screen
  makes disjoint object slices unreachable at the destination too.
- **`State::draw()` finding graded high** — re-graded to medium. Real, but no live defect
  and the same mechanical edit as the `dt` finding; merged the `StateContext` false-const
  half into it rather than leaving it implied.
- **`PHILOSOPHY.md:366-369`** (renderer interface) — the clause is at 367-370. Corrected.
- **`PHILOSOPHY.md:308` "names it `GameObject`"** — line 308 is about the OOP/performance
  spectrum. The name appears at 304, 312 and 329. Corrected.
- **`CONVENTIONS.md:60-61`** (abbreviation allowlist) — the bullet runs 59-61. Corrected.
- **`matt_math.h:400-402`** for `Vector2F`'s definition — the struct opens at 399.
  Corrected.

<a id="g-core-registry"></a>

## core-registry — Registry, Handle, NameTable

*Group `core-registry` · 15 findings (1 high, 3 medium, 11 low) · source `review2/verified/core-registry.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened all three headers line by line, both test files, `tests/core/CMakeLists.txt`, and every
consumer the reviewer named plus three they did not (`engine/audio/sound_bank_object.h/.cpp`,
`engine/render/animation_object.h`, `engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp`). Every line number in
the raw report checks out against the current tree; the quoted source is accurate everywhere I
looked, which is not something I could say of most reports at this scale. I also re-ran the git
archaeology the reviewer leaned on, and re-derived the reachability of each consequence from the
shipped manifest.

The reviewer's central judgement is right and I have kept it: there is no critical here, nothing is
UB on a reachable path, and the defect shape of this group is that its load-bearing invariants are
enforced in prose where T5 says they belong in the type system. What I changed is severity and one
mechanism claim. I dropped `Handle` table-identity from high to medium: the phantom type already
catches the frame-vs-strip class of mistake, the shipped manifest declares exactly one sprite sheet
and one sound bank (`game/content/manifest.json`), `set_sound_bank` has no caller at all and
`set_sprite_sheet`'s only two callers re-resolve in the same function — so the consequence is real
but wholly latent. I kept the const-hole at high, because that one is not latent in the same way: it
is the only thing standing between the codebase and a re-introduction of the data race that
`ca4d228` was written to make impossible, and `DrawObject::render_resources() const` returning a
non-const `RenderResources*` is a two-hop path from inside any `draw() const` to
`SpriteSheet::set_texture`. I rejected the claim that `RegistryStorage` cannot be specialised from
game code: C++17 relaxed both [temp.expl.spec]/2 and [temp.class.spec]/5 so a client may declare the
specialisation from their own scope with a qualified name, never opening `namespace artattack` — the
finding survives only as a documentation gap, at low. Four other over-reaches were trimmed and are
listed at the bottom. Five findings that were graded medium on aesthetic or coverage grounds went to
low; I would rather the author's eye land on the four things above the fold than on eleven equal-
looking items.

What the reviewer missed, and I added: `Registry::add` cannot tell a first insert from a replace, so
two manifest entries sharing a name — including the cross-kind case where a `sprite_sheet` entry and
a `texture` entry collide, which the current loader makes easy — silently collapse into one slot
with no diagnostic, in an asset pipeline whose every other layer is scrupulously loud (T6). Also:
the concurrency contract that four consumer headers advertise is stated in neither of the two
headers that actually provide it; and every failure in this group is a `std::out_of_range`,
including "was never loaded", so a caller cannot tell a content typo from a programming error. I
also strengthened the `add()`-ordering finding — the corrupt state it leaves does not merely cross
two names, it makes `contains()` and the replace path of `add()` index the vector out of bounds.

### Themes

- The invariants that carry this group — table identity, `kind_` lifetime, "const after loading",
  const-ness on the draw path, "mutate only at load" — are all enforced by comment. That is the
  exact trade T5 says to take the other way, and the comments are good enough that the gap is easy
  to miss.
- Silence where the pipeline is otherwise loud: a duplicate asset name, and a released-then-crossed
  slot, both pass without a word, in an engine whose T6 is its most-quoted tenet.
- `Registry` and `NameTable` have diverged on three axes that a stranger meets as noise — error
  grammar, `contains()` semantics, and pointer-vs-reference for the same never-absent contract.
- The naming rule the whole conventions document falls out of is broken in this group's newest
  public API, and the lowercase spelling has already propagated to 23 sites across engine, game and
  tests.
- The tests pin the device-loss story unusually well and skip the two paths production depends on;
  one test's title asserts a property the implementation does not have.

#### `Registry::get()` is `const` but lends mutable access, so the wall under "drawing is a pure read" cannot be built

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:98-120`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time), T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** a `const Registry` hands out a non-const `Resource*`, so const-ness stops propagating at
the registry. Everything above it — `RenderResources`, `AudioResources`, `SoundBank`, every
`draw() const` — is const in signature and unconstrained in fact, and `registry.h`'s otherwise
exhaustive commentary never raises the question.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:98` and `:117` — both reads are `const` members returning a mutable pointer:

    Resource* get(handle resource_handle) const
    ...
    Resource* get(const std::string& name) const

The two-hop escape path from inside a pure-read `draw()`. `engine/render/draw_object.h:21` hands out
a non-const services pointer from a const member:

    virtual RenderResources* render_resources() const;

`engine/render/render_resources.h:57-62` — const member, mutable resource out:

    // Per-draw, and const and non-mutating because they are called from
    // thread-pool workers. Each throws std::out_of_range if the handle is
    // unresolved or its slot has been released.
    ID3D11ShaderResourceView* texture(TextureHandle texture) const;
    DirectX::SpriteFont* sprite_font(FontHandle font) const;
    SpriteSheet* sprite_sheet(SpriteSheetHandle sprite_sheet) const;

and `engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:43` is public and non-const:

    void set_texture(ID3D11ShaderResourceView* texture);

So `this->sprite_sheet()->set_texture(nullptr);` compiles inside any `draw() const`. The affordance
is already relied on deliberately: `engine/audio/sound_bank_object.cpp:15-18` turns a
`const AudioResources*` into a mutable `SoundBank*`,

    SoundBank* SoundBankObject::sound_bank() const
    {
        return this->audio_resources_->sound_bank(this->sound_bank_);
    }

and `engine/assets/resource_loader.cpp:155-162` is a `const` member function that mutates a
`SpriteSheet` reached through the registry:

    void ResourceLoader::reload_sprite_sheet_texture(const std::string& directory,
        const std::string& name) const
    {
        this->load_texture(directory, name);

        this->render_resources_->sprite_sheet(name)->set_texture(
            this->render_resources_->texture(name));
    }

**Why it matters:** `game/objects/level.cpp:404-417` dispatches `draw_player_view_level` to N
thread-pool workers over one shared object graph, and `engine/render/texture_object.h:60-64` states
that `Level::draw_active_level` runs `draw()` on the *same* object from every worker simultaneously.
`docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md` records that the pure-read contract is "the *only* thing making this
sound", and `ca4d228` made `draw()` const precisely so the compiler would enforce it. That
enforcement stops at the registry: resources — the one thing every worker genuinely shares — are
handed out mutable from a const path. There is no live race today; the defect is that nothing but
review can keep it that way, and the review that would catch it is the one that already had to catch
finding #16 once. Deferring it is not free either: fixing it later touches every caller of
`RenderResources::texture/sprite_font/sprite_sheet`, `AudioResources::sound_bank` and
`SoundBank::sound_effect_instance`.

**Remedy:** give `Registry` a `const Resource* get(...) const` alongside a non-const overload, and
name the exception explicitly in the header — DirectXTK and COM types have no const-correct API, so
the audio and texture paths need the mutable one and should say why. The point is that the exception
becomes a documented, greppable list rather than the default.

#### `Handle` carries no table identity, so mixing two tables of the same element type stays silent

- **File:** `engine/core/handle.h:16-38`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time), T6 (loud failure)

**What:** `Handle` stores nothing but an index. The phantom `Resource` parameter separates a frame
handle from a strip handle, but not sheet A's frames from sheet B's, nor bank A's effects from bank
B's — so a handle resolved against one table is accepted by any other table of the same element type
and reads the wrong element whenever the index is in range.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/handle.h:16-38` — the entire state of a handle:

    template <typename Resource>
    class Handle
    {
    public:
        Handle() = default;
        explicit Handle(int index) : index_(index) {}

        bool valid() const { return this->index_ >= 0; }
        int index() const { return this->index_; }

        friend bool operator==(Handle a, Handle b) { return a.index_ == b.index_; }
        friend bool operator!=(Handle a, Handle b) { return a.index_ != b.index_; }

    private:
        int index_ = -1;
    };

`engine/core/registry.h:98-105` — the only gate is a range test, and the message it produces for an
in-type but foreign handle is factually wrong:

    Resource* get(handle resource_handle) const
    {
        const size_t index = static_cast<size_t>(resource_handle.index());
        if (!resource_handle.valid() || index >= this->entries_.size())
        {
            throw std::out_of_range(std::string(this->kind_) +
                " was read through an unresolved handle.");
        }

The missing mechanism is written out in prose at **six** places, not the four the reviewer counted:
`handle.h:12-14`, `sprite_sheet.h:31-32`, `sprite_sheet_object.h:33-36`, `texture_object.h:29-32`,
`sound_bank.h:36-39`, and `sound_bank_object.h:47-49`:

    // Points this object at a different bank. Every handle resolved from the
    // old one is meaningless against the new one, so a caller doing this
    // re-resolves everything it holds.
    void set_sound_bank(const std::string& sound_bank_name);

**Why it matters:** the widest door is `engine/render/texture_object.h:65-72`, `draw_with(...,
SpriteSheet::frame_handle frame, ...)`, which takes a frame handle from its caller and draws it
against `SpriteSheetObject::sprite_sheet()` with nothing connecting the two. The reachability is
genuinely nil today and I have graded accordingly: `game/content/manifest.json` declares one sprite
sheet and one sound bank, `set_sound_bank` (`sound_bank_object.cpp:79-83`) has no caller anywhere,
and `set_sprite_sheet`'s only callers (`texture_object.cpp:33`, `animation_object.cpp:165`)
re-resolve the element in the next statement. It stays a medium rather than a low because the engine
is offered to strangers, for whom a second sprite sheet is the first thing they add, and the failure
mode is a wrong sprite drawn with no diagnostic (T6 inverted) or a throw saying "unresolved handle"
about a handle that resolved perfectly. Cost of delay is real: `Handle` is already spelled at 23
sites across engine, game and tests, so widening it later is a wide edit.

**Remedy:** issue each `Registry`/`NameTable` a small table id at construction, stamp it into
`Handle` beside the index, and check it in `get()` — debug-only if the four extra bytes are
unacceptable on the frame path. The same field is where a generation counter would later live.

#### `Registry::add` cannot tell a first insert from a replace, so two assets sharing a name collapse silently

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:63-76`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation), T7 (data over code)

**What:** `add()` replaces the resource in an existing slot and returns `void`. Replacement is
required — it is how a device restore refills slots under live handles — but there is no signal
distinguishing "reloading a slot I own" from "a second asset just claimed a name that was already
taken", so a duplicate name anywhere in the manifest is absorbed without a word and the later asset
silently wins.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:63-71`:

    void add(const std::string& name, Storage resource)
    {
        const auto it = this->indices_.find(name);
        if (it != this->indices_.end())
        {
            this->entries_[static_cast<size_t>(it->second)].resource =
                std::move(resource);
            return;
        }

The manifest walk feeds it directly, one entry at a time, with no duplicate check of its own
(`engine/assets/resource_loader.cpp:74-86`):

    for (const AssetEntry& entry : manifest.entries)
    {
        const auto kind = this->kinds_.find(entry.kind);
        ...
        kind->second.load(entry.directory, entry.name);
    }

and the cross-kind collision needs no user error at all to be surprising —
`engine/assets/resource_loader.cpp:143-152` loads a sprite sheet's texture *under the sheet's name*:

    void ResourceLoader::load_sprite_sheet(const std::string& directory,
        const std::string& name) const
    {
        // The sheet's texture is loaded under the sheet's own name: they are one
        // asset with two files, and the manifest names it once.
        this->load_texture(directory, name);

so a `texture` entry and a `sprite_sheet` entry that share a stem overwrite one another in
`textures_`. Every other layer of this pipeline is loud by design: `asset_manifest_loader.cpp:11-20`
exists solely so a hand-edited manifest reports its own typos by name, and `load_manifest` throws
naming the asset, the file and the kind for an unregistered kind.

**Why it matters:** this is exactly the class of content bug T6 was written for — a person edits
JSON, the wrong image draws, and nothing anywhere says why. It is reachable by ordinary authoring
(two directories, one stem; a `names` array with a repeated entry; a texture named after a sheet),
it survives to runtime, and the only symptom is visual. The engine cannot simply throw on re-add,
because the restore path depends on silent replacement — which is precisely why the distinction has
to be made in `Registry`'s API rather than guessed at by loaders.

**Remedy:** have `add()` report whether it claimed a new slot or refilled one (a bool return, or a
separate `reload(name, resource)`), and let `ResourceLoader` throw naming both entries when a first
load lands on an occupied slot. The device-restore path calls the replacing form deliberately and
stays silent.

#### Rename `Registry::handle` and `Registry::entry` to PascalCase — they are types

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:53`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Types

**What:** two type names in the engine's newest public primitive are lowercase, against the single
rule the whole conventions document falls out of, and the codebase already spells the same concept
the other way three lines further out.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:53`:

    using handle = Handle<Resource>;

`engine/core/registry.h:149-153`:

    struct entry
    {
        Storage resource;
        std::string name;
    };

The same spelling was copied outward — `engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:18-19`:

    using frame_handle = Handle<SpriteFrame>;
    using strip_handle = Handle<AnimationStrip>;

while the neighbours get it right: `TextureHandle`, `FontHandle`, `SpriteSheetHandle`
(`render_resources.h:38-40`), `SoundBankHandle` (`audio_resources.h:17`), `WaveHandle`,
`EffectHandle` (`sound_bank.h:25-26`). `CONVENTIONS.md:18`: "Types — classes, structs, enums,
aliases | `PascalCase`".

**Why it matters:** `sound_bank.h:26` puts both spellings on one line —
`using EffectHandle = Registry<DirectX::SoundEffectInstance>::handle;` — and
`tests/core/registry_tests.cpp:67` reads like a variable declaration:
`const Registry<Resource>::handle unresolved;`. The lowercase form has spread to 23 sites, including
game code (`game/objects/weapon.h:154`, `game/objects/interface_gameplay.h:92-93`), so it is now the
engine teaching its client the wrong rule. Git puts the chronology beyond doubt: `registry.h` was
created in `7949655`, the two lowercase names were introduced in `10a2eac`, and three later
conventions commits — `6175c6b`, `52fe513`, `2fa12fe` — edited the file without catching them. This
is not old code awaiting a pass; it is new code the passes walked through.

**Remedy:** `using Handle = Handle<Resource>;` would shadow, so spell it `ResourceHandle` (and
`Entry`, `FrameHandle`, `StripHandle`) and update the call sites plus the two tests that name it.

#### `add()` inserts the name before the slot exists, so a throw between them corrupts the table

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:73-75`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed), T6 (loud failure)

**What:** the name is committed to `indices_` before the slot it points at exists. If the vector
growth throws, the name is left mapped to an index one past the end — and every later operation on
that name reads out of bounds or crosses onto another name's slot.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:73-75`:

    const int index = static_cast<int>(this->entries_.size());
    this->indices_.emplace(name, index);
    this->entries_.push_back(entry{ std::move(resource), name });

`engine/core/name_table.h:46-47` has the identical ordering:

    this->indices_.emplace(name, static_cast<int>(this->elements_.size()));
    this->elements_.push_back(std::move(element));

**Why it matters:** the reviewer described the crossed-slot outcome, which is right — the next
`add("b", …)` computes the same index, so `resolve("a")` and `resolve("b")` return equal handles and
`"a"` reads `"b"`'s resource. Two more consequences they missed are worse than that one, because
they are not merely wrong answers: in the corrupt state `contains("a")` indexes `entries_`
**unchecked** (`registry.h:129-131`), and the replace path of `add("a", …)` does the same
(`registry.h:68`) — both are out-of-bounds `std::vector::operator[]`, i.e. undefined behaviour,
where `get()` at least throws. The grade stays low only because the sole reachable trigger is
`std::bad_alloc`: the `entry` temporary's `std::string` copy and the vector's reallocation both
allocate, while every move involved is `noexcept`. But the promise T6 makes is that the engine stops
loudly, and this stops quietly and then lies.

**Remedy:** push the entry first and let the `indices_.emplace` be the commit point; if the emplace
then throws, the orphaned slot is invisible rather than reachable. Same edit in both headers.

#### `Registry` and `NameTable` have diverged on three axes a stranger meets as noise

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:63-132`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness — "Not a licence for: copy-paste")

**What:** the two headers share one lookup — `std::map<std::string,int>` plus a `std::vector`, with
"a repeated name keeps its index" written twice — and the copies have drifted apart in their error
grammar, in what `contains()` means, and in how they express "this never comes back empty".

**Evidence:**

The error grammars. `registry.h:89-90`:

    throw std::out_of_range(
        std::string(this->kind_) + " '" + name + "' was never loaded.");

`name_table.h:58-59`:

    throw std::out_of_range(std::string("no ") + this->kind_ +
        " named '" + name + "'");

The `kind` strings follow the grammar of whichever type they were written for: `"Texture"`,
`"SpriteFont"`, `"SpriteSheet"` (`render_resources.h:88-91`), `"SoundBank"`
(`audio_resources.h:40`) against `"sprite frame"`, `"animation strip"`
(`sprite_sheet_loader.cpp:13,40`). So one content typo is reported as
`Texture 'plyer_sheet' was never loaded.` and its neighbour as `no sprite frame named 'wlak'`.

`contains()` means two things — "loaded now" (`registry.h:125-132`, which tests the stored pointer)
versus "named at all" (`name_table.h:77-80`, which tests the map alone) — documented on `Registry`
and undocumented on `NameTable`.

And the same never-absent contract is expressed two ways: `registry.h:26-27` promises "It never
returns nullptr" in prose while returning `Resource*`, where `name_table.h:66` says it in the type:

    const Element& get(Handle<Element> element_handle) const

**Why it matters:** none of this is wrong, which is why it is a low — but the two types are meant to
be learned as one bargain ("the same names-in, handles-out bargain as Registry", `name_table.h:13`),
and a stranger who learns one is mildly misinformed about the other. The user-visible half is the
log: two grammars for one event, which a tool over the log has to know about. The maintenance half
is that the two findings above this line each have to be fixed twice.

**Remedy:** settle on one message grammar and one `kind` convention, and state `contains()`'s
meaning in both headers. Extracting a shared `detail::NameIndex` is optional and probably not worth
it — the duplication is about ten lines, and both types read well alone.

#### The concurrency contract every consumer advertises is stated in neither header that provides it

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:24-48`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/The public face, T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `Registry` and `NameTable` are read concurrently by every render worker and mutated only
at load and device-restore time. That contract is what makes the parallel draw sound, it is
advertised by four consumer headers, and neither of the two headers that actually provide it
mentions threads at all.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/render_resources.h:57-58` states it as a property of the registry:

    // Per-draw, and const and non-mutating because they are called from
    // thread-pool workers. Each throws std::out_of_range if the handle is
    // unresolved or its slot has been released.

`engine/audio/audio_resources.h:26-27`: "Const and non-mutating, like every other registry getter".
`engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:45-47`: "Every draw overload is const: a single SpriteSheet is shared
by every drawable in the level and is entered concurrently by the render workers, so nothing here
may mutate the frame or strip tables." `engine/render/texture_object.h:60-62` says the same about
`draw()`. `engine/core/registry.h`'s 36 lines of class comment (`:24-48`) cover the two-way lookup,
slot stability, device loss and the names-not-meanings boundary — and never say that `add()` and
`release_all()` may not run while a read is in flight.

**Why it matters:** the guarantee holds today for a reason nothing in this group records: device
loss is signalled from `DeviceResources::Present` on the main thread, and
`Level::draw_active_level` joins its workers at `level.cpp:417` before returning, so
`Application::OnDeviceLost` → `reset_all_textures()` → `release_all()` can never interleave with a
worker's `get()`. That is a whole-program argument a reader of `registry.h` cannot make. The engine
is for strangers, and a stranger who calls `add()` from a loading thread while a frame is in flight
gets silent corruption from a type whose documentation is otherwise excellent.

**Remedy:** two sentences in both class comments — concurrent `get`/`resolve`/`contains` are safe;
`add` and `release_all` are load-time and device-restore only and must not overlap a read — and name
the join that makes it true.

#### Every failure in this group is a `std::out_of_range`, including the ones that are not

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:89-112`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation), T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** a content typo, a read through an unresolved handle, and a read of a released slot all
throw the same standard exception type, and so does the neighbouring asset code for a missing file —
so nothing above can distinguish a broken content file from a programming error except by matching
on the message text.

**Evidence:**

Three different failures, one type — `engine/core/registry.h:89-90`, `:103-104`, `:111-112`:

    throw std::out_of_range(
        std::string(this->kind_) + " '" + name + "' was never loaded.");
    ...
    throw std::out_of_range(std::string(this->kind_) +
        " was read through an unresolved handle.");
    ...
    throw std::out_of_range(std::string(this->kind_) + " '" +
        slot.name + "' has been released.");

`name_table.h:58` and `:71` follow suit, and so does the loader for a missing file —
`resource_loader.cpp:138-139`:

    throw std::out_of_range(
        "SpriteFont " + name + " not found at " + font_path + ".");

while its sibling three functions down throws `std::runtime_error` for the same category of failure
(`resource_loader.cpp:179-180`), as does the manifest reader
(`asset_manifest_loader.cpp:18-19`).

**Why it matters:** T6 asks for loud failure that names things, and the messages do that well. The
gap is the layer above: a game that wants to report "your content is broken" differently from "the
engine has a bug" has no handle on the distinction, and `std::out_of_range` — whose standard meaning
is an argument outside a valid range — is the wrong word for "this name is not in the manifest".
This is cheap to fix now and progressively less so: the two exception types are already spelled at
26 sites in `engine/`, and the tests pin `std::out_of_range` in six places.

**Remedy:** one engine exception type for content failures (`artattack::ContentError`, deriving from
`std::runtime_error`), thrown by both tables for a name miss, with the handle-misuse throws left as
`std::out_of_range` where the word is accurate.

#### `kind_` is a borrowed `const char*` whose lifetime contract is enforced only by a comment

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:55-58`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** both tables store the caller's `const char*` without owning it, so a table named from
anything but a literal dangles, and the type system permits it.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:55-58`:

    // `kind` names the resource type in error messages: "Texture",
    // "SpriteFont". It is stored, not copied, so it must outlive the
    // registry - pass a literal.
    explicit Registry(const char* kind) : kind_(kind) {}

`engine/core/registry.h:155`:

    const char* kind_ = nullptr;

`engine/core/name_table.h:32` and `:83` are identical.

**Why it matters:** every construction site in the tree passes a literal
(`render_resources.h:88-91`, `audio_resources.h:40`, `sprite_sheet.h:90-91`,
`sprite_sheet_loader.cpp:13,40`), so nothing dangles today. The trap is for the stranger who names a
registry from data — `Registry<Foo> r(kind_name.c_str());` where `kind_name` is a local — which
compiles cleanly and then reads freed memory inside the throw, i.e. it fails in the one place the
engine promises to be loud. A `std::string` member costs one allocation at construction and nothing
on the frame path reads it, as the header itself notes at `:147-148` ("Nothing on the draw path
reads it").

**Remedy:** store a `std::string`, or take `const char (&kind)[N]` so only a literal binds.

#### `[[nodiscard]]`, `noexcept` and `constexpr` are absent from every pure read in these headers

- **File:** `engine/core/handle.h:30-34`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time), PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** none of the accessors, predicates or comparisons carry the annotations PHILOSOPHY names as
compiler-enforced information, so discarding their result compiles silently.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/handle.h:30-34` — four functions that cannot throw and whose results are their entire
purpose:

    bool valid() const { return this->index_ >= 0; }
    int index() const { return this->index_; }

    friend bool operator==(Handle a, Handle b) { return a.index_ == b.index_; }
    friend bool operator!=(Handle a, Handle b) { return a.index_ != b.index_; }

`engine/core/registry.h:125` and `engine/core/name_table.h:77` (`contains`) are the same shape.
`docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:450-452`: "Warnings are errors with zero suppressions; the language
standard is current; `const`, `noexcept` and `[[nodiscard]]` carry information the compiler
enforces (T5)."

**Why it matters:** `handle.valid();` and `registry.contains(name);` as full statements compile
without a word, and both are the residue of an `if` that lost its condition. `Handle`'s members are
additionally the only ones in this group that could be `constexpr`, which is what would let a game
hold a known-invalid handle as a class constant. For scope: `[[nodiscard]]` appears nowhere in
`engine/`, `game/` or `tests/` — this group is where a codebase-wide habit is cheapest to start,
because these are the newest headers and have five call sites between them. `resolve()` and `get()`
are the honest exceptions: discarding them for their throw is a legitimate validation idiom.

**Remedy:** `[[nodiscard]] constexpr ... noexcept` on `Handle`'s four members, `[[nodiscard]]` on
both `contains()`.

#### `Registry` has no way to release one name, enumerate, or report its size

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:49-158`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** the public surface is `add`, `resolve`, `get` ×2, `contains` and `release_all`. There is no
per-name release, no iteration and no `size()`/`empty()`, so within one registry the only unload is
all-or-nothing and there is no way to audit what is cached.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/registry.h:138-144`:

    void release_all()
    {
        for (entry& slot : this->entries_)
        {
            slot.resource = Storage{};
        }
    }

with `registry.h:39-40` making it deliberate: "A name owns its slot for the registry's lifetime."

**Why it matters:** this is the price `Handle`-as-index bought, and the trade is the right one — the
device-loss story depends on slots outliving resources. I have corrected the reviewer's framing: a
client is *not* unable to free per-level content, because nothing stops them owning a second
`Registry` per level and destroying it whole. What is missing is finer-grained release *within* a
registry, plus any way to measure occupancy, and the header discusses release only in the
device-loss framing, so a reader cannot tell whether the omission is a decision or a gap.

**Remedy:** either add `release(const std::string&)` and `size()`, or — cheaper and probably better
— one sentence saying a registry is whole-program-lifetime by design and per-level content belongs
in a registry of its own.
