  consequence; libstdc++ (`<bits/stl_algobase.h>` via `<vector>`) and libc++ both
  supply `std::min`/`std::max` through headers this file already includes. Observation
  kept, regraded medium → low.
- **`triangles_intersect` graded medium** — rejected; I re-derived the reviewer's proof
  including the three-arc case they omitted, and it holds, so there is no reachable
  wrong answer for non-degenerate triangles. Regraded medium → low; the plan correction
  in the remedy is the part worth acting on.
- **`RectangleF(c, 5.0f)` graded medium** — rejected as severity; the resolution is
  exactly as described and no other two-argument overload is viable, but it needs an
  authoring mistake to fire and no caller in the tree makes one. Regraded medium → low.
- **"the NaN contact point propagates into whatever it is assigned to"** — rejected as a
  live consequence; the sole in-tree caller iterates `RectangleRotated::edges()`, and
  that type validates its extents and axes on construction and on every setter, so no
  degenerate segment reaches it. Observation kept, regraded medium → low.
- **"`edges_valid()` already contains code that would be wrong if handed a
  RectangleF-style ordering"** — rejected as framing; `edges_valid()` calls
  `this->edges()` on a `RectangleRotated` and can never receive another shape's
  ordering. The finding stands on the missing contract and the absent tests instead.
- **"Two test cases assert nothing" graded medium, remedy `CHECK_FALSE(...)` at 333** —
  the missing assertions are confirmed but the proposed fix at 333 would fail the suite,
  because `10.0f + FLT_EPSILON == 10.0f` and the library treats a vertex on the corner
  as intersecting. Regraded medium → low and split: the epsilon defect is now its own
  finding.
- **"MattMath's `<algorithm>` uses number 54 in this range"** — not claimed by the
  reviewer, but worth recording that I checked: 54 is correct file-wide (28 + 26
  occurrences), of which 8 fall in lines 1-1500. No adjustment needed.
- **"The Shape dispatch layer has zero tests" (previous review #96)** — not re-filed;
  `tests/math/collision_tools_tests.cpp:21-62` now drives `Shape::intersects(const Shape*)`
  indirectly through `CollisionTools` for rectangle-rectangle and rectangle-triangle,
  so the claim no longer holds as stated.

<a id="g-math-impl-b"></a>

## math-impl-b — `engine/math/matt_math.cpp` lines 1450–3100

*Group `math-impl-b` · 15 findings (2 high, 9 medium, 4 low) · source `review2/verified/math-impl-b.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every line the reviewer cited — all ten findings, every `.cpp` coordinate, every
`matt_math.h` coordinate, and every off-file citation (`engine/math/collision_tools.cpp`,
`game/objects/player.cpp`, `engine/render/drawer.{h,cpp}`, `engine/math/colour.h`,
`tests/math/math_tests.cpp`, `engine/math/CMakeLists.txt`, `cmake/settings.cmake`) — plus
`docs/review/findings.json` to establish which of these the previous review already proved and
`docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md` to establish what has since been fixed. The line numbers are accurate:
of roughly sixty citations, two are off by one (`matt_math.h:1128-1133` should be `1127-1133`;
`player.cpp:268-271` should be `267-270`), and both are corrected below. Every finding survives as an
*observation*. What did not survive is severity and provenance. I regraded three: the reviewer's
`critical` on `MatrixF`'s unsized storage goes back to `high` (the previous review's own grade) —
the CMake split created the *possibility* of an external consumer, not one, and nothing in
`engine/`, `game/`, `samples/` or `tests/` names `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F` or `Vector4F`; and the two
`high`s on `divide` and on `cross`/`rotate_vector_by_ref` go back to `medium`, because the
reviewer's own text concedes there is no first-party caller and nothing about the defects changed.
I struck one factual premise outright: **`/fp:fast` is not set anywhere in this build.**
`cmake/settings.cmake` carries `/W4 /WX /permissive- /sdl` and nothing else, and a grep for
`fp:fast` across every `CMakeLists.txt`, `.cmake`, `CMakePresets.json` and `.vcxproj` in the tree
returns hits only inside `docs/review/`. The CMake conversion dropped it; `IMPLEMENTED.md` still
describes it as live. Finding 6 leaned on it twice and finding 3 of the previous review's DNA runs
through several others, so I removed the claim everywhere it appeared. I also corrected the report's
provenance paragraph: the reviewer wrote that findings 1 and 3 restate previous work and "everything
else is new", but findings 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 all correspond to entries in `findings.json` that
`IMPLEMENTED.md` does not record as fixed — only finding 2 (`divide`) is genuinely new. That does
not weaken anything, but a report that miscounts its own novelty invites the author to skip the
parts they think they have already read. What the reviewer missed is more interesting than what they
overstated. Finding 5's consequence is **understated**, not overstated: they wrote "I could not reach
the bad state from a real caller", having missed that `shape_shape_collision_direction` returns
`ZERO` for shapes that *are* intersecting when their centres coincide, and that
`player.cpp:299`'s `else if (direction == Vector2F::ZERO) { throw }` is unreachable dead code
precisely because the primitive launders `ZERO` into `DIRECTION_RIGHT` one line earlier. I added
five findings they did not file: `angle_between`'s unclamped `acos` (in their range, at 1803,
reachable from live shape code, previously reported, still unfixed), `set_from_hex`'s two silent
failure modes, `saturate`/`desaturate` being byte-identical (both of which the reviewer buried as
asides in finding 6's closing paragraph rather than filing), `Vector2I`'s unguarded *integer*
division — a hardware trap, not a NaN — and the total absence of `explicit`, `[[nodiscard]]` and
`noexcept` from the header (zero occurrences of each, measured). I folded the reviewer's strongest
missing observation into finding 6: `Colour`'s channels are **public mutable fields**, so the
0..1 invariant `clamp_colours()` supposedly enforces is defeated by `c.r = 5.0f;` without needing
NaN at all.

### Themes

- **The dead half of MattMath is the broken half.** `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F`, `Vector4F`, `Vector3F`,
  `Vector2F::cross`, `rotate_vector_by_ref`, `angle_between` and `Vector2I::scale(Vector2)` have zero
  first-party callers, and every one of them is defective. The library split changed who would pay,
  not whether it is broken — and the right remedy for most of it is deletion, which makes the
  severity argument largely moot.
- **Degenerate input has no contract.** The zero vector silently becomes "right"; NaN survives the
  colour clamp; a malformed hex string becomes opaque black; `acos` runs off its domain; integer
  division traps. `Vector2F::direction()` at `:1647` — twenty lines above the worst offender —
  returns `Direction::none` for the zero vector, so the library already contains the correct pattern.
- **`MattMath` is not the dependency-free library both design documents describe.** Its public header
  includes `<d3d11.h>` and DirectXTK's `SimpleMath.h`, the target links DirectXTK `PUBLIC`, and the
  build file's own opening comment concedes the contradiction.
- **The value layer has no compile-time guardrails at all.** Zero `constexpr`, zero `explicit`, zero
  `[[nodiscard]]`, zero `noexcept` in 1150 lines of public header, and the named constants are
  dynamically initialised SCREAMING_SNAKE objects defined in the `.cpp` and used as default member
  initialisers in the header.
- **Coverage stops at the shape trunk.** One of roughly 120 public members in this range has a test,
  which is why every defect below except `divide` also appears in the previous review.

*(Correcting one theme the reviewer asserted: contracts are not undocumented "anywhere". The last
remediation pass added them at `matt_math.h:442-449`, `:464-465`, `:489` and `:705`. Four contracts
for ~120 members is thin, which is the real point — but the absolute claim is false.)*

#### Size `MatrixF`'s storage in its constructor, or delete the matrix subsystem

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2473-2477`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2

**What:** `MatrixF(int rows, int columns)` records the dimensions but never sizes `elements_`, so
every factory that builds a matrix through it writes past the end of an empty `std::vector<float>`.

**Evidence:**

    MatrixF::MatrixF(int rows, int columns)
    {
        this->rows_ = rows;
        this->columns_ = columns;
    }

`elements_` is declared `std::vector<float> elements_;` with no initialiser (`matt_math.h:731`), so
it is empty. The only guards are dimension guards (`:2499-2508`):

    void MatrixF::set_element(int row, int column, float value)
    {
        // check if the row and column are valid
        if (!row_valid(row) || !column_valid(column))
        {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Row or column is not valid");
        }
        int index = calculate_index(row, column);
        this->elements_[index] = value;
    }

`row_valid`/`column_valid` (`:2696-2703`) test against `rows_`/`columns_` and never against
`elements_.size()`. Every producer uses the two-argument constructor: `add` (`:2737`), `subtract`
(`:2756`), `multiply` (`:2773`), `divide` (`:2795`), `multiply(a, float)` (`:2814`),
`divide(a, float)` (`:2828`), `transpose` (`:2896`), `identity` (`:2911`), `zero` (`:2920`), the
cofactor submatrix in `determinant` (`:2951`), and `Matrix3x3F` (`:2990-3004`):

    Matrix3x3F::Matrix3x3F(float e11, float e12, float e13,
        float e21, float e22, float e23,
        float e31, float e32, float e33) :
        MatrixF(3, 3)
    {
        this->set_element(0, 0, e11);
        this->set_element(0, 1, e12);
        ...

— nine out-of-bounds writes, and every `Matrix3x3F::rotation`/`scale`/`translation` factory
(`:3005-3043`) routes through it.

Three further defects confirm the subsystem has never been executed:

- `MatrixF::operator==` (`:2642-2661`) iterates `i` over `dimensions.x` and `j` over `dimensions.y`,
  but `dimensions()` returns `Vector2I(columns_, rows_)` (`:2518-2521`, documented at
  `matt_math.h:705`), so `i` runs over columns and `j` over rows before being passed to
  `element(i, j)`. Comparing two identical 2x3 matrices throws `std::invalid_argument` out of an
  equality operator.
- `Matrix3x3F::Matrix3x3F(const std::vector<float>&)` (`:2982-2988`) checks `elements.size() != 9`
  in its body, after `MatrixF(3, 3, elements)` in its mem-initialiser list has already thrown for
  exactly that condition (`:2478-2488`). The derived check is unreachable.
- `Matrix3x3F` derives publicly from a `MatrixF` that has no virtual destructor and no virtual
  functions at all (`matt_math.h:692-773`).

No constructor rejects negative dimensions either: `MatrixF(-3, -3, nine_elements)` passes the
`rows * columns != elements.size()` check because `-3 * -3` is `9`.

**Why it matters:** a grep of `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/` and `tests/` finds zero references to
`MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F` or `Vector4F` outside `matt_math.h`/`.cpp` — which is why this is `high` and
not `critical`: no code in this repository can corrupt its heap through it today, and the library has
no external consumers yet. What the split changed is the *audience*: `MattMath` is now a static
library target with a public header that `ARCHITECTURE.md` presents as one of the two libraries a
game project links, and `mattmath::Matrix3x3F::rotation(a)` is the most natural first line anyone
would write against it. T2 is unambiguous that a fast engine nobody can trust is worthless, and a
store through an empty vector's data pointer is the exact "unfalsifiable" failure it names.

**Remedy:** delete `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F`, `Vector4F` and the free `add`/`subtract`/`multiply`/
`divide`/`gaussian_elimination`/`transpose`/`identity`/`zero`/`determinant` functions — a 2D engine
has no use for a heap-allocating dynamically-sized dense matrix, and T9's standing obligation
("contracts, tests, documentation — or it was not worth building") has gone unpaid since it was
written. If it stays: `elements_.assign(static_cast<size_t>(rows) * columns, 0.0f)` in the
constructor, reject negative dimensions, validate against `elements_.size()`, fix `operator==`, and
ship behavioural tests in the same commit.

#### `MattMath` depends on D3D11 and DirectXTK, which contradicts both design documents

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5`, `engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:1-18`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`math` — may depend on: nothing), PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout

**What:** the math library's public header includes `<d3d11.h>` and DirectXTK's `SimpleMath.h`, the
target links DirectXTK `PUBLIC`, and a large share of this range is conversion members that exist
only to serve them — so PHILOSOPHY's target table (`MattMath` | static library | `engine/math/` |
**nothing**) and ARCHITECTURE's module table are both false as written.

**Evidence:** the header opens

    #pragma once

    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"
    #include <d3d11.h>

and this range implements the members that require them:

    DirectX::SimpleMath::Rectangle RectangleI::sm_rectangle() const   (:2031-2037)
    RECT RectangleI::win_rect() const                                 (:2038-2047)
    XMVECTOR Vector4F::xm_vector() const                              (:2172-2176)
    DirectX::SimpleMath::Color Colour::sm_colour() const              (:2425-2428)
    DirectX::XMVECTOR Colour::xm_vector() const                       (:2429-2432)

plus `Vector2I::set(const XMINT2&)` (`:1475-1479`), `Vector2I::scale(const SimpleMath::Vector2&)`
(`:1460-1464`), and the `SimpleMath::Vector2` / `XMFLOAT2` constructors and assignment operators for
`Vector2F` (`:1524-1558`). `Viewport::d3d_viewport()` (`matt_math.h:797`) returns a
`D3D11_VIEWPORT` by value, which is what makes `<d3d11.h>` structurally load-bearing rather than
incidental. The build file states the contradiction in its own opening comment:

    # MattMath — the math static library. Depends on nothing but the
    # DirectXTK headers it currently wraps (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md).
    ...
    target_link_libraries(MattMath
        PUBLIC Microsoft::DirectXTK
        PRIVATE artattack_settings
    )

**Why it matters:** `PUBLIC` propagates, so every consumer of `MattMath` — including
`MattMathTests`, which should be the cheapest and most portable target in the tree — compiles
DirectXTK and a Windows graphics header. `matt_math.h` is included by every shape user, so
`Vector2F` costs `<d3d11.h>`, which PHILOSOPHY's "compile speed is a maintained property" clause
makes a defect in its own right. It also pre-commits the second platform: `Vector2F` cannot exist on
a non-Windows build without `SimpleMath` or an `#ifdef` farm, which is the "second platform is a
rewrite, not an addition" outcome ARCHITECTURE exists to prevent. The conversions are one-way
adapters to a specific backend, which by ARCHITECTURE's own rule belongs behind the render module's
edge, not in the module everything else points at.

**Remedy:** move the `sm_*`/`xm_*`/`win_rect`/`d3d_viewport` conversions into `engine/render/` (or
`engine/render/d3d11/`) as free functions over the plain math types and drop the DirectXTK and
`<d3d11.h>` includes from `matt_math.h`, dropping the link to `PRIVATE` or removing it — or amend
both design documents to state that `math` depends on the DirectXTK headers, in the same PR, as
PHILOSOPHY's amendment rule requires.

#### `mattmath::divide(MatrixF, MatrixF)` is not matrix division under any definition

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2788-2809`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T9

**What:** `divide(a, b)` — exported as `operator/` and `operator/=` on `MatrixF` — computes, for each
output cell, the *sum of elementwise quotients* along a row/column pair, which is neither `a * b⁻¹`,
nor an elementwise divide, nor anything else with a name.

**Evidence:**

    MatrixF mattmath::divide(const MatrixF& a, const MatrixF& b)
    {
        // check if the dimensions are correct
        if (a.columns() != b.rows())
        {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Matrix dimensions are not correct");
        }
        MatrixF result(a.rows(), b.columns());
        for (int i = 0; i < a.rows(); i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < b.columns(); j++)
            {
                float sum = 0.0f;
                for (int k = 0; k < a.columns(); k++)
                {
                    sum += a.element(i, k) / b.element(k, j);
                }
                result.set_element(i, j, sum);
            }
        }
        return result;
    }

It is `multiply` (`:2766-2787`) with `*` changed to `/`. `a / identity(n)` does not return `a`; it
returns a matrix of row sums with a division by zero in every off-diagonal term.

**Why it matters:** it is public API (`matt_math.h:746`) reachable through `MatrixF::operator/=`
(`:2681-2685`) and the free `operator/` (`:2720-2723`), and a function's name is the strongest claim
it makes. A user who trusts it gets silently wrong numbers plus infinities, with no throw and no way
to tell. This is the one finding in the group the previous review did not have, which is a fair
measure of how little of this subsystem has ever been read. Graded `medium` rather than the
reviewer's `high` for the same reason as the finding above: nothing calls it, and the recommended
fix deletes it.

**Remedy:** delete it with the rest of the matrix subsystem. A "divide" that is not multiplication by
an inverse must not carry the name.

---

#### `Vector2F::cross` and `rotate_vector_by_ref` are still wrong verbatim after the split

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1705-1708`, `:1795-1802`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2

**What:** `Vector2F::cross` returns a vector holding the two *unsubtracted* terms of the 2D perp-dot
product, and `rotate_vector_by_ref` overwrites `vec.x` before using it to compute `vec.y`. Both were
named by the previous review (each at `medium`); neither appears in `IMPLEMENTED.md`; I confirmed
both unchanged at the coordinates above.

**Evidence:**

    Vector2F Vector2F::cross(const Vector2F& other) const
    {
        return Vector2F(this->x * other.y, this->y * other.x);
    }

    void Vector2F::rotate_vector_by_ref(Vector2F& vec, float angle)
    {
        float cos_angle = std::cos(angle);
        float sin_angle = std::sin(angle);

        vec.x = vec.x * cos_angle - vec.y * sin_angle;
        vec.y = vec.x * sin_angle + vec.y * cos_angle;
    }

The by-value sibling seven lines above (`:1787-1794`) computes both components from the originals
and is correct, which is direct proof that the by-ref version is a typo and not a different
convention:

    Vector2F Vector2F::rotate_vector(const Vector2F& vec, float angle)
    {
        ...
        return Vector2F(vec.x * cos_angle - vec.y * sin_angle,
            vec.x * sin_angle + vec.y * cos_angle);
    }

**Why it matters:** `a.cross(a)` must be zero and returns `(a.x*a.y, a.y*a.x)`. The correct scalar
`x*other.y - y*other.x` is exactly the primitive a separating-axis or winding test reaches for, and
its absence is why `mattmath::sign` (`:87-92`) exists in a truncated-to-`int` form that the previous
review filed separately. `rotate_vector_by_ref` produces a vector that is neither the input nor a
rotation of it for almost every angle. Neither has a first-party caller — I grepped `engine/`,
`game/`, `samples/` and `tests/` and found none — so nothing in this repository is currently wrong
because of them, which is why this stays at the previous review's `medium` rather than the
reviewer's `high`. What makes them worth fixing rather than ignoring is placement: they sit at
`matt_math.h:440` and `:471`, immediately beside the correct `dot` and `rotate_vector`, so they read
as vetted siblings, and PHILOSOPHY's promise is that a stranger starts from the headers.

**Remedy:** make `cross` return `float` (`x*other.y - y*other.x`) with a static overload mirroring
`dot`; fix the second assignment in `rotate_vector_by_ref` to use a saved copy of `vec.x`; pin both
with tests in the same commit.

---

#### `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` launders the collision layer's "no collision" sentinel into "right"

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1865-1900`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** the function branches on `direction.angle()`, and `std::atan2(0, 0)` is `0`, so a
zero-length input falls into the first branch and is returned as `DIRECTION_RIGHT` — undocumented,
and indistinguishable from a genuine rightward direction.

**Evidence:**

    Vector2F Vector2F::direction_to_8_cardinal_direction(const Vector2F& direction)
    {
        float angle = direction.angle();
        if (angle >= -PI / 8.0f && angle < PI / 8.0f)
        {
            return Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT;
        }

with `float Vector2F::angle() const { return std::atan2(this->y, this->x); }` (`:1744-1747`). The
library already knows how to do this correctly twenty lines earlier — `Vector2F::direction()`
(`:1647-1700`) returns an enum whose first case is exactly the missing one:

    Direction Vector2F::direction() const
    {
        if (are_equal(this->x, 0.0f) && are_equal(this->y, 0.0f))
        {
            return Direction::none;
        }

**Why it matters:** the reviewer wrote that they "could not reach the bad state from a real caller".
That is not correct, and the finding is stronger than they filed it. `CollisionTools` uses
`Vector2F::ZERO` as its sentinel in *two* places, and only one of them means "not colliding":

    Vector2F CollisionTools::shape_shape_collision_direction(
        const Shape* collider, const Shape* collidee)
    {
        Vector2F direction = collidee_center - collider_center;

        if (direction == Vector2F::ZERO)
        {
            return Vector2F::ZERO;
        }

(`engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:120-134`) — that is two shapes that *are* intersecting whose
centres coincide. `calculate_object_collision_direction` (`:136-145`) returns `ZERO` for the
not-intersecting case and otherwise forwards to it, so the sentinel survives the intersection guard.
The single first-party caller then feeds it straight in:

    Vector2F direction = CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_direction(
        this->shape(), other->shape());

    direction = Vector2F::direction_to_8_cardinal_direction(direction);

(`game/objects/player.cpp:256-259`). After that line `direction` can never be `ZERO` again, which
makes the author's own guard forty lines below unreachable dead code:

    else if (direction == Vector2F::ZERO)
    {
        throw std::runtime_error("No collision direction.");
    }

(`player.cpp:299-302`). What actually happens to a concentric player/ramp overlap is a silent
misclassification: `DIRECTION_RIGHT` against a `structure_ramp_left` satisfies
`side_wall_collision` (`player.cpp:267-270`) and is routed to the flat-structure response, and
against a `structure_ramp_right` it is handled at `:319` as a ramp-surface contact. Both are
plausible-looking wrong answers. T6 exists for exactly this: the engine says so when it cannot do
what was asked, rather than picking a direction.

**Remedy:** document the zero-length contract in the header beside the three
`normalized()`/`to_unit_vector()`/`unit_vector()` contracts already there, and return
`Vector2F::ZERO` for a zero-length input so the caller's existing `== ZERO` guard becomes live
again — or return `Direction` and reuse `Direction::none`. Either way, pin it with a test; the
existing `test_8_cardinal_direction` (`tests/math/math_tests.cpp:212-247`) checks all eight axis
directions and not the ninth case.

---

#### `Colour`'s 0..1 invariant is not an invariant

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2433-2439`, `engine/math/matt_math.h:594-599`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T2, T6

**What:** every `Colour` mutator ends in `clamp_colours()`, which is presented as the type's
invariant. It is not one, for two independent reasons: the channels are public mutable fields that
bypass every mutator, and `mattmath::clamp` returns its input unchanged for NaN.

**Evidence:** the type's data is public (`matt_math.h:594-599`), sitting above a full set of
clamping accessors and setters:

    struct Colour
    {
        float r = 0.0f;
        float g = 0.0f;
        float b = 0.0f;
        float a = 0.0f;

so `c.r = 5.0f;` is legal, compiles, and never reaches `clamp_colours()`. Separately, the clamp
itself does not reject non-finite values:

    void Colour::clamp_colours()
    {
        this->r = clamp(this->r, 0.0f, 1.0f);
        this->g = clamp(this->g, 0.0f, 1.0f);
        this->b = clamp(this->b, 0.0f, 1.0f);
        this->a = clamp(this->a, 0.0f, 1.0f);
    }

    float mattmath::clamp(float value, float min, float max)   // :35-49
    {
        if (value < min)      { return min; }
        else if (value > max) { return max; }
        else                  { return value; }
    }

Both comparisons are false for NaN, so the `else` returns it. The producers are the division
operators — `operator/(Colour, Colour)` (`:2456-2459`), `operator/(Colour, float)` (`:2460-2463`),
`operator/=(const Colour&)` (`:2284-2292`), `operator/=(float)` (`:2293-2301`) — and a
default-constructed `Colour` is `{0,0,0,0}`, so `some_colour / Colour()` is `0.0f/0.0f` in all four
channels. Note also that the default alpha is `0.0f` while `Colour(float, float, float)`
(`:2182-2186`) sets it to `1.0f`: a default-constructed `Colour` is invisible and a three-argument
one is opaque.

**Why it matters:** `clamp_colours()` is called from fifteen places in this region and is the only
thing making "a `Colour` always holds four values in [0,1]" true; a reader of the constructors
reasonably concludes the type defends itself. Unlike most of this group, `Colour` is live — it is
what the renderer and the asset loaders pass around — so the gap is in shipped API, not dead code.

**Corrected from the raw report:** the reviewer attributed part of the consequence to `/fp:fast`
licensing the compiler to assume NaNs do not occur. **`/fp:fast` is not set in this build.**
`cmake/settings.cmake` sets `/W4 /WX /permissive- /sdl` only, and no `CMakeLists.txt`, `.cmake`
file or preset anywhere in the tree names a floating-point model, so every target compiles at the
default `/fp:precise`. `IMPLEMENTED.md` still describes `/fp:fast` as live, which is stale. I have
removed the claim; the observation stands without it.

**Remedy:** make the channels private behind the accessors that already exist (they are already
declared: `red()`/`set_red()` and siblings, `matt_math.h:624-632`), or delete the setters and accept
that `Colour` is a plain aggregate with a clamping helper and say so. Guard or drop the division
operators — neither has a first-party caller. Make `clamp_colours` map non-finite channels to a
defined value. Pin the whole invariant with tests.

#### `Vector3F` is a 3D type in a declared-2D library, serving two near-dead `Drawer` helpers

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3049-3132` (header `engine/math/matt_math.h:663-690`)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Non-goals ("**3D.** MattMath is a 2D library; the dimension is a design
  constant, not a parameter"), T1

**What:** `Vector3F` and its seven free operators are implemented in full inside a library whose
philosophy names 3D a permanent non-goal, and the type's only first-party use is as an ad-hoc
`(x, y, zoom)` camera triple in two `protected` `Drawer` members that no derived class calls.

**Evidence:** the implementation runs from `Vector3F::Vector3F(float, float, float)` at `:3049` to
`operator*(float, const Vector3F&)` at `:3129-3132`. Its consumers, in their entirety:

    mattmath::RectangleI calculate_draw_rectangle(
        const mattmath::RectangleI& rec,
        const mattmath::Vector3F& camera) const;
    mattmath::RectangleI calculate_draw_rectangle(
        const mattmath::Vector2F& position,
        const mattmath::Vector2F& size,
        const mattmath::Vector3F& camera) const;

(`engine/render/drawer.h:22-28`), whose body reads it as a camera:

    Vector2F draw_pos = (position - Vector2F(camera.x, camera.y)) * camera.z;
    Vector2F draw_size = Vector2F(size) * camera.z;

(`engine/render/drawer.cpp:35-36`). Grepping `calculate_draw_rectangle` across `engine/`, `game/`,
`samples/` and `tests/` returns only the two declarations, their two definitions, and one internal
call: the `RectangleI` overload forwards to the `Vector2F` one at `drawer.cpp:26`. Nothing outside
`drawer.cpp` calls either. *(The reviewer wrote "no call sites at all"; that internal forward is the
one exception, and it does not change the conclusion.)*

**Why it matters:** the correct type already exists in the same header —
`Camera { Vector2F translation; float scale; }` (`matt_math.h:1020-1058`) — and it is what the rest
of the render path passes around. So there are two encodings of a camera, the one that contradicts
the stated dimension constant is the one nothing calls, and a stranger reading `matt_math.h` finds a
general-purpose 3D vector type and reasonably concludes 3D is on the roadmap. The block also carries
two commented-out member-operator bodies (`:3133-3140`) that duplicate free operators defined nine
lines above them.

**Remedy:** delete `Vector3F`, its seven free operators and the commented-out pair; delete the two
`Drawer` overloads with it, or give them `const Camera&` if the helpers are wanted.

#### `Vector2F::angle_between` feeds an unclamped quotient to `acos` and has no zero-length guard

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1803-1806`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T3 ("a simple model still has exact, documented, tested semantics"), T6

**What:** the quotient handed to `std::acos` is not clamped to `[-1, 1]`, so float rounding on
nearly-parallel vectors puts it outside the domain and the function returns NaN; and a zero-length
input makes the denominator zero, giving `0.0f/0.0f`. Neither is documented. This was reported by the
previous review at `medium`, is absent from `IMPLEMENTED.md`, sits inside this group's range, and
the reviewer did not file it.

**Evidence:**

    float Vector2F::angle_between(const Vector2F& a, const Vector2F& b)
    {
        return std::acos(Vector2F::dot(a, b) / (a.length() * b.length()));
    }

**Why it matters:** unlike `cross` and `rotate_vector_by_ref`, this one has callers inside the
library: `Triangle::angle_0/1/2` (`:3506-3520`) are implemented entirely in terms of it, `angles()`
(`:3522-3529`) collects all three, and `TriangleRightAxisAligned::find_hypotenuse` (`:3659-3678`)
compares each against `PI_OVER_2` with `are_equal`. Every comparison against NaN is false, so a
degenerate triangle makes `find_hypotenuse` return `-1` and both `hypotenuse()` (`:3630-3633`) and
`hypotenuse_gradient()` (`:3640-3643`) throw "Triangle is not a right triangle" for a triangle that
is one. That chain has no first-party caller outside `matt_math.cpp` today, so this is latent rather
than live — but it is the third instance in this range of the same missing contract, in the module
PHILOSOPHY singles out for "documented contracts — edge ordering, winding, zero-length behaviour,
what throws".

**Remedy:** clamp the quotient with the `mattmath::clamp` already in the file, decide and document
what a zero-length operand returns, and pin both with tests.

#### `Colour::set_from_hex` turns malformed input into black, and throws before `main`

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2354-2379`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** the parser validates the string's *length* and nothing else. Any length other than 6 or 8
silently yields opaque black, and any non-hex digit inside a correct-length string escapes as an
`std::invalid_argument` thrown from `std::stoi`. The reviewer noted both in a closing aside to
another finding rather than filing them; they were separately reported by the previous review and are
absent from `IMPLEMENTED.md`.

**Evidence:**

    void Colour::set_from_hex(const std::string& hex)
    {
        size_t hex_length = hex.length();
        if (hex_length == 6)
        {
            this->r = static_cast<float>(std::stoi(hex.substr(0, 2), nullptr, 16)) / 255.0f;
            ...
        }
        else if (hex_length == 8)
        {
            ...
        }
        else
        {
            this->r = 0.0f;
            this->g = 0.0f;
            this->b = 0.0f;
            this->a = 1.0f;
        }
        this->clamp_colours();
    }

So `"#ff0000"` — seven characters, the form every CSS and design tool emits — is black, and
`"gg0000"` throws.

**Why it matters:** `engine/math/colour.h` calls this constructor 153 times at namespace scope
(`:159-312`, one `const mattmath::Colour` per HTML colour name, each built from one of 148
`const std::string` hex literals at `:9-156`). None of those objects is `inline` or `constexpr`, so
each has **internal linkage and is constructed once per translation unit**, before `main`, in
seventeen headers' worth of includes — 301 dynamically initialised objects per TU, 153 of them
running `substr` and three `std::stoi` calls apiece. A throw from there is unattributable and
unrecoverable, and a silent black is a colour constant that renders wrong with no diagnostic. T6
names this exact failure mode: "a missing texture is a launch-time error naming the file, not an
invisible sprite."

**Remedy:** accept an optional leading `#`, validate that every remaining character is a hex digit,
and throw a diagnostic naming the offending string — or, better for the namespace-scope case, parse
at compile time so a bad literal is a build error (T5). Pin success and failure cases with tests.

#### The value layer of `MattMath` has no behavioural tests at all

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1450-3100` (tests: `tests/math/math_tests.cpp`)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests ("A new public primitive ships with behavioural tests in the same
  commit"), PHILOSOPHY/Collision, T9

**What:** of roughly 120 public members implemented in this range, exactly one —
`direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` — is exercised by a test; the rest of `MattMathTests` tests
shape-vs-shape intersection and the `RectangleRotated`/OBB work.

**Evidence:** `tests/math/math_tests.cpp` (1013 lines, 36 `TEST_CASE`s) contains
`test_8_cardinal_direction` (`:212-247`) and then `test_rectangles_intersect` onwards — every
remaining case constructs shapes and calls an intersection free function. Nothing in the file names
`Vector2F::normalized`, `normalize`, `to_unit_vector`, `rotate`, `rotate_vector`,
`rotate_vector_by_ref`, `cross`, `angle_between`, `lerp`, `clamp`, `clamped`, `min_vec`, `max_vec`,
`direction`, `Vector2I` (any member), `RectangleI` (any member), `Vector4F`, `Colour` (any member,
including `set_from_hex`), `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F` or `Vector3F`.

**Why it matters:** this is the direct cause of everything above surviving to a second review —
`Matrix3x3F::rotation(0.0f)` in a single `CHECK` would have tripped the debug iterator assertion the
day it was written, and `CHECK(a.cross(a) == 0.0f)` would not compile against the current signature,
which is itself the diagnosis. It is sharpest for `normalized()`/`normalize()`: the last remediation
pass *changed their contract* to return zero for a zero-length vector and wrote that contract into
the header (`matt_math.h:442-449`), and shipped no test pinning it — so the one documented promise in
this range is the one nothing enforces. PHILOSOPHY/Collision asks for contracts "each pinned by
behavioural tests in the commit that creates them", and T9 makes it the price of building rather than
buying.

**Remedy:** add `vector2f_tests.cpp` and `colour_tests.cpp` covering the arithmetic identities, the
three documented zero-length contracts, and the hex parser's success and failure cases; delete
whatever remains untested *and* uncalled rather than testing it.

#### Rename the SCREAMING constants and make them `constexpr`

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1902-1911` (also `:1480`, `:2133`, `:1119`)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never ("SCREAMING constants — screaming means macro, nothing else"), T5

**What:** the library's named constants are SCREAMING_SNAKE, which CONVENTIONS lists under *Never*
and whose own worked example of the correct form is `Colour::white`. They are also non-`constexpr`
namespace-scope objects with dynamic initialisation, defined in the `.cpp` and used as default member
initialisers in the public header.

**Evidence:**

    const Vector2F Vector2F::ZERO = { 0.0f, 0.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::ONE = { 1.0f, 1.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT = { 1.0f, 0.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::DIRECTION_DOWN = { 0.0f, 1.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::DIRECTION_LEFT = { -1.0f, 0.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP = { 0.0f, -1.0f };
    const Vector2F Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP_RIGHT = Vector2F::unit_vector(Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP + Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT);
    ...

plus `const Vector2I Vector2I::ZERO` (`:1480`), `const RectangleI RectangleI::ZERO` (`:2133`),
`const RectangleF RectangleF::ZERO` (`:1119`) and `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (`matt_math.h:1057`).
The header then uses them as NSDMIs: `Circle::center_` (`matt_math.h:853`), `Triangle::points`
(`:858`), `Quad::points_` (`:991-992`), `Segment::point_0`/`point_1` (`:997-998`),
`Camera::translation` (`:1022`) and `RectangleRotated`'s five members (`:1127-1133`, including
`x_axis_ = Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT`). *(The raw report cited `1128-1133`; the block starts at
1127.)*

Note the four diagonal constants are not literals — they are computed by calling
`Vector2F::unit_vector` on two other constants during dynamic initialisation, so their correctness
depends on `DIRECTION_UP`/`DIRECTION_RIGHT` being initialised first, which holds only because they
are defined earlier in the same translation unit.

**Why it matters:** two separate costs. (1) Four conventions passes have run — `#pragma once`,
trailing underscores, enum and namespace renames, dropping `get_` — and these survived all four, so
the most-typed names in the library still contradict the document that says a screaming name always
signals preprocessor danger. (2) Because the constants are dynamically initialised in
`matt_math.cpp`, no shape can ever be `constexpr`, default-constructing a `Quad` is four loads from
`.data` rather than zero-initialisation, and any namespace-scope object in another translation unit
whose constructor reads one of them depends on cross-TU initialisation order — a hazard the previous
review already found realised once in this codebase, and one `colour.h`'s 301 namespace-scope objects
keep live.

**Remedy:** rename to value case (`Vector2F::zero`, `Vector2F::direction_right`) and make the
constructors `constexpr` so these become `static constexpr` inline members in the header, which
removes the ordering hazard and the loads at once.

#### `Vector2I::scale(const SimpleMath::Vector2&)` truncates the scale factor before applying it

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1460-1464`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T4

**What:** the overload that exists specifically to scale an integer vector by a *float* vector casts
each factor to `int` first, so every fractional scale is either a no-op or zeroes the vector.

**Evidence:**

    void Vector2I::scale(const DirectX::SimpleMath::Vector2& amount)
    {
        this->x *= static_cast<int>(amount.x);
        this->y *= static_cast<int>(amount.y);
    }

`scale({0.5f, 0.5f})` yields `(0, 0)`; `scale({1.9f, 1.9f})` yields exactly what
`scale({1.0f, 1.0f})` yields.

**Why it matters:** the integer overload `scale(int, int)` sits immediately above it (`:1455-1459`),
so the float overload's only reason to exist is fractional scaling, which it cannot do. It has no
first-party caller, so nothing is currently wrong because of it — but it is public API
(`matt_math.h:383`), the failure is silent, and it is one of the members forcing the DirectXTK
dependency described above.

**Remedy:** scale in float and round (`static_cast<int>(std::lround(x * amount.x))`), or delete the
overload with the rest of the `SimpleMath` adapters.

#### `Vector2I`'s division operators have no zero guard, and integer division by zero is a hardware fault

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1497-1504`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** both free `operator/` overloads on `Vector2I` divide without checking the divisor. Unlike
every float division in this file, integer division by zero is not an infinity — on x86 it raises
`#DE` and the process dies with `STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`. The previous review reported this
merged with the truncation above; the reviewer kept only the truncation half.

**Evidence:**

    Vector2I mattmath::operator/ (const Vector2I& V1, const Vector2I& V2)
    {
        return Vector2I(V1.x / V2.x, V1.y / V2.y);
    }
    Vector2I mattmath::operator/ (const Vector2I& V, int S)
    {
        return Vector2I(V.x / S, V.y / S);
    }

The compound forms `Vector2I::operator/=` (`:1424-1441`) have the same hole. `Vector2I::ZERO` is
defined twenty lines below (`:1480`), so the divisor most likely to be passed by accident is a named
constant the type ships.

**Why it matters:** no first-party caller divides a `Vector2I` today, so this is exported surface
rather than a live crash — but it is the loudest possible failure with the quietest possible
contract, in the module PHILOSOPHY requires to document "zero-length behaviour, what throws". A
`Vector2I` is the natural type for a tile-grid or resolution calculation, which is exactly where a
zero divisor arrives from data.

**Remedy:** throw `std::invalid_argument` naming the operand, or document that the caller owns the
precondition. Pin it with a test either way.

---

#### `Colour::saturate` and `Colour::desaturate` are byte-identical, so one of the two names is a lie

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2380-2395`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T4

**What:** the two functions have character-for-character identical bodies, so `saturate(0.5f)` and
`desaturate(0.5f)` both move the colour halfway toward its luminance grey. One of the two public
names does the opposite of what it says. Reported by the previous review, absent from
`IMPLEMENTED.md`, and mentioned by the reviewer only as an aside inside another finding.

**Evidence:**

    void Colour::saturate(float amount)
    {
        float grey = this->r * 0.3f + this->g * 0.59f + this->b * 0.11f;
        this->r = grey + amount * (this->r - grey);
        this->g = grey + amount * (this->g - grey);
        this->b = grey + amount * (this->b - grey);
        this->clamp_colours();
    }
    void Colour::desaturate(float amount)
    {
        float grey = this->r * 0.3f + this->g * 0.59f + this->b * 0.11f;
        this->r = grey + amount * (this->r - grey);
        this->g = grey + amount * (this->g - grey);
        this->b = grey + amount * (this->b - grey);
        this->clamp_colours();
    }

**Why it matters:** neither has a first-party caller, which is why this is `low` — but two public
methods with one implementation is a duplication defect *and* a naming defect at once, and
CONVENTIONS opens by calling names the engine's first API. Nothing in the test suite touches
`Colour`, so there is no mechanism that would ever notice.

**Remedy:** keep one, expressed as a lerp toward grey with a documented `amount` convention, and
express the other as its complement — or delete both until a caller exists.

---

#### Nothing in the value layer is `explicit`, `[[nodiscard]]` or `noexcept`, so every lossy conversion is silent

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h` (constructors implemented at `matt_math.cpp:1962-1997`,
  `:1514-1538`, `:2206-2209`)
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5

**What:** `matt_math.h` contains zero occurrences of `explicit`, zero of `[[nodiscard]]` and zero of
`noexcept` across 1150 lines and roughly 400 declarations. Every single-argument constructor is
therefore an implicit conversion, including the ones that quietly truncate.

**Evidence:** measured with `grep -c` over `engine/math/matt_math.h`: `explicit` 0, `nodiscard` 0,
`noexcept` 0. The conversions this enables include

    RectangleI::RectangleI(RectangleF rectangle)          // :1977-1983
    {
        this->x = static_cast<int>(rectangle.x);
        this->y = static_cast<int>(rectangle.y);
        this->width = static_cast<int>(rectangle.width);
        this->height = static_cast<int>(rectangle.height);
    }

— so `RectangleI r = some_rectangle_f;` compiles and truncates position and size independently,
toward zero, with no rounding and no range check — plus `Vector2F(float f)` (`:1514-1518`), which
makes `some_vector == 3.0f` compile, and `Colour(const std::string& hex)` (`:2206-2209`), which makes
any `std::string` implicitly a colour by way of the parser above.

**Why it matters:** T5 is the tenet that says push every error to the earliest stage that can catch
it, and PHILOSOPHY/Tests names `const`, `noexcept` and `[[nodiscard]]` specifically as walls that
"carry information the compiler enforces". These are the cheapest and most boring walls available —
exactly the kind T5 says to prefer — and the value layer has none of them, on roughly 120 pure
accessors whose results are the whole point of calling them. The previous review filed the truncation
half of this; the `explicit` half is what makes it reachable by accident.

**Remedy:** mark every single-argument constructor `explicit` unless the conversion is genuinely
lossless and intended, mark the pure accessors `[[nodiscard]]`, and fix the fallout the build reports.
Round rather than truncate in the float-to-int conversions, or name them `from_*` so the loss is
visible at the call site.

---

### Rejected

- **`/fp:fast` is on for every target via `artattack_settings`** (finding 6's supporting claim, and
  an implicit premise elsewhere) — false. `cmake/settings.cmake` sets `/W4 /WX /permissive- /sdl`
  and no floating-point model; a grep for `fp:fast` across every `CMakeLists.txt`, `.cmake` file,
  `CMakePresets.json` and `.vcxproj` in the tree hits only `docs/review/`. The CMake conversion
  dropped it. Claim removed; the NaN observation stands without it.
- **Severity `critical` on `MatrixF`'s unsized storage** — regraded to `high`, the previous review's
  own grade. Nothing in `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/` or `tests/` references `MatrixF`,
  `Matrix3x3F` or `Vector4F`; the split created the possibility of an external consumer, not one.
- **Severity `high` on `mattmath::divide`** — regraded to `medium`. Exported, wrong, and uncalled;
  the recommended remedy deletes it.
- **Severity `high` on `cross` / `rotate_vector_by_ref`** — regraded to `medium`, matching the
  previous review. The reviewer's own text concedes no first-party caller and nothing about the
  defects changed since they were first reported.
- **"Findings 1 and 3 restate defects the previous review proved … everything else is new"** —
  false. Findings 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 all correspond to entries in `docs/review/findings.json` that
  `IMPLEMENTED.md` does not record as fixed. Only finding 2 (`divide`) is new. All are kept; the
  provenance sentence is corrected.
- **Theme: "Zero contracts are documented anywhere in 1650 lines"** — false. `matt_math.h:442-449`,
  `:464-465`, `:489` and `:705` document the zero-length contracts of `normalized()`,
  `to_unit_vector()` and `unit_vector()` and the axis order of `dimensions()`. Four contracts for
  ~120 members is the real complaint, and it is made in the tests finding instead.
- **"Grepping `calculate_draw_rectangle` … returns no call sites at all"** — overstated. The
  `RectangleI` overload calls the `Vector2F` overload at `drawer.cpp:26`. No caller exists outside
  `drawer.cpp`; the conclusion is unchanged and the wording is corrected in the finding.
- **"149 hex strings and ~153 `Colour`s … 302 namespace-scope constants"** — measured as 148
  `const std::string` and 153 `const mattmath::Colour` (301). More importantly the figure is
  *per translation unit*, not once: none is `inline` or `constexpr`, so each of the 17 files that
  includes `colour.h` gets its own copy. Corrected and strengthened inside the `set_from_hex`
  finding.
- **No finding was rejected outright.** Every observation in the raw report was reproduced in the
  current tree at the cited coordinates.

<a id="g-math-impl-c"></a>

## math-impl-c — `engine/math/matt_math.cpp` lines 3050-4594

*Group `math-impl-c` · 26 findings (3 high, 13 medium, 10 low) · source `review2/verified/math-impl-c.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every line the reviewer cited — all nineteen findings, in both
`matt_math.cpp` and `matt_math.h` — and every line number is right. I also
re-derived the four pieces of geometry the report leans on rather than trusting
them: the right-triangle vertex/edge indexing, the concave-quad worked example
(`p0=(0,0), p1=(5,3), p2=(10,0), p3=(5,10)`, cross products `-30/+35/+100/+35`,
so `p1` is reflex; ray-casting `(5,1)` gives two crossings, i.e. outside, while
`triangle_0` contains it), the camera round trip against
`calculate_view_rectangle`, and the `Quad` vs `RectangleRotated` storage
comparison. All four hold. Nothing here is already recorded as fixed in
IMPLEMENTED.md; the `RectangleRotated` items it lists (#21, transactional
setters, `edges_valid`, `normalize`) are all genuinely present in the code and
the report correctly credits them.

I rejected no finding outright but corrected three consequence claims and
regraded five. The consequence corrections matter: the unused
`calculate_points(Segment, float)` overload does **not** produce NaN corners —
`normalize()` was fixed to return zero for a zero-length vector (IMPLEMENTED.md
records exactly this), so it produces four *coincident* corners; and the
zero-width camera divisor is not reachable via a missing JSON key defaulting to
`RectangleF::ZERO`, because `Level`'s constructor always supplies the value and
a missing rapidjson key trips an assert long before that — a `"width": 0` typo
in a level file is the honest reach, which drops it to low. I regraded the
undefined `operator==` down (a link error is loud and diagnosable, which is what
T5 asks of a failure), the `RectangleRotated` heap corners down (real, but on no
frame path today), and `rectangle_rotated_to_axis` down (a comment, on a
three-line method whose one caller is itself unreachable).

I added seven findings. The largest is that `Triangle::angle_0/1/2()` return
`π` minus the interior angle — the *exterior* turn angle — which the reviewer
walked past while working the `find_hypotenuse` example; `find_hypotenuse` is
only correct because `π/2` is its own supplement, so the two defects share a
root. The next is that `RectangleRotated` **cannot be rotated at all** through
its public API: `set_x_axis` validates the candidate against the *current*
`y_axis_`, and vice versa, so neither order of the two setters can reach a new
orientation, there is no `rotate()` or `set_angle()`, and the angle constructor
is commented out — `angle()` is a getter with no setter. Also added: both `Quad`
and `RectangleRotated` are `= default` default-constructible into a state their
own `is_valid()` rejects; `TriangleRightAxisAligned` never checks that it is a
right triangle even though `level_object_builder.cpp:147` builds one straight
from JSON; it has no `clone()` override, so `Structure`'s `collision_shape_->clone()`
silently slices every level ramp back to a plain `Triangle`; `Shape::edges()` is
a pure virtual whose *return type* mandates a heap allocation per call; and
`Segment::direction()` is un-normalised with nothing saying so — the exact trap
that produced already-fixed finding #21. One out-of-scope note for whoever holds
lines 1-3050: `Vector2F::rotate_vector_by_ref` (1795-1802) assigns `vec.x` and
then uses the *new* `vec.x` to compute `vec.y`, which `Vector2F::rotate` (1752)
correctly avoids with temporaries.

### Themes

- The transactional-setter fix landed inside `RectangleRotated` and stopped at
  the class boundary: `Quad`'s four point setters still assign, then validate,
  then throw.
- Validation is applied at some doors and not others. Every real constructor
  throws on an invalid shape; the `= default` default constructor does not, and
  `inflate()` does not (except in `RectangleRotated`), so the invariant a caller
  is invited to rely on is not actually an invariant.
- Predicates check the cheap half. `Quad::is_valid()` rejects bow-ties but
  accepts concave and partially-degenerate quads, even though `triangles()` —
  the basis of every quad query — is only correct for convex ones.
- Angular geometry is systematically off by a supplement or a sign:
  `Triangle::angle_N()` returns the exterior angle, `hypotenuse()` indexes edges
  with a vertex index, `RectangleRotated::angle()` uses `acos` and cannot sign a
  rotation.
- Fixed-size geometry travels by `std::vector`, and the `Shape::edges()` virtual
  locks that in for every implementation (PHILOSOPHY/Performance: "fixed-size
  geometry returns fixed-size containers"). The newest class in the file,
  `RectangleRotated`, went further and put four corners in a heap vector where
  the older `Quad` uses `Point2F points_[4]`.
- Names carry the contract because nothing else does, and where the name is
  wrong (`calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle`'s parameters,
  `rectangle_rotated_to_axis`, `Segment::direction`, `minDepth`) nothing catches
  it (T4, PHILOSOPHY/The public face).
- Public API exists in the header that does not exist in the object file
  (`RectangleRotated::operator==`), or exists but answers wrongly
  (`hypotenuse()`, `angles()`), or exists but can never do its job
  (`set_x_axis`), or has never had a caller (`d3d_viewport_ptr()`).
- `Camera` and `Viewport` are render-layer, D3D11-shaped types living in the
  library ARCHITECTURE says depends on nothing, and neither has a single test.

#### `TriangleRightAxisAligned::hypotenuse()` returns a leg, not the hypotenuse

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3627-3646`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T9 (built over bought — built code must meet library standard)

**What:** `find_hypotenuse()` returns the index of the *vertex* carrying the
right angle, and both `hypotenuse()` and `hypotenuse_gradient()` use it as an
*edge* index. The hypotenuse is the edge opposite the right angle, not one of
the two that contain it.

**Evidence:**

    Segment TriangleRightAxisAligned::hypotenuse() const
    {
        int hypotenuse = this->find_hypotenuse(*this);
        if (hypotenuse == -1)
        {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Triangle is not a right triangle");
        }

        return this->edges()[hypotenuse];
    }
    float TriangleRightAxisAligned::hypotenuse_gradient() const
    {
        int hypotenuse = this->find_hypotenuse(*this);
        ...
        return this->calculate_gradient(hypotenuse);
    }

`find_hypotenuse` (3659-3678) tests `are_equal(tri.angle_0(), PI_OVER_2)` and
returns `0` — vertex 0. `edge_0()` (3484) is `Segment(points[0], points[1])`,
which *contains* vertex 0. Worked through with `p0=(0,0), p1=(1,0), p2=(0,1)`:
the right angle is at `p0`, `find_hypotenuse` returns `0`, and `hypotenuse()`
returns `Segment((0,0),(1,0))` — length 1, a leg. The hypotenuse is
`edge_1 = Segment((1,0),(0,1))`, length `sqrt(2)`. `hypotenuse_gradient()`
returns `(0-0)/(1-0) = 0.0f` where the answer is `(1-0)/(0-1) = -1.0f`. The edge
opposite vertex `i` is `edges()[(i + 1) % 3]` for all three vertices.

**Why it matters:** answering these two questions is the entire reason
`TriangleRightAxisAligned` exists as a distinct type, and it answers both
wrongly, silently. `grep -rn hypotenuse engine/ game/ tests/` finds no caller
outside this file and no test, so nothing has caught it — but the type *is*
constructed from level data (`game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:147`, every
`StructureRamp`), so the first ramp feature that needs the slope gets a wrong
number with no diagnostic. T9's standing obligation is that hand-rolled code
meet library standard.

**Remedy:** return `(right_angle_vertex + 1) % 3`, or have `find_hypotenuse`
return the edge index directly, and add a behavioural test with a 3-4-5 triangle
in each of the three vertex orderings.

#### Fix the inverted parameter names on `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle`

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4149-4162`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness), PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** the two `RectangleF` parameters are named the opposite of what they
receive — the world rectangle arrives in `view_rectangle` and the view rectangle
in `world_rectangle` — so the function is correct only when called against its
own naming.

**Evidence:**

    Camera Camera::calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle(
        const RectangleF& view_rectangle,
        const RectangleF& world_rectangle)
    {
        //return Camera(world_rectangle.x - view_rectangle.x,
        //	world_rectangle.y - view_rectangle.y,
        //	world_rectangle.width / view_rectangle.width);


        return Camera(view_rectangle.x - world_rectangle.x,
            view_rectangle.y - world_rectangle.y,
            world_rectangle.width / view_rectangle.width);

    }

The only caller, `game/objects/level.cpp:151-157`, passes them the other way up:

    Camera start_camera = Camera::calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle(
        this->zoom_out_start_bounds_,
        RectangleF(Vector2F::ZERO, this->resolution_manager_->resolution_vec()));

`zoom_out_start_bounds_` is world-space (`game/content/levels/close_quarters.json:67`
gives `x: 0, y: 4000, width: 1920, height: 1080` — a region of the level); the
second argument is the screen rect. Against `calculate_view_rectangle`
(4109-4116, `view = (world - translation) * scale`), the camera showing world
`W` in view `V` at the origin is `translation = W.position`,
`scale = V.width / W.width`. The body computes exactly that from the arguments
it actually receives, and exactly the inverse from the arguments its names ask
for.

**Why it matters:** a stranger reading the signature passes `(V, W)` and gets
`Camera(V.x - W.x, V.y - W.y, W.width / V.width)`. For `W = (100,100,200,200)`
into `V = (0,0,800,800)` the right answer is `Camera(100, 100, 4.0)`; they get
`Camera(-100, -100, 0.25)` — translation negated, scale reciprocal. Nothing
fails loudly; the view is somewhere else at the wrong zoom. This is a public
static factory in a library written for people who will read the header and not
the body.

**Remedy:** swap the parameter names (and the function name, which describes the
wrong direction) so the signature states what the body does, and fix the one
call site's argument order to match.

#### Make `Quad`'s point setters transactional, as `RectangleRotated`'s already are

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3876-3914`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed), T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** all four `Quad::set_point_N` overwrite the member, then validate, then
throw — leaving the object holding a value its own constructor would have
rejected.

**Evidence:**

    void Quad::set_point_0(const Point2F& point)
    {
        this->points_[0] = point;

        if (!this->is_valid())
        {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Quad is not valid");
        }
    }

Identical bodies at 3886, 3896 and 3906. This is precisely the defect just fixed
one class down, with the reason written into the source at 4367-4370:

    // Each setter validates the candidate value before committing it, so a
    // rejected argument leaves the rectangle exactly as it was. Assigning to
    // the member first and throwing afterwards left the object corrupt: it
    // held the bad value and a stale points_ cache.

`tests/math/math_tests.cpp:984` (`test_rectangle_rotated_setters_are_transactional`)
pins the fixed behaviour for `RectangleRotated`. There is no equivalent for
`Quad`.

**Why it matters:** `Quad`'s five constructors throw on an invalid quad
precisely so the invariant can be relied on afterwards — `triangles()`,
`quad_point_intersect` and `quad_segment_intersect` all assume it. After a caught
`set_point_2` exception the quad is a bow-tie, and every subsequent intersection
query against it returns a wrong answer with no further throw. No in-repo caller
uses these setters (`grep -rn set_point_ engine/ game/ tests/` finds only the
declarations and definitions), so it is not reachable from the game; it is
reachable from any user of the shape API.

**Remedy:** build the candidate value, validate it, and only then commit —
matching `RectangleRotated::set_x_axis` (4371-4383). Since `is_valid()` reads the
whole array, the cheapest form is to save the old point, assign, validate, and
restore on failure.

#### `Triangle::angle_0/1/2()` return the exterior angle, not the interior one

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3506-3531`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T3 (simplicity over accuracy — "a simple model still has exact, documented, tested semantics")

**What:** each accessor measures the angle between an edge's direction and the
*incoming* edge's direction, which is `π` minus the interior angle at that
vertex — the turn angle. `angles()` therefore sums to `2π`, not `π`.

**Evidence:**

    float Triangle::angle_0() const
    {
        return Vector2F::angle_between(this->edge_0().direction(),
            this->edge_2().direction());

    }

`edge_0().direction()` is `p1 - p0`; `edge_2().direction()` is `p0 - p2`, i.e.
`-(p2 - p0)`. The interior angle at `p0` is between `p1 - p0` and `p2 - p0`, so
this returns `π - interior`. Equilateral check with `p0=(0,0), p1=(1,0),
p2=(0.5, 0.866)`: `dot((1,0), (-0.5,-0.866)) = -0.5`, both unit, so
`acos(-0.5) = 2π/3 = 120°` for a triangle whose every interior angle is `60°`.
`angle_1()` and `angle_2()` have the same shape.

**Why it matters:** `angles()` is public API on the engine's own triangle
primitive, with no doc comment and no test, returning a number a reader will
take for the interior angle. It is also the shared root of the `hypotenuse()`
defect above: `find_hypotenuse` (3662-3673) survives this only because `π/2` is
its own supplement, so the one consumer that would have exposed the convention
is blind to it. PHILOSOPHY/Collision requires math primitives to carry
documented contracts pinned by behavioural tests; this one has neither, and the
undocumented convention is the surprising one.

**Remedy:** return the interior angle — `angle_between(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)` and
its rotations — or, if the turn angle is genuinely wanted, rename to
`turn_angle_N()`/`exterior_angle_N()` and say so in the header. Either way, pin
it with an equilateral and a 3-4-5 test.

#### `RectangleRotated` cannot be rotated through its own API

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4371-4396`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy), PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** `set_x_axis` validates the candidate against the *current* `y_axis_`,
and `set_y_axis` against the current `x_axis_`, so neither ordering of the two
setters can reach a new orientation. There is no `rotate()`, no `set_angle()`,
and the angle-taking constructor is commented out — so the OBB type has an
`angle()` getter and no way to change it.

**Evidence:**

    void RectangleRotated::set_x_axis(const Point2F& x_axis)
    {
        const Vector2F candidate = x_axis.normalized();

        if (!are_equal(candidate.length(), 1.0f, EPSILON) ||
            !are_equal(Vector2F::dot(candidate, this->y_axis_), 0.0f, EPSILON))
        {
            throw std::invalid_argument("Axes are not valid");
        }

        this->x_axis_ = candidate;

`set_y_axis` (4384-4396) is the mirror. Starting from the default
`x = (1,0), y = (0,-1)` and trying to reach 45°: `set_x_axis((0.707, 0.707))`
throws because `dot` with the old `y` is `-0.707`; `set_y_axis((-0.707, 0.707))`
throws because `dot` with the old `x` is `-0.707`. The only values `set_x_axis`
accepts are `±(1,0)` — a flip. The header confirms there is nothing else:

    // matt_math.h:1116-1117
    //RectangleRotated(const mattmath::Point2F& center,
    //	float angle, const mattmath::Vector2F& hw_extents);

**Why it matters:** the transactional-setter fix is right and the perpendicularity
check is right; together they make the pair unusable for the one thing an
oriented bounding box is for. A user's only route is to discard and rebuild —
`rr = RectangleRotated(rr.center(), new_x, new_y, rr.half_extents())` — which
nothing documents and which is exactly the value-semantics workaround a stranger
will not guess when the class ships two axis setters.

**Remedy:** add `void rotate(float radians)` / `set_angle(float)` that sets both
axes together (deriving `y` as `Vector2F::normal(x)`, so the pair is
perpendicular by construction), or make `set_x_axis` re-derive `y_axis_` rather
than validate against the stale one. Uncomment the angle constructor while you
are there.

#### `Quad::is_valid()` accepts concave and degenerate quads that `Quad::triangles()` cannot represent

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3826-3843`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `is_valid()` only rejects self-intersection, but every quad query
decomposes via `triangle_0`/`triangle_1`, a fan from point 0 that is a correct
triangulation only of a *convex* quad — so a concave quad passes construction
and then reports points outside itself as inside.

**Evidence:**

    bool Quad::is_valid() const
    {
        // check if the edges intersect
        std::vector<Segment> edges = this->edges();

        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
        {
            for (int j = i + 1; j < 4; j++)
            {
                if (edges[i].intersects(edges[j]))

    Triangle Quad::triangle_0() const
    {
        return Triangle(this->points_[0], this->points_[1], this->points_[2]);
    }
    Triangle Quad::triangle_1() const
    {
        return Triangle(this->points_[0], this->points_[2], this->points_[3]);
    }

Take `p0=(0,0), p1=(5,3), p2=(10,0), p3=(5,10)`. `test_2D_segment_segment`
(`ericson_math.cpp:704`) uses a strict `a1 * a2 < 0.0f`, so shared endpoints do
not count, and the two non-adjacent pairs genuinely miss: `e0 ∩ e2` would be at
`x = 7.69`, outside `e0`'s span `[0,5]`; `e1 ∩ e3` at `x = 2.31`, outside `e1`'s
span `[5,10]`. So `is_valid()` returns true. But the cross products at the four
vertices are `+35, -30, +35, +100`, so `p1` is reflex and the interior diagonal
is `p1-p3`, not `p0-p2`. `triangle_0 = (0,0),(5,3),(10,0)` is the notch, outside
the quad, so `quad.contains(Point2F(5, 1))` returns `true` for a point that
ray-casting places outside (two boundary crossings). Degeneracy slips through the
same gap: `[P, P, Q, R]` — a triangle with a doubled vertex — has one zero-length
edge whose signed areas are all `0`, so no pair reports an intersection and the
quad is accepted. The header's stated contract is never checked either
(`matt_math.h:929-932`: "The points are ordered in a clockwise direction,
starting from the top left").

**Why it matters:** every in-repo `Quad` comes from a `RectangleF` or a
`RectangleRotated` and is convex, so the wrong answer is not reachable from the
game. It is reachable from the two public constructors that take arbitrary
points, and a predicate named `is_valid()` that validates half the invariant is
worse than none — it tells the caller the object is safe to use.

**Remedy:** require a consistent turn direction at all four vertices (which
subsumes the bow-tie test and rejects the doubled-vertex case), or triangulate
on the interior diagonal instead of always from point 0.

#### `Quad` and `RectangleRotated` are default-constructible into a state their own `is_valid()` rejects

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:935, 1062`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed), T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** every written constructor of both shapes ends by calling `is_valid()`
and throwing — and both then declare `= default` default constructors that skip
it, producing objects for which `is_valid()` returns `false`.

**Evidence:**

    // matt_math.h:935 / :1062
    Quad() = default;
    RectangleRotated() = default;

    // matt_math.h:1127-1133 — the default member state
    Point2F center_ = Point2F::ZERO;
    Vector2F x_axis_ = Vector2F::DIRECTION_RIGHT;
    Vector2F y_axis_ = Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP;
    Vector2F hw_extents_ = Vector2F::ZERO;

`RectangleRotated::half_widths_valid()` (4526-4535) rejects `hw_extents_.x <= 0`,
so a default-constructed OBB fails `is_valid()`. The tests already assert that
this exact state is rejected when it arrives through a constructor
(`math_tests.cpp:974-977`, "zero half extents"). For `Quad`, the four points
default to `ZERO`, so all four edges are `Segment(ZERO, ZERO)` and
`segments_intersect`'s `if (a == b) return true` fast path (`matt_math.cpp:566`)
makes `is_valid()` false as well.

**Why it matters:** the type's contract — "a constructed shape is valid" — is
what `triangles()`, `contains()` and the intersection routines rely on, and it
is not true. A default-constructed OBB answers `contains()` without complaint:
`quad()` builds a `Quad` from four coincident points, which passes `Quad`'s own
validation for the degenerate reason above, and the query returns a silent
`false`. This is the last unpatched hole in the validation pass IMPLEMENTED.md
records.

**Remedy:** either give both types a genuinely valid default (unit extents), or
delete the defaulted default constructors so an unusable shape cannot be spelled.
If a default-constructible "empty" state is wanted deliberately, say so in the
header and make `is_valid()` accept it.

#### `TriangleRightAxisAligned` never checks that it is a right triangle

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3603-3625`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** all three constructors forward straight to `Triangle` and validate
nothing, so the type's whole premise — that a hypotenuse exists — is unchecked
at the only place it could be checked cheaply.

**Evidence:**

    TriangleRightAxisAligned::TriangleRightAxisAligned(
        float x0, float y0, float x1, float y1, float x2, float y2) :
        Triangle(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2)
    {

    }

`find_hypotenuse` already exists (3659) and returns `-1` for a non-right
triangle; the constructors do not call it. Nor is axis alignment — the other
half of the name — checked anywhere. The type is built directly from authored
data:

    // game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:147
    TriangleRightAxisAligned triangle = TriangleRightAxisAligned(
        json["triangle"]["x1"].GetFloat(),
        ...

**Why it matters:** `Quad` and `RectangleRotated` both throw from their
constructors when the invariant fails, and the recent work made that stick. This
one accepts anything and defers the complaint to `hypotenuse()`, which nothing
calls — so a mistyped ramp in a level file produces a silently wrong collision
shape rather than a load-time error naming the file, which is exactly the
inversion T6 exists to prevent.

**Remedy:** validate in the constructor —
`if (find_hypotenuse(*this) == -1) throw std::invalid_argument(...)` — and add a
matching check for axis alignment if the name is to keep that word. Test all
three constructors.

#### `Shape::edges()` mandates a heap allocation on every call

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:88`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap), PHILOSOPHY/Performance

**What:** the base-class virtual returns `std::vector<Segment>` by value for
geometry whose size is fixed and known per shape (3 for a triangle, 4 for a quad
or OBB, 0 for a circle), so every implementation must allocate, and no caller can
opt out.

**Evidence:**

    // matt_math.h:88
    virtual std::vector<Segment> edges() const = 0;

    // matt_math.cpp:3936-3946 — one of five identical shapes
    std::vector<Segment> Quad::edges() const
    {
        std::vector<Segment> edges =
        {
            this->edge_0(),
            this->edge_1(),
            this->edge_2(),
            this->edge_3()
        };
        return edges;
    }

`Triangle::edges()` (3496), `Triangle::angles()` (3522), `Quad::points()` (3865),
`Quad::triangles()` (3958) and `RectangleRotated::edges()` (4290) are the same
shape. `Quad::is_valid()` calls `edges()` once per validation, and
`RectangleRotated::edges_valid()` (4555) once per construction — so validating a
shape costs a `malloc`/`free` before it computes anything.

PHILOSOPHY/Performance: "Per-frame code performs no heap allocation and no
string-keyed lookups; **fixed-size geometry returns fixed-size containers**".

**Why it matters:** the allocation is not incidental — it is written into a pure
virtual, which means it survives every implementation and every future shape, and
changing it later breaks every override and every caller at once. `Circle` has to
return an empty vector to satisfy it. It is also the multiplier behind the
allocation count in the OBB finding below.

**Remedy:** `edges()` cannot return a single fixed-size type across shapes with
different edge counts, so either drop it from `Shape` and keep the per-type
`std::array<Segment, N> edges()` accessors (callers that need polymorphism can
use `edge_count()` + `edge(i)`), or have the virtual write into a caller-supplied
span. The per-type helpers — `points()`, `triangles()`, `angles()` — should be
`std::array` today.

#### Stop storing and re-deriving `RectangleRotated`'s four corners on the heap

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4275-4281, 4463-4468, 4495-4512`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap), PHILOSOPHY/Performance

**What:** the four corners of an OBB live in a `std::vector<Point2F>` member that
is freed and reallocated by every mutator, while `quad()` — on the containment
path — ignores that cache and computes a fifth copy.

**Evidence:**

    // matt_math.h:1132
    std::vector<Point2F> points_ = { Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO,
                Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO };

    // matt_math.cpp:4275
    void RectangleRotated::offset(const Vector2F& amount)
    {
        this->center_ += amount;

        this->points_ = this->calculate_points();

    }

    // matt_math.cpp:4463
    Quad RectangleRotated::quad() const
    {
        auto points = this->calculate_points();

        return Quad(points);
    }

    // matt_math.cpp:4504
    std::vector<Point2F> points(4);

The comparison that makes this a regression rather than a habit: the older
`Quad`, which holds the same four points, uses a plain array —
`Point2F points_[4] = { ... };` (`matt_math.h:990-991`). `calculate_points()`
returns a fresh vector by value, so `offset()`, `set_center()`, the three
`set_half_*` and `inflate()` each cost one allocation and one free to update 32
bytes the object already owns, where `points_[i] += amount` would have been exact
and free for `offset()`.

The compounded cost is on the query path. `rectangles_rotated_intersect`
(619-662) calls `contains()` up to eight times; each goes
`point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (612) → `quad()` → one vector from
`calculate_points()` → `Quad(const std::vector<Point2F>&)` (3710) → `is_valid()`
→ `edges()` → a second vector → `quad_point_intersect` (531) → `triangles()` → a
third — around two dozen allocations and forty-eight orientation tests per
OBB-vs-OBB query, most of it re-proving that a rectangle built from validated
perpendicular axes is not a bow-tie.

**Why it matters:** no shipping game object holds a `RectangleRotated` today
(`ProjectileJet::shape()` and friends return `&rectangle_`, a `RectangleF`), so
this is not currently hot in the paint-shooter — which is why it is graded medium
rather than high. It is the public OBB type a stranger reaches for, in the newest
code in the file, and the cost is baked into the class layout *and* into the
public signature `const std::vector<Point2F>& points() const`, so undoing it later
is a source-breaking change for every user.

**Remedy:** make `points_` a `std::array<Point2F, 4>` (matching `Quad`), have
`offset()` add to the cached corners rather than recompute them, have `quad()`
build from `points_`, and change `points()` to return the array by const
reference.

#### Define `RectangleRotated::operator==` and `operator!=`, or delete the declarations

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:1123-1124`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time), PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** `RectangleRotated`'s equality operators are declared in the public
header and defined nowhere in the library.

**Evidence:**

    // matt_math.h:1123-1124
    bool operator==(const RectangleRotated& other) const;
    bool operator!=(const RectangleRotated& other) const;

The `RectangleRotated` region runs from `matt_math.cpp:4177` to `4593` and
contains no `operator==`; `grep -rn "RectangleRotated::operator" engine/ game/
tests/` returns nothing. Every peer type has both: `Circle` at 3346, `Triangle`
at 3532, `Quad` at 3968, `Segment` at 4038, `Camera` at 4100, `Viewport` at 3282.

**Why it matters:** `RectangleRotated`/`OBB` is the only public shape you cannot
compare. A user writing `if (a == b)`, or putting an OBB in a container or a test
assertion that needs equality, gets `LNK2019` on a symbol the header promised.
Regraded down from the reviewer's `high` because the failure is a link error —
loud, immediate and unambiguous, which is the outcome T5 asks for — not a wrong
answer at run time. Nothing in the repo compares two OBBs, which is why the
library links today.

**Remedy:** define both in the `RectangleRotated` region, comparing `center_`,
`x_axis_`, `y_axis_` and `hw_extents_` (`points_` is derived), or remove the
declarations.
