## app-shell — Application shell

*Group `app-shell` · 16 findings (4 high, 8 medium, 4 low) · source `review2/verified/app-shell.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every cited line in `engine/app/application.h` and
`engine/app/application.cpp` and checked each quotation character by character, then
re-derived each consequence from the code it depends on rather than from the finding's
own narrative: `engine/core/state_context.{h,cpp}`, `engine/core/state.h`,
`engine/core/step_timer.h`, `engine/render/device_resources.{h,cpp}` (in particular
`WindowSizeChanged`, `CreateWindowSizeDependentResources`, `Present`,
`HandleDeviceLost`, `create_deferred_contexts`), `engine/render/resolution_manager.cpp`,
`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp`, `engine/core/thread_pool.cpp`, and every client —
`samples/minimal/main.cpp`, `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp`, `game/main.cpp`,
`game/game_data.cpp`, `game/states/main_menu.cpp`, `game/objects/level.h`,
`game/objects/weapon.h`. Every line number in the raw report was correct; the only
citation I corrected is finding #1, whose evidence block quotes the header comment at
`application.h:137-143` while the range said `144-166`.

**What I threw out.** One finding, and only one: the `transition_to` contract
(`engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`). It is a true and serious observation, but it is
not in this group's files and the group that owns them — `core-objects` — filed it
against the identical anchor (`state_context.h:10-18`, `state_context.cpp:21-26`). Two
copies of one defect is exactly the duplication I am here to remove.

**What I re-graded.** Two, both downward, both because the consequence outran the
trigger. `target_fps == 0` really does hang inside `StepTimer`, and I confirmed the MSVC
x64 double→`uint64_t` sequence plausibly yields `0` for `+inf` — but both live clients
(`game/main.cpp:37`, and the sample's defaults) pass valid values, so this is a
hardening gap and not a live hang: **high → medium**. And `window_proc`'s function-local
statics genuinely cross-wire two windows, but nothing in the repo opens two, so it is
latent in a scenario no client reaches: **medium → low**. I also trimmed two overstated
sub-claims: `max_threads = 0` does *not* leave `deferred_contexts_` null
(`device_resources.cpp:745` allocates the vector unconditionally, so `clear()` iterates
an empty vector safely), and `run()` before `initialize()` does not reach
`PIXBeginEvent` — it dies one frame earlier on `*this->dt_` at `application.cpp:259`.

**What I confirmed that surprised me.** Finding #4's window-sizing claim is stronger than
the reviewer knew, and I found the mechanism that makes it permanent:
`DeviceResources::WindowSizeChanged` opens with `if (!m_window) return false;`
(`device_resources.cpp:406-407`), and `create_window` calls `ShowWindow` at
`application.cpp:124` *before* `SetWindow` at `:61` — so the one `WM_SIZE` that would
have delivered the real client size is silently dropped, and the swap chain is built at
the requested resolution and stretched for the whole session. I also found that the
reviewer's remedy for finding #3 is wrong: `ResolutionManager::set_resolution(const
Vector2I&)` does not store an arbitrary size, it runs
`convert_ivec_to_resolution` (`resolution_manager.cpp:153-176`), which silently returns
`s_1280_720` for anything that is not one of four hardcoded pairs. Pushing a dragged
window size into it makes the divergence worse, not better. I rewrote that remedy.

**What they missed.** Three things I added. The shell's public face publishes
`DirectX::SpriteBatch*`, `DirectX::CommonStates*`, `DirectX::GamePad*` and a raw `HWND`
— the backend the rest of the design keeps behind a seam — and `window()` has zero
callers in the entire repo, so it is dead Win32 in the first header a stranger reads.
`set_fullscreen` sets `WS_EX_TOPMOST` with `SetWindowLongPtr`, which the Win32 contract
says does not change z-order. And the accessor block's own contract is false on its first
line: "Every one of these is null until `initialize()` has run" — `device_resources_` is
constructed in the constructor.

### Themes

- The shell holds two competing notions of "the size" — `ResolutionManager`'s enum and
  the window's real client area — and never reconciles them. Three separate findings
  (#1, #2, and half of #5's cousin) fall out of that one confusion, and the two halves
  mask each other: fix the stretch and the viewports drift; drag the window and the
  stretch disappears while the viewports break.
- `ApplicationOptions` is taken entirely on trust. `target_fps`, `min_threads` and
  `max_threads` reach `SecondsToTicks`, `SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum` and
  `vector::resize` unchecked, in the struct that is the first thing a stranger fills in.
- Failure signals from the platform edge are discarded rather than raised:
  `AudioEngine::Update()`'s bool, `SetWindowLongPtr`'s return, `SetWindowPos`'s return,
  and the absence of any device-lost notification to the game.
- `Application` inherits two things it should own, and both leak: `StateContext` puts the
  live state tree in the wrong destruction slot, and `IDeviceNotify` puts a
  macro-keyword, `I`-prefixed type in the public signature.
- The header documents contracts the code does not keep — a three-step protocol enforced
  by nothing, a "created once and never reseated" promise that `common_states()`
  contradicts four lines later, and a "null until `initialize()`" claim that is false for
  the first accessor listed.
- Teardown is incomplete in the direction the header does not discuss: the window class
  is never unregistered, `window_` is never nulled, and `GWLP_USERDATA` keeps pointing at
  a destroyed `Application`.
- Nothing in `tests/` constructs, links against or exercises this file.

#### Size the window from the client rectangle, not from the requested resolution

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:59-61,96-125,215-224`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `create_window` and `set_resolution` pass the requested resolution as
`CreateWindowExW`/`SetWindowPos`'s *overall window* size, which for a titled, bordered
window is never the client size — and the one `WM_SIZE` that would have corrected it is
dropped, so the back buffer is stretched non-uniformly for the whole session.

**Evidence:**

    const mattmath::Vector2I size =
        this->resolution_manager_->resolution_ivec();
    ...
        this->window_ = CreateWindowExW(0,
            this->options_.window_class_name.c_str(),
            this->options_.window_title.c_str(), WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW,
            CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, size.x, size.y,
            nullptr, nullptr, instance, this);
    ...
    ShowWindow(this->window_,
        this->options_.fullscreen ? SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED : show_command);

`initialize` then tells `DeviceResources` the same number (`application.cpp:59-61`):

    const mattmath::Vector2I size =
        this->resolution_manager_->resolution_ivec();
    this->device_resources_->SetWindow(this->window_, size.x, size.y);

and `set_resolution` repeats it (`application.cpp:222-223`):

    SetWindowPos(this->window_, HWND_TOP, 0, 0, size.x, size.y,
        SWP_NOMOVE | SWP_NOZORDER);

**Why it matters:** `nWidth`/`nHeight` and `SetWindowPos`'s `cx`/`cy` are window
dimensions including caption and borders, and there is no `AdjustWindowRect`
anywhere in the repo. A 1280x720 request yields a client area of roughly 1264x681 at
96 DPI. The `ShowWindow` at `:124` does send a `WM_SIZE` carrying the true client size,
but it runs *inside* `create_window` at `:51` — before `SetWindow` at `:61` — and
`DeviceResources::WindowSizeChanged` opens with `if (!m_window) return false;`
(`device_resources.cpp:406-407`), so that message is discarded. `SetWindow` then stamps
`m_outputSize` as 1280x720, `CreateWindowSizeDependentResources` builds a 1280x720 swap
chain from it, and `DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH` (`device_resources.cpp:330`) stretches it into
1264x681 — a 4.4% aspect error on every frame the engine has ever drawn. Nothing after
startup corrects it: `on_window_moved` passes `m_outputSize` back to itself, so
`WindowSizeChanged` early-returns. `ScreenResolution::s_1280_720` does not mean 1280x720
anywhere the player can see. The `set_resolution` path, reachable from the options menu
(`game/states/main_menu.cpp:338`), has the same bug plus the divergence in the next
finding. `WM_GETMINMAXINFO` (`application.cpp:534-541`) confuses the same two units,
setting `ptMinTrackSize` — a window size — from `min_window_width`/`min_window_height`.

**Remedy:** Run the requested resolution through `AdjustWindowRectEx` with the actual
style and exstyle before both `CreateWindowExW` and `SetWindowPos`, and keep passing the
*client* size to `DeviceResources::SetWindow`. Moving `ShowWindow` after `SetWindow`
would also let the initial `WM_SIZE` do the reconciling for free.

#### Tell ResolutionManager when the window resizes, or stop computing viewports from it

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:226-248,359-362`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `on_window_size_changed` resizes the swap chain to the new client size and
never updates `resolution_manager_`, so every viewport, divider and UI position is
computed against a resolution the render target no longer has.

**Evidence:**

    void Application::on_window_size_changed(int width, int height)
    {
        std::ignore = this->device_resources_->WindowSizeChanged(width, height);
    }

`WindowSizeChanged` (`device_resources.cpp:404-424`) assigns `m_outputSize = newRc` and
calls `CreateWindowSizeDependentResources()`, which sizes the back buffer and
`m_screenViewport` from it. Every viewport comes from the *other* number —
`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:47`:

            this->layout_, player_num, this->resolution_manager_->resolution_vec());

and the same at `:56`, `:76` and `:115` for the split-screen dividers. `set_fullscreen`
(`application.cpp:226-248`) is the third door into the divergence: it changes the window
style and size and never touches `resolution_manager_` either.

**Why it matters:** The window is `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` (`application.cpp:114`), so
dragging its border is a one-gesture path from a real user to this state. Drag a
1280x720 window down to 1000x600: the back buffer becomes 1000x600 while
`ViewportManager::calculate_viewport` still divides 1280x720 into quadrants, so in a
four-player match the right column is set to `x=640, width=640` on a 1000-pixel target —
D3D clips 280 pixels off every right-hand player's view, and `viewport_dividers()` draws
the split lines somewhere they do not belong. Nothing reports it. Note this defect and
the previous one mask each other: today the swap chain is *wrong* (stretched) and the
viewports are *right*; the first time the user drags the window the swap chain becomes
right and the viewports become wrong.

**Remedy:** Make one of the two the single source of truth — the cleaner direction is to
have `ViewportManager` take its screen size from `DeviceResources::GetOutputSize()` and
delete the `ResolutionManager*` it holds. Do **not** push the new client size into
`ResolutionManager::set_resolution(const Vector2I&)`: that overload runs
`convert_ivec_to_resolution` (`resolution_manager.cpp:153-176`), which silently maps
anything outside four hardcoded pairs to `s_1280_720`, so a dragged window would report
1280x720 no matter what size it actually is.

#### Destroy the state tree before the services it borrows, not after

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:71,137-166`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY, Services and lifetimes ("Construction and destruction order are designed")

**What:** `Application` inherits `StateContext`, which owns the live `State`, so C++
destroys every service member *before* the base subobject destroys the state tree that
borrows them — the exact inversion of the ordering the header declares load-bearing.

**Evidence:**

    class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext

`application.h:137-144`:

        // DECLARATION ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING BELOW THIS LINE.
        //
        // Members destruct in reverse declaration order. DirectXTK requires the
        // AudioEngine to outlive every WaveBank and SoundEffectInstance - their
        // destructors unregister themselves from it - and AudioResources owns the
        // SoundBanks that own those. So audio_engine_ is declared FIRST and dies
        // LAST.
        std::unique_ptr<DirectX::AudioEngine> audio_engine_ = nullptr;

and `engine/core/state_context.h:17`:

        std::unique_ptr<State> state_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** Non-static data members are destroyed before direct base
subobjects, so `audio_engine_` dies last *among members* only — `StateContext::state_`
dies after it. The real order on `~Application` is: body (`audio_engine_->Suspend()`,
`CoUninitialize()`), then `sprite_batch_ptrs_` … `audio_resources_` …
`device_resources_`, then `audio_engine_`, and only then `~StateContext()` →
`~GameMenu`/`~GameLevel` → `~Level` → `~Player` → `~Weapon`. Every one of those holds
borrowed pointers into memory that is already freed: `Weapon::sound_bank_`
(`game/objects/weapon.h:55`) points into the `AudioResources` destroyed several members
earlier, and `Level::sampler_state_` (`game/objects/level.h:149`) into the
`CommonStates` destroyed before that. I verified the reviewer's latency claim and it
holds — `~Level`, `~Player`, `~Weapon` and all five menu-page destructors are implicit
or `= default` (`game/states/*.h`), so nothing dereferences a back-pointer today. But
that is latent by accident, not by design: the first stranger who writes
`~MyState() { level_->stop_sounds(); }` — the ordinary thing to do, and a method that
already exists — gets a use-after-free at exit that the header's own comment promised
was impossible. `IMPLEMENTED.md` marks old finding #10 fixed, and the member half
genuinely is (`audio_resources_` is destroyed before `audio_engine_`); the base-class
half was never addressed and is now papered over by a comment asserting the opposite.

**Remedy:** Hold a `StateContext` by composition as the *first-declared* member so it
dies first, or give `StateContext` a `clear_state()` and make it the first statement of
`~Application()`. Either way the header comment needs the base-class sentence it is
currently missing.

#### Stop discarding AudioEngine::Update()'s failure — audio dies silently for the session

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:257-262`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** The shell throws away the only signal DirectXTK gives it that the audio device
has gone, so a headset unplug or a default-device change silences the game permanently
with no diagnostic and no recovery.

**Evidence:**

    void Application::update()
    {
        *this->dt_ = static_cast<float>(this->timer_.GetElapsedSeconds());
        StateContext::update();
        std::ignore = this->audio_engine_->Update();
    }

**Why it matters:** `AudioEngine::Update()` returns `false` when the engine is not
running; the documented recovery is to test `IsCriticalError()` and call `Reset()` to
re-acquire the new default endpoint. Without that call DirectXTK never re-acquires a
device, so the silence is for the life of the process. The path is reached by any player
who unplugs a USB headset, switches Bluetooth output, or has Windows move the default
device mid-session: `SoundBank::play_effect`/`play_wave` keep being called from `Player`,
`Weapon` and `StructurePaintable`, every call succeeds, and nothing is ever heard again.
`std::ignore` makes the discard look deliberate, which is the part that will keep the
next reader from fixing it. This is the "limping" T6 forbids, in the module whose own
header cites T6 twice. Note the correct fix is not an unconditional throw: `Update()`
also returns `false` in DirectXTK's silent mode, where there is no device and nothing to
recover, and that is the "expected absence" T6 explicitly excludes.

**Remedy:** Test the result; on `IsCriticalError()` call `audio_engine_->Reset()` and let
`AudioResources` re-seat its banks; on the silent-mode case do nothing, quietly and on
purpose, with a comment saying so.

#### Validate ApplicationOptions — target_fps == 0 hangs the process inside StepTimer

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:73-75`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation) / T5

**What:** No field of `ApplicationOptions` is checked. `target_fps = 0` produces an
out-of-range double-to-`uint64_t` conversion (undefined behaviour) and, on the result
MSVC x64 actually produces, a non-terminating loop in the fixed-step update.

**Evidence:**

        this->timer_.SetFixedTimeStep(true);
        this->timer_.SetTargetElapsedSeconds(
            1.0 / static_cast<double>(this->options_.target_fps));

`engine/core/step_timer.h:68`:

        static constexpr uint64_t SecondsToTicks(double seconds) noexcept { return static_cast<uint64_t>(seconds * TicksPerSecond); }

`engine/core/step_timer.h:134-142`:

                while (m_leftOverTicks >= m_targetElapsedTicks)
                {
                    m_elapsedTicks = m_targetElapsedTicks;
                    m_totalTicks += m_targetElapsedTicks;
                    m_leftOverTicks -= m_targetElapsedTicks;
                    m_frameCount++;

                    update();
                }

**Why it matters:** `1.0 / 0` is `+inf`, and `static_cast<uint64_t>(inf)` is undefined
behaviour. MSVC x64 lowers the conversion as "subtract 2^63, `cvttsd2si`, flip bit 63";
for `+inf` that is `0x8000000000000000` with bit 63 flipped, i.e. **0**. With
`m_targetElapsedTicks == 0` the loop condition `m_leftOverTicks >= 0` is always true and
`m_leftOverTicks -= 0` never progresses, so the first `tick()` never returns and the
window stops pumping messages — a hang with no output at all. A negative `target_fps`
is the same conversion UB. The sibling fields are equally unguarded:
`max_threads = 0` leaves `sprite_batches_` empty so the sample's `sprite_batches()->at(0)`
throws `out_of_range` from inside `draw()`; a negative `max_threads` reaches
`sprite_batches_.resize(static_cast<size_t>(-16))` and
`SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum(pool_, static_cast<DWORD>(-16))` (`thread_pool.cpp:15-16`);
`min_threads > max_threads` makes `SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum` fail with nobody looking
(`thread_pool.cpp:18-19`). Graded medium rather than high because both live clients pass
valid values (`game/main.cpp:37-38`, and the sample takes the defaults), so this is a
hardening gap and not a live hang — but this struct is the first thing a stranger fills
in, which is precisely why it should be the loudest thing in the file.

**Remedy:** Validate every field at the top of `initialize()` and throw naming the field
and its constraint, the way the CPU-support and COM checks already do six lines above.

#### Expose the device-lost/restored signal the shell already receives

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:364-383`, `engine/app/application.h:110-129`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** `Application` is the sole `IDeviceNotify` listener and publishes no hook, so a
game caching a `CommonStates*` or `SpriteBatch*` either dangles across a device loss or
must re-fetch through the shell every frame — and the header contradicts itself about
which of those it is.

**Evidence:**

    void Application::OnDeviceLost()
    {
        ...
        this->common_states_.reset();

The header promises stability at `application.h:110-111`:

        // After that they are created once and never reseated, so an object may
        // hold one for its whole life - device loss recreates GPU objects in place
        // and leaves service identity alone (PHILOSOPHY, Services and lifetimes).

and withdraws it fifteen lines later, at `application.h:126-129`:

        // Recreated on device loss, so these change identity across one. The
        // vector's own address is stable; only the pointers inside it move.
        DirectX::CommonStates* common_states() const;
        std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches() const;

**Why it matters:** `OnDeviceLost`/`OnDeviceRestored` are private overrides; there is no
`on_device_restored` callback in `ApplicationOptions`, no virtual on `State`, no version
counter. The only contract a game can infer is "re-read `common_states()` every frame",
which is unenforceable and is exactly the per-frame service indirection the frame loop
was meant not to need. The live casualty already exists: `Level::sampler_state_`
(`game/objects/level.h:149`) is snapshotted from `common_states()->PointClamp()` at
construction (`game/states/game_states.cpp:119`), and `IMPLEMENTED.md`'s "Known remaining
issues" files it as a game bug. It is not: the shell owns the only signal and publishes
none, so every client will make the same mistake. PHILOSOPHY's "service identity is
stable across [device loss]" is the invariant `common_states_` breaks, and the header
knows it.

**Remedy:** Either keep the promise — hold `CommonStates` by a stable handle whose
contents are rebuilt in place — or publish the event: an optional callback pair on
`ApplicationOptions`, or a `device_restored()` the current `State` may override. Then
delete whichever of the two header paragraphs is no longer true.

#### Enforce the three-step protocol the header documents

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:180-185,187-205,215-224`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** Every public method that depends on `initialize()` having run dereferences a
null `unique_ptr` if it has not, instead of naming the step that is missing.

**Evidence:**

    void Application::load_manifest(const std::string& manifest_path)
    {
        this->resource_loader_->load_manifest(
            read_asset_manifest(manifest_path.c_str()));
        this->content_loaded_ = true;
    }

    void Application::set_resolution(ScreenResolution resolution)
    {
        this->options_.resolution = resolution;
        this->resolution_manager_->set_resolution(resolution);

**Why it matters:** The header opens with a worked example presented as *the* way the
class is used ("It is used in three steps", `application.h:59-66`) and the accessor block
warns "Every one of these is null until `initialize()` has run" — so the ordering is
known, documented and load-bearing, and enforced nowhere. `load_manifest` before
`initialize` is a null `resource_loader_->` call. `run()` before `initialize` calls
`transition_to`, whose `init()` reaches null services, and if the state survives that it
dies one line into `Application::update` on `*this->dt_` (`application.cpp:259`) — a null
float deref, not the `PIXBeginEvent` the raw report named. A second `initialize()` leaks
the first window and then throws "Could not register the window class", a message that
blames the class name for a duplicated call. For the class the header itself calls the
first thing a stranger writes, a null-pointer crash is the worst available diagnostic.

**Remedy:** Keep an `initialized_` flag and throw `std::runtime_error` naming the missing
or duplicated step from every entry point that requires one.

#### Null window_ on quit(), and unregister the window class on teardown

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:21-31,91-94,207-213`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** `quit()` destroys the window synchronously but is `const`, so it cannot null
`window_`; `~Application` never unregisters the window class or clears the window's
`GWLP_USERDATA`.

**Evidence:**

    void Application::quit() const
    {
        if (this->window_ != nullptr)
        {
            DestroyWindow(this->window_);
        }
    }

    Application::~Application()
    {
        if (this->audio_engine_)
        {
            this->audio_engine_->Suspend();
        }
        if (this->com_initialized_)
        {
            CoUninitialize();
        }
    }

**Why it matters:** `DestroyWindow` is synchronous for a window owned by the calling
thread, and `WM_DESTROY` (`application.cpp:583-585`) only posts the quit message — the
`HWND` is invalid the moment `quit()` returns. `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:49`
calls `app_->quit()` from inside `update()`; control then returns through
`StateContext::update` → `Application::update` → the `StepTimer::Tick` lambda → `tick()`
→ `render()`, which runs a full `clear()`/`draw()`/`Present()` against a swap chain whose
window no longer exists before `PeekMessage` picks up `WM_QUIT`. Because `window_` is
still non-null, `window()`, `set_resolution()` and `set_fullscreen()` all stay callable
on the dangling handle and fail silently — every one of them ignores its return value.
Separately, `RegisterClassExW` at `:91-94` is never paired with `UnregisterClassW`, and a
class registered by an `.exe` lives for the process, so constructing a second
`Application` with the same `window_class_name` — even strictly after the first is
destroyed — always throws "Could not register the window class." The header's note at
`application.h:32-33` explains the uniqueness requirement as being about opening two
windows simultaneously; the real cause is that the class is leaked for good.

**Remedy:** Make `quit()` non-`const` and null `window_` (or null it in the `WM_DESTROY`
case, which also covers the user clicking the close box), clear `GWLP_USERDATA` on
`WM_NCDESTROY`, and destroy any surviving window plus unregister the class in
`~Application`.

#### Publish DirectXTK and Win32 types out of the shell's public API, or don't publish them at all

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:15-19,115-134`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T10 (one language, teachable API) / ARCHITECTURE ("platform-specific code lives at the edge behind engine-owned interfaces")
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** The first header a stranger reads returns `DirectX::SpriteBatch*`,
`DirectX::CommonStates*`, `DirectX::GamePad*` and a raw `HWND` from its public accessors,
so every game that touches the shell is source-coupled to DirectXTK and Win32 — and one
of those accessors has no callers at all.

**Evidence:**

    #include <Audio.h>
    #include <CommonStates.h>
    #include <GamePad.h>
    #include <SpriteBatch.h>
    #include <Windows.h>
    ...
        DirectX::GamePad* gamepad() const;
        HWND window() const;

        // Recreated on device loss, so these change identity across one. The
        // vector's own address is stable; only the pointers inside it move.
        DirectX::CommonStates* common_states() const;
        std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches() const;

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE lets `app` *depend* on everything; it does not let `app`
*re-export* the backend. PHILOSOPHY puts the rendering backend, input devices and
windowing "at the edge behind engine-owned interfaces, so that a second platform is an
addition, not a rewrite" — but a second platform now breaks the signature of the class
every game constructs, not just the implementation behind it. T10's acceptance test is
the sharper one: the game-facing API must stay teachable to a beginner, and what this API
teaches is visible in the minimal sample, where drawing one string requires
`ID3D11CommandList*`, `FinishCommandList`, `ExecuteCommandList` and a manual `Release()`
(`samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:68-84`). `HWND window() const` is the cheapest
evidence that the leak is not load-bearing: grepping `game/`, `samples/` and `engine/`
for callers returns the declaration and the definition and nothing else.

**Remedy:** Delete `window()` — nothing uses it. Take the other three behind the renderer
and input seams the design already names, so the shell hands out engine types and the
DirectXTK includes move to `application.cpp`. That is the same seam the memory note
"OPEN: renderer seam" already tracks for `IGameObject`; this is its other end.

#### Stop const_casting the sprite-batch vector out of a const accessor

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:429-432`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** `sprite_batches()` is declared `const` and hands the caller a mutable pointer to
a private member vector by casting its own constness away.

**Evidence:**

    std::vector<SpriteBatch*>* Application::sprite_batches() const
    {
        return const_cast<std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*>(&this->sprite_batch_ptrs_);
    }

**Why it matters:** The cast is not needed to hand out mutable `SpriteBatch`es — a
`const std::vector<SpriteBatch*>&` already does that, because the pointees are not const.
What the cast actually buys the caller is the ability to `push_back`, `clear` or `assign`
the vector the shell itself rebuilds on device loss (`application.cpp:368-372`), from any
state or render worker. It is the only `const_cast` in `engine/` — I grepped the whole
tree — and the game has already copied the lesson: `GameData::dt()`
(`game/game_data.cpp:68`) does `const_cast<float*>(this->application_->dt())`, with a
comment explaining why the shell's `const` may be ignored. T5 asks the compiler to be the
reviewer; this line tells it to look away, and the only other `const_cast` in the repo
cites it as precedent.

**Remedy:** Return `const std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>&` (or a span) and delete the
cast; `GameData::dt()`'s cast goes with the `dt` change below.

---

#### Stop rendering while the window is minimized

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:187-205,264-279`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8 (performance over customisability)

**What:** The message loop calls `tick()` unconditionally, so a minimized game keeps
running the full update and render path and presenting to an occluded swap chain.

**Evidence:**

        MSG message = {};
        while (message.message != WM_QUIT)
        {
            if (PeekMessage(&message, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE))
            {
                TranslateMessage(&message);
                DispatchMessage(&message);
            }
            else
            {
                this->tick();
            }
        }

**Why it matters:** `WM_SIZE`/`SIZE_MINIMIZED` calls `on_suspending()`
(`application.cpp:499`), which suspends the gamepad and the audio engine — the shell
clearly intends to idle — but nothing stops the loop, so `render()` keeps recording
command lists into every deferred context and calling `Present`. `DeviceResources::Present`
uses `m_swapChain->Present(1, 0)` (`device_resources.cpp:493`), and the vsync throttle it
relies on is not guaranteed for an invisible window: DXGI returns
`DXGI_STATUS_OCCLUDED`, a success code `ThrowIfFailed` waves through, at exactly the
moment the frames are worthless. A minimized game can therefore spin a core and keep the
GPU busy on work nobody will see — the opposite of the throughput this engine leads with.

**Remedy:** Track the minimized flag on the `Application` (see the `window_proc` finding
below) and skip `render()`, or the whole `tick()`, while it is set. `DXGI_PRESENT_TEST`
is the cheap way to detect the occluded case if the flag is not trusted.

---

#### Make dt a value, not a heap float behind a pointer

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:131-134,159`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap) / PHILOSOPHY, Services and lifetimes

**What:** Frame time is a `std::unique_ptr<float>` exposed as a `const float*`, justified
by a rationale that commit `c6696af` deleted.

**Evidence:**

        // Seconds the last fixed step covered. A pointer because the objects that
        // read it are built once and outlive any particular frame; the value
        // behind it is rewritten every update.
        const float* dt() const;
    ...
        std::unique_ptr<float> dt_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY states the target plainly — "Frame time is a parameter —
`update(float dt)` — not shared state" — and T11 makes a lone heap-allocated `float` the
canonical anti-example. The header's justification described the eleven classes that held
a `const float*`, and `c6696af` ("Pass dt to update() instead of holding a pointer to
it") removed every one of them. I grepped: the only readers left are three call sites
that dereference it on the spot — `game/states/game_states.cpp:196`,
`game/states/results_menu.cpp:34`, `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:55`. So the
allocation, the indirection, the null-until-`initialize()` accessor and the stale
rationale all outlived the reason for them, and the sample — the file a stranger copies —
repeats the dead rationale verbatim at `hello_state.cpp:53-54`. `GameData::dt()` then
`const_cast`s the pointer back to mutable, which is what a pointer-shaped API invites.

**Remedy:** `float dt_ = 0.0f;` with a `float dt() const` accessor. That deletes the
allocation, the null case, `GameData`'s `const_cast`, and both stale comments.

---

#### window_proc's function-local statics are shared by every Application in the process

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:441-446`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY, Services and lifetimes (ownership is explicit and lexical)

**What:** The window procedure's three pieces of per-window state are function-local
statics in a `static` member function, so two `Application`s in one process share one
`in_sizemove`, one `in_suspend` and one `minimized`.

**Evidence:**

    LRESULT CALLBACK Application::window_proc(HWND window, UINT message,
        WPARAM w_param, LPARAM l_param)
    {
        static bool in_sizemove = false;
        static bool in_suspend = false;
        static bool minimized = false;

**Why it matters:** The header contemplates exactly this case — "The window class name has
to be unique per process, so a game that ever opens two windows needs two of these"
(`application.h:32-33`) — and this is the state that makes two windows misbehave.
Dragging window A sets `in_sizemove`, so window B's `WM_SIZE` stops resizing its swap
chain (`:513`) and its `WM_PAINT` starts calling `app->tick()` on the wrong window
(`:465`). Even sequentially, a second `Application` constructed after the first was
minimized starts with `minimized == true` and swallows its first restore. Graded low
rather than medium because nothing in the repo opens two windows, so the defect is latent
in a scenario no client currently reaches — but the `Application*` is already correctly
threaded through `GWLP_USERDATA`, so these three flags are ambient for no reason, and
moving them is the same edit that fixes the minimized-rendering finding above.

**Remedy:** Move the three flags to `Application` members and reach them through the `app`
pointer the procedure already recovers.

---

#### Inherit IDeviceNotify privately — it is a macro-keyword, I-prefixed type in the public API

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:71`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12 (the language over a dialect) / CONVENTIONS, Never (no `I` prefix)

**What:** The first line of the class a stranger reads publicly inherits `IDeviceNotify`,
which is both an `I`-prefixed name and declared with the Windows `interface` macro, and
public inheritance makes the device-lost teardown callable by anyone.

**Evidence:**

    class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext

`engine/render/device_resources.h:17-24`:

        interface IDeviceNotify
        {
            virtual void OnDeviceLost() = 0;
            virtual void OnDeviceRestored() = 0;

**Why it matters:** `interface` is `#define interface struct` from `combaseapi.h` — a
macro that reads like a keyword, which T12 names as precisely the thing this engine is
not — and `I` is on CONVENTIONS' Never list. The conventions passes renamed enums,
namespaces, members and accessors but stopped at the DirectXTK-derived headers, so the
one place the leftover is visible is the public signature of the class every game
constructs. Public inheritance also makes
`static_cast<IDeviceNotify*>(&app)->OnDeviceLost()` legal from game code even though
`Application` declares both overrides private — a caller can tear down every sprite batch
and the `CommonStates` at will. `Application` *has-a* device-loss listener; it is not one.

**Remedy:** Rename the type to `DeviceNotify` (a plain `struct`) and inherit it privately
— private inheritance still binds the virtual overrides.

---

#### set_fullscreen sets WS_EX_TOPMOST with SetWindowLongPtr, which does not change z-order

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:226-248`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** The fullscreen toggle writes `WS_EX_TOPMOST` into the extended style and then
calls `SetWindowPos` with `SWP_NOZORDER`, so the window never actually becomes topmost —
and every one of the five Win32 calls in the function has its return value discarded.

**Evidence:**

        if (fullscreen)
        {
            SetWindowLongPtr(this->window_, GWL_STYLE, WS_POPUP);
            SetWindowLongPtr(this->window_, GWL_EXSTYLE, WS_EX_TOPMOST);
            SetWindowPos(this->window_, HWND_TOP, 0, 0, 0, 0,
                SWP_NOMOVE | SWP_NOSIZE | SWP_NOZORDER | SWP_FRAMECHANGED);
            ShowWindow(this->window_, SW_SHOWMAXIMIZED);
        }

**Why it matters:** The `SetWindowLongPtr` contract is explicit that `WS_EX_TOPMOST` is
not honoured when set this way — the documented way to add or remove it is
`SetWindowPos(hwnd, HWND_TOPMOST, ...)` — and this call passes `HWND_TOP` *and*
`SWP_NOZORDER`, which asks for no z-order change at all. So a game that toggles
fullscreen from its options menu (`game/states/main_menu.cpp:428`) gets a maximized
borderless window that other windows can still cover, while the style bits claim
otherwise. The `CreateWindowExW` path at startup (`application.cpp:104-108`) passes
`WS_EX_TOPMOST` at creation, where it *is* honoured, so the same option behaves
differently depending on whether it came from the save file or the menu. Nothing reports
any of it: `SetWindowLongPtr` returning 0 and `SetWindowPos` returning FALSE are both
discarded, which is the same silence T6 rules out.

**Remedy:** Pass `HWND_TOPMOST`/`HWND_NOTOPMOST` to `SetWindowPos` and drop
`SWP_NOZORDER`; check the returns and throw naming the call, the way `create_window`
already does for `RegisterClassExW`.

#### Correct the accessor block's contract: device_resources() is non-null from construction

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:104-115`, `engine/app/application.cpp:12-19`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY, The public face ("a stranger starts from the headers")
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** The header's contract for the service accessors says all of them are null before
`initialize()`; the first one listed is created in the constructor.

**Evidence:** `application.h:104-115`:

        // The services. Every one of these is null until initialize() has run -
        ...
        DeviceResources* device_resources() const;

`application.cpp:12-19`:

        Application::Application(ApplicationOptions options) :
            options_(std::move(options))
        {
            // Renders only 2D, so no depth buffer.
            this->device_resources_ = std::make_unique<DeviceResources>(
                DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM, DXGI_FORMAT_UNKNOWN);
            this->device_resources_->RegisterDeviceNotify(this);
        }

**Why it matters:** This is the block PHILOSOPHY's "The public face" is about — the
documentation a stranger reads instead of the implementation — and its universal claim is
false for the accessor it lists first. The error is in the safe direction today, but it
is the kind of inaccuracy that decides a design question later: the reason
`device_resources_` is special is that it must exist before `RegisterDeviceNotify`, and
that reason is worth one sentence rather than an incorrect blanket statement. The same
block is also where the "created once and never reseated" promise sits that
`common_states()` contradicts fifteen lines further down (see the device-lost finding).

**Remedy:** Say what is true: the services are null until `initialize()` has run, except
`device_resources()`, which is constructed with the `Application` because it must be
registered before anything can be lost — and reconcile the reseating promise with the
`common_states()` note below it.

Corrections applied to surviving findings, recorded so the diff against the raw report is
visible:

- **State-tree destruction order** — citation `application.h:71,144-166` corrected to

# Game modules

<a id="g-game-shell"></a>

## game-shell — Game entry point, shared data, save

*Group `game-shell` · 27 findings (1 high, 16 medium, 10 low) · source `review2/verified/game-shell.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every line the reviewer cited, in all nine assigned files plus the seven
engine and game files they reached into, and I checked the mechanical claims by
measurement rather than by reading: I counted the game's translation units and the
transitive include closure of `directory_consts.h`, `save.h`, `game_data.h` and
`rapidjson/document.h` with a script, counted references to every DirectXTK symbol
`pch.h` supplies, grepped every call site of `dt()`, `game_data()` and `save_data()`,
read the generated `build.ninja` and `rules.ninja` for the flags the game is actually
compiled with, and rebuilt `ArtAttackGame` from a cleared PCH to see the build the
report is describing.

**Everything the reviewer filed is real; I rejected no finding outright.** What I did
reject is a scattering of *sub-claims and consequences* attached to true observations,
and every one of them was a number or a mechanism: eleven forwarding accessors, not
twelve; fourteen translation units reach `directory_consts.h`, not "~20"; sixteen of
the twenty PCH headers are unreferenced, not fifteen, and `SimpleMath.h` — which the
reviewer's remedy proposes keeping — is one of the unused ones; `screen_resolution.h`
does expose a `max` enumerator, so "no way to size it" is wrong even though the
duplication it explains is real; `save_data.txt` is seeded once beside the exe, not
"shipped and installed", because the project has no `install()` rule at all; the window
title is `main.cpp:34`, not `:35`. I regraded three findings down — the DPI item from
high to medium, and `ctime_s` and the duplicate-level-name item from medium to low —
because each carried a consequence larger than the code supports; and I regraded
nothing up.

The most substantive correction is to the DPI finding. Its headline — the resolution
you save is not the resolution you get — is **true, and true for a second reason the
reviewer missed and did not need DPI scaling to find**: `create_window` passes the
saved resolution to `CreateWindowExW` as the *outer* window rectangle with no
`AdjustWindowRect` anywhere in the repository, so in windowed mode the client area is
always smaller than the setting by the border and caption, while `ViewportManager`
keeps building viewports from the nominal number. I also chased and confirmed by
experiment two things nobody could have found by reading: CMake's generated PCH wrapper
carries `#pragma system_header` and the game is compiled with `-external:W0`, so
`game/pch.h` and everything it includes is compiled at warning level 0 — which is the
only reason its duplicate `#define NOMINMAX` is not a hard `/WX` error, and which I
verified by reproducing both the error and its suppression with `cl`. And `game/pch.h`
pins `_WIN32_WINNT` to Windows 7 while an engine TU compiles at `0x0A00` (measured with
`#pragma message`), so one binary is built against two Windows API surfaces — and that
floor is what would block the DPI remedy. Four findings added; none rejected.

### Themes

- The game shell's only diagnostic channel is `std::cout`/`stderr` in a
  `/SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS` process, so T6 is structurally impossible on the save path — and
  the one channel it has reports success it never verified.
- Every failure signal `save.cpp` produces is dropped: `write_save_file`'s `bool`, the
  `error_code` from `create_directories`, the parse exception's `what()`, and the return
  of `fclose`. A permanently unwritable save directory and a working one are
  indistinguishable from inside and outside the process.
- `GameData` survived the engine/game split unchanged in shape: default-constructible
  into an invalid state, publicly reseatable for life, and re-exporting an API its own
  callers already reach directly in the same function.
- The number the whole group exists to persist does not survive the trip to the screen —
  twice, independently: the window is sized as an outer rect, and the process is
  DPI-unaware.
- `game/pch.h` is a dialect the sample does not speak *and* a warning-free zone the build
  does not inspect: force-included, hand-included, sixteen-twentieths unused, pinned to a
  Windows version nothing else in the build shares.
- The engine exposes `ScreenResolution` publicly but keeps every conversion off it
  private, so the first client that had to persist one copied the table — duplication
  manufactured by an API gap.
- Constants that should be parameters (`MANIFEST_PATH`, `SAVE_FILE_PATH`, `IDI_ICON`,
  `max_threads = 16`) are compiled in at three layers, each breaking a different rule.
- The game claims the global namespace for `GameData`, `Save`, `SaveData`, `Stage` and
  `StageList` while opening three `using namespace` directives over it — the opposite of
  what the reference client should teach.

---

#### Report save failures somewhere a GUI-subsystem process can be heard

- **File:** `game/save.cpp:107-133`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** `save_to_file()`'s only report of success or failure is `std::cout`, in an
executable linked `/SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS`, and both callers discard the result, so a save
that cannot be written fails completely silently.

**Evidence:**

    void Save::save_to_file() const
    {
        auto start = std::chrono::system_clock::now();
        auto legacy_start = std::chrono::system_clock::to_time_t(start);
        char buffer[30];
        std::cout << ctime_s(buffer, sizeof(buffer), &legacy_start) << " Saving...\n";
        if (write_save_file(this->save_data_))
        {
    		std::cout << "Save was successful.\n";
    	}
        else
        {
    		std::cout << "Save was unsuccessful.\n";
    	}
    }

    void Save::set_resolution_and_save(ScreenResolution resolution)
    {
        this->save_data_.resolution = resolution;
        this->save_to_file();
    }

Verified: `game/CMakeLists.txt:11` is `add_executable(ArtAttackGame WIN32 ...)`, and the
generated link line carries `LINK_FLAGS = /machine:x64 /debug /INCREMENTAL
/subsystem:windows`. `write_save_file` returns `bool` (`save.cpp:71`); `save_to_file`
returns `void`; both setters return `void`. Two lines earlier the other failure signal is
also dropped (`save.cpp:78-79`):

    std::error_code ec;
    std::filesystem::create_directories(save_path.parent_path(), ec);

`ec` is never read. There is no `[[nodiscard]]` anywhere in the repository — zero hits
across `engine/` and `game/` — so nothing at the type level objects either.

**Why it matters:** Run the game anywhere the process cannot write and the path is:
`create_directories` fails, `ec` is dropped; `fopen_s` fails; `write_save_file` returns
`false`; `save_to_file` writes to a stream with no handle behind it; the setter ignores
it; and `MainMenuSettings` (`main_menu.cpp:334`) has already applied the resolution on
screen, so the user watches it work. Every launch thereafter reverts to 1280x720
windowed and nothing on the machine ever says why. This is the exact failure mode T6
exists to forbid, on the game's only persistence path.

**Remedy:** Give `Save` a failure channel that exists in this process: throw from
`write_save_file` naming the path and `errno`, or return `std::error_code` up to the
settings menu so it can tell the user. Mark the returning functions `[[nodiscard]]` so
the next caller cannot drop it. `std::cout` is not a channel this executable has.

---

#### The saved resolution is not the resolution the game gets

- **File:** `game/settings.manifest:1-16`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2; T6

**What:** The manifest declares OS compatibility but never DPI awareness, and nothing
calls `SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext`, so the process is DPI-unaware and on a scaled
display Windows virtualises its coordinates.

**Evidence:**

    <assembly xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v1" manifestVersion="1.0" xmlns:asmv3="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3" >
       <compatibility xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:compatibility.v1">
           <application>
               <!-- Windows Vista -->
               <supportedOS Id="{e2011457-1546-43c5-a5fe-008deee3d3f0}"/>
               ...
           </application>
       </compatibility>
    </assembly>

The `asmv3` namespace is declared on line 1 and never used — the file was cut down from a
template that had an `<asmv3:application>` block. A case-insensitive grep for `dpi` across
`engine/`, `game/`, `samples/`, `cmake/` and every `.manifest` returns nothing outside
vendored DirectXTK. The manifest *is* embedded: the generated link statement carries
`MANIFESTS = C:\VSProjects\ArtAttack\game\settings.manifest`. `samples/minimal` has no
manifest of any kind.

**Why it matters:** Two things follow, and only the first needs a scaled display.
On a 150%-scaled monitor the window is created in virtualised (logical) pixels and the
composited result is bitmap-stretched, so the game is blurry; and `s_3840_2160` becomes
unreachable, because a 150%-scaled 4K panel reports a 2560x1440 virtual desktop that a
3840x2160 window will not fit. Windows defaults to scaling on laptops and 4K monitors, so
this is the common case, not the edge one. The remedy is also gated by something else in
this group: `game/pch.h:9-10` pins `_WIN32_WINNT` to `0x0601`, which hides
`SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext` from every game translation unit (see the API-floor
finding below).

Note for whoever fixes this: the reviewer's headline was right for a *second* reason that
has nothing to do with DPI, filed separately below — `create_window` passes the saved
resolution as the window's outer rectangle, so even at 100% scaling the client area is
smaller than the setting.

**Remedy:** Add an `<asmv3:application><asmv3:windowsSettings>` block declaring
`dpiAwareness = PerMonitorV2` with the legacy `dpiAware` fallback, raise or delete the
`_WIN32_WINNT` floor so the modern API is visible, handle `WM_DPICHANGED` in the engine,
and give `samples/minimal` the same manifest so the template is not worse than the
reference game.

---

#### `write_save_file` reports success it never verified

- **File:** `game/save.cpp:71-105`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** Once `fopen_s` succeeds, `write_save_file` returns `true` unconditionally. It
checks neither the stream state after `d.Accept(writer)` nor the return of `fclose`, so a
write that fails after the file is open is reported as a successful save.

**Evidence:**

    FILE* fp = nullptr;
    if (fopen_s(&fp, SAVE_FILE_PATH.c_str(), "wb") != 0 || fp == nullptr)
    {
        return false;
    }
    // Allocate buffer on the heap
    auto write_buffer = std::make_unique<char[]>(65536);
    FileWriteStream os(fp, write_buffer.get(), 65536);
    ...
    Writer<FileWriteStream> writer(os);
    d.Accept(writer);

    fclose(fp);
    return true;

`rapidjson::FileWriteStream::Flush()` calls `fwrite` and discards its result; the
document is 53 bytes so it never leaves the 64 KB buffer until `fclose` flushes it, and
`fclose`'s return — the one value that reports whether those bytes reached the disk — is
ignored. The `bool` this function returns is therefore only ever "did the open succeed".

**Why it matters:** A full disk, a quota, a network path that drops, or an antivirus
lock after open all produce the same outcome: `save_to_file` announces "Save was
successful", the file on disk is truncated or empty, and the *next* launch's
`load_from_json` throws and is swallowed into defaults (the finding below). The one
diagnostic the group has is not merely inaudible — it is wrong. It also means the fix
for the previous finding is not enough on its own: a propagated `false` still would not
fire here.

**Remedy:** Check `fclose(fp) == 0` and fold it into the result; return `false` if the
`Accept` call reports failure. Better, drive the write through the engine's RAII file
wrapper (see the last finding) so the close is both checked and exception-safe.

---

#### The window is sized as an outer rectangle, so the client area is never the chosen resolution

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:96-117`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2

**What:** The resolution the save file persists is handed to `CreateWindowExW` as the
window's *outer* dimensions. `AdjustWindowRect` appears nowhere in the repository, so in
windowed mode the client area — and therefore the swap chain — is always smaller than the
setting by the border and caption, while `ViewportManager` keeps laying out from the
nominal number.

**Evidence:**

    const mattmath::Vector2I size =
        this->resolution_manager_->resolution_ivec();
    ...
        this->window_ = CreateWindowExW(0,
            this->options_.window_class_name.c_str(),
            this->options_.window_title.c_str(), WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW,
            CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, size.x, size.y,
            nullptr, nullptr, instance, this);

`nWidth`/`nHeight` on `CreateWindowExW` are the whole window including non-client area.
`grep -rn "AdjustWindowRect" engine/ game/` returns nothing. `WM_SIZE` then reports the
real client size and resizes the swap chain (`application.cpp:515`,
`on_window_size_changed` at `:359`), but `ViewportManager` sizes every viewport from
`resolution_manager_->resolution_vec()` (`viewport_manager.cpp:17`, `:47`, `:56`, `:115`),
which still says 1920x1080. `Application::set_resolution` (`:215-224`) repeats the same
mistake with `SetWindowPos`.

**Why it matters:** At default DPI a 1920x1080 setting produces roughly a 1904x1041
client area, so the viewport is larger than the render target and the bottom ~39 and
right ~16 pixels of every frame are clipped — including whatever menu content the game
placed near those edges. It is on for every windowed launch on every machine, with no
scaled display required, and it is the concrete form of "the setting this whole group
persists is not what the game renders at".

**Remedy:** Call `AdjustWindowRectEx` (or `AdjustWindowRectExForDpi` once the process is
DPI-aware) on the desired client rect before `CreateWindowExW` and before `SetWindowPos`,
so the client area is the resolution. *Dedupe note:* this lives in `engine/app/`; the
`app` group may raise it too.

---

#### Rewrite or report a corrupt save instead of silently reverting to defaults forever

- **File:** `game/save.cpp:50-69`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** A save file that exists but does not parse is swallowed by an unbound catch,
replaced in memory by defaults, and left on disk unchanged, so the corruption survives
every launch.

**Evidence:**

    void Save::load_save_file()
    {
        if (!check_if_save_file_exists())
        {
            // First run, or the save directory was never created. Write the
            // defaults out so the file exists from here on.
            this->save_to_file();
        }

        try
        {
            this->save_data_ = this->load_from_json(SAVE_FILE_PATH.c_str());
        }
        catch (const std::exception&)
        {
            // A missing, unreadable or corrupt save is not fatal - the defaults are
            // perfectly playable, and the next settings change overwrites the file.
            this->save_data_ = SaveData();
        }
    }

`read_json_file` (`engine/assets/json_loader.cpp:63-72`) throws a `runtime_error`
carrying the path, the rapidjson error string and the byte offset — all of it discarded
here by a catch with no binding.

**Why it matters:** T6 carves out expected absence, but a file that exists and is
malformed is a broken contract, not the world being the world. The comment's escape
hatch — "the next settings change overwrites the file" — only fires if the user goes
back into the options menu, which they have no reason to do if they believe they already
set their resolution. Note the asymmetry the code already has: a *missing* file is
rewritten, a *corrupt* one is not. Meanwhile the most informative error message in the
codebase is constructed and thrown away.

**Remedy:** Bind the exception, keep `e.what()`, surface it through whatever channel the
first finding establishes, and rewrite the file with the defaults immediately so the
corruption does not survive the launch — the same treatment the missing-file case
already gets.

#### Stop labelling mid-match exceptions "startup failure"

- **File:** `game/main.cpp:24-101`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6

**What:** The single `try` block spans `app.run()`, and `Application::run` has no handler
of its own, so an exception thrown an hour into a match is presented to the user as a
startup failure.

**Evidence:**

    		return app.run(std::make_unique<GameMenu>(&data));
    	}
    	catch (const std::exception& e)
    	{
    		// T6: a broken contract stops the game dead with the reason on screen,
    		// never a silent abort.
    		fprintf(stderr, "startup failure: %s\n", e.what());
    		MessageBoxA(nullptr, e.what(), "ArtAttack - startup failure",
    			MB_OK | MB_ICONERROR);
    		return 1;
    	}

`Application::run` (`engine/app/application.cpp:187-205`) is a bare `PeekMessage`/`tick()`
loop with no `try`, so everything the simulation throws lands here.

**Why it matters:** `docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md` records live throw paths on the tick
path that were deliberately left loud — `Player` leaving the level bounds, and the
`default:` cases in `Weapon`, `Projectile` and `Player`. Each of those now produces a
dialog titled "ArtAttack - startup failure" reading "Collision object out of bounds",
which points a stranger at the wrong half of the program. Two smaller things ride along:
only `std::exception` is caught, so anything else reaches `std::terminate` with no
dialog; and the `fprintf(stderr, ...)` beside the `MessageBoxA` is the same dead channel
`save.cpp` relies on — harmless only because the dialog follows it.

**Remedy:** Split the block — one `try` around construction, `initialize` and
`load_manifest` reporting "startup failure", another around `run()` reporting "the game
stopped" — and add a `catch (...)`.

#### Give `GameData` one constructor instead of a default constructor plus four setters

- **File:** `game/game_data.h:24-30`, `game/game_data.cpp:14-32`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T5; PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes

**What:** `GameData` is default-constructible with all four members null and stays
publicly reseatable for its whole life, while every forwarding accessor dereferences
`application_` unchecked — so the invariant its header states in a comment is one the
type never enforces.

**Evidence:**

    GameData() = default;
    explicit GameData(const GameData* game_data);

    void set_application(artattack::Application* application);
    void set_save(Save* save);
    void set_level_infos(artattack::Registry<LevelLoadedInfo>* level_infos);
    void set_stages(const StageList* stages);

    ...
    artattack::Application* application_ = nullptr;
    Save* save_ = nullptr;

and every forwarder is unguarded (`game_data.cpp:57-60`):

    ResolutionManager* GameData::resolution_manager() const
    {
    	return this->application_->resolution_manager();
    }

`main.cpp` uses exactly the two-phase shape this enables — `GameData data;` at `:50`,
`data.set_application(&app);` at `:86`.

**Why it matters:** Between `main.cpp:50` and `main.cpp:89` — spanning `app.initialize`,
`register_kind` and `load_manifest`, the lines new code is most likely to be added to —
`data` is a live object on which any of eleven forwarding accessors is a null
dereference. The header's own comment ("All four are borrowed and all four outlive it")
is a promise the type does not keep, and PHILOSOPHY is explicit that services are
"created once, at initialisation, and never reseated" while this one can be reseated by
anybody holding it. Not currently reachable — nothing calls an accessor in that window —
which is precisely why it should be a constructor, where the compiler holds it (T5).

**Remedy:** Replace the default constructor and the four setters with
`GameData(Application&, Save&, Registry<LevelLoadedInfo>&, const StageList&)`, and build
it after `load_manifest` in `main.cpp`.

#### Delete `GameData`'s forwarding half; it is a hand-maintained copy of an API callers already bypass

- **File:** `game/game_data.h:40-56`, `game/game_data.cpp:54-114`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4

**What:** Eleven of `GameData`'s sixteen accessors do nothing but re-export
`Application`'s public API under the same names, across a target boundary, while game
code reaches `Application` directly as well.

**Evidence:**

    // Everything below forwards. There is deliberately no cached copy of any of
    // them: a copy would be a second place for a service pointer to be wrong.

    ResolutionManager* GameData::resolution_manager() const
    {
    	return this->application_->resolution_manager();
    }
    ...
    const Partitioner* GameData::partitioner() const
    {
    	return this->application_->partitioner();
    }

The eleven are `resolution_manager`, `dt`, `render_resources`, `audio_resources`,
`gamepad`, `device_resources`, `viewport_manager`, `thread_pool`, `partitioner`,
`common_states`, `sprite_batches`. Both routes are used inside one function —
`game/states/main_menu.cpp:334-342`:

    				this->save()->set_resolution_and_save(this->resolution_selection_);
    				...
    				this->data()->application()->set_resolution(
    					this->resolution_selection_);

**Why it matters:** This is the post-split residue of the old service-locator shape, and
the split changed its cost: `GameData` now lives in a different target from the services
it re-exports, so every service `Application` gains is two edits in two projects, and a
signature change is a compile break in the game long after the engine change looked
done. The comment's justification argues against *caching*, not for *forwarding* —
holding an `Application*` and spelling `application()->thread_pool()` has the same
property with none of the duplication, and `application()` is already public and already
used.

**Remedy:** Keep `application()`, `save()`, `level_infos()` and `stages()`; delete the
eleven forwarders (and `game_data()`, below) and let callers spell
`application()->thread_pool()`.

#### Delete `GameData::dt()`'s `const_cast` — the cost its comment cites no longer exists

- **File:** `game/game_data.cpp:62-69`, `game/game_data.h:44`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5

**What:** `GameData::dt()` casts away the `const` the engine deliberately carries on the
frame timestep, and the comment defending it cites "several dozen call sites" when there
are two.

**Evidence:**

    float* GameData::dt() const
    {
    	// The shell hands out a const float* because nothing downstream should be
    	// writing the frame's own timestep. The game's older signatures still take
    	// a float*, so the cast lives here, in one place, rather than at each of
    	// the several dozen call sites - and goes when those signatures do.
    	return const_cast<float*>(this->application_->dt());
    }

`grep -rn "dt()" game/` returns five hits: the declaration, the definition, the cast, and
these two call sites —

    game/states/game_states.cpp:196:                *this->game_data_->dt());
    game/states/results_menu.cpp:34:	const float dt = *this->data()->dt();

Both dereference immediately to a value. `grep -rn "float\*" game/` finds only this
declaration, this comment, and a note at `level.h:118` recording that the pointer member
was already removed.

**Why it matters:** `Application::dt()` returns `const float*` (`application.h:134`)
precisely so game code cannot write the timestep, and this line hands every state a
writable pointer to it. Not UB — the underlying `float` is non-const — but the guarantee
the engine spent a signature on is void for its own first client. Commit `c6696af`
("Pass dt to update() instead of holding a pointer to it") already did the migration the
comment is waiting for; the comment now describes a codebase that does not exist.

#### `pch.h` is force-included *and* hand-included, so no game header is proven to compile alone

- **File:** `game/pch.h:1-79`, `game/CMakeLists.txt:72`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12; CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** CMake force-includes `pch.h` into every game translation unit, and all 46 game
`.cpp` files also open with `#include "game/pch.h"` as their first line, so the
own-header-first rule proves nothing.

**Evidence:**

`game/CMakeLists.txt:72`

    target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)

`game/game_data.cpp:1-2`

    #include "game/pch.h"
    #include "game/game_data.h"

Measured: `find game -name '*.cpp'` returns 46; `grep -rl '#include "game/pch.h"' game/`
returns 46; and a check of the first line of each confirms all 46 open with it. No game
*header* includes it. The generated flags carry
`/FI.../cmake_pch.hxx` on every game TU, so the include is doubly redundant. `pch.h`
supplies `Windows.h`, `d3d11_1.h`, `<memory>`, `<algorithm>`, `<stdexcept>`, all of
DirectXTK and one engine header (`engine/core/throw_if_failed.h`).
`samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt` declares no precompiled header and the sample has no
`pch.h`.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS is explicit — "Include order: own header first — proving
every header compiles on its own." Nothing proves it here: a game header may reference
`HWND`, `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr` or `DirectX::SpriteBatch` with no include and still
build. The concrete cost is that the paint-shooter and `samples/minimal` — the directory
ARCHITECTURE says a new project is copied from — compile under two different sets of
ambient includes, so a header lifted from one into the other may not compile. That is
the "reading the source is not sufficient to know what the source does" property T12 was
written to rule out.

**Remedy:** Keep the precompiled header as a build accelerator only: delete the
`#include "game/pch.h"` line from all 46 `.cpp` files, put each file's own header first,
and add the includes that turn out to be missing. Expect that list to be long — see the
warning-level finding below for why nothing has been complaining.

#### Sixteen of the twenty headers in the game's precompiled header are unreferenced

- **File:** `game/pch.h:59-79`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain; Non-goals (3D)

**What:** The precompiled header pulls nineteen DirectXTK headers plus one engine header
into all 46 translation units. Sixteen of the twenty have no referenced symbol anywhere
in `game/`, and four of those are DirectXTK's 3D facilities.

**Evidence:**

    #include "BufferHelpers.h"
    #include "CommonStates.h"
    #include "DDSTextureLoader.h"
    #include "DirectXHelpers.h"
    #include "Effects.h"
    #include "GamePad.h"
    #include "GeometricPrimitive.h"
    #include "GraphicsMemory.h"
    #include "Keyboard.h"
    #include "Model.h"
    #include "Mouse.h"
    #include "PostProcess.h"
    #include "PrimitiveBatch.h"
    #include "ScreenGrab.h"
    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "SpriteBatch.h"
    #include "SpriteFont.h"
    #include "VertexTypes.h"
    #include "WICTextureLoader.h"

    #include "engine/core/throw_if_failed.h"

Counting references across `game/` with `pch.h` excluded, exactly four headers earn their
place: `SpriteBatch` (59 hits), `GamePad` (10), `SpriteFont` (3), `CommonStates` (2). The
other fifteen DirectXTK headers score zero, and so does `ThrowIfFailed`. Two traps I
checked: the 50 hits for "Effects" are all `SpriteEffects`, which comes from
`SpriteBatch.h`, not `Effects.h`; and the only DirectXMath-flavoured types in `game/` are
two `XMFLOAT2` uses in `interface_gameplay.cpp`, which come from `<DirectXMath.h>` at

**Why it matters:** `Model.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h` and `Effects.h`
are DirectXTK's 3D model loader, 3D primitive renderer, 3D batch renderer and 3D effect
library, in a project whose Non-goals name 3D as "a design constant, not a parameter".
All of them, plus `PostProcess.h`, `ScreenGrab.h`, `Keyboard.h`, `Mouse.h` and
`GraphicsMemory.h`, are parsed into the PCH that all 46 TUs consume. That is a permanent
tax on the build time PHILOSOPHY names as an engine responsibility, paid for facilities
the engine has declared it will never have.

**Remedy:** Reduce `pch.h` to `SpriteBatch.h`, `SpriteFont.h`, `CommonStates.h` and
`GamePad.h`, drop `throw_if_failed.h`, and rebuild — the deletions and the hand-include
cleanup above are one job, because both surface the same missing real includes.

#### Game translation units compile against a Windows 7 API floor nothing else in the build shares

- **File:** `game/pch.h:8-12`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** T5; T4

**What:** `game/pch.h` pins `_WIN32_WINNT` to `0x0601` before including `<sdkddkver.h>`.
Nothing else in the build sets it, so the engine, the sample and the tests compile
against the SDK's default — one binary, two Windows API surfaces.

**Evidence:**

    #include <winsdkver.h>
    #ifndef _WIN32_WINNT
    #define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0601
    #endif
    #include <sdkddkver.h>

`grep -rn "_WIN32_WINNT\|WINVER" engine/ game/ samples/ cmake/` finds this definition and
one consumer (`engine/render/device_resources.cpp:532`, `#if ... _WIN32_WINNT >= 0x0603`)
and nothing else; the game's compile command line (`build.ninja`, `DEFINES`) does not
predefine it. I measured both sides with `#pragma message`: a TU compiled the way the
engine is compiled reports `WIN32_WINNT=0x0A00`; the game's `pch.h` forces `0x0601`.

**Why it matters:** Three consequences, ascending. First, the debug-layer block at
`device_resources.cpp:532` is compiled in the engine TU and would not be in a game TU —
the same source, two meanings, which is exactly what T5's "the build is the cheapest
reviewer" is supposed to prevent. Second, every game TU is blind to anything newer than
Windows 7, `SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext` included, which is why the DPI remedy above
cannot simply be written. Third, `settings.manifest` claims support down to Vista, the
game compiles at Windows 7, and the engine at Windows 10 — three different answers to
"what Windows does this support", none of them written down. The whole block is leftover
DirectX Visual Studio template boilerplate that the CMake conversion carried across.

**Remedy:** Delete the `_WIN32_WINNT` block from `pch.h`, or move a single deliberate
floor into `artattack_settings` as a `target_compile_definition` so every target shares
it, and make `settings.manifest`'s `supportedOS` list agree with it.

#### `game_data.h` drags rapidjson and the level-definition type into most of the game

- **File:** `game/game_data.h:3-7`, `game/save.h:3-8`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain; CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** The service bag's header includes four heavyweight headers by value when all
four of its members are pointers, and `save.h` adds three includes it does not use — in
an order the conventions forbid.

**Evidence:**

`game/game_data.h:3-7`

    #include "engine/app/application.h"
    #include "engine/core/registry.h"
    #include "game/objects/level_loaded_info.h"
    #include "game/objects/stage.h"
    #include "game/save.h"

Every member is a pointer:

    artattack::Application* application_ = nullptr;
    Save* save_ = nullptr;
    artattack::Registry<LevelLoadedInfo>* level_infos_ = nullptr;
    const StageList* stages_ = nullptr;

`game/save.h:3-8`

    #include <iostream>
    #include <chrono>
    #include "game/directory_consts.h"
    #include <rapidjson/document.h>
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"
    #include "engine/render/screen_resolution.h"

`rapidjson::Document`, `std::cout`, `<chrono>` and `SAVE_FILE_PATH` appear only in
`save.cpp`. Measured over the transitive include closure of all 46 game TUs: **18 reach
`rapidjson/document.h`**, of which eleven are menu, menu-page and menu-data files that
never parse anything; 16 reach `level_loaded_info.h`; 14 reach `save.h` and
`directory_consts.h`; 13 reach `game_data.h`. `application.h` itself does *not* pull
rapidjson — the parser arrives entirely through `level_loaded_info.h` and `save.h`.
`<iostream>` in `save.h` also plants a `std::ios_base::Init` static in each of those 14
TUs. Separately, `save.h`'s include order is standard library, then game, then external,
then engine — the reverse of CONVENTIONS' "own header first, then engine, then external,
then standard library".

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE's rule for the engine is that "`rapidjson` reaches
`assets` and stops there — drawing a sprite does not compile a JSON parser." The game has
no such discipline: a JSON parser compiles into 18 of 46 TUs, most of which are menus.
That is the build-time regression PHILOSOPHY calls a defect, and it is avoidable — every
member here is a pointer.

**Remedy:** Forward-declare `LevelLoadedInfo` in `game_data.h` (the `Registry`
forward-declaration needs care because of its default template argument — declaring it in
one place, ideally `registry.h` itself, is cleaner than repeating it); drop `<iostream>`,
`<chrono>`, `<rapidjson/document.h>` and `directory_consts.h` from `save.h`; reorder the
survivors.

#### `directory_consts.h` breaks three naming rules and instantiates two `std::string` globals per TU

- **File:** `game/directory_consts.h:8-12`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never; CONVENTIONS/Namespaces; T7

**What:** Two SCREAMING_SNAKE `const static std::string`s sit at namespace scope in a
header, inside a `_consts` namespace whose name is neither one lowercase word nor the
game's own.

**Evidence:**

    namespace directory_consts
    {
    	const static std::string MANIFEST_PATH = "./manifest.json";
    	const static std::string SAVE_FILE_PATH = "./save/save_data.json";
    }

**Why it matters:** Three rules, each stated explicitly in CONVENTIONS: SCREAMING_SNAKE is
reserved for macros so that "a screaming name always signals preprocessor danger and
nothing else ever does"; namespaces are "one lowercase word"; and "constants that stay in
code live next to the one thing they configure, not in a `consts` namespace collecting
strays" — of which `grep -rn "^namespace" game/` finds sixteen, every one a `*_consts`
namespace and not one a namespace for the game itself. Mechanically, `const` at namespace
scope gives internal linkage (the `static` is redundant), so each of the fourteen
translation units that reach this header through `save.h` ← `game_data.h` gets its own
`std::string` with a dynamic initialiser and an `atexit` destructor, for two string
literals. Against T7 the file defends itself honestly — these genuinely are the two paths
known before anything is read — but `SAVE_FILE_PATH` being a hardcoded relative write
path is what makes the read-only-install failure above unreportable rather than
configurable.

**Remedy:** `inline constexpr std::string_view manifest_path` / `save_file_path` in the
game's own namespace, next to `main()`, which is the only place either is chosen; better
still, pass them as parameters so a test can point them somewhere writable.

#### Give the game its own namespace

- **File:** `game/game_data.h:21`, `game/save.h:10-16`, `game/main.cpp:10-12`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Namespaces

**What:** Every type this group defines — `GameData`, `Save`, `SaveData`, and the
`Stage`/`StageList` it hands around — is declared in the global namespace, under
file-scope `using namespace` directives.

**Evidence:**

`game/main.cpp:10-12`

    using namespace DirectX;
    using namespace directory_consts;
    using namespace artattack;

`game/save.h:10-16`

    struct SaveData
    {
    	artattack::ScreenResolution resolution = artattack::ScreenResolution::s_1280_720;
    	bool fullscreen = false;
    };

    class Save

`save.cpp:10-13` opens four more (`rapidjson`, `directory_consts`, `mattmath`,
`artattack`), which is past CONVENTIONS' "used sparingly". `grep -rn "^namespace" game/`
returns sixteen matches, every one a `*_consts` namespace; not one is the game's.

**Why it matters:** The engine took its namespace in commit `2fa12fe` and the game did

#### `Save` re-implements the engine's private resolution table

- **File:** `game/save.cpp:134-174`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T4; T1

**What:** `Save::convert_resolution_to_ivec` is a verbatim duplicate of
`ResolutionManager::convert_resolution_to_ivec`, and `convert_ivec_to_resolution`
duplicates the same table in reverse, because the engine keeps both conversions private.

**Evidence:**

`game/save.cpp:158-174`

    Vector2I Save::convert_resolution_to_ivec(
        ScreenResolution resolution) const
    {
        switch (resolution)
        {
        case ScreenResolution::s_1280_720:
            return {1280, 720};
        ...
        default:
            return {-1, -1};
        }
    }

`engine/render/resolution_manager.cpp:48-64` is the same function, character for
character apart from the class name; `save.cpp:134-157` and
`resolution_manager.cpp:153-176` are the same reverse map. `resolution_manager.h:28-37`
declares five conversions, all `private`. `screen_resolution.h` is thirteen lines holding
the enum — it *does* carry a `max = s_3840_2160` enumerator, so the reviewer's "no way to
size it" is wrong; what it has no public route to is the one meaningful operation, the
pixel pair.

**Why it matters:** Adding a fifth resolution to the engine's enum requires an
unprompted edit inside the game's save code, in a different build target, and the failure
is silent: `Save`'s reverse map falls through to `s_1280_720` for any pair it does not
recognise (`save.cpp:153-156`), so a save written by a newer build reads back as 720p on
an older one, and a round trip through `{-1,-1}` lands there too. This is duplication
manufactured by an API gap rather than by carelessness — the enum is public, the only
thing you can usefully do with it is not. Both `Save` conversions are also non-`static`
`const` members that touch no state.

**Remedy:** Add `mattmath::Vector2I size_of(ScreenResolution)` and its inverse to
`engine/render/screen_resolution.h` as free functions, delete both members from `Save`,
and have `ResolutionManager` call them too so there is one table.
