#### Stop caching the sampler state — device loss frees it in two places, not one

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:149`, `game/objects/level_builder.h:39`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes

**What:** Both `Level` and `LevelBuilder` cache a raw `ID3D11SamplerState*` taken from
`CommonStates`, which `Application::OnDeviceLost` destroys, so after a device-lost/restored cycle
every `SpriteBatch::Begin` in the level passes a freed COM object to D3D — and because
`LevelBuilder` outlives every level it builds, restarting the match re-injects the same dangling
pointer into each rebuilt `Level`.

**Evidence:**

    game/game_data.h:53-56
        // Recreated on device loss, so unlike the rest these change identity
        // across one and must be read through this each time they are needed.
        DirectX::CommonStates* common_states() const;

    game/states/game_states.cpp:114-122
        this->level_builder_ = std::make_unique<LevelBuilder>(
            ...
            this->data()->common_states()->PointClamp(),

    game/objects/level_builder.h:39
        ID3D11SamplerState* sampler_state_ = nullptr;

    game/objects/level_builder.cpp:77
            this->sampler_state_,

    game/objects/level.h:149
        ID3D11SamplerState* sampler_state_ = nullptr;

    game/objects/level.cpp:531
        sprite_batches->at(i)->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, this->sampler_state_);

    engine/app/application.cpp:374
        this->common_states_.reset();

**Why it matters:** `IMPLEMENTED.md` records this under "Known remaining issues" as a defect in
`Level` alone. It is not alone. `LevelBuilder` is constructed once in `GameLevel::init`
(`game_states.cpp:114`) and outlives every level it builds; `build_and_enter_level()`
(`game_states.cpp:131-137`) is the restart path, reached from `PauseMenuAction::restart`
(`:213`) and `EndMenuAction::restart` (`:289`). So the one action a player takes after a graphics
hiccup — restart — constructs a fresh `Level` and hands it the same freed pointer
(`level_builder.cpp:77`). It is then consumed three times per view per frame: `level.cpp:531`,
`level.cpp:585` (forwarded into `InterfaceGameplay::draw_gameplay_interface`, which passes it to
a second `Begin` at `interface_gameplay.cpp:39`), and `level.cpp:650` on the zoom-out path.
`SpriteBatch` stores it and calls `PSSetSamplers` at `End()`, so this is a use-after-free reaching
the driver on a path a TDR, a driver update or a remote-desktop session reaches on a real machine.
The engine already solved this shape once: `Registry` handles are slot indices precisely so a
name survives a device restore (`registry.h:39-44`). The sampler is the one D3D object that opted
out.

**Remedy:** Do not store it. Read `common_states()->PointClamp()` through the service at the top
of `draw`, or better, hoist sampler choice behind the renderer interface so no game object ever
names a D3D state object. Delete `sampler_state_` from both classes and both constructors.

#### Split Level into an engine Scene and a game ruleset — the line, member by member

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:53-187`, `game/objects/level.cpp:181-340`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (also PHILOSOPHY/Structural types)

**What:** `Level` is simultaneously the scene container the engine must own and the paint-battle
ruleset the game must own, interleaved member by member rather than layered, and the view count,
each view's viewport and each view's camera are all derived from `player_objects_`, so `Scene`
cannot be extracted at all until it owns an explicit view list.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:92-102
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<artattack::IGameObject>>>
            non_collision_objects_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>>>
            collision_objects_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Player>>>
            player_objects_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<artattack::IGameObject>>>
            viewport_dividers_ = nullptr;

    game/objects/level.cpp:400-401     (the view count comes from the player list)
        auto partitioned_players =
            this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);

    game/objects/level.cpp:521-529     (each view's viewport and camera come from a Player)
        const int player_num = this->player_objects_->at(i)->player_num();

        this->viewport_manager_->apply_player_viewport(
            player_num, deferred_contexts->at(i), sprite_batches->at(i));

        const Camera& camera = this->player_objects_->at(i)->camera();

**Why it matters:** This is finding `#18` from the previous review, still **Outstanding** in
`IMPLEMENTED.md`; what follows is the specific information it lacked — where the line runs, and
what crossing it costs. I re-checked every citation below against the files.

*Becomes engine `Scene`.* Members: `non_collision_objects_` (h:92-93), `collision_objects_`
(h:95-96), `viewport_dividers_` (h:101-102), `camera_tools_` (h:124), `resolution_manager_`
(h:127), `viewport_manager_` (h:128), `render_resources_` (h:129), `out_of_bounds_` (h:140),
`camera_bounds_` (h:141), `thread_pool_` (h:154), `partitioner_` (h:155). Methods: the two
object-update loops (cpp:185-188, 228-231), the whole collision dispatch (cpp:233-305), the
out-of-bounds sweep (cpp:310-317), the swap-and-pop compaction (cpp:320-329),
`is_object_out_of_bounds` (cpp:709-714), the per-view fan-out `draw_active_level` (cpp:393-418)
and `draw_player_view_level` (cpp:509-612), the single-view `draw_zoom_out_level_component`
(cpp:625-675), and the three `bounds().intersects(camera_view)` culls (cpp:536, 545, 554).

*Stays game.* `player_objects_` (h:98-99); the FSM — `LevelState` (h:21-28), `state_` (h:148),
`state()`/`set_state()` (h:84-85), the branch in `update` (cpp:68-176) and the branch in `draw`
(cpp:376-390); the four timers (h:131-134) and `zoom_out_camera_ratio` (cpp:177-180); the
zoom-out camera (h:136) and its two bounds (h:142-143); all audio — `sound_bank_`, `music_`,
`zoom_out_sound_`, `countdown_sound_`, `music_volume_` (h:104-112), `stop_music` (cpp:60-63),
`stop_player_sounds` (cpp:341-348); all HUD — `frame_dt_` (h:120), `countdown_text_` (h:122),
`interface_gameplay_` (h:125), `debug_text_` (h:152), `draw_countdown_text` (cpp:759-767),
`count_projectiles` (cpp:682-706); scoring — `team_colours_` (h:138), `level_end_info`
(cpp:726-757); and `level_consts` (h:30-51).

*Crossings that must be deleted or re-expressed.* (1) `collision_objects_` is typed on
`ICollisionGameObject`, and Scene-side code reads the game's content enum through it —
`is_structure(other_object->collision_object_type())` at cpp:250. (2) `player_objects_` is a third
registration list existing only so Scene-side code can call Player-only methods: `player_num()`
(cpp:196, 521, 562), `camera()`/`set_camera()` (cpp:84, 86, 213, 215), `set_player_input()`
(cpp:201, 205), `update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()` (cpp:219),
`update_weapon_position()`/`update_prev_rectangle()` (cpp:266-267), `on_no_collision()` (cpp:259).
(3) `update(const std::vector<PlayerInputData>&, float)` (h:79) puts the game's input type in the
tick signature. (4) `draw`'s three D3D/DirectXTK vector parameters (h:80-82) and `sampler_state_`
(h:149). (5) `IPaintableGameObject`/`PaintTotal` (cpp:741-749), game-side already, crossing only
because it is reached by walking the Scene's list.

*What the fix costs.* Folding `player_objects_` into the single registered-object list removes
crossing 2 and most of 4's motivation, but it deletes the only source of view information the
renderer has: the number of tasks (cpp:401), each view's viewport (cpp:523) and each view's camera
(cpp:526) are all derived from `Player`. `Scene` therefore cannot be built at all until it owns an
explicit view list — N × (viewport, camera) — that the game refills each tick. Second,
`update_weapon_and_get_projectiles` (cpp:218-224) is the only place objects enter the world
mid-frame, so `Scene` needs an `add()` with insertion deferred to end of tick. Third,
`update_weapon_position()`/`update_prev_rectangle()` (cpp:264-268) is an unnamed post-resolution
phase only `Player` has — `Scene` either names that phase for everyone, or the game runs it itself
after `Scene::resolve()`.

**Remedy:** Introduce `Scene` with the three things `Level` does not have — an explicit view list,
`add()` with deferred insertion, and a named post-resolution phase — then move the eleven members
and nine methods listed above into it, and leave `Level` owning a `Scene` plus the ruleset.

#### Take the D3D11 backend out of Level's public signature

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:80-82`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering; PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** `Level::draw` takes three raw pointers to vectors of D3D11/DirectXTK objects, one of them
an output parameter carrying three obligations stated nowhere, which welds the renderer backend
into the prototype for `Scene` and puts the D3D11 headers in the link line of anything that wants
to test a level.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:80-82
        void draw(std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
            std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
            std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

    game/states/game_states.cpp:322-339
        std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*> command_lists(deferred_contexts->size(), nullptr);

        this->level_->draw(this->data()->device_resources()->deferred_contexts(),
            &command_lists,
            this->data()->sprite_batches());
        ...
        for (int i = 0; i < command_lists.size(); i++)
        {
            if (command_lists[i] == nullptr)
            {
                continue;
            }

            immediate_context->ExecuteCommandList(command_lists[i], TRUE);
            command_lists[i]->Release();
        }

**Why it matters:** Three obligations are placed on the caller and stated nowhere. The
`command_lists` vector must be at least as long as the player count — `level.cpp:606` does
`command_lists->at(i)` with `i` a *player* index. It must be pre-filled with `nullptr`, because
the zoom-out path writes only index 0 (`level.cpp:670`) and leaves the rest for the caller's loop
to skip. And every non-null entry must be `Release`d by the caller, from a loop that only runs
*after* `Level::draw` returns — so any of the three reachable throws inside a render worker
(`level.cpp:516-519`, `:606-610`, or anything a game object's `draw` throws) propagates through
`ThreadPool::wait_for_tasks_to_complete` (`thread_pool.cpp:72-75`) and skips the release of every
command list the other workers already produced. That particular leak is inert today — `main.cpp:93`
catches, message-boxes and returns 1 — but a raw-`Release` contract is exactly what a `Scene` API
must not hand to a game, and a second game copying this shape can learn none of the three rules
from the header. It also means PHILOSOPHY's "everything below the platform edge is testable
headlessly" is false for the class that most needs a test: there is no `tests/` folder for the
game (only `tests/{assets,core,math}`) and there cannot be one while `Level`'s header names
`ID3D11DeviceContext`, `ID3D11CommandList`, `ID3D11SamplerState` and `DirectX::SpriteBatch`.

**Remedy:** Replace the three parameters with the renderer interface PHILOSOPHY already specifies
(`draw_sprite(...)` plus a per-view handle), and let the D3D11 backend own deferred contexts,
sprite batches and command-list lifetime behind it — with `ComPtr`, so a throw releases them.

#### `update_level_logic` is declared `const` and rewrites the entire world

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:161-162`, `game/objects/level.cpp:181-340`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T5

**What:** The function that performs every mutation in the frame — input assignment, object
updates, projectile spawning, collision response, deletion — is a `const` member function, which
it compiles as only because every object list sits behind an outer `unique_ptr` that does not
propagate `const`.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:161-162
        void update_level_logic(const std::vector<PlayerInputData>& player_inputs,
            float dt) const;

    game/objects/level.cpp:201
                object->set_player_input(player_inputs[player_index]);

    game/objects/level.cpp:223
                this->collision_objects_->push_back(std::move(proj));

    game/objects/level.cpp:324-326
                this->collision_objects_->at(i) = std::move(
                    this->collision_objects_->back());
                this->collision_objects_->pop_back();

**Why it matters:** `IMPLEMENTED.md` and `i_game_object.h:10-15` both present `draw() const` as the
compiler-enforced guarantee that makes the render fan-out sound, and `ca4d228` was spent buying it.
This function is the standing proof that `const` on `Level` guarantees nothing about the world
`Level` owns: a `draw_player_view_level(...) const` could `push_back` into `collision_objects_`
tomorrow and the build would stay green. `stop_music() const` (h:89) and `stop_player_sounds()
const` (h:174) are smaller instances of the same thing. There is no live defect here — nothing on
the draw path currently mutates — so this is graded on what it fails to prevent, not on what it
breaks. For the class that becomes `Scene`, and that a stranger will read to learn what the
guarantee is, the signature actively misleads. (While the signatures are being fixed:
`state()`, `level_end_info()`, `zoom_out_camera_ratio()`, `count_projectiles()` and
`is_object_out_of_bounds()` are pure reads with no `[[nodiscard]]`, which PHILOSOPHY/Tests and
toolchain lists beside `const` as compiler-enforced information.)

**Remedy:** Drop `const` from `update_level_logic`, and hold the object lists by value
(`std::vector<std::unique_ptr<...>>`, no outer `unique_ptr`) so the compiler enforces the
read/write split on the scene itself and not merely on its contents.

#### Collision fires both objects' responses off one object's predicate, and tests every pair twice

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:233-305`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Collision

**What:** The dispatch runs three nested loops that between them cover every ordered pair, and in
each hit invokes `on_collision` on *both* participants although only one participant's
`is_colliding` was consulted — so whether an object responds at all is decided by the other
object's filter.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.cpp:245-248     (players against objects: the player's filter decides)
                if (player->is_colliding(other_object.get()))
                {
                    player->on_collision(other_object.get());
                    other_object->on_collision(player.get());

    game/objects/level.cpp:280-284     (objects against players: the object's filter decides)
                    if (object->is_colliding(player.get()))
                    {
                        object->on_collision(player.get());
                        player->on_collision(object.get());
                    }

    game/objects/level.cpp:289-303     (every ordered pair of collision objects, both directions)
            for (auto& object_2 : *this->collision_objects_)
            {
                ...
                if (object == object_2)
                {
                    continue;
                }
                if (object->is_colliding(object_2.get()))
                {
                    object->on_collision(object_2.get());
                    object_2->on_collision(object.get());
                }
            }

**Why it matters:** The first two blocks cover the identical player × object pair set with opposite
predicates and identical handler calls. The only reason a player/structure contact does not apply
its push-out twice per frame is that `Player::is_matching_collision_object_type` accepts structures
only (`player.cpp:151-156`) while `Structure::is_colliding` returns `false` unconditionally
(`structure.cpp:40-43`). Give `Structure` a real predicate — the obvious thing to do the day a
structure needs to react to being hit — and `Player::on_collision` runs twice per contact per
frame, applying the MTV resolution twice. Nothing in the code or a comment records that this is
load-bearing. Separately, the pair loop at `:289` is a full O(n²) with no broad phase, visiting
each unordered pair in both directions: `collision_objects_` holds the level's whole static
geometry as well as the live projectiles, so a few hundred entries is ~10⁵ virtual `is_colliding`
calls per tick — precisely what `IGameObject::bounds()` was introduced to make unnecessary
(`i_game_object.h:53-56`).

**Remedy:** Produce a pair list once — each unordered pair at most once, pruned by a
`bounds()`-driven broad phase — consult a symmetric layer/mask test rather than one object's
predicate, then call both responders exactly once per pair.

#### The render fan-out allocates several times per frame

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:397-417`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8 (PHILOSOPHY/Performance)

**What:** Each frame the draw path allocates a partition vector, copies that whole vector into
every task lambda, then heap-allocates each lambda into a `std::function` and again into a
`task_item`.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.cpp:400-415
        auto partitioned_players =
            this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);

        // draw player objects
        for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
        {
            this->thread_pool_->add_task([this, i, partitioned_players,
                deferred_contexts, command_lists, sprite_batches]()
                {
                    this->draw_player_view_level(partitioned_players[i].first,
                    partitioned_players[i].second,
                    ...

    engine/core/thread_pool.cpp:39-41
        void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)
        {
            auto item = std::make_unique<task_item>(task_item{ std::move(task), this });

**Why it matters:** `Partitioner::partition` returns by value (`partitioner.cpp:5-23`) and the
lambda captures the whole vector by copy — one heap buffer per task, when each task reads exactly
one `std::pair<int,int>`. The capture set is `this` + `int` + a 24-byte vector + three pointers,
far past MSVC's `std::function` small-object buffer, so `add_task`'s by-value `std::function`
parameter allocates, and `std::make_unique<task_item>` allocates again. At four players that is
roughly seventeen allocations per frame, about a thousand per second, on the path PHILOSOPHY says
performs none. It is also pure waste: the partition is recomputed every frame from a player count
that cannot change during a match.

**Remedy:** Capture `partitioned_players[i]` by value — a `pair`, no allocation — and compute the
partition once when the level is built.

#### Per-team spawn arrays are indexed by the global player ordinal

- **File:** `game/objects/player_builder.cpp:27-38` (reached from `game/objects/level_builder.cpp:53-56`)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (also T2)

**What:** `build_players`, the only path `LevelBuilder::build_level` has for creating players,
increments one counter across all players and uses it to subscript whichever team's spawn array
the player belongs to, so a level whose spawn lists are sized per team reads out of bounds.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/player_builder.cpp:27-38
        int i = 0;
        for (auto& setting : settings.player_settings())
        {
            Vector2F position = Vector2F::ZERO;
            if (setting.team == PlayerTeam::a)
            {
                position = team_a_spawns[i];
            }
            else
            {
                position = team_b_spawns[i];
            }

    game/objects/level_builder.cpp:53-56
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Player>>> players =
            this->player_builder_->build_players(settings, load_info, team_colours,
                this->render_resources_, this->audio_resources_,
                this->viewport_manager_);

**Why it matters:** With four players split two-and-two, the team B players read `team_b_spawns[2]`
and `[3]`. All three shipped levels list exactly four spawns per team
(`game/content/levels/{turbulence,close_quarters,king_of_the_hill}.json`, `spawn_locations`), so it
does not fire today — but the natural authoring of a two-versus-two level is two spawns per team,
and `operator[]` on a `std::vector` gives no diagnostic: it is an out-of-bounds read producing a
garbage spawn position, in a file the level author edits (T7) with no validation at load (T6). The
spawn counts are never checked against the player count anywhere. This file is outside the
group's file list; it is filed here because `LevelBuilder` is its only caller.

**Remedy:** Track a per-team index, and validate at load that each team's spawn list is at least as
long as the maximum supported player count, naming the level file if it is not.

#### `level_consts` screams, and puts match tuning in code

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:30-51`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never (also T7)

**What:** Every level constant is SCREAMING_SNAKE inside a `consts` namespace, which CONVENTIONS
reserves for macros and explicitly rules out, and the match length and countdown length — the two
most-tuned numbers in the game — are compiled in rather than read from the level definition that
already supplies the music, the bounds and the spawns.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:30-51
    namespace level_consts
    {
        constexpr float TIMER = 240.0f;
        constexpr float START_TIMER = 3.0f;
        const static std::string COUNTDOWN_TEXT = "3";
        const static std::string COUNTDOWN_FONT_NAME = "gill_sans_mt_bold_144";
        ...
        constexpr float ZOOM_OUT_TIMER = 2.0f;
        constexpr float OVERVIEW_TIMER = 2.0f;

        const std::string COUNTDOWN_SOUND = "smash_countdown";

    engine/render/viewport_manager.h:15-21     (the engine's own counter-example)
        // How a split-screen divider is drawn. They live on the class that shapes
        // the dividers rather than in a `consts` namespace of strays (CONVENTIONS,
        // Constants and enumerators); a game asks for the rectangles and then for
        // these to fill them.
        static inline const std::string DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1";

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Never says "SCREAMING constants — screaming means macro, nothing
else", and Constants and enumerators says "a header full of numeric constants is usually tuning
data in the wrong place … Constants that stay in code live next to the one thing they configure,
not in a `consts` namespace collecting strays". Both apply exactly, and `ViewportManager` shows
the engine already following its own rule, so the game contradicts the engine's example. Concretely,
changing the match from four minutes to three is a rebuild today, which T7 says it must not be —
while `sound`, `spawn_locations` and `level_bounds` in the same level file already rebuild nothing.
The four `std::string` constants also have internal linkage at namespace scope, so every
translation unit including `level.h` gets its own dynamically-initialised copy.

**Remedy:** Rename to `snake_case` and move each next to what it configures; move `TIMER`,
`START_TIMER`, `ZOOM_OUT_TIMER` and `OVERVIEW_TIMER` into the level JSON beside `sound` and
`level_bounds`.

- **Severity:** low

**What:** The same camera-update block exists twice; the steady-state copy was corrected to index
viewports by the player's own pad slot and carries a comment saying why, while the first-update
copy thirty lines above still uses a running loop counter.

**Evidence:**

#### Twenty-one positional constructor parameters, four of them adjacent rectangles

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:57-77`, `game/objects/level_builder.cpp:62-83`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T5 (also T4, T10)
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** `Level`'s constructor takes twenty-one positional parameters, including four consecutive
`const RectangleF&`, two consecutive `const std::vector<Vector2F>&` and two consecutive
`const std::string&` — so transposing any pair within those runs compiles clean and type-checks
clean, and produces a level with the camera bounds and the level bounds swapped.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:62-69
            const mattmath::RectangleF& out_of_bounds,
            const mattmath::RectangleF& camera_bounds,
            const mattmath::RectangleF& zoom_out_start_bounds,
            const mattmath::RectangleF& zoom_out_finish_bounds,
            const std::vector<mattmath::Vector2F>& team_a_spawns,
            const std::vector<mattmath::Vector2F>& team_b_spawns,
            const std::string& sound_bank_name,
            const std::string& music_name,

    game/objects/level_builder.cpp:68-75
            load_info->out_of_bounds_rectangle(),
            load_info->camera_bounds_rectangle(),
            load_info->zoom_out_start_bounds_rectangle(),
            load_info->zoom_out_finish_bounds_rectangle(),
            load_info->team_a_spawns(),
            load_info->team_b_spawns(),
            load_info->sound_bank_name(),
            load_info->music_name(),

**Why it matters:** The call site is correct today — I checked all twenty-one against the
declaration. That is the whole problem: nothing but that check protects it, and the failure mode
is silent. Swap `out_of_bounds` and `camera_bounds` and the game still runs, with the camera
clamped to the wider rectangle and players deleted at the narrower one; swap `team_a_spawns` and
`team_b_spawns` and both teams start in the other's base. T5 says push every error to the earliest
stage that can catch it, and four same-typed adjacent parameters push it past the compiler
entirely. It is also the API a sample-game reader meets: T10 asks the game-facing surface to stay
in the simple subset of the language, and a twenty-one-argument positional call is not that.

**Remedy:** Group the four rectangles into a named `LevelBounds` struct with bare fields (the
schema already groups them under `level_bounds` in the JSON), pass the sound trio as one struct,
and hand the services in as one bag — the constructor drops to about six parameters, and every
transposition that survives is between differently-typed arguments.

#### `out_of_bounds_` holds the in-bounds rectangle, and the test is "touches at all"

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:140`, `game/objects/level.cpp:709-714`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** T4

**What:** The member named `out_of_bounds_` stores the rectangle an object must stay *inside*, and
`is_object_out_of_bounds` returns true only when the object's bounding box does not intersect it at
all — neither of which the name, the JSON key, or any comment says.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:140
        mattmath::RectangleF out_of_bounds_ = mattmath::RectangleF::ZERO;

    game/objects/level.cpp:709-714
    bool Level::is_object_out_of_bounds(const ICollisionGameObject* object) const
    {
        bool object_in_bounds =
            this->out_of_bounds_.intersects(object->shape()->bounding_box());
        return !object_in_bounds;
    }

    game/content/levels/turbulence.json:51-58
        "level_bounds":
        {
            "out_of_bounds":
            {
                "x": -100.0, "y": -100.0, "width": 6200.0, "height": 6200.0
            },

**Why it matters:** The local variable inside the function is called `object_in_bounds` and is
assigned from a member called `out_of_bounds_`, so the function reads as its own negation. The
misnomer reaches the content schema too — the JSON key is `out_of_bounds` and its value is the
containment rectangle, larger than `camera_bounds` beside it — so fixing the name is a schema
change, which is an argument for doing it now rather than after the engine has users. Two callers
depend on the exact semantics with opposite consequences: projectile retirement (`level.cpp:310-317`)
and a `throw` that kills the process (`level.cpp:333-339`). A reader tuning the rectangle to make
projectiles retire sooner will find that an object counts as out of bounds only once its bounding
box has left entirely, not when its centre leaves — a distinction worth exactly one sentence that
isn't there.

**Remedy:** Rename member and JSON key to `level_bounds`, and state the containment rule
(bounding box, any overlap counts as inside) on `is_object_out_of_bounds`.

#### Seven borrowed pointers in `Level`, none documented as a loan

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:104`, `127-129`, `149`, `154-155`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** PHILOSOPHY requires a non-owning pointer to be a documented loan — "the member
declaration says who owns the object and why it outlives the holder". `Level` holds seven and
documents none, in a class whose author documents lifetimes carefully two lines above and two
lines below.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:104-120     (the two members that do carry the comment)
        artattack::SoundBank* sound_bank_ = nullptr;

        // The level's own music comes from its definition file, so its name is not
        // known until here - but it is known once, at construction, which is where
        // it stops being a name. Same for the two fixed sounds the level plays.
        ...
        // This frame's dt, for the debug overlay's dt/fps readout ...
        // It replaces a const float* handed in at construction, so what used
        // to be a pointer that device loss could invalidate is now a value.
        float frame_dt_ = 0.0f;

    game/objects/level.h:127-129, 149, 154-155     (the seven that do not)
        const artattack::ResolutionManager* resolution_manager_ = nullptr;
        artattack::ViewportManager* viewport_manager_ = nullptr;
        artattack::RenderResources* render_resources_ = nullptr;
        ...
        ID3D11SamplerState* sampler_state_ = nullptr;
        ...
        artattack::ThreadPool* thread_pool_ = nullptr;
        const artattack::Partitioner* partitioner_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** `frame_dt_`'s comment shows the author already knows what this rule is for —
it exists because a borrowed `const float*` was invalidated by device loss. Six of the seven
undocumented pointers are genuinely safe (`GameData`'s header states that the engine services it
forwards are "created once by the shell and never reseated, so anything here may be held for an
object's whole life"). The seventh, `sampler_state_`, is the one that breaks the rule — and it is
indistinguishable from the other six at the declaration, which is exactly how it survived a
review that fixed everything around it. A one-line comment per member is the cheapest possible
place to catch the next one.

**Remedy:** Give each borrowed pointer the one-line loan comment the two documented members
already model; the sampler's would have to say "freed by device loss", which is the finding that
deletes it.

#### The music's lifetime is a seven-call-site convention, not the level's

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:89`, `game/states/game_states.cpp:212-295`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes (T11)
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** `Level` starts its music in `update` but never stops it in a destructor; instead every
one of the seven exits from `GameLevel` must remember to call the public `stop_music()` first, and
one that forgets leaves the track playing over the menus for the rest of the session.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:89
        void stop_music() const;

    game/objects/level.cpp:74     (started here, on the level's first update)
                this->sound_bank_->play_effect(this->music_, true, this->music_volume_);

    game/states/game_states.cpp     (stopped here, seven times, by hand)
        212:            this->level_->stop_music();
        217:            this->level_->stop_music();
        258:            this->level_->stop_music();
        268:            this->level_->stop_music();
        278:            this->level_->stop_music();
        288:            this->level_->stop_music();
        295:            this->level_->stop_music();

**Why it matters:** `Level` has no user-declared destructor, and the `SoundBank` it plays through
is owned by `AudioResources` and outlives it — so destroying a `Level` stops nothing. All seven
sites are correct today; I checked each. The eighth transition someone adds will not be, and the
symptom (music that never stops) is a long way from the cause. PHILOSOPHY asks for lexical
ownership and designed destruction order, and this is the one resource in the class whose release
is neither. It is also a crossing worth resolving *before* the split, because "the level's music"
is unambiguously the game half of finding 2 and should end up owned by whatever object the
ruleset becomes.

**Remedy:** Stop the music in `~Level()` and make `stop_music()` private (or delete it): the
transitions then only have to destroy the level, which they already do.

#### The draw path's three throws discard the diagnostic they were thrown for

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:606-610`, `516-519`, `670-674`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** Every failure the render path can report throws a bare string: the `FinishCommandList`
failure discards the `HRESULT` it just tested and the index of the view that failed, and the
deferred-context check discards the index too — so the message names neither what broke nor where.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.cpp:606-610
            HRESULT hr = deferred_contexts->at(i)->FinishCommandList(TRUE, &command_lists->at(i));
            if (FAILED(hr))
            {
                throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list");
            }

    game/objects/level.cpp:516-519
            if (deferred_contexts->at(i)->GetType() != D3D11_DEVICE_CONTEXT_DEFERRED)
            {
                throw std::exception("Deferred context not created");
            }

    game/objects/level.cpp:630-633     (the same check, a different exception type)
        if (deferred_contexts->at(0)->GetType() != D3D11_DEVICE_CONTEXT_DEFERRED)
        {
            throw std::runtime_error("Deferred context not created");
        }

**Why it matters:** T6 is "it says so immediately, with names and paths"; these say so immediately
with neither. `FAILED(hr)` on a deferred context is most often `DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED`, which
is the one HRESULT that would tell the reader this is a device-loss problem and send them straight
at the critical finding above — and it is thrown away one line after being read. The two spellings
of the identical check also disagree on exception type, and `std::exception(const char*)` is an
MSVC extension with no standard equivalent, so both of these are edits waiting at the second
platform PHILOSOPHY keeps a seam open for. Since this exception kills the process
(`main.cpp:93-101` catches, message-boxes and returns 1), the string in it is the entire bug
report the user can send.

**Remedy:** Throw `std::runtime_error` uniformly, and put the HRESULT (hex) and the view index in
the message.

#### Game types sit in the global namespace

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:21`, `53`; `game/objects/level_builder.h:17`; `game/objects/stage.h:18`, `26`; `game/objects/level_mode.h:3`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Namespaces

**What:** `LevelState`, `Level`, `LevelBuilder`, `LevelMode`, `Stage` and `StageList` are all
declared at global scope, while the engine they link against is correctly inside
`namespace artattack`.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level.h:21
    enum class LevelState

    game/objects/level.h:53
    class Level

    game/objects/level_builder.h:17
    class LevelBuilder

    game/objects/stage.h:18, 26
    struct Stage
    ...
    using StageList = std::vector<Stage>;

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Namespaces says "Game code owns its own namespace and never
reopens the engine's". The engine half of that rule landed; the game half did not. `Stage`,
`Level` and `LevelBuilder` are common enough words that a project copying `samples/minimal/` and
linking a second library will collide — and the sample is the file a stranger copies.
`level.h:3-19` also mixes game and engine includes in arbitrary order (game, game, game, game,
engine, engine, game, engine, game, game, engine, engine, game, engine, engine, engine, engine),
against CONVENTIONS/Files.

**Remedy:** Wrap the game in one namespace and sort the include blocks.

### Rejected

- **A throwing render worker leaks every command list already finished** (low, lifetime) —
  observation true, consequence nil. The only reachable throws are inside a render worker;
  `ThreadPool::wait_for_tasks_to_complete` rethrows on the caller, and `main.cpp:93` is the next
  handler — it message-boxes and returns 1, so the process is exiting and the leaked
  `ID3D11CommandList` references die with it. There is no path where the leak accumulates. Its
  durable content — that `Release`ing the output vector is an undocumented obligation on the
  caller — was already the third item in "Take the D3D11 backend out of Level's public signature",
  where I folded the throw-site detail so nothing is lost.
- **`for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); ...)` breaks the `/W4 /WX` build** (raised and dropped by the
  reviewer) — correctly dropped, and I verified it rather than inferring it: compiling a reduction
  with `cl /W4 /WX /std:c++20 /permissive-` produces no diagnostic, and the committed `out/` tree
  has `level.cpp.obj` and a linked `ArtAttackGame.exe` both newer than `level.cpp`.
- **The swap-and-pop compaction's unsigned wraparound** (raised and dropped by the reviewer) —
  correctly dropped. `i--` at `size_t i == 0` wraps to `SIZE_MAX` and the loop's `i++` returns it
  to `0`, which is defined behaviour for unsigned types and re-tests the swapped-in element, which
  is what the loop needs.

<a id="g-game-player"></a>

## game-player — Player

*Group `game-player` · 26 findings (2 high, 12 medium, 12 low) · source `review2/verified/game-player.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every cited line in all nine assigned files and in each file the reviewer reached
for as corroboration: `game/objects/level.cpp` (the only caller of Player's update/draw/collision
surface), `weapon.cpp`, `weapon.h`, `weapon_consts.h`, `collision_object_type.h`,
`i_collision_game_object.h`, `structure.cpp` and `structure_paintable.cpp`, `projectile.cpp`,
`paint_tile.cpp`, `level_loaded_info.cpp` plus the three shipped level JSONs (parsed, spawn counts
checked), `menu_level_settings.cpp` / `menu_player_settings.h` / `main_menu.cpp`,
`engine/core/i_game_object.h` and `moving_object.h`, the whole
`draw_object` → `sprite_sheet_object` → `texture_object`/`animation_object` chain,
`engine/math/collision_tools.cpp` (`calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge`,
`calculate_containing_collision_direction`), `Vector2F::direction_to_8_cardinal_direction`,
`game/CMakeLists.txt` and the generated `build.ninja`, `game/pch.h`, and DirectXTK's own
`GamePad.cpp`.

Every cited line number is right except three, which I corrected in place. The core observations
survive; what did not survive is a set of consequences and arithmetic attached to them. I threw
out the claim that the mutating-`const` methods "reintroduce the data race" — nothing on the draw
path calls them today, so it is a hole in a compiler-enforced wall, not a live race, and I say so
while keeping the finding at high because that wall is the thing IMPLEMENTED.md #16 claims to have
built. I regraded the spawn-indexing finding from high to medium: all three shipped levels carry
exactly four spawns per team and the menu caps at four players, so the out-of-bounds read is latent
and content-conditional, while the live consequence is misplaced spawn slots. I regraded the input-
seam finding from high to medium (it is a not-yet-built boundary the roadmap already names, and it
restates an unfixed finding from the previous review) and the SCREAMING-constants finding from
medium to low. I corrected the `bounds()` arithmetic (452x520 against 52x120 is ~38x the area, not
"four and a half times"), the translation-unit count for `player_consts.h` (seven, not ten;
`interface_gameplay.h` does not include `player.h`), the dead-field count (three, not two —
`primary_type_` is dead too), and the header-self-containment evidence (`std::string` and `FLT_MIN`
reach `player_consts.h` through `colour.h` → `matt_math.h`, not through the PCH; only
`DirectX::GamePad` genuinely depends on it). That last one also had the wrong remedy: CMake
force-includes the PCH with `/FI`, so no include reordering can restore the self-containment proof
and the `#include "game/pch.h"` at the top of every `.cpp` is now dead text.

I added six findings the reviewer missed. The sharpest is that the left-stick deadzone is applied
twice — DirectXTK's `DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR` already removes the hardware deadzone and rescales to
[0,1] specifically "to remove the deadzone discontinuity", and `PlayerInput` then re-imposes a 0.5
threshold on the raw x component with no rescale, so the player has no analog movement below half
speed and a fully-deflected stick at 60 degrees is dead. The second is that `respawn()` restores
position, velocity, health, ammo and state but leaves `move_state_`, `prev_rectangle_`, `air_time_`
and the two timers holding their values from the moment of death — so the one-way jump-through
platform test is evaluated against the death position on the respawn frame. The rest are smaller:
`PlayerBuilder` heap-allocates a stateless builder to call a `static` function, `Player::update`
silently overrides `AnimationObject::update` as well as `IGameObject::update`, twelve throws use
MSVC's non-standard `std::exception(const char*)` with messages that name no value, and the game's
types sit in the global namespace CONVENTIONS reserves.

I checked and discarded two hypotheses of my own before they became findings: paint tiles never
reach `Player::on_collision` (they are owned by `StructurePaintable`, not registered), and
structures never double-dispatch collision response (`Structure::is_colliding` returns `false`
unconditionally), so the trailing `throw` in `Player::on_collision` is not reachable that way.

### Themes

- The const/`dt`/`bounds()` remediation passes declared the right contracts and `Player` still
  breaks them from the inside: `const` methods that mutate the weapon, a `bounds()` padded with a
  guessed constant, and a `for_deletion()` hardwired to `false` that leaves `Level` with `throw` as
  its only verb.
- Death is a drawing-and-collision flag, not a simulation state. Shooting, ammo drain, weapon
  positioning, camera tracking and the looping fire sound all continue while `state_ == dead`, and
  `respawn()` puts back only half of what death changed.
- No single place owns `PlayerMoveState`. Transitions are written from eight collision handlers,
  from `update_movement`, from `do_jump` and from `on_no_collision` — and the one state nobody
  clears (`on_ceiling`) is exactly the one that is wrong.
- Indices are trusted rather than checked: the per-team spawn arrays are subscripted with
  `operator[]` by a global player counter, under an invariant nobody states and no loader validates.
- Tuning, asset names and sound names are compiled in, in SCREAMING_SNAKE, in a `consts` namespace —
  the three things CONVENTIONS names in a row as the wrong answer.
- The game owns its own input device layer, and having taken ownership it gets the deadzone wrong on
  top of a library that had already got it right.
- Nothing in this group is tested, including `PlayerInput::calculate_player_input`, which is a
  `static` pure function of two PODs.

#### Stop a dead player from firing

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:776-785`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** —

**What:** `update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()` does not check `state_`, and `Level` calls it for
every player unconditionally, so a player who dies while holding the fire trigger keeps spawning
damaging projectiles, draining ammo and looping the fire sound for the whole three-second respawn
delay.

**Evidence:**

    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>>
        Player::update_weapon_and_get_projectiles(float dt) const
    {
        return this->primary_->update_and_get_projectiles(
            this->input(),
            this->center(),
            MovingObject::velocity(),
            this->facing_right(),
            dt);
    }

`game/objects/level.cpp:191-225` runs this over `*this->player_objects_` with no state filter, and
`set_player_input` two lines above keeps feeding the corpse live input:

    for (const auto& object : *this->player_objects_)
    {
        ...
        object->set_player_input(player_inputs[player_index]);
        object->update(dt);
        ...
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>> new_projs =
            object->update_weapon_and_get_projectiles(dt);

`Player::update` (player.cpp:746-755) does nothing but tick `respawn_timer_` while dead, so the
corpse never moves; `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update` (weapon.cpp:194-241) gates only on
`input.primary_shoot && gun_player_aligned()`, and `gun_player_aligned_` defaults to `true`
(weapon.h:161) and is assigned only by `WeaponRoller`.

**Why it matters:** Reachable in every match — get killed with the right trigger down. The
projectiles are spawned from `center()`, are registered into `collision_objects_`, and
`Projectile::is_colliding` (projectile.cpp:106-116) accepts a live enemy player, so they paint tiles
and deal damage while `Player::draw` early-outs on `state_ == dead` and shows nothing firing them.
`Weapon::handle_shoot_sound` (weapon.cpp:242-260) keeps the looping fire instance playing for the
same three seconds. `respawn()` calls `reset_ammo()`, which hides the ammo drain and is why this
survived a `/W4` pass and a const pass.

**Remedy:** Return an empty vector when `state_ != PlayerState::alive` (and stop the weapon's
looping sound on the frame the player dies), or have `Level` skip the call for dead players. The
first is better: it keeps the rule inside the object that owns the state.

#### Stop declaring `const` on Player methods that mutate the weapon

- **File:** `game/objects/player.h:86-87,131`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** `update_weapon_and_get_projectiles()` and `update_weapon_position()` are declared `const`
but mutate `Weapon` through a `std::unique_ptr`, which does not propagate constness — so on the one
class whose `draw()` every render worker enters simultaneously, `const` no longer certifies a pure
read.

**Evidence:**

    // player.h:86-87
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>>
        update_weapon_and_get_projectiles(float dt) const;
    // player.h:131
    void update_weapon_position() const;

    // player.cpp:671-674
    void Player::update_weapon_position() const
    {
        this->primary_->set_player_center(this->center());
    }

`Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles` and `Weapon::set_player_center` are both non-`const`
(weapon.h:40-49). Between them they assign the weapon's rotation, ammo, shoot timer, ammo timer,
`shooting_this_update_`, `invert_x`/`invert_y`, and start or stop its looping `SoundEffectInstance`.
`weapon.h:34-36` already records that the author found this hole once:

    // The const does not come for free through Player - primary_ is a
    // unique_ptr, and a const unique_ptr still hands out a non-const pointee -
    // so it has to be declared here to be enforced at all.

**Why it matters:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:14-15` states that `const` "is how the compiler
holds a new object to it instead of a comment nobody reads", and IMPLEMENTED.md #16 records that
the const pass exists so that a mutating `draw()` is a compile error rather than something an audit
has to keep catching. Both of these are public `const` members of `Player`, so `Player::draw() const`
can call either and compile. **No current path does** — this is a gap in the wall, not a live race —
but it is a gap on exactly the class that shipped this bug twice before (IMPLEMENTED.md #23
`Player::draw` and #34 `Weapon::draw`, both "mutates shared state on several render threads"). And
neither `const` buys anything: `Level::update_level_logic` reaches players through
`unique_ptr<vector<unique_ptr<Player>>>` and already calls the non-`const` `update()` and
`update_prev_rectangle()` from a `const` member (level.cpp:207, 267).

**Remedy:** Drop `const` from both declarations. If the goal was to let a `const Level` drive them,
fix that at the `Level` end rather than by lying about `Player`.

#### Index spawn points per team, and check the count

- **File:** `game/objects/player_builder.cpp:27-38`
- **Severity:** medium *(regraded from high)*
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** Both per-team spawn arrays are subscripted with the *global* player counter using
unchecked `operator[]`, so spawn slots are assigned wrongly whenever the teams are not a prefix
split, and nothing at load validates that either array is long enough.

**Evidence:**

    int i = 0;
    for (auto& setting : settings.player_settings())
    {
        Vector2F position = Vector2F::ZERO;
        if (setting.team == PlayerTeam::a)
        {
            position = team_a_spawns[i];
        }
        else
        {
            position = team_b_spawns[i];
        }

`i` increments once per player (player_builder.cpp:65), never per team. `team_a_spawns` /
`team_b_spawns` are plain `std::vector<Vector2F>` copies (lines 24-25) and
`LevelLoadedInfo::team_a_spawns()` / `team_b_spawns()` (level_loaded_info.cpp:37-46) validate
nothing — no presence check, no count check, and `decode_team_spawns_json` returns whatever the
array held.

**Why it matters:** I parsed all three shipped levels: each carries exactly four spawns per team,
and `MainMenuPlayerCount` caps players at four (main_menu.cpp:881-921), so **the read is in range
today** — which is why this is medium rather than high. What is live is the slot assignment: in a
1v3 the three team-B players take `team_b_spawns[1..3]` and slot 0 is never used, and in a 2v2 team
B spawns at its third and fourth points. A level author's spawn layout is not what they wrote. What
is latent is the rest: content is data (T7), and a stage authored with two team-B spawns for a 2v2
map makes `team_b_spawns[2]` and `[3]` undefined behaviour on load with no diagnostic naming the
file. The invariant "each team's spawn list must be at least as long as the *total* player count"
is nowhere written down, and it is not even the invariant anyone would guess.

**Remedy:** Keep a counter per team and index with it. Validate at load that each team's spawn list
has at least as many entries as that team's player count, throwing with the level file name and the
two counts (T6).

#### The stick deadzone is applied twice, the second time without rescaling

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.cpp:21,87-110`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `raw_input` asks DirectXTK for a radial deadzone, which removes the hardware deadzone
*and rescales the remainder back to [0,1] precisely so there is no discontinuity*. `calculate_player_input`
then imposes a second, much larger threshold on the raw component with no rescale, reintroducing the
discontinuity the library had removed.

**Evidence:**

    // player_input.cpp:21
    auto pad = this->gamepad_->GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR);

    // player_input.cpp:87-94
    if (std::fabs(current.left_analog_stick.x) > STICK_DEADZONE)
    {
        result.x_movement = current.left_analog_stick.x;
    }
    else
    {
        result.x_movement = 0.0f;
    }

`STICK_DEADZONE` is `0.5f` (player_input.h:11). DirectXTK's own implementation
(`Src/GamePad.cpp`, `ApplyLinearDeadZone`) is explicit about what it already did:

    // Decrease positive values to remove the deadzone discontinuity.
    value -= deadZoneSize;
    ...
    // Scale into 0-1 range.
    const float scaledValue = value / (maxValue - deadZoneSize);

**Why it matters:** Two live consequences in every match. `x_movement` feeds
`X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input` and `X_ACCELERATION * dt * x_input` (player.cpp:803, 808), so the
player has **no analog movement below half speed**: the axis is 0 up to 0.5 and then jumps. And the
test is on the x *component*, not the vector magnitude, so a stick at full deflection 60 degrees
above horizontal (x = 0.5) is dead for movement while a stick at half deflection horizontally is
not — which is the opposite of what the circular deadzone one line earlier was chosen for. The right
stick has the same 0.5 gate on `length()` (lines 97-110), so aiming needs half the stick's already-
rescaled travel before it registers. This restates a finding from the previous review
(`docs/review/findings.json`, "Pick one deadzone") that IMPLEMENTED.md does not record as fixed, and
the code confirms it is not.

**Remedy:** Ask for `DEAD_ZONE_NONE` and apply one deadzone with a rescale
(`x = sign(x) * (|x| - dz) / (1 - dz)`), or keep `DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR` and drop `STICK_DEADZONE`
entirely. Test the magnitude, not the component. 0.5 is enormous for a movement axis; 0.15-0.25 is
typical.

#### Clear `on_ceiling` when the player leaves the ceiling

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:1287-1298`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T3 (simplicity over accuracy — "a simple model still has exact, documented, tested semantics")

**What:** `on_no_collision()` resets every ground state to `in_air` but not `on_ceiling`, so after
any head-bump the player's move state stays `on_ceiling` for the entire fall.

**Evidence:**

    void Player::on_no_collision()
    {
    	PlayerMoveState move_state = this->move_state();

    	if (move_state == PlayerMoveState::on_ground ||
    		move_state == PlayerMoveState::on_drop_down_ground ||
    		move_state == PlayerMoveState::on_ramp_left ||
    		move_state == PlayerMoveState::on_ramp_right)
    	{
    		this->set_move_state(PlayerMoveState::in_air);
    	}
    }

`on_top_collision` (player.cpp:574-582) is the only writer of `on_ceiling`. Nothing clears it except
landing on something: `on_bottom_collision`, the two ramp handlers, and
`on_structure_jump_through_collision`. `calculate_animation_state` (player.cpp:1058-1061) then does:

        else if (move_state == PlayerMoveState::on_ceiling)
        {
    		return PlayerAnimationState::idle;
    	}

and `do_jump` (player.cpp:915-918) treats `on_ceiling` as "do nothing", so the state cannot decay
from there either.

**Why it matters:** Reachable by jumping into any overhang. From the frame the player's head touches
a ceiling until the frame they land, `calculate_animation_state()` returns `idle`, so the falling
player plays the standing-still clip — and `update_animation_state()` will not switch back, because
it early-outs when the computed state has not changed and `move_state_` never changes. It also
survives death: `respawn()` does not reset `move_state_` (see the respawn finding below), so a player
who dies while `on_ceiling` respawns into the idle-while-falling state.

*(I dropped the reviewer's second consequence — that a simultaneous floor-and-ceiling overlap would
make `do_jump` refuse a visibly-grounded jump. `do_jump` tests `is_on_ground()` first, so that
requires `on_top_collision` to run after `on_bottom_collision` in the same frame, which I could not
demonstrate from the level content.)*

**Remedy:** Add `on_ceiling` to the list in `on_no_collision()`. Better: give one function ownership
of every `PlayerMoveState` transition, so the set of states that decay to `in_air` is written once.

#### `respawn()` leaves half the player's state at its death values

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:1028-1038`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `respawn()` restores position, rotation, velocity, `dx`, health, ammo and state, and stops
there. `move_state_`, `prev_rectangle_`, `air_time_`, `animation_state_`, `damage_sound_timer_` and
`health_regen_timer_` all still describe the moment of death, on a player who has just been
teleported across the level.

**Evidence:**

    void Player::respawn()
    {
        this->rectangle_.set_position(this->respawn_position_);
        MovingObject::set_rotation(0.0f);
        MovingObject::set_velocity(Vector2F::ZERO);
        MovingObject::set_dx(Vector2F::ZERO);
    	this->health_ = 1.0f;
    	this->primary_->reset_ammo();
    	this->state_ = PlayerState::alive;
        this->sound_bank_->play_wave(this->respawn_sound_, RESPAWN_SOUND_VOLUME);
    }

`prev_rectangle_` is the load-bearing one. `on_structure_jump_through_collision` (player.cpp:390-418)
decides whether a one-way platform is solid with

        bool was_above = this->prev_rectangle_.bottom() <= other_rect.top();

and `Level` runs the collision pass in the same frame as the `update()` that respawned the player
(level.cpp:207 then 234-261), updating `prev_rectangle_` only afterwards (level.cpp:267).

**Why it matters:** For exactly one frame after respawn, `was_above` is evaluated against the
position the player *died* at, which is the single frame in the whole simulation where the previous
rectangle carries no information about where the player is now. A player who dies below a jump-through
platform and respawns above one falls straight through it. The other stale members are milder but
of a piece: `move_state_` carrying `on_ceiling` through a respawn is the failure described above,
and `air_time_` carrying a value means the first jump after respawn may get a shortened hold window.

**Remedy:** Set `prev_rectangle_ = rectangle_` and reset `move_state_` to `in_air`, `air_time_` to
zero and both timers in `respawn()` — or, better, make `respawn()` construct the mutable half of the
player's state from one place so a new member cannot be forgotten.

#### The game owns the input device, so there is no input seam to test or port

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.cpp:18-37`
- **Severity:** medium *(regraded from high)*
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree; T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** `PlayerInput` is game code that holds a `DirectX::GamePad*` and polls XInput directly,
deciding device enumeration, deadzone shape and trigger thresholds — all of which ARCHITECTURE
assigns to `engine/input/` with an `engine/input/xinput/` backend — while `engine/input/` contains
nothing but `connection_state.h`.

**Evidence:**

    // player_input.h:34,45
    explicit PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad);
    ...
    DirectX::GamePad* gamepad_ = nullptr;

    // player_input.cpp:18-24
    RawPlayerInput PlayerInput::raw_input(int gamepad_num) const
    {
    	auto result = RawPlayerInput();
        auto pad = this->gamepad_->GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR);
        if (pad.IsConnected())
        {
            result.left_analog_stick = Vector2F(pad.thumbSticks.leftX,
                -pad.thumbSticks.leftY);

`ls engine/input/` returns exactly one file. The pad itself comes from `engine/app/application.h:123`,
which hands the game the raw DirectXTK object: `DirectX::GamePad* gamepad() const;`. The same
device-polling loop is duplicated in `game/states/menu_input.cpp:18-35`, differing only in
`DEAD_ZONE_NONE` and which buttons it reads.

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE's tree names `input/` with `xinput/` inside it, and the boundary
table splits this as "input devices and action mapping" (engine) against "which actions exist and
their bindings" (game); today the game does both. Three concrete costs: the second platform is a
game rewrite rather than an engine addition, `PlayerInput` cannot be constructed in a test without
DirectXTK (see the testing finding), and every game built on this engine reimplements pad
enumeration and deadzones — which, as the deadzone finding above shows, is not a thing this codebase
has got right once. Regraded to medium because this is a boundary that has not been built yet rather
than a defect in code that exists, and because it restates an open finding from the previous review.

**Remedy:** Put a device/action-mapping layer behind an engine interface in `engine/input/` with the
XInput implementation in `engine/input/xinput/`, and let `PlayerInput` become the game-side binding
table only. `RawPlayerInput` and both consumers move with it.

#### Move player tuning out of a compiled header and into JSON

- **File:** `game/objects/player_consts.h:19-77`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T7 (data over code)

**What:** Every gameplay number the player has — gravity, jump curve, max velocity, acceleration,
health, regen, per-weapon damage — plus the sprite sheet, animation strip, sound bank and four sound
names, are compile-time constants in a header.

**Evidence:**

    const mattmath::Vector2F MAX_VELOCITY = { 800.0f, 1900.0f };
    constexpr float X_INITIAL_VELOCITY = 100.0f;
    constexpr float X_ACCELERATION = 900.0f;
    constexpr float X_DEACCELERATION = 2500.0f;
    constexpr float GRAVITY = 2000.0f;
    constexpr float JUMP_LAUNCH_VELOCITY = -600.0f;
    ...
    constexpr float SPRAY_DAMAGE = 0.01f;
    constexpr float JET_DAMAGE = 0.334f;
    ...
    const std::string SOUND_BANK = "sound_bank_1";
    const std::string DAMAGE_SOUND = "SplittingFireWood";

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY says "Tuning changes rebuild nothing", and CONVENTIONS says outright
that "A header full of numeric constants is usually tuning data in the wrong place — *which* and
*how much* belong in JSON (T7). Constants that stay in code live next to the one thing they
configure, not in a `consts` namespace collecting strays." `player_consts.h` is included by
`player.h`, which is included by `debug_text.h`, `level.h` and `player_builder.h`; I traced the
closure and it reaches **seven** translation units — `player.cpp`, `debug_text.cpp`, `level.cpp`,
`level_builder.cpp`, `player_builder.cpp`, `game_states.cpp` and `main.cpp`. (The reviewer said ten,
via `interface_gameplay.h`; that header does not include `player.h`.) So changing `GRAVITY` by 1.0
recompiles the level builder, the HUD and the whole state machine. The projectile damage constants
are worse than misplaced: they are a *weapon* property living in the player, sitting next to but
independent of `weapon_consts.h`, where the rest of each weapon's definition lives.

**Remedy:** Load the movement/health block from a player definition JSON at level load, and move the
per-projectile damage into the projectile definitions.

#### `Player` inherits two independent sprite layers, and pays for it twice

- **File:** `game/objects/player.h:63-64`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap — "inheritance and virtual dispatch are tools of last resort")

**What:** `Player` derives from both `TextureObject` and `AnimationObject`, which each derive from
`SpriteSheetObject` → `DrawObject` non-virtually, so it carries two `RenderResources*`, two sheet
handles for the *same* sheet, and two independent colour / rotation / origin / effects / layer-depth
sets.

**Evidence:**

    class Player final : public artattack::MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject,
                         public artattack::AnimationObject, public artattack::TextureObject

The cost is visible at every use site. The author has already had to document it inside `draw()`
(player.cpp:91-93):

    // Every base call is explicitly qualified: Player inherits DrawObject
    // twice, once through TextureObject and once through AnimationObject, and
    // the two subobjects carry independent colour/origin/rotation.

In `update_animation_state()` (player.cpp:64-67), one logical clip change costs two string→handle
resolutions of the same sheet name:

    const PlayerAnimationInfo& info = this->animation_info(new_animation_state);
    TextureObject::set_frame(info.sprite_sheet, info.uniform_texture);

    set_animation_strip_and_reset(info.sprite_sheet, info.animation);

And the constructor (player.cpp:27-32) hands `rotation` to both drawable bases but not to
`MovingObject`, giving `Player` three rotations; `respawn()` then resets the one that is never
drawn (player.cpp:1031, `MovingObject::set_rotation(0.0f)`).

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY permits a game to choose its own grammar behind the engine interfaces,
but also states that "everything it ships — the sample game, the tutorials — are value-first (T11)",
and Structural types designates the traditional player class as starter code "to copy into your game
and own". What is being handed over teaches quadruple inheritance with a duplicated base, where an
unqualified `origin()` is a compile error and `set_origin()` on one subobject silently does not
affect the other layer.

**Remedy:** Hold the uniform frame and the animated body as two named member sub-objects rather than
two base classes, so `Player` has one `DrawObject`-shaped concern and the two layers are named
rather than inherited.

#### Delete the seventeen dead private members

- **File:** `game/objects/player.h:221-255`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness)

**What:** Seventeen private members of `Player` are declared, defined and called from nowhere —
including a `set_input` that duplicates the live `set_player_input` verbatim — and three data
members exist only to serve them.

**Evidence:** I grepped each name across `game/` and `engine/` and confirmed every one has exactly
two hits, its declaration and its definition: `set_player_num`, `set_team`, `primary`, `set_primary`,
`secondary`, `set_secondary`, `set_team_colour`, `set_viewport`, `set_input`, `alter_health`,
`set_health`, `set_respawn_timer`, `alter_respawn_timer`, `score`, `set_score`, `alter_score`,
`set_showing_debug`. The duplicate pair:

    // player.cpp:957-960
    void Player::set_player_input(const PlayerInputData& input)
    {
    	this->input_ = input;
    }

    // player.cpp:1172-1175
    void Player::set_input(const PlayerInputData& input)
    {
    	this->input_ = input;
    }

Three fields are dead as a result, not two: `score_` (player.h:148) is written only by the dead
`set_score`/`alter_score` and read only by the dead `score()`; `secondary_type_` (player.h:159) and
`primary_type_` (player.h:158) are assigned in the constructor and read only by the dead
`secondary()` and `primary()`.

**Why it matters:** About eighty lines of `player.cpp` are definitions nothing reaches, and three
members carry values no code ever consumes — so a reader working out what a `Player` *is* has to
disprove seventeen of its verbs. In a file CONVENTIONS' no-huge-files guideline already has in its
sights ("a reader can no longer hold what it does in their head"), this is the cheapest third of the
fix. `set_score` in particular reads as an unimplemented scoring feature rather than as dead code.

**Remedy:** Delete all seventeen and the three members they are the only users of. If scoring is
planned, leave it out until it is written.

#### `Player::for_deletion()` is why leaving the level has to be fatal

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:141-144`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T6 ("not a licence for … treating expected absence as failure")

**What:** `Player` hardwires `for_deletion()` to `false` and does not override `set_for_deletion`, so
`Level`'s out-of-bounds handler has no verb available except `throw`, which kills the process.

**Evidence:**

    bool Player::for_deletion() const
    {
    	return false;
    }

`ICollisionGameObject::set_for_deletion` (i_collision_game_object.h:20) has an empty default body and
`Player` does not override it. `level.cpp:331-339` therefore reads:

    	// A player leaving the level is a genuine simulation failure, not a
    	// gameplay event, so it still reports loudly.
    	for (auto& player : *this->player_objects_)
    	{
    		if (this->is_object_out_of_bounds(player.get()))
    		{
    			throw std::runtime_error("Player out of bounds");
    		}
    	}

versus the projectile case twenty lines earlier (level.cpp:310-317), which calls
`object->set_for_deletion(true)` because `Projectile` overrides it (projectile.h:46).

**Why it matters:** This is new information about the item IMPLEMENTED.md records under "Known
remaining issues": the reason a player out of bounds is still a process kill is not only that the
author chose loudness, it is that `Player` exposes no other outcome to choose. And the recovery
already exists and is already correct — `respawn()` (player.cpp:1028-1038) teleports to
`respawn_position_`, zeroes velocity and `dx` and restores health and ammo, and `set_state(PlayerState)`
is public (player.h:125). Killing and respawning an out-of-bounds player is one line at the `Level`
end, so the cost of not terminating the process is approximately zero.

**Remedy:** Treat out-of-bounds as lethal (`set_state(PlayerState::dead)`) so the existing respawn
path recovers it, and keep the throw only for a bounds rectangle that is itself invalid.

#### `bounds()` is padded by a magic 200 because the weapon draws from inside the player

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:949-956`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T8 (performance over customisability); ARCHITECTURE/The boundary

**What:** `Player::bounds()` inflates its rectangle by an unexplained `(200, 200)` in all four
directions to cover a weapon that is not part of the player.

**Evidence:**

    RectangleF Player::bounds() const
    {
        // Inflated to take in the weapon, which is drawn from Player::draw but
        // is not inside the player's own rectangle.
        RectangleF player_and_weapon_rect = this->rectangle_;
        player_and_weapon_rect.inflate(Vector2F(200.0f, 200.0f));
        return player_and_weapon_rect;
    }

`RectangleF::inflate` (matt_math.cpp:924-930) subtracts the amount from the origin and adds twice it
to each extent, so a 52x120 player (`player_consts.h:20`) reports **452x520 — about 38 times the
area**, not the "four and a half times" the raw review claimed. The actual requirement is derivable:
the largest weapon in `weapon_consts.h` is 100x50 with a 20px offset, so about 120px from the
player's centre in x and about 45 in y. Nothing in the code derives 200 from either.

**Why it matters:** `bounds()` is brand-new API whose whole justification (i_game_object.h:43-60) is
that reporting an extent lets the scene build an index and query it, and that "It is the input a
broad phase wants too". An object that pads its extent by a guessed constant makes that index answer
wrong for the future broad phase, not just for culling — and wrong in the expensive direction, since
every player is a 452x520 query box. The underlying cause is that `Player::draw` draws a second
entity (`primary_->draw(...)`, player.cpp:103) that the level never registered, so the weapon has no
bounds of its own to contribute.

**Remedy:** Have `Weapon` report its own drawn rectangle and union it into `Player::bounds()`, so the
number is derived rather than guessed.

#### Nothing in this group has a test, including the one pure function

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.cpp:39-118`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** `PlayerInput::calculate_player_input` is a `static` pure function from two PODs to a POD —
the one piece of logic in this group that needs no window, no device and no engine — and it has no
test, as does nothing else here.

**Evidence:**

    PlayerInputData PlayerInput::calculate_player_input(
        const RawPlayerInput& current, const RawPlayerInput& previous)

`tests/` contains only `tests/assets/asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp`, `tests/core/name_table_tests.cpp`,
`tests/core/registry_tests.cpp`, `tests/math/collision_tools_tests.cpp` and `tests/math/math_tests.cpp`.
There is no `tests/game/` directory and `game/CMakeLists.txt` builds one target, `ArtAttackGame`.

**Why it matters:** The behaviours this function encodes are exactly the ones that are hard to reason
about and easy to break: the jump edge is the OR of a button edge and a trigger threshold crossing,
the pause and debug edges fire on *release*, the shoot trigger is a level and not an edge, and the
stick deadzone is applied to the x component rather than the magnitude — which is a live defect
filed above and would have been a one-line table test. The rest of the group is harder: `Player`'s
constructor takes a `RenderResources*` and an `AudioResources*` and resolves four wave handles out of
a `SoundBank` in its body (player.cpp:44-49), so constructing one headlessly needs those services to
be constructible without a device. That is worth recording as a consequence of the renderer-seam work,
but `calculate_player_input` needs none of it.

**Remedy:** Add `tests/game/player_input_tests.cpp` covering the four edge behaviours and the
deadzone. It requires only compiling `player_input.cpp` into a test target.

#### The headers are not self-contained, and the PCH is force-included so nothing proves it

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.h:34`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files ("own header first — proving every header compiles on its own")

**What:** `player_input.h` names `DirectX::GamePad` without including `<GamePad.h>`, and the PCH is
force-included into every translation unit by the build, so the "does this header compile on its own"
proof the include-order rule exists to provide cannot happen at all.

**Evidence:**

    // player_input.h — includes are <vector>, player_input_data.h, engine/math/matt_math.h
    explicit PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad);
    ...
    DirectX::GamePad* gamepad_ = nullptr;

`engine/math/matt_math.h` includes `SimpleMath.h`, `shape_type.h`, `<d3d11.h>`, `<cmath>`, `<memory>`,
`<string>`, `<vector>` — no `GamePad.h`. The only `#include "GamePad.h"` in the tree is
`game/pch.h:64`. And `game/CMakeLists.txt:72` says

    target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)

which the generated `build.ninja` turns into `/FI…/cmake_pch.hxx` on every source file. So the PCH
arrives before line 1 of every `.cpp` regardless of what that `.cpp` writes, and the
`#include "game/pch.h"` at the top of `player.cpp`, `player_input.cpp` and `player_builder.cpp` is
now dead text left over from the vcxproj build — it hits `#pragma once` and does nothing.

*(I checked and rejected the reviewer's second example: `player_consts.h` gets `std::string` through
`engine/math/colour.h` → `matt_math.h` → `<string>`, and `FLT_MIN` through `SimpleMath.h` →
`DirectXMath.h` → `<float.h>`. Both are include-what-you-use violations, but neither depends on the
PCH.)*

**Why it matters:** Every header in the game currently has an unknown number of missing includes, and
the count will only be discovered when something outside `ArtAttackGame` includes one — a test target,
or a user copying `Player` into their own project as the sample is meant to invite. That is precisely
the moment "copy this file into your game and own it" has to work.

**Remedy:** Include what each header uses. Then prove it: a small target that compiles each header
alone, with no PCH, is the only thing that keeps this from regressing — reordering the `.cpp`
includes cannot, because `/FI` wins. Deleting the now-dead `#include "game/pch.h"` lines is a
separate, free cleanup.

#### Rename the constants: SCREAMING means macro

- **File:** `game/objects/player_consts.h:19-120`
- **Severity:** low *(regraded from medium)*
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never ("SCREAMING constants — screaming means macro, nothing else")

**What:** All ~60 constants in `player_consts.h` are SCREAMING_SNAKE, and `player_input.h` adds four
more, so a reader cannot tell a macro from a value anywhere in this group.

**Evidence:**

    constexpr float STARTING_HEALTH = 1.0f;
    constexpr float HEALTH_REGEN_DELAY = 5.0f;
    constexpr auto DEFAULT_TEAM = PlayerTeam::a;
    const mattmath::Colour DEFAULT_TEAM_COLOUR = colour_consts::GRAY;

    // player_input.h:9-15
    constexpr float TRIGGER_SHOOT_THRESHOLD = 0.6f;
    constexpr float TRIGGER_JUMP_THRESHOLD = 0.6f;
    constexpr float STICK_DEADZONE = 0.5f;
    constexpr int MAX_PAD_COUNT = 4;

`player.cpp:6` then does `using namespace player_consts;`, dropping all sixty names into the file's
lookup so that `GRAVITY`, `MAX_VELOCITY` and `DEFAULT_SIZE` read at the use site exactly like
preprocessor symbols.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS names this in the "Never" list precisely so that "a screaming name
always signals preprocessor danger and nothing else ever does". Four conventions passes have already
run over this tree and this one was not among them, so the file now mixes freshly-conformant
`PlayerTeam::a` enumerators with `DEFAULT_TEAM`. Low rather than medium because the consequence is
reader confusion with no runtime effect — but it is in an exemplar file a stranger is invited to copy.

**Remedy:** Rename to `snake_case` in the same pass that moves the tuning to JSON — most of these
names disappear rather than get renamed.

#### The debug overlay prints "invalid" for a real move state

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:1251-1271`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** —

**What:** `player_move_state_string()` has no case for `PlayerMoveState::dropping_down`, so the debug
HUD reports a legitimate state as `"invalid"`.

**Evidence:**

    switch (this->move_state_)
    {
    case PlayerMoveState::on_ground:
    ...
    case PlayerMoveState::in_air:
        return "in_air";
    case PlayerMoveState::jumping:
        return "jumping";
    };
    	return "invalid";

`dropping_down` is a real enumerator (player.h:28), set by `update_movement` (player.cpp:879) and read

`move_state_string += player->player_move_state_string();`. `/W4` does not catch it — C4061/C4062 are
off by default.

**Why it matters:** The state lasts one frame, so the reader most likely to hit it is someone
debugging the drop-through-platform path — the exact case where being told the state is "invalid"
sends them looking for a bug that is not there.
