#### Make the level JSON type keys snake_case like every other name in the project

- **File:** `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:20-36`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Data

**What:** The registry keys the builder dispatches on are PascalCase type names and
SCREAMING_SNAKE collision names, while the surrounding JSON keys are snake_case — so a level
object reads in three casing conventions at once.

**Evidence:**

    std::string type = json["type"].GetString();
    if (type == "Structure")
    {
        CollisionObjectType col_type;
        std::string collision_type = json["collision_type"].GetString();
        if (collision_type == "STRUCTURE")
        {
            col_type = CollisionObjectType::structure;
        }
        else if (collision_type == "STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH")

with the same shape at `:68` (`"StructurePaintable"` / `"STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE"`) and `:130`
(`"StructureRamp"` / `"STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT"` / `"STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT"`).

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Data is unambiguous — "JSON keys, asset names, registry
keys, spawn-group names: snake_case, same as code-side variables, so a definition reads
continuously from file to loader" — and the JSON *keys* here (`type`, `collision_type`,
`sheet_name`, `paintable_faces`) already follow it; only the values do not. A level file
currently reads `"type": "StructurePaintable", "collision_type": "STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE"`.
These strings are the registry keys PHILOSOPHY (Content and assets) says the object builder
will be keyed on — "The object builder is a `map<string, factory>` the game registers into"
— so fixing them after that registry exists means migrating every level file of every game
built on the engine, rather than three files in this repo. The SCREAMING values are also
among the last places in the tree where a screaming name is not a macro, which is the exact
property CONVENTIONS says the rule is protecting.

**Remedy:** Rename to `structure`, `structure_paintable`, `structure_ramp` and
`structure_jump_through` in the three level files and the builder, before the string set
becomes a published format.

#### Fix the include discipline: PCH first, own header never, and no block ordered

- **File:** `game/objects/structure.cpp:1-2`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** Every `.cpp` in this group opens with `#include "game/pch.h"` before its own
header while CMake force-includes the same PCH anyway, so the "proving every header compiles
on its own" guarantee is not merely skipped but *unavailable* — and the headers themselves
prove it, because none of the four is self-contained and none orders its includes.

**Evidence:**

    #include "game/pch.h"
    #include "game/objects/structure.h"

Identical at `paint_tile.cpp:1-2`, `structure_paintable.cpp:1-2` and
`level_object_builder.cpp:1-2`; all 46 game translation units open this way. The CMake side,
`game/CMakeLists.txt:72`:

    target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)

The headers that never get compiled first, and so never get checked:

    // level_object_builder.h — uses std::vector at :17, includes only <memory>
    #include "game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h"
    #include <memory>
    #include "rapidjson/document.h"
    #include "game/objects/structure_paintable.h"
    #include "engine/audio/audio_resources.h"

    // paint_tile.h — uses std::string at :14, includes no <string>
    #include "game/objects/player_team.h"
    #include "engine/render/texture_object.h"
    #include "game/objects/team_colour.h"
    #include "game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h"
    #include "engine/render/animation_object.h"

Both compile only because `engine/math/matt_math.h` happens to include `<string>` and
`<vector>` (matt_math.h:8-9) several levels down.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Files gives the rule and its purpose in one sentence:
"Include order: own header first — proving every header compiles on its own — then engine
headers, then external, then standard library." The engine already follows it
(`engine/render/animation_object.cpp:1` is its own header, and there is no PCH anywhere in
`engine/`), so the two halves of the same repo build under different rules. Because
`target_precompile_headers` injects `pch.h` ahead of the first line of every game TU, a game
header that forgets `<string>` or `<vector>` can never fail — and two of the four here have.
`game/pch.h:63,65,68,70` also pulls `Effects.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `Model.h` and
`PostProcess.h` into all 46 game TUs — 3D DirectXTK headers in a project whose non-goals list
3D — which is a standing tax on the build time PHILOSOPHY calls "a maintained property" and a
"build-time regression is a defect".

**Remedy:** Delete the explicit `#include "game/pch.h"` lines, put each file's own header
first, order the remaining blocks engine → external → standard library, add the standard
headers each file actually uses, and either drop the PCH or trim it to what a 2D game needs.

#### Reconcile the extents: StructurePaintable reports neither what it draws nor what it collides on

- **File:** `game/objects/structure_paintable.h:32-56`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering

**What:** `StructurePaintable` never overrides `bounds()`, so it inherits `Structure`'s
sprite rectangle while drawing splashes that extend up to 10 units outside it; and
`Structure` carries two independent extents — the sprite rectangle and the cloned collision
shape — with nothing in the header saying which is authoritative or that they must agree.

**Evidence:** `StructurePaintable` overrides `update`, `draw`, `on_collision` and
`paint_total`, and nothing else:

    void update(float dt) override;
    void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
        const mattmath::Camera& camera) const override;
    void on_collision(const ICollisionGameObject* other) override;

    PaintTotal paint_total() const override;

so culling uses `structure.cpp:36-39`:

    RectangleF Structure::bounds() const
    {
        return this->sprite_rectangle_;
    }

while the drawn splash is 24x24 centred on a 4x12 tile (`paint_tile.h:19`,
`paint_tile.cpp:24-30`, `:49`):

    const static mattmath::RectangleF SPLASH_RECTANGLE = { 0.0f, 0.0f, THICKNESS * 2.0f, THICKNESS * 2.0f };
    ...
    this->splash_.set_rectangle_center(rectangle.center());
    ...
    this->splash_.draw_with_colour(sprite_batch, camera, tint);

**Why it matters:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:43` documents `bounds()` as "The object's
drawn extent, in world space", and PHILOSOPHY says "Objects expose bounds; the scene culls."
A top-band tile at `(left + 4i, top, 4, 12)` has centre `(left + 4i + 2, top + 6)`, so its
splash spans `y ∈ [top − 6, top + 18]` and `x ∈ [left + 4i − 10, left + 4i + 14]` — 6 units
above the structure and 10 to its left. `Level::draw_player_view_level` culls collision
objects on `object->bounds().intersects(camera_view)` (`level.cpp:545`), so a painted
structure is dropped while a fringe of its splashes would still be on screen. Separately,
`Level::is_object_out_of_bounds` reads `object->shape()->bounding_box()`
(`level.cpp:711-715`) off the cloned `collision_shape_`, not `bounds()`, so two different
extents answer two different questions about the same object and `structure.h` documents
neither.

I regraded this from the reviewer's medium. Their anchor, `PaintTile::bounds()`
(`paint_tile.cpp:128-131`), is unreachable — no pointer of any interface type points at a
`PaintTile`, so the scene never culls on it (see the first finding). What is live is the
missing override, and its worst case is a 10-unit under-report on a structure hundreds of
units wide, at the exact viewport edge. The splash overhang itself is already on record from
the previous review (`PaintTile.cpp` finding 1). The reason to fix it anyway is forward-looking
and stated in the header comment that introduced `bounds()` (`c040c36`): it exists so a future
`Scene` can build an index once instead of interrogating objects one at a time, and an index
built from an under-reported extent is wrong everywhere at once.

**Remedy:** Override `bounds()` on `StructurePaintable` to return the sprite rectangle
inflated by the splash half-extent, and state in `structure.h` whether the sprite rectangle
is required to contain the collision shape — asserting it in the constructor if so.

#### Cut the using-directive stack in structure_paintable.cpp

- **File:** `game/objects/structure_paintable.cpp:4-8`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Namespaces

**What:** Five `using namespace` directives open the file, two of them constant namespaces,
so `WIDTH`, `HEIGHT` and `THICKNESS` appear unqualified in `generate_paint_tiles` with no
indication at the use site of which namespace owns them.

**Evidence:**

    using namespace DirectX;
    using namespace mattmath;
    using namespace paint_tile_consts;
    using namespace structure_paintable_consts;
    using namespace artattack;

used at `:98` and `:116`:

    static_cast<int>(std::fabs(this->rectangle().width / WIDTH));
    ...
    THICKNESS);

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Namespaces allows `using namespace mattmath;` in a `.cpp`
because "math reads badly fully qualified" and says others "are used sparingly". Five is not
sparingly, and the two constant namespaces are the ones that cost clarity rather than buy it:
a reader of `generate_paint_tiles` — the function with two shipped face-mapping bugs behind
it — cannot tell from the line that `WIDTH` is the paint tile's width rather than the
structure's, and the day `structure_paintable_consts` gains a `WIDTH` this file either
becomes ambiguous or silently changes meaning depending on declaration visibility. T4 is
explicit that a clever line is a tax levied on every future visit.

**Remedy:** Keep `mattmath` and `artattack`, drop the two constant namespaces, and qualify
`paint_tile_consts::WIDTH` at the six use sites in `generate_paint_tiles`.

#### Document the non-owning pointers as loans

- **File:** `game/objects/structure_paintable.h:66`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes

**What:** The `SoundBank*`, `RenderResources*` and `const AudioResources*` members carry no
note of who owns them or why they outlive the holder, even though the members declared
immediately beside them carry three lines of history each.

**Evidence:**

    // By value. This was a reference bound to a vector local to
    // LevelObjectBuilder::build_collision_object, so it dangled for the whole
    // life of every paintable structure in the level.
    PaintableFaces faces_ = PaintableFaces();
    std::vector<PaintTile> generate_paint_tiles() const;
    artattack::SoundBank* sound_bank_ = nullptr;

and `level_object_builder.h:28-29`:

    artattack::RenderResources* render_resources_ = nullptr;
    const artattack::AudioResources* audio_resources_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes states "A non-owning pointer is a
documented loan: the member declaration says who owns the object and why it outlives the
holder." The contrast sits inside one class: `faces_` and `paint_sound_` each carry three
lines of history, and the `SoundBank*` between them — the one member whose validity depends
on something outside the object — carries none. The answer is not obvious: the bank is owned
by `AudioResources`, which is owned by the application shell, and the deliberate decision
recorded at `engine/audio/audio_resources.h:34-37` is that banks are never released on device
loss *because* live objects hold exactly this pointer. That reasoning is written down in the
engine and invisible at the place that depends on it.

One correction to the reviewer's version: they claimed the `const` on `audio_resources_`
guarantees nothing "because `sound_bank() const` returns a mutable pointer that `on_collision`
plays through". `SoundBank::play_wave` is itself `const` (`sound_bank.h:45`), so nothing is
mutated through that pointer. The real, smaller T5 point stands: `AudioResources::sound_bank()
const` hands back a non-const `SoundBank*`, so the `const` on the parameter and the member
propagates nothing a reader can rely on, and `sound_bank_` could be `const SoundBank*` today.

**Remedy:** Add the one-line ownership note to each of the three members, naming the
application shell as the owner and the reason it outlives the level; make `sound_bank_` a
`const SoundBank*`.

#### set_for_deletion is a request half the implementers silently refuse

- **File:** `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:17-20`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T6 (also T5)
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `for_deletion()` is pure virtual, so every collidable must answer it, while its
setter is a defaulted no-op — so `set_for_deletion(true)` followed by `for_deletion()`
returning `false` is a documented, silent outcome, and `Level` drives the deletion path
through exactly that pair.

**Evidence:**

    virtual bool for_deletion() const = 0;

    // Requests removal at the end of the frame. Objects that are part of the
    // level's fixed geometry (structures, paint tiles) cannot be removed and
    // ignore this by default.
    virtual void set_for_deletion(bool /*for_deletion*/) {}

`Structure` accepts the default and hardcodes the answer (`structure.cpp:56-59`), as does
`PaintTile` (`paint_tile.cpp:124-127`); only `Projectile` overrides the setter
(`projectile.h:46`). `Level::update_level_logic` (`level.cpp:310-317`) calls it on every
collision object in the list:

    for (auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
    {
        if (!object->for_deletion() &&
            this->is_object_out_of_bounds(object.get()))
        {
            object->set_for_deletion(true);
        }
    }

**Why it matters:** T6 is "loud failure over graceful degradation" — "when the engine can't
do what was asked, it says so immediately". Here the caller asks an object to retire, the
object declines, and nothing anywhere records that the request was made and dropped. The
loop above runs over structures as well as projectiles, so a level whose `out_of_bounds`
rectangle does not cover a structure produces a request that vanishes: no error, no log, no
change. That is a level-authoring mistake with no failure mode. T5's framing is the sharper
one: an object that cannot be removed should not have a removal setter to ignore — the
distinction belongs in the type system or in two lists, not in a virtual that returns
silence. Nothing in the shipped levels triggers it today, which is why this is low rather
than higher; the comment documenting the behaviour is what makes it a design choice worth
questioning rather than an oversight.

Note this is *new* code relative to the previous review, whose `ICollisionGameObject`
finding 5 complained about the opposite problem — "an object can only be *asked* whether it
wants to die … there is no interface to tell one to die". The setter that answered it was
added with a silent-refusal default.

**Remedy:** Make `set_for_deletion` pure virtual and have fixed geometry throw or assert on
`true`; or, better, take lifetime off the object entirely — a `destroy(handle)` queue the
level drains at a defined point, which is where PHILOSOPHY's `Scene` will need it anyway.

#### An engine header documents itself against a type that lives in the game

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:53-56`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/The boundary
- **Origin:** added-by-verifier

**What:** `IGameObject`'s documentation for `bounds()` explains the design by referring to
`ICollisionGameObject::shape()` — a type that lives in `game/objects/` and that the engine
target cannot see.

**Evidence:**

    // It is the input a broad phase wants too: "what overlaps this view"
    // and "which pairs overlap each other" are one query against one
    // structure. ICollisionGameObject::shape() stays the fine half of that
    // pair; this is the coarse half.

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY/The boundary sets the test: "Engine headers contain no game
nouns … The litmus test for any file: if a game built on the engine — yours or a stranger's
— would need to edit it, it is game code." This creates no compile dependency, which is why
it is low, but it is the only place in `engine/` that mentions a game type at all (I grepped
`engine/` for both `CollisionObjectType` and `ICollisionGameObject`; this comment is the sole
hit), and it makes an engine header's own explanation unverifiable from inside the engine —
a stranger reading `engine/core/i_game_object.h` cold is pointed at a header that is not
theirs and will not exist in their project. It also goes stale the moment the engine grows
the `CollisionObject` interface PHILOSOPHY/The object model promises, at which point the
comment names the wrong type.

**Remedy:** Rewrite the sentence in engine vocabulary — "a shape interface supplies the fine
half of that pair; this is the coarse half" — and re-point it at the engine's own
`CollisionObject` when that lands.

Nothing was rejected in full; the corrections applied to surviving findings are listed here

## game-hud — HUD, debug text, match info

*Group `game-hud` · 16 findings (1 critical, 7 medium, 8 low) · source `review2/verified/game-hud.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened all ten assigned files in full and every line the reviewer cited,
including the ones outside the group: `game/objects/level.cpp` (the per-viewport
parallel draw), `level_builder.cpp/.h`, `player.cpp`, `weapon.cpp`, `main.cpp`,
`states/results_menu.cpp`, `engine/math/matt_math.h/.cpp`, `engine/math/colour.h`,
`engine/render/drawer.h`, `render_resources.h`, `sprite_sheet.cpp`,
`text_object.cpp`, `resolution_manager.h`, `engine/assets/json_loader.cpp`,
`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp`, the vendored `rapidjson/document.h` and
`rapidjson.h`, the vcpkg-built `DirectXTK/Src/SpriteFont.cpp` and `Inc/SpriteFont.h`,
plus `CMakeLists.txt`, `game/CMakeLists.txt` and `CMakePresets.json`.

**This reviewer's evidence held up unusually well.** Every quoted source line
matched the file, and every line number was right or within two lines. I could
not falsify a single observation. What needed correcting was severity and three
counts, not facts.

The critical finding is real and I strengthened it: I confirmed by overload
resolution — not by assumption — that these call sites bind to the UTF-8
`DrawString`, because `mattmath::Vector2F::xm_vector()` returns `XMFLOAT2` and
`Colour::xm_vector()` returns `XMVECTOR`, which selects `SpriteFont.cpp:581`
exactly. That overload is `const` and mutates a `unique_ptr<wchar_t[]>` owned by
the one shared `SpriteFont`. IMPLEMENTED.md records finding #16 as *partial* and
says outright that "the pure-read contract is the **only** thing making this
sound" — this is the hole in that contract, so it is not covered by anything
already fixed.

What I threw out is all consequence, not observation. I re-graded four findings
down. `LevelLoadedInfo`'s unchecked keys go high→medium: the crash is real but it
needs an authoring error in a hand-written level file that is correct today, so
it is a T6 robustness gap, not a live bug. `LevelEndInfo`'s six broken members and
the `TeamColourTools` heap allocation go medium→low: I verified all four of the
reviewer's arithmetic walks (900%/-800%, ±inf, 100%/0%, NaN) and they are exactly
right, and I re-confirmed by repo-wide grep that nothing calls them — which is
precisely why today's blast radius is zero. I also corrected three counts: it is
eleven of thirteen accessors unchecked (not nine of eleven), root `CMakeLists.txt`
lines 15-17 (not 14-16), and at least 16 of 46 TUs reach rapidjson (not "roughly
half"). And I removed one overclaim: ARCHITECTURE's "rapidjson reaches assets and
stops there" governs *engine module* direction, not game code, so that finding
stands on PHILOSOPHY's compile-speed and T7 rules instead.

I added four findings. The largest is one the reviewer noticed in their own summary
and then never filed: `colour_consts::TEAM_BLUE`…`TEAM_GREEN` are a team palette
sitting in `engine/math/colour.h` — game nouns inside MattMath, the module that is
supposed to depend on nothing. The second is a defect hiding immediately beneath
their `TeamColourPair::max` finding: `srand` is called nowhere in the repository,
so `rand()` runs from the default seed and the "random" team palette — and the
random weapon and random slot in `main_menu.cpp` — are identical on every launch.
The other two are `DebugText` building twenty-odd heap-allocated strings inside
`draw()`, and the MSVC-only `std::exception(const char*)` constructor in live code.

### Themes

- The one shared mutable object in an otherwise correct per-worker render design
  is inside a third-party `const` method, where neither the compiler nor the
  header comment claiming safety can see it.
- Validation is all-or-nothing per accessor: two keys throw naming the file, the
  other eleven index straight through rapidjson and return a null pointer, a
  silent `0.0f` or a silently empty array depending only on which getter was called.
- Copy-paste has already diverged where it matters: `draw_ammo` and `draw_health`
  are the same forty lines, but `Weapon` clamps its input and `Player` does not.
- Dead code carries wrong code forward: six `LevelEndInfo` members, `InterfaceDraw`,
  and two of three `TeamColourTools` statics have no caller, and every one of them
  is either wrong or contradicts a live function of the same name.
- The randomness in this game is not random, and nothing above it says so.
- Every header here declares tuning as `const static` SCREAMING_SNAKE at global
  namespace scope, and every `.cpp` includes `pch.h` before its own header — so
  the two conventions that would have caught this are both unenforced.

#### Fix the data race on `SpriteFont`'s shared UTF-8 conversion buffer

- **File:** `game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:156-202`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** threading
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed); PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering

**What:** Every text draw in this group passes a `const char*`, which binds to
DirectXTK's UTF-8 `DrawString`. That overload is declared `const` but converts the
string into a scratch `wchar_t` buffer owned by the `SpriteFont`, and one
`SpriteFont` is shared by all render workers — so N viewports concurrently write
and read the same array.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:156-166` — one shared font, two writes per call:

    SpriteFont* sprite_font = this->render_resources()->
        sprite_font(this->timer_font_);

    sprite_font->DrawString(
        sprite_batch,
        std::to_string(static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))).c_str(),
        (pos + (TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET * scale)).xm_vector(),
        TIMER_SHADOW_COLOUR.xm_vector(),
        0.0f,
        XMFLOAT2(0.0f, 0.0f),
        scale);

`game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:186-195` — the respawn timer, whose text
differs per player:

    SpriteFont* sprite_font = this->render_resources()->
        sprite_font(this->respawn_timer_font_);

    std::string text = std::to_string(static_cast<int>(timer) + 1);

    sprite_font->DrawString(
        sprite_batch,
        text.c_str(),

`game/objects/debug_text.cpp:106-117` — twenty lines, all per-player, in a loop:

    SpriteFont* sprite_font = this->render_resources()->sprite_font(
        this->font_);
    ...
        sprite_font->DrawString(
            sprite_batch,
            lines[i].c_str(),

The shared mutable state, `DirectXTK/Src/SpriteFont.cpp:66-67` and `365-371`:

    size_t utfBufferSize;
    std::unique_ptr<wchar_t[]> utfBuffer;
    ...
    const wchar_t* SpriteFont::Impl::ConvertUTF8(_In_z_ const char *text) noexcept(false)
    {
        if (!utfBuffer)
        {
            utfBufferSize = 1024;
            utfBuffer.reset(new wchar_t[1024]);
        }

and the exact overload these three call sites bind to, `SpriteFont.cpp:580-584`:

    // UTF-8
    void XM_CALLCONV SpriteFont::DrawString(_In_ SpriteBatch* spriteBatch, _In_z_ char const* text, XMFLOAT2 const& position, FXMVECTOR color, float rotation, XMFLOAT2 const& origin, float scale, SpriteEffects effects, float layerDepth) const
    {
        DrawString(spriteBatch, pImpl->ConvertUTF8(text), XMLoadFloat2(&position), color, rotation, XMLoadFloat2(&origin), XMVectorReplicate(scale), effects, layerDepth);
    }

**Why it matters:** I verified the overload resolution rather than assuming it.
`Vector2F::xm_vector()` returns `DirectX::XMFLOAT2` and `Colour::xm_vector()`
returns `XMVECTOR` (`engine/math/matt_math.h:413, 650`), so `(position=XMFLOAT2,
color=FXMVECTOR, origin=XMFLOAT2, scale=float)` selects `SpriteFont.cpp:581` —
the UTF-8 overload — at all three sites.

The path is fully reachable in the only mode this game has. `Level::draw` →
`draw_active_level` (`game/objects/level.cpp:392-416`) partitions the players
across the thread pool, and `Partitioner::partition(4, 16)`
(`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:5-23`) returns `(0,1) (1,2) (2,3) (3,4)` — I
traced the loop bound `i < num_partitions && i < num_elements`, so a 4-player
match is exactly four concurrent workers. Each worker runs
`draw_player_view_level` (`level.cpp:509-612`), which calls
`draw_gameplay_interface` at `:578` and `draw_debug_info` at `:594`. The font they
use is one object: `RenderResources::sprite_font(FontHandle)` returns a borrowed
pointer into a single `Registry<DirectX::SpriteFont>` (`render_resources.h:61, 90`).

Everything else in this design is correctly per-worker — its own `SpriteBatch`,
its own deferred context, a disjoint player slice — so this buffer is the only
shared writable object on the path, and it is invisible because the method is
`const` and mutates through `pImpl`. Two concrete failures: two players dead at
once write different respawn digits into one buffer, so a player can see the
other's number; two players with the overlay on interleave each other's debug
lines. Worse, on a font's first UTF-8 draw `utfBuffer` is null, so two workers can
both execute `utfBuffer.reset(new wchar_t[1024])` — one `reset` frees the array
the other is about to write through. I confirmed the exposure is asymmetric:
`courier_new_bold_16` is named by nothing but `DebugText::DEBUG_FONT`
(`debug_text.h:10`) and `samples/minimal`, so its buffer is genuinely still null
the first time the overlay is drawn concurrently; the two `gill_sans_*` fonts are
warmed single-threaded because `TextObject::remeasure()`
(`engine/render/text_object.cpp:112-118`) calls `MeasureString(text_.c_str())`,
which routes through the same `ConvertUTF8`. Those two race on content only.

IMPLEMENTED.md marks review finding #16 **partial** and states that "workers do
not own disjoint slices — every worker draws every object, so the pure-read
contract is the *only* thing making this sound." This is the hole in that
contract, and the comment at `interface_gameplay.h:51-57` asserts the opposite as
fact — "the only reason it is safe is that all of it arrives as parameters" —
which the next reader will believe.

**Remedy:** convert to `std::wstring` once and call the `wchar_t const*`
overloads, which touch no font state; or give each render worker its own
conversion buffer and pass `wchar_t const*` down. Then correct the comment in
`interface_gameplay.h`.

#### Check the level-file keys `LevelLoadedInfo` reads, or stop returning what rapidjson hands back

- **File:** `game/objects/level_loaded_info.cpp:37-101`
- **Severity:** medium *(re-graded from high)*
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** Eleven of the thirteen accessors index the document with unchecked
`operator[]` chains. Under `NDEBUG` a missing key yields a null value whose
`GetString()` returns a null pointer, whose `GetFloat()` returns `0.0f`, and whose
`GetArray()` is empty — so an authoring typo produces a crash, a silent zero, or a
silent empty list depending only on which getter you happened to call.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_loaded_info.cpp:90-101`:

    std::string LevelLoadedInfo::sound_bank_name() const
    {
        return this->json_doc_["sound"]["sound_bank_name"].GetString();
    }
    std::string LevelLoadedInfo::music_name() const
    {
        return this->json_doc_["sound"]["music_name"].GetString();
    }
    float LevelLoadedInfo::music_volume() const
    {
        return this->json_doc_["sound"]["music_volume"].GetFloat();
    }

`external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/document.h:1214` — the const `operator[]`
these calls take, which forwards to the mutating one:

    RAPIDJSON_DISABLEIF_RETURN(...,(const GenericValue&)) operator[](T* name) const { return const_cast<GenericValue&>(*this)[name]; }

`document.h:1226-1236` — the missing-member path:

    GenericValue& operator[](const GenericValue<Encoding, SourceAllocator>& name) {
        MemberIterator member = FindMember(name);
        if (member != MemberEnd())
            return member->value;
        else {
            RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(false);    // see above note
            alignas(GenericValue) thread_local static char buffer[sizeof(GenericValue)];
            return *new (buffer) GenericValue();

`external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/rapidjson.h:437` — the guard that is compiled out:

    #define RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(x) assert(x)

`document.h:1853, 2107-2109` — what `GetString()` does to that null value:

    const Ch* GetString() const { RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(IsString()); return DataString(data_); }
    ...
    static RAPIDJSON_FORCEINLINE const Ch* DataString(const Data& data) {
        return (data.f.flags & kInlineStrFlag) ? data.ss.str : RAPIDJSON_GETPOINTER(Ch, data.s.str);
    }

**Why it matters:** `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` (`CMakePresets.json:24`) defines
`NDEBUG`, so `assert` is a no-op and the three outcomes above are what actually
happen. A default-constructed `GenericValue` has a zeroed union, so `DataString`
returns `nullptr` and the implicit `const char*` → `std::string` conversion at
`:92` runs `strlen(nullptr)` — an access violation with no message.
`music_volume()` returns a silent `0.0f`; `out_of_bounds_rectangle()` returns a
zero rect; `decode_team_spawns_json` walks an empty array and returns no spawns.
`LevelBuilder::build_level` (`level_builder.cpp:34-83`) calls eight of these in a
row on a `LevelLoadedInfo` built from a hand-written file (`main.cpp:64-68`), and
the header names adding a stage as the expected workflow (`level_loaded_info.h:16-17`).
The class already knows how to do this right — `required_string`
(`level_loaded_info.cpp:17-27`) throws naming the file and the key.

*Re-graded from high.* The reviewer's mechanism is exactly right and I could not
break any step of it, but reaching it requires an authoring mistake in content
that is correct in the repository today. This is a T6 robustness gap that will
bite the next person adding a stage, not a live defect — and the header comment at
`:42-46` calling the rest "the loaders' standing validation debt" is an accurate
description of a defect, not a retirement of one.

**Remedy:** add `required_object` / `required_float` / `required_array` beside
`required_string`, each throwing with the path and the key, and route the eleven
accessors through them. Also reject a document whose root is not an object.

#### `TeamColourPair::max` aliases the last enumerator, so `blue_yellow` can never be rolled

- **File:** `game/objects/team_colour.cpp:27-42`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** `rand() % static_cast<int>(TeamColourPair::max)` computes `rand() % 2`
because `max` is *equal to* `blue_yellow` rather than one past it, so one of the
three palettes is never selected and `case 2:` is unreachable.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/team_colour.h:16-22`:

    enum class TeamColourPair
    {
        blue_orange,
        pink_green,
        blue_yellow,
        max = blue_yellow
    };

`game/objects/team_colour.cpp:27-42`:

    TeamColour TeamColourTools::generate_random_team_colour()
    {
        int enum_max = static_cast<int>(TeamColourPair::max);
        int random = rand() % enum_max;
        switch (random)
        {
        case 0:
            return BLUE_ORANGE;
        case 1:
            return PINK_GREEN;
        case 2:
            return BLUE_YELLOW;

**Why it matters:** `blue_yellow` is `2`, so `enum_max` is `2` and `random` is
`{0, 1}`. `BLUE_YELLOW` is dead — and it is also the pair the `TeamColour` default
member initialisers name (`team_colour.h:8-9`), so the default and the roll
disagree about what the palette set is. The single caller is
`LevelBuilder::build_level` (`level_builder.cpp:39`), so every match ever played
picks from two of the three palettes. `case 2:` compiles to nothing and `/W4 /WX`
cannot see it because the switch is over a runtime `int`.

The correct mapping is already in the file and unused:
`TeamColourTools::team_colours(TeamColourPair)` (`team_colour.cpp:44-57`) is an
exhaustive switch over the enum. `generate_random_team_colour` re-implements it by
hand over integers, which is how the two got out of step.

**Remedy:** make the sentinel one past the end (`count`, not `max = blue_yellow`)
and index a `constexpr std::array<TeamColour, 3>` — or call the existing
`team_colours(static_cast<TeamColourPair>(roll))` — so adding a palette cannot
desynchronise the two.

#### `srand` is never called, so the "random" team palette is the same on every launch

- **File:** `game/objects/team_colour.cpp:30`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time); T9 (built over bought — built code meets library standard)
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** `generate_random_team_colour()` draws from `rand()`, and `srand` is
called nowhere in the repository, so the sequence starts from the implementation's
default seed on every run. The palette a match gets is a deterministic function of
how many `rand()` calls the session has made — identical across launches.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/team_colour.cpp:29-30`:

    int enum_max = static_cast<int>(TeamColourPair::max);
    int random = rand() % enum_max;

A repo-wide grep for `srand` across every `.cpp` and `.h` returns nothing. The
only three `rand()` call sites are:

    game/objects/team_colour.cpp:30   int random = rand() % enum_max;
    game/states/main_menu.cpp:1499    int random = rand() % static_cast<int>(WeaponType::max_prim_wep);
    game/states/main_menu.cpp:1886    return rand() % this->random_slot();

**Why it matters:** C's `rand()` behaves as if `srand(1)` had been called, so the
whole sequence is fixed at process start. Two of the three consumers are
player-facing features whose entire purpose is variety — the random weapon pick
and the random slot pick in the main menu — and the third decides the colours of
the match. Start the game, take the same path through the menus, and you get the
same "random" weapon and the same palette every single time. Nothing above these
calls seeds anything, and no test covers them (see the testing finding below), so
this has never had a chance to be noticed.

It compounds the off-by-one above: with `max = blue_yellow` the roll already only
reaches two of three palettes, and with a fixed seed a given session reaches one
of those two by a fixed rule.

**Remedy:** T9 says built code must meet library standard, and `rand()` does not —
use a `std::mt19937` seeded once from `std::random_device` at start-up, handed to
the game as an explicit service (or, keeping it small, a file-local
`std::mt19937` behind a `random_index(n)` free function), and delete all three
`rand()` calls. That also removes the modulo bias and makes the roll testable by
injecting a seed.

#### Clamp the health bar, or stop drawing a rectangle whose right edge is left of its left edge

- **File:** `game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:128-146`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness — duplication is the opposite of clarity)

**What:** `draw_health` multiplies the fill width by an unclamped `health`, and
`Player::health_` goes negative on the killing blow and stays negative into the
respawn, so the HUD builds a `RectangleI` with a negative width.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:128-139`:

        //fill box
        float border = resolution.x * BOX_FILL_BORDER;
        Vector2F fill_pos = position + Vector2F(border, border);
        Vector2F fill_size = Vector2F(size.x - 2.0f * border,
            size.y - 2.0f * border);
        fill_size.x *= health;

        RectangleI fill_rect = RectangleI(
            static_cast<int>(fill_pos.x),
            static_cast<int>(fill_pos.y),
            static_cast<int>(fill_size.x),
            static_cast<int>(fill_size.y));

`engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2038-2047` — width becomes `right`:

    RECT RectangleI::win_rect() const
    {
        RECT result = {
            static_cast<long>(this->x),
            static_cast<long>(this->y),
            static_cast<long>(this->x + this->width),
            static_cast<long>(this->y + this->height)
        };

`engine/render/sprite_sheet.cpp:67-85` — that `RECT` is the destination rectangle
handed straight to `SpriteBatch::Draw`.

The twin, `game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:84-101`, is the same block with
`ammo` in place of `health`.

**Why it matters:** `Player::on_projectile_collision` subtracts damage with no
floor (`game/objects/player.cpp:682-707`); death is only *detected* on the next
`update` (`player.cpp:738-742`) and health is only reset in `respawn()`
(`player.cpp:1034`), so between the killing hit and the respawn — up to
`RESPAWN_DELAY = 3.0f` (`player_consts.h:42`) — `health()` is negative and
`Level::draw_player_view_level` passes it to the HUD unconditionally
(`level.cpp:581`). With `BALL_DAMAGE = 0.201f` (`player_consts.h:67`) landing on a
player at 0.05 health, `fill_size.x` comes out around −21 px in a quarter-screen
viewport and around −42 px full-screen, which `win_rect()` turns into
`right = x − 21`; SpriteBatch computes `right − left`, so it draws a mirrored fill
bar extending left out of the health box, over the rest of the HUD, once per death
per match. (The reviewer's "about −55" was arithmetically optimistic; the defect
is not.)

The reason this is worth more than its pixel count is the second half:
`draw_ammo` and `draw_health` are forty duplicated lines, and `Weapon` *does*
clamp its input on both sides (`game/objects/weapon.cpp:216-218, 227-229`) while
`Player` clamps only the upper bound (`player.cpp:769-771`) — so the copies have
silently diverged in exactly the property that makes one of them safe. That is
the failure mode CONVENTIONS' "no copy-paste in the name of readability" exists
to prevent.

**Remedy:** clamp the fraction to `[0, 1]` at the top of one shared
`draw_bar(sprite_batch, resolution, fraction, colour, position)` and delete the
duplicate. Clamping `Player::health_` at zero on damage is the better fix but a
wider one.

#### The team palette is a game noun living in MattMath

- **File:** `game/objects/team_colour.h:8-9, 26-40`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** architecture
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy); ARCHITECTURE/Modules and The boundary
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** `team_colour.h` correctly does not duplicate the engine's colour
constants — but the dependency runs the wrong way. The five team colours it names
are defined in `engine/math/colour.h`, inside `MattMath`, the module ARCHITECTURE
says may depend on nothing and which contains no game vocabulary at all.

**Evidence:**

`engine/math/colour.h:308-312` — a paint-shooter's team palette, in the maths library:

    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_BLUE = { 6, 52, 204, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_YELLOW = { 255, 255, 0, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_ORANGE = { 255, 127, 0, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_PINK = { 255, 0, 127, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_GREEN = { 0, 255, 0, 255 };

`game/objects/team_colour.h:8-9, 26-40` — the whole of this group's palette is
built from them:

    mattmath::Colour team_a = colour_consts::TEAM_BLUE;
    mattmath::Colour team_b = colour_consts::TEAM_YELLOW;
    ...
    const TeamColour BLUE_ORANGE =
    {
        colour_consts::TEAM_BLUE,
        colour_consts::TEAM_ORANGE
    };

Every consumer of the five names is game code — `team_colour.h` and three menu
headers (`end_menu.h:21`, `main_menu.h:28`, `pause_menu.h:17`). Nothing in
`engine/` reads them.

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY's litmus test is explicit — "Engine headers contain
no game nouns — no team, weapon, paint, menu or asset name… if a game built on the
engine — yours or a stranger's — would need to edit it, it is game code."
ARCHITECTURE puts `math` at the bottom of the dependency graph with "may depend
on: nothing", and names `Team` among the types the engine must not have. A
stranger's game linking `MattMath` gets this game's team colours. This is small
and cheap to fix now and gets harder once the split lands, because the five
constants have to land on the game side of a wall they currently sit behind — and
they are reachable today only because `colour.h` is a global-namespace header the
game can reopen.

**Remedy:** move the five `TEAM_*` constants into `team_colour_consts` in
`game/objects/team_colour.h` (or into the level/HUD JSON, per T7), and have the
three menu headers name a game-side constant rather than `colour_consts::TEAM_ORANGE`.

#### Take `rapidjson::Document` out of a header that reaches every game state

- **File:** `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4, 30-31, 38`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** T7 (data over code — resolved at load); PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain
  ("Compile speed is a maintained property… a build-time regression is a defect")

**What:** `LevelLoadedInfo` stores a `rapidjson::Document` by value and returns
`const rapidjson::Value&` from two public accessors, which forces
`rapidjson/document.h` into its header and, through `game_data.h`, into every game
state and menu translation unit.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4, 30-31, 38`:

    #include "rapidjson/document.h"
    ...
    const rapidjson::Value& collision_objects_json() const;
    const rapidjson::Value& non_collision_objects_json() const;
    ...
    rapidjson::Document json_doc_;

`game/game_data.h:5`:

    #include "game/objects/level_loaded_info.h"

**Why it matters:** `game_data.h` is the service bag "every state, object and
drawable in this game is handed at construction" (its own header comment), and it
is included by `game/states/game_states.h` and `game/states/menu_data.h`. I
enumerated the includers: at least 16 of the game target's 46 translation units
reach `document.h` — a 3,044-line header that itself pulls in rapidjson's reader,
encodings and allocators — to hold two accessors returning a `const Value&`. The
game uses a PCH, but `game/pch.h` does not include rapidjson, so this cost is paid
per TU. PHILOSOPHY makes compile speed a maintained property and a build-time
regression a defect outright.

The public `const rapidjson::Value&` returns are the harder half, and they are the
T7 problem rather than the build one: they hand the parser's own type to
`LevelObjectBuilder`, so the level *format* is welded to rapidjson, and the
`Document` stays alive in the registry for the whole process rather than being
resolved to plain values at load — "Data is read, validated and resolved to
handles at load; the frame loop never sees it."

*Correction to the raw report:* it cited ARCHITECTURE's "rapidjson reaches
`assets` and stops there" as forbidding this. That sentence governs the *engine's*
module dependency direction; `LevelLoadedInfo` is game code, and a game is
entitled to parse JSON. The finding stands on compile speed and on T7, not on that
rule, and "roughly half of 46 TUs" is corrected to "at least 16".

**Remedy:** parse the document once in the constructor into plain structs (bounds,
spawns, sound settings) and drop the `Document` member, keeping the object-array
handoff behind a pimpl or a game-owned `LevelObjectsJson` type so `document.h`
stops at `level_loaded_info.cpp`.

#### Test `LevelEndInfo` and `TeamColour` — they need no device and there is nowhere to put a test

- **File:** `game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:5-129`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** No test covers any file in this group, although `LevelEndInfo` is
fourteen pure functions over two floats and `TeamColour` is a palette lookup —
neither touches D3D, a file, or a thread.

**Evidence:** the entire test tree is

    tests/assets/  asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp
    tests/core/    name_table_tests.cpp  registry_tests.cpp
    tests/math/    collision_tools_tests.cpp  math_tests.cpp

and the root `CMakeLists.txt:15-17` adds exactly those three directories. The
structural half is `game/CMakeLists.txt:11` — the game is
`add_executable(ArtAttackGame WIN32 …)`, so there is no library or object library
for a test target to link against.

`LevelEndInfo`'s entire dependency surface is `float team_a_area`,
`float team_b_area` and a `TeamColour` (`level_end_info.h:8-10`).

**Why it matters:** three of the correctness defects in this report are each one
assertion away from having been caught on the commit that wrote them.
`winning_percentage()` on `{90, 10}` returns 900. `generate_random_team_colour()`
called a hundred times returns two distinct values, not three — and returns the
*same* hundred values on every run. PHILOSOPHY's claim is that everything below
the platform edge is headlessly testable *because* the boundary makes it linkable;
these two types are the easiest possible demonstration of it, and the build offers
nowhere to demonstrate it.

**Remedy:** add `tests/game/` and give the game an object library (or a small
`ArtAttackGameLib`) that both the executable and the tests link, then pin
`winning_team`, the ratio guards, the percentage strings and the palette roll.

#### Delete or fix `LevelEndInfo`'s six callerless members — every one of them is wrong

- **File:** `game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:80-129`
- **Severity:** low *(re-graded from medium)*
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T3 (simplicity over accuracy — "a simple model still has exact, documented, tested semantics")

**What:** `winning_score`, `losing_score`, `winning_ratio`, `losing_ratio`,
`winning_percentage` and `losing_percentage` have no caller anywhere in the
repository, and each is arithmetically broken.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:97-129`:

    float LevelEndInfo::losing_score() const
    {
        PlayerTeam winning = this->winning_team();
        if (winning == PlayerTeam::a)
        {
            return this->team_b_area;
        }
        if (winning == PlayerTeam::b)
        {
            return this->team_a_area;
        }
        if (winning == PlayerTeam::none)
        {
            return this->team_a_area;
        }
        throw std::exception("No winning team");
    }
    float LevelEndInfo::winning_ratio() const
    {
        return this->winning_score() / this->losing_score();
    }
    float LevelEndInfo::losing_ratio() const
    {
        return this->losing_score() / this->winning_score();
    }
    float LevelEndInfo::winning_percentage() const
    {
        return 100.0f * this->winning_ratio();
    }
    float LevelEndInfo::losing_percentage() const
    {
        return 100.0f - this->winning_percentage();
    }

**Why it matters:** I re-ran the grep and confirmed all six appear only in
`level_end_info.h` and `level_end_info.cpp`; the only consumers of the type are
`results_menu.cpp:134, 145, 160, 231, 244`, which use
`team_a_percentage_string`, `team_b_percentage_string`, `winning_team_string`,
`team_a_ratio` and `team_b_ratio` — the five that are correct. I also re-walked
all four of the reviewer's cases and every one holds: a landslide (90 vs 10) gives
`winning_ratio() == 9.0`, `winning_percentage() == 900` and
`losing_percentage() == −800`; a shutout (90 vs 0) gives `+inf` and `−inf`; a draw
takes the `none` branch in *both* `winning_score` and `losing_score` so both return
`team_a_area`, reporting 100%/0%; and a 0-0 draw is `0.0f / 0.0f`, the NaN that
the surviving `team_a_ratio` guard at `:21-24` explicitly exists to avoid.
`losing_percentage` is defined over a different quantity than `winning_percentage`
— a share of the total versus a ratio of the two scores — which is why it can go
negative.

*Re-graded from medium.* The arithmetic is wrong in every case, and the six names
read exactly like what a results screen wants, so this is a genuine landmine for
whoever adds a "beat them by X%" line. But nothing calls them today, so today's
impact is zero, and severity should say so.

**Remedy:** delete all six. If they are wanted, define them over the total
(`winning_score() / (team_a_area + team_b_area)` with the guard `team_a_ratio`
already has) and fix the `none` branch of `losing_score` to return `team_b_area`.

#### Stop heap-allocating a stateless class to call a static function

- **File:** `game/objects/team_colour.h:43-54`
- **Severity:** low *(re-graded from medium)*
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap)

**What:** `TeamColourTools` has no data members and three `static` functions, yet
`LevelBuilder` owns one through a `unique_ptr`, allocates it in the constructor,
and calls a static member through the resulting pointer. Two of the three statics
have no caller, and one of those contradicts a live member function of the same name.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/team_colour.h:43-54`:

    class TeamColourTools
    {
    public:
        TeamColourTools() = default;

        static TeamColour generate_random_team_colour();

        static TeamColour team_colours(TeamColourPair team_colour);

        static mattmath::Colour team_colour(TeamColour team_colours,
            PlayerTeam team);
    };

`game/objects/level_builder.h:32` and `level_builder.cpp:26, 39`:

    std::unique_ptr<TeamColourTools> team_colour_ = nullptr;
    ...
    this->team_colour_ = std::make_unique<TeamColourTools>();
    ...
    const TeamColour team_colours = team_colour_->generate_random_team_colour();

The two policies under one name — `team_colour.cpp:14-25` (member, throws) against
`team_colour.cpp:59-71` (static, silently returns team A):

    const Colour& TeamColour::team_colour(PlayerTeam team) const
    {
        ...
        default:
            throw std::exception("Invalid team.");
    ...
    Colour TeamColourTools::team_colour(TeamColour team_colours, PlayerTeam team)
    {
        ...
        default:
            return team_colours.team_a;
    }

**Why it matters:** this is a heap allocation, an eight-byte member, a `unique_ptr`
destructor and an indirection whose entire purpose is to let
`generate_random_team_colour()` be spelled with a `->`. T11's argument is that
value-first C++ is what distinguishes this engine from the pointer-linked object
webs of the majors, and everything the engine ships is supposed to demonstrate it
— this is the anti-pattern, in game code that sits beside the sample. A grep
confirms `TeamColourTools::team_colours` and the static `team_colour` have no
caller, and the latter's `PlayerTeam::none` policy is the opposite of the live
member's, so whichever one the next reader finds first decides what a draw does.

*Re-graded from medium.* It is a clear tenet violation with a two-line fix and no
runtime consequence beyond one allocation at level-build time.

**Remedy:** delete the class and the `unique_ptr`, keep
`generate_random_team_colour()` and `team_colours()` as free functions in the
file's namespace, and delete the callerless static `team_colour`.

#### `DebugText` builds its whole overlay inside `draw()`

- **File:** `game/objects/debug_text.cpp:44-102`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Performance ("Per-frame code performs no heap allocation")
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** `draw_debug_info` constructs a `std::vector<std::string>` and twenty-odd
`std::string`s by concatenation, on the render worker, once per viewport per frame.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/debug_text.cpp:44-52` (the shape repeats for eighteen more lines):

    std::vector<std::string> lines;

    lines.push_back("rect: " + std::to_string(rect.x) + ", " +
        std::to_string(rect.y) + ", " + std::to_string(rect.width) + ", " +
        std::to_string(rect.height));
    lines.push_back("center: " + std::to_string(center.x) + ", " +
        std::to_string(center.y));

and `debug_text.cpp:82`, which also divides by a parameter with no zero guard:

    lines.push_back("fps: " + std::to_string(1.0f / dt));

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY states the rule flatly under Performance:
"Per-frame code performs no heap allocation and no string-keyed lookups." Most of
these lines exceed the small-string buffer, so this is on the order of twenty
allocations plus the vector's reallocation growth, per viewport, per frame, inside
the thread-pool workers — the exact loop the engine's headline value is about.
It is guarded by `showing_debug()` (`level.cpp:592`), so it is a developer-facing
cost rather than a shipping one, which is why this is low and not medium.

The same file also hand-rolls drop-shadow text (draw at `pos + offset` in the
shadow colour, then at `pos`), as do `draw_timer` and `draw_respawn_timer` in
`interface_gameplay.cpp` — three copies of one idiom the engine already has as
`TextDropShadow`, though that type carries per-object state and so cannot be used
directly from this const, per-viewport path.

**Remedy:** build the line list in `Player::update` (or a small `DebugSnapshot`
the level fills once per frame) into a reused buffer, and have `draw_debug_info`
walk it. That also removes the last per-frame allocation from the render workers.

#### Move the group's constants out of global-namespace SCREAMING_SNAKE

- **File:** `game/objects/interface_gameplay.h:9-34`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never ("SCREAMING constants — screaming means macro, nothing else"); CONVENTIONS/Namespaces ("Game code owns its own namespace")

**What:** All five headers in this group define their tuning as `const static`
SCREAMING_SNAKE objects in namespaces hung off the global namespace, which
CONVENTIONS forbids twice over and which gives every including TU its own
dynamically-initialised copy.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/interface_gameplay.h:9-17`:

    namespace interface_consts
    {
        constexpr float RIGHT_MARGIN = 0.18f;
        constexpr float AMMO_TOP_MARGIN = 0.15f;
        constexpr float HEALTH_TOP_MARGIN = 0.05f;
        const static mattmath::Vector2F TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE = { 0.15f, 0.07f };
        constexpr float BOX_FILL_BORDER = 0.003f;
        const static mattmath::Vector2F TIMER_OFFSET = { 0.01f, 0.05f };
        const static std::string TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_48";

`game/objects/debug_text.h:8-18` (`debug_text_consts`, which also spells two
constants `COLOR` in a codebase whose header is `colour.h`) and
`game/objects/team_colour.h:24-41` (`team_colour_consts`) have the same shape.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS reserves screaming names for macros precisely so a
screaming name is a reliable preprocessor warning, and none of these is a macro.
All three namespaces sit at global scope, where the same document says game code
owns its own namespace — the engine did this work (everything is in `artattack::`)
and the game did not. Mechanically, `const` at namespace scope already implies
internal linkage, so each TU that reaches these headers — via `level.h`,
`level_builder.h`, `player_builder.h` and `results_menu_data.h`, which is most of
`game/objects/` and `game/states/` — gets its own `std::string`, `Vector2F` and
`Colour`, each with a dynamic initialiser the linker cannot fold. The `Colour`
ones are worse than they look: `mattmath::Colour` has a `Colour(const std::string& hex)`
constructor (`matt_math.h:609`) and `colour_consts::GREEN` is built from
`html::GREEN = "008000"`, so `HEALTH_COLOUR` is a hex-string parse at static-init
time in every TU.

CONVENTIONS also notes that a header full of tuning is usually data in the wrong
place (T7): `TIMER_FONT`, `SPRITE_SHEET`, `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME`, `FILL_FRAME` and
`DEBUG_FONT` are asset names compiled into the binary, so re-skinning the HUD is a
rebuild.

**Remedy:** put the game in its own namespace, rename to snake_case, make the
scalars `constexpr` and the objects `inline constexpr` where the type permits
(which requires `Vector2F` and `Colour` to gain `constexpr` constructors — worth
doing anyway), and move the five asset names into the level or HUD JSON.

---

#### `DEBUG_POSITION` reads a cross-TU dynamically-initialised object

- **File:** `game/objects/debug_text.h:13`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** A namespace-scope constant in a header is initialised from
`mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO`, a non-`constexpr` static data member defined in
another translation unit — and another static library — so the read happens in an
unspecified order relative to the definition.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/debug_text.h:13`:

    const static mattmath::Vector2F DEBUG_POSITION = mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO;

`engine/math/matt_math.h:496` declares it, `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:1902` defines it:

        static const Vector2F ZERO;
    ...
    const Vector2F Vector2F::ZERO = { 0.0f, 0.0f };

and `matt_math.h:406` is why that initialisation is dynamic rather than constant —
the constructor is user-provided and defined out of line:

        Vector2F(float x, float y);

**Why it matters:** `Vector2F::ZERO` is dynamically initialised in
`matt_math.cpp`'s TU inside `MattMath`; `DEBUG_POSITION` is dynamically
initialised in each TU that includes `debug_text.h`. Nothing orders the two. Today
it is harmless only by coincidence — zero-initialisation runs first and the
intended value is also zero. The moment someone writes
`const static Vector2F FOO = Vector2F::ONE;` in the same idiom, the answer becomes
a silent `{0, 0}` in some TUs and `{1, 1}` in others, with no diagnostic. The
engine has ten such constants (`matt_math.cpp:1902-1911`), four of which are
computed by calling `Vector2F::unit_vector` at static-init time, so the pattern is
already in place to be copied. (I checked the sibling case in this group:
`team_colour_consts::BLUE_ORANGE` reads `colour_consts::TEAM_BLUE`, but
`team_colour.h` includes `colour.h` above it, so within every TU the order is
defined. Only the cross-library read is unordered.)

**Remedy:** write `mattmath::Vector2F{0.0f, 0.0f}` here, and give `Vector2F` and
`Colour` `constexpr` constructors so the MattMath constants can be
`inline constexpr` and no consumer can depend on their initialisation order.

---

#### `std::exception(const char*)` is an MSVC extension, in live code

- **File:** `game/objects/team_colour.cpp:23`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** portability
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout ("a second platform is an addition, not a rewrite")
- **Origin:** added by verifier

**What:** Both files in this group that throw do so through
`std::exception(const char*)`, a Microsoft extension — the standard `std::exception`
has no such constructor — and the throws sit at `default:` labels over exhaustive
`enum class` switches.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/team_colour.cpp:16-25`:

    switch (team)
    {
    case PlayerTeam::a:
        return this->team_a;
    case PlayerTeam::b:
        return this->team_b;
    default:
        throw std::exception("Invalid team.");
    }

`game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:78` — the same, at the end of a chain that has
already handled all three enumerators of `PlayerTeam` (`player_team.h:3-8`):

        throw std::exception("No winning team");

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY commits to a second platform as an addition rather
than a rewrite, and CONVENTIONS justifies its all-lowercase filename rule by
"deletes the trap before the second platform arrives" — this is the same class of
trap, and it will be a compile error on the first non-MSVC build of every file
that uses it. Separately, the messages are lost: `std::exception::what()` is the
only channel and the standard constructor cannot carry a string, so this idiom
works *only* on MSVC. IMPLEMENTED.md already records `stop_sounds()` and match-end
throws from `default:` cases as a live hazard pattern; this group is two more
instances of it, one of which (`TeamColour::team_colour(PlayerTeam::none)`) is the
opposite policy from the `TeamColourTools` static of the same name.

**Remedy:** use `std::runtime_error` (or `std::invalid_argument`) with a message
naming the value, here and in `level_end_info.cpp:78, 95, 112`. Better for the two
switches: drop the `default:` label so `/W4` reports a missing enumerator at
compile time (T5) instead of a throw at run time.

---

#### Tidy the group's includes — two unused, the order scrambled, and `pch.h` ahead of every own header

- **File:** `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:3-8`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files ("Include order: own header first — proving every header compiles on its own — then engine headers, then external, then standard library")

**What:** `level_loaded_info.h` includes `<cstdio>` and `<map>`, neither of which
it uses, and interleaves standard, external and engine includes in no order. More
broadly, every `.cpp` in the group puts `game/pch.h` ahead of its own header, so
nothing in the group proves its headers are self-contained.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:3-8`:

    #include <cstdio>
    #include "rapidjson/document.h"
    #include <string>
    #include <vector>
    #include <map>
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"

and the first two lines of all five `.cpp` files in the group, e.g.
`game/objects/team_colour.cpp:1-2`:

    #include "game/pch.h"
    #include "game/objects/team_colour.h"

**Why it matters:** `<cstdio>` is left over from when this class opened the file
itself — it now delegates to `artattack::read_json_file`
(`level_loaded_info.cpp:114-117`) and holds no `FILE*` — and `<map>` names a type
the header never mentions. The order breaks the stated rule in three places at
once, and the file writes `"rapidjson/document.h"` where `engine/assets/json_loader.h:3`
writes `<rapidjson/document.h>` for the same header.

The `pch.h`-first line is the part with teeth. `game/CMakeLists.txt:70` already
declares `target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)`, so the compiler
force-includes it — the explicit line is redundant *and* it is what voids the
guarantee the own-header-first rule exists to provide. `level_end_info.h` names
`std::string` and includes neither `<string>` nor anything that obviously supplies
it; it compiles only because `team_colour.h` → `colour.h` → `matt_math.h:8` pulls
in `<string>`. Nothing in the build would catch it if that chain changed. The
group's other headers repeat the ordering problem (`interface_gameplay.h:3-7` puts
`game/objects/player_team.h` in the middle of three engine includes), and a
stranger reading these files as the sample's neighbours learns the wrong habit.

**Remedy:** delete `<cstdio>` and `<map>`; order the rest engine → external →
standard; delete the explicit `#include "game/pch.h"` from all five `.cpp` files
and let the build's forced include do its job, so the own header comes first and
each header is compiled on its own at least once.

### Rejected and corrected claims

No finding was rejected outright — every one of the twelve raw findings survived
verification, three of them at a lower severity. What was cut or corrected:

- **"Nine of the eleven accessors"** (level_loaded_info) — wrong count. It is
  eleven of thirteen unchecked; `display_name` and `icon_frame` are the two
  checked. Corrected in place.
- **"Severity high"** (level_loaded_info) — rejected. The mechanism is verified
  and the crash is real, but it requires an authoring error in content that is
  correct in the repo; re-graded to medium as a T6 robustness gap.
- **"a mistyped key yields… an access violation"** — kept only for `GetString()`.
  I traced `GetFloat()` and `GetArray()` on the null value: under `NDEBUG` those
  return `0.0f` and an empty range, they do not crash. The report now says which
  getter does which.
- **"the exact crossing ARCHITECTURE forbids… rapidjson reaches assets and stops
  there"** — rejected. That rule governs engine module direction; `LevelLoadedInfo`
  is game code. The finding was re-founded on PHILOSOPHY's compile-speed rule and T7.
- **"roughly half the game target… 46 TUs"** — overstated. I enumerated the
  includers: at least 16 of 46. Corrected.
- **"`fill_size.x` is about −55"** — overstated. Re-computed at ~−21 px in a
  quarter-screen viewport and ~−42 px full-screen for the case given. The negative
  rectangle and the mirrored draw are confirmed; the number was corrected.
- **"Severity medium"** (LevelEndInfo's six dead members) — re-graded to low. All
  four arithmetic walks are correct and I re-confirmed there are no callers, which
  is exactly why present impact is zero.
- **"Severity medium"** (TeamColourTools heap allocation) — re-graded to low. A
  real T11 violation with a two-line fix and no runtime consequence.
- **`level_builder.cpp:26,39` as the finding's file** — re-anchored to
  `team_colour.h:43-54`, which is in this group; `level_builder.cpp` is evidence,
  not the site.
- **`CMakeLists.txt:14-16`** — off by one; the three `add_subdirectory(tests/…)`
  lines are 15-17. Corrected.
- **`interface_gameplay.cpp:84-95` as the ammo twin** — the duplicated block runs
  to `:101`. Corrected.
- **`weapon.cpp:216-218, 227-229`** — verified exactly right, unchanged.
- **"`team_colour.h` does not duplicate `colour.h`, but the dependency runs the
  wrong way"** — this was in the raw summary and never filed. Promoted to a
  finding (added by verifier).

<a id="g-game-menu-framework"></a>

## game-menu-framework — Menu framework

*Group `game-menu-framework` · 18 findings (3 high, 7 medium, 8 low) · source `review2/verified/game-menu-framework.md`, verified report.*

I re-opened every cited line in all fifteen assigned files and in the twenty-odd files the
reviewer traced through: `viewport_manager.cpp`, `matt_math.cpp` (`Camera`), `widget.cpp`,
`state.h`, `state_context.cpp`, `thread_pool.cpp`, `partitioner.cpp`, `application.cpp`,
`game_data.cpp`, `game_states.cpp`, `level.cpp`, `player_input.cpp`, `main.cpp`,
`main_menu.cpp`, `pause_menu.cpp`, `results_menu.cpp`, `end_menu.cpp`, both `CMakeLists.txt`
files and `cmake/settings.cmake`. Every line number in the raw report checked out; the only
drift I found was cosmetic (the raw report cited `menu_input.cpp:104-124` for a block that
starts at 116, and quoted `set_player_count` without its `else if` arm). The two behavioural
claims are both real and I confirmed them by hand-composing the transforms: the three-player
menu pass is worse than reported — no pass covers the top-right quadrant at all, so a
three-player menu is missing a quarter of itself as well as showing a shifted duplicate — and
the `prev_inputs_` staleness is exactly reproducible in the order the raw report gives, with a
symmetric twin in `PlayerInput` that I verified and folded into the same finding.

I merged two findings into one (the three-player viewport bug and the per-viewport redundancy
are the same eighteen lines with the same fix), regraded four downward, corrected one remedy
that would have introduced a new bug, and trimmed one table. Nothing was fabricated, so
nothing is rejected outright; the regrades are all the same shape — a true observation with a
consequence that no reachable input produces today. Specifically: both `throw new
std::exception` arms are provably dead (I re-derived the unreachability from the `else if`
chains), every page that inherits `MenuHighlight` does seed it in `init()` (seven pages, seven
seed calls — I checked each), and every `MenuLevelSettings` index is bounded by
`player_count()`, which its own setter keeps in step with the vector. Those are latent traps,
not live defects, and they are graded as such. I also checked and did *not* raise the
signed/unsigned loop at `menu_page.cpp:143`: the object file is newer than the source and the
exe links, so it demonstrably compiles clean under `/W4 /WX`.

What the reviewer missed, and I added: the const-`draw()` contract that `ca4d228` made
compiler-enforced for `IGameObject` stops dead at `State` — `MenuPage`'s three draw helpers
are all non-`const` and all three run on sixteen thread-pool workers, while `Level`'s
equivalents are `const`; and the menu frame path allocates on the heap several times per
frame, including from inside the render workers, against an explicit PHILOSOPHY/Performance
rule. I also sharpened the deferred-context finding: the sixteen-object cap is structural, not
incidental, because `draw_mobject_in_viewports` calls `FinishCommandList` once per MObject, so
the obvious "index by partition ordinal" fix would leak command lists.

### Themes

- One line of code, two identities: the menu draw loop's index is a player number for
  `apply_player_viewport` and a subscript into `all_viewports()`, and the render worker's
  index is an MObject ordinal and a deferred-context slot. Both are the defect class the
  previous review already fixed twice (`IMPLEMENTED.md` #11, #14, #15).
- Frame-to-frame input state is stored but not maintained. `MenuInput::prev_inputs_` and
  `PlayerInput::prev_inputs_` each advance only on frames where their owner happens to be the
  active state, and neither class offers a way to prime or reset across a transition.
- `engine/ui/` is a widget *set*, not a widget *system*: containers and drawables, no focus,
  no navigation, no input, no per-viewport anything — so all three live in `game/states/` in
  entirely game-agnostic form, and the split-screen one does not exist at all.
- `MenuPage` is a renderer wearing a state base class. Ninety lines of deferred contexts,
  command lists, thread pool and partitioner sit in `game/`, which is what makes menus
  undrawable headlessly and unavailable to `samples/minimal/`.
- The contracts that were tightened elsewhere stop at this module boundary: `draw()` is const
  all the way down for `IGameObject` but not for `State`; headers compile on their own
  everywhere the PCH is not force-included.
- Preconditions are neither documented nor checked — seed the highlight, size the settings
  before indexing, pass at most sixteen MObjects — and none of the three is written down.
- The naming passes have not reached this corner: SCREAMING constants in a `*_consts`
  namespace, in the first menu header a new reader opens.

#### The three-player menu pass draws with the wrong viewport, and no pass covers the top-right quadrant

- **File:** `game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-118`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** The draw loop uses its index `i` both as a *player number* for
`apply_player_viewport(i, …)` and as a *subscript* into `all_viewports()`. Those two disagree
in the three-player layout, so the fourth pass rasterises into the bottom-right quadrant with
a camera built from the fullscreen viewport. The same loop also redraws every screen-space
menu once per player viewport of a layout no menu state ever sets.

**Evidence:**

`game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-118`

        std::vector<Viewport> viewports =
         	this->viewport_manager()->all_viewports();

        size_t num_viewports = viewports.size();
        for (size_t i = 0; i < num_viewports; i++)
        {
            this->viewport_manager()->apply_player_viewport(
                static_cast<int>(i), deferred_context, sprite_batch);

            sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, sampler_state);

            widget->draw(sprite_batch, viewports[i]);

            sprite_batch->End();
        }

`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:79-93` — four entries for three players, the fourth asked
for by a player number that does not exist:

        std::vector<Viewport> ViewportManager::all_viewports() const
        {
            std::vector<Viewport> result;
            int player_count = this->player_count_from_layout(this->layout_);
            for (int i = 0; i < player_count; i++)
            {
                result.push_back(this->player_viewport(i));
            }
            // Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
            if (player_count == 3)
            {
                result.push_back(this->player_viewport(4));
            }
            return result;
        }

`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:173-233` — the `three_player` switch has no `break` after
its inner switch, so both `player_num == 3` and `player_num == 4` fall through into the
`four_player` switch; `3` lands on `case 3` (bottom-right quadrant), `4` falls through again
to `default` (fullscreen):

            case ScreenLayout::three_player:
                switch (player_num)
                {
                ...
                default:
                    break;
                }
            case ScreenLayout::four_player:
                switch (player_num)
                {
                ...
                case 3:
                    result.x = screen_size.x / 2.0f;
                    result.y = screen_size.y / 2.0f;
                    ...
                default:
                    break;
                }
            default: //1P screen
                result.x = 0.0f;
                result.y = 0.0f;
                result.width = screen_size.x;
                result.height = screen_size.y;
                return result;

`engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4093-4098` — the camera translates by the viewport origin, which is
what makes the two transforms cancel when (and only when) they name the same viewport:

        Camera::Camera(const Viewport& viewport, float scale)
        {
            this->translation.x = viewport.x;
            this->translation.y = viewport.y;
            this->scale = scale;
        }

**Why it matters:** Pick 3 players (`main_menu.cpp:909-911` sets `player_count(3)` and
`ScreenLayout::three_player`), start a match, press Start. `GameLevel::update`
(`game_states.cpp:158-172`) puts up `PauseMenuInitial`, whose `draw` (`pause_menu.cpp:213-223`)
calls `draw_mobjects_in_viewports`. The three-player layout covers top-left (player 0),
bottom-right (player 1) and bottom-left (player 2) — the top-right quadrant is the empty one,
which is what the `all_viewports()` special case was clearly trying to fill. It fills nothing:

- Passes 0–2 draw the menu correctly, each clipped to its own quadrant. **Nothing draws the
  top-right quadrant**, so a quarter of every three-player pause, results and end menu — the
  right half of the top half, which for the centred pause box is a quarter of the box — is
  simply absent.
- Pass 3 sets the rasterizer and `SpriteBatch` viewport to the bottom-right quadrant while
  `viewports[3]` is fullscreen, so `Camera(viewports[3]).translation` is `(0, 0)` instead of
  `(w/2, h/2)` and every widget lands at `p + (w/2, h/2)`: a shifted copy of the menu's
  top-left quarter, painted over the content pass 1 already put in the bottom-right quadrant.

The redundancy is the second half of the same loop. In every other layout the two transforms
compose to the identity in screen space, so all N passes place a widget at the same absolute
pixel and differ only in the clip — N full command-list recordings, N `Begin`/`End` pairs and
N viewport applications per MObject per frame to produce one screen of pixels. And nothing
resets `ViewportManager::layout_` on the way out of a match: `set_layout` is called from
exactly one place in the tree (`game_states.cpp:133-134`, `grep -rn set_layout game/ engine/`
returns that line and the declaration), so quitting a four-player match
(`game_states.cpp:216-223`) leaves `MainMenuHome::draw` running four passes over the whole main
menu — gameplay state leaking into an unrelated state.

**Remedy:** Menus are screen-space; draw them once with the fullscreen viewport. That deletes
the index/player-number conflation, the missing quadrant, the duplicate and the 3–4x cost in
one edit. If a page ever genuinely needs per-player passes, iterate viewport *records* and
apply the same `Viewport` value you draw with — never an index that two different functions
interpret differently — and fix `all_viewports()` to stop synthesising an entry from a player
number the layout does not have.
