# Cross-cutting sweeps

<a id="g-sweep-module-graph"></a>

## sweep-module-graph — Module dependency directions and include graph

*Group `sweep-module-graph` · 13 findings (5 high, 5 medium, 3 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-module-graph.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I extracted every `#include` line from all 100 `.h`/`.cpp` files under `engine/`, plus
`game/`, `samples/`, `tests/`, and read all seven `CMakeLists.txt` and the presets/manifest.
The good news first, and it is real: **there is no cycle.** The engine's folder-level include
graph has a clean topological order — `math` → `core` → {`render`, `audio`} → {`ui`, `assets`}
→ `app` — nothing points back at `app` or at `assets`, and **no engine file includes a game
header**. The four namespace/`pragma once`/accessor passes landed and the module tree exists on
disk. What does not exist is any of the *outward* discipline the same table promises. Every
external edge in ARCHITECTURE/Modules is violated: `math`, the module that "may depend on
nothing", is the one that includes `d3d11.h`; `assets` takes an `ID3D11Device1*` in a
constructor; `core` puts `PTP_POOL` and `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` in public headers; and the two
backend folders the whole cross-platform story rests on (`render/d3d11/`, `input/xinput/`) do
not exist at all. Two modules are hollow — `collision/` holds a generic index splitter with no
collision in it, and `input/` holds one enum that no engine file includes, while the actual
input API is `DirectX::GamePad*` handed out raw by `Application`. Underneath all of it, the
compile-time wall the documents cite twice as "the feature (T5)" is not built: the repository
root is a `PUBLIC` include directory on both libraries, so an engine `.cpp` can include
`game/objects/collision_object_type.h` and compile. What surprised me most is that the newest,
least-reviewed code carries the leak furthest: `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp` — the
file a stranger copies to start a project — calls `FinishCommandList` and `ExecuteCommandList`
by hand.

### The actual module graph

Derived mechanically from the `#include` lines of every file under `engine/`, then confirmed by
opening each violating file. "External" collapses `d3d11.h`/`d3d11_1.h`/`dxgi1_6.h` into
`d3d11/dxgi`, and `windows.h`/`objbase.h`/`wrl/client.h` into `Win32`.

| Module | Permitted (ARCHITECTURE/Modules) | Actual engine edges | Actual external edges | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `math` | *nothing* | — | `DXTK:SimpleMath.h`, `d3d11/dxgi` (+`RECT` via it) | **violation** |
| `core` | math | math | `DXTK:SpriteBatch.h`, `Win32` (`PTP_POOL`, `HRESULT`) | **violation** |
| `collision` | core, math | *none* | *none* | hollow (see finding) |
| `render` | core, math — D3D11/DirectXTK inside `d3d11/` only | core, math | `DXTK:SpriteBatch.h`, `DXTK:SpriteFont.h`, `DXTK:DirectXMath.h`, `d3d11/dxgi`, `Win32` | **violation** (no `d3d11/` folder exists) |
| `input` | core, math — XInput inside `xinput/` only | *none* | *none* | hollow; XInput lives in `app` |
| `audio` | core, math — backend at its edge only | core, math | `DXTK:Audio.h` | borderline (module *is* the edge) |
| `ui` | core, math, render, input | core, render | *none* | OK |
| `assets` | core, math, render, audio, rapidjson | audio, core, render | `rapidjson`, `d3d11/dxgi`, `DXTK:Audio.h`, `DXTK:DDSTextureLoader.h`, `Win32` | **violation** (`d3d11`, DXTK) |
| `app` | everything | assets, audio, collision, core, math, render | `DXTK:{Audio,CommonStates,GamePad,SpriteBatch,DirectXMath}.h`, `Win32` | OK by the table |

Checks the brief asked for, answered:

- **Cycles:** none, at module level or file level.
- **Engine including a game header:** none today — but nothing prevents it (finding 1).
- **Does `math` include anything:** yes — `SimpleMath.h` and `<d3d11.h>` (finding 2).
- **Does rapidjson reach past `assets`:** inside the engine, no. Out of it, yes — `assets/json_loader.h` returns `rapidjson::Document` and the engine exports `external/rapidjson/include` `PUBLIC` (finding 6).
- **Does D3D11/DirectXTK reach outside `render` and `app`:** yes — `math`, `core`, `assets` (findings 2, 4, 5).

### Themes

- The module walls are documentation, not build structure: the include root is the repository root for every target, so no `#include` anywhere in the tree can fail for reasons of module direction.
- Every violation of the module table is an *outward* one — a first-party module reaching into DirectXTK, D3D11 or Win32 — never a sideways or backward one between engine modules.
- The two modules whose whole purpose is to hide a platform, `render/d3d11/` and `input/xinput/`, do not exist; their contents are spread flat across `render/` and `app/`.
- Two named modules are hollow (`collision/`, `input/`) while the work they are named for is filed elsewhere (`math/collision_tools.*`, `game/objects/player_input.*`), so the disk layout misdescribes the design in both directions.
- `math` is not a math library: it holds `Viewport`, `Camera` and `Colour`, which is the direct and only cause of its dependency on the graphics API.
- The new, unreviewed code — the sample game and the test targets — routes *around* the engine library rather than through it, which is the clearest available evidence that the boundary is not yet load-bearing.
- Include ordering and quoted-vs-angled external includes are inconsistent across the engine, in a codebase whose one enforcement mechanism for module direction is reading includes.

#### Build the engine/game compile wall the documents claim exists

- **File:** `engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** T5 / ARCHITECTURE/The targets

**What:** Both static libraries put the repository root on their `PUBLIC` include path, so an
engine translation unit can `#include "game/..."` and compile, contradicting the claim — made
twice, as the justification for the whole split — that it cannot.

**Evidence:**

    engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49
    target_include_directories(ArtAttackEngine PUBLIC
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/rapidjson/include"
    )

    engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:14
    target_include_directories(MattMath PUBLIC "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}")

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:14-16
    An arrow reads "links against"; no arrow ever points the other way — an
    engine file including a game header fails to compile, and that is the
    feature (T5).

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:271-272
    ... every file picks its home the day it is created. An engine
    file including a game header fails to compile; that is the feature (T5).

**Why it matters:** `CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR` is `C:/VSProjects/ArtAttack`, so
`#include "game/objects/collision_object_type.h"` from, say, `engine/collision/partitioner.cpp`
resolves and compiles. Twenty-one game headers have no matching `.cpp` at all —
`collision_object_type.h`, `player_team.h`, `weapon_type.h`, `level_mode.h`, `player_consts.h`,
`weapon_consts.h`, `projectile_consts.h`, `menu_element.h`, `stage.h`, `directory_consts.h`
among them — so such an include produces no link error either, in any target. For headers that do have a `.cpp`, `ArtAttackGame` still links
cleanly because the game objects and the engine archive land in the same executable; only
`ArtAttackSample` and the tests would fail, and only at link. There is no CI (`.github` does not
exist), no include-what-you-use step and no lint, so the "wall" is one reviewer noticing a line.
Note the specific thing lost: `#13` (collision interface carries a game enum) is exactly the
kind of regression this wall is supposed to make impossible, and today it would not even warn.

**Remedy:** Give each target a narrow include root (`${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}` on the engine, but
game/sample targets receive it only via the engine's `INTERFACE`, and never let the engine see
`game/`), or add a build step that greps engine sources for `#include "game/` and fails.

#### Stop MattMath depending on DirectXTK and d3d11.h — and stop the build file endorsing it

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5`, `engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:1-2,15-18`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`math` | nothing)

**What:** The module the table says may depend on nothing includes `SimpleMath.h` and
`<d3d11.h>`, links `Microsoft::DirectXTK` `PUBLIC`, and its `CMakeLists.txt` states the
violation as if it were the design, citing the document that forbids it.

**Evidence:**

    engine/math/matt_math.h:1-9
    #pragma once

    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"
    #include <d3d11.h>
    #include <cmath>
    #include <memory>
    #include <string>
    #include <vector>

    engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:1-2
    # MattMath — the math static library. Depends on nothing but the
    # DirectXTK headers it currently wraps (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md).

    engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:15-18
    target_link_libraries(MattMath
        PUBLIC Microsoft::DirectXTK
        PRIVATE artattack_settings
    )

**Why it matters:** `PUBLIC` is transitive, so every target in the repository — including
`MattMathTests`, which exists to test pure geometry — compiles `d3d11.h` and links DirectXTK.
`matt_math.h` is included by 30+ first-party headers, and through `engine/core/i_game_object.h`
by every renderable in the engine and the game, so `d3d11.h` is in essentially every
translation unit; that is a standing compile-time cost against "build time is iteration time"
(PHILOSOPHY, Tests and toolchain). Structurally it means the one library extracted specifically
because it depends on nothing cannot be reused, cannot be ported, and cannot be built on a
machine without the DirectX SDK — which removes the entire reason it is a separate target. The
old review named the header (`MattMath.h:4-8`); what is new is that the CMake conversion *wrote
the violation into the build system* as a documented `PUBLIC` dependency, so it now propagates
by construction rather than by include.

**Remedy:** Move `Viewport`, `Camera` and the `SimpleMath` conversion helpers out of `math`
(next finding), then drop `Microsoft::DirectXTK` from MattMath's link line and `d3d11.h` from
its header.

#### Move Viewport, Camera and Colour out of the math module and into render

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:775-811, 1020-1057, 594-649`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree (`render/` — renderer interface, cameras, viewports)

**What:** `math` contains the render module's types — `Viewport` (with `D3D11_VIEWPORT`
constructors and accessors), `Camera`, and `Colour` — which is the sole reason `math` cannot be
dependency-free.

**Evidence:**

    engine/math/matt_math.h:775-798
    struct Viewport
    {
    public:
        float x = 0.0f;
        ...
        Viewport(const DirectX::SimpleMath::Viewport& viewport);
        ...
        Viewport(const D3D11_VIEWPORT& viewport);

        DirectX::SimpleMath::Viewport sm_viewport() const;
        D3D11_VIEWPORT d3d_viewport() const;
        const D3D11_VIEWPORT* d3d_viewport_ptr() const;

    engine/math/matt_math.h:810
        Viewport& operator=(const RECT& rect);

    engine/math/matt_math.h:1020-1029
    struct Camera
    {
        ...
        Camera(const mattmath::Viewport& viewport, float scale = 1.0f);

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:84-85
    │   ├── render/             renderer interface, cameras, viewports

**Why it matters:** Trace the chain. `Viewport` exists to convert to and from `D3D11_VIEWPORT`,
which forces `#include <d3d11.h>` at `matt_math.h:5`; `Viewport(const DirectX::SimpleMath::…)`
forces `SimpleMath.h` at line 3; `RECT` at line 810 forces `windows.h` transitively. So the
previous finding is not independently fixable — the graphics API is in `math` *because the
render module's types are*, and no amount of build-file editing removes it while they stay. The
consequence for the stated goal is direct: ARCHITECTURE promises "a second platform is an
addition, not a rewrite", but a second backend means editing `mattmath::Viewport`, a type that
30+ headers depend on. This is a decision that gets more expensive to undo with every file that
includes `matt_math.h`.

**Remedy:** Move `Viewport` and `Camera` to `engine/render/` and `Colour` to `engine/render/` or
keep a backend-free `Colour` in math; leave the `D3D11_VIEWPORT`/`SimpleMath` conversions in the
(not yet existing) `render/d3d11/` backend as free functions.

#### Take the D3D11 device and the DirectXTK AudioEngine out of the assets module's API

- **File:** `engine/assets/resource_loader.h:6-7,47-49,92-93`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`assets` | core, math, render, audio, rapidjson)

**What:** `assets` includes `<d3d11_1.h>` and `<Audio.h>` and names `ID3D11Device1*` and
`DirectX::AudioEngine*` in a public constructor, though the table grants it only
core/math/render/audio/rapidjson — the graphics API is not among them.

**Evidence:**

    engine/assets/resource_loader.h:3-10
    #include "engine/assets/asset_manifest.h"
    #include "engine/audio/audio_resources.h"
    #include "engine/render/render_resources.h"
    #include <Audio.h>
    #include <d3d11_1.h>

    engine/assets/resource_loader.h:47-49
        ResourceLoader(RenderResources* render_resources,
            AudioResources* audio_resources, ID3D11Device1* device,
            DirectX::AudioEngine* audio_engine);

    engine/assets/resource_loader.h:87
        void set_device(ID3D11Device1* device);

    engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.h:4,16-17
    #include <d3d11_1.h>
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<SpriteSheet> read_sprite_sheet(const char* json_path,
        ID3D11ShaderResourceView* texture);

    engine/assets/sound_bank_loader.h:4,17-18
    #include <Audio.h>
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<SoundBank> read_sound_bank(const char* json_path,
        std::unique_ptr<DirectX::WaveBank> wave_bank);

**Why it matters:** The module that is furthest from the platform is compiled against it
directly, so the loaders cannot be built, tested, or ported without D3D11 and XAudio2 headers.
The cost is already visible in the tree: `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-5` says outright that it
compiles two engine `.cpp` files rather than linking the engine "and everything the engine drags
in" — the first test written against `assets` had to route around the library. A second render
backend must edit `ResourceLoader`'s constructor, `set_device`, and `read_sprite_sheet`'s
signature, all of which the game calls.

**Remedy:** Have `render` own a backend-neutral texture/device handle type and pass that;
`assets` should name `render`'s and `audio`'s types, never the SDK's.

#### Rewrite the sample so a new project does not have to drive D3D11 command lists

- **File:** `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:3,44,62-85`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 / ARCHITECTURE/A game project

**What:** The sample — the permanent second client and the file a new project copies — includes
`<SpriteBatch.h>`, calls `DirectX::GamePad` directly, and hand-writes a deferred-context
record/execute/`Release` sequence, so a stranger's first contact with the engine is the
graphics API.

**Evidence:**

    samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:62-85
    void HelloState::draw()
    {
        // Drawing goes through a deferred context so it can be recorded off the
        // main thread; ...
        artattack::DeviceResources* device = this->app_->device_resources();
        ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred = device->deferred_context(0);
        SpriteBatch* sprite_batch = this->app_->sprite_batches()->at(0);

        sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred);
        this->greeting_->draw(sprite_batch);
        this->hint_->draw(sprite_batch);
        sprite_batch->End();

        ID3D11CommandList* commands = nullptr;
        if (FAILED(deferred->FinishCommandList(FALSE, &commands)))
        {
            throw std::runtime_error("HelloState::draw - FinishCommandList failed");
        }

        device->GetD3DDeviceContext()->ExecuteCommandList(commands, FALSE);
        commands->Release();
    }

    samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:44
        const GamePad::State pad = this->app_->gamepad()->GetState(0);

    samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:21-25
    target_link_libraries(ArtAttackSample PRIVATE
        ArtAttackEngine
        Microsoft::DirectXTK
        artattack_settings
    )

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:173-174
    A project is an ordinary C++ application that links two static
    libraries.

**Why it matters:** The sample is described as "the standing answer to 'how do I start a project
on this engine'" (PHILOSOPHY, The public face) and as the target-graph client that keeps the
boundary honest. As written it is the opposite: it proves the boundary does not hold, because
the smallest possible client cannot draw one string without `FinishCommandList`,
`ExecuteCommandList` and a manual COM `Release()` — five lines that are pure backend and that a
`/W4 /WX` reader of the sample must understand. Its link line also names a third-party SDK
beyond the engine and the shared settings target, and the `Microsoft::DirectXTK` on line 23 is a
real requirement rather than a redundancy: line 3 of `hello_state.cpp` includes
`<SpriteBatch.h>`. Every one of these lines is code a copied project
inherits and owns. This is the renderer-seam decision made concrete in the newest file in the
repository.

**Remedy:** The sample's `draw()` should be one call against an engine-owned draw target; until
the renderer seam exists, at minimum hide the record/submit sequence behind an
`Application`-level helper so the sample does not teach it.

#### Create the backend folders, or stop claiming platform code lives behind interfaces

- **File:** `engine/render/device_resources.h:7-10`, `engine/core/thread_pool.h:3,40-50`, `engine/core/i_game_object.h:4,41-42`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree (`render/d3d11/`, `input/xinput/`)

**What:** Neither `engine/render/d3d11/` nor `engine/input/xinput/` exists; D3D11, DXGI and Win32
sit at the top level of `render/` and inside `core/`'s public headers, so nothing is behind an
engine-owned interface.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/device_resources.h:7-11
    #include <Windows.h>
    #include <wrl/client.h>
    #include <d3d11_1.h>
    #include <dxgi1_6.h>
    #include <memory>

    engine/core/thread_pool.h:3
    #include <windows.h>

    engine/core/thread_pool.h:40-50
        static void CALLBACK work_callback(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE,
            PVOID parameter, PTP_WORK);
        ...
        std::vector<PTP_WORK> work_items_;
        TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON callback_environment_ = {};
        PTP_POOL pool_ = nullptr;
        PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP cleanup_group_ = nullptr;

    engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:3,13,23
    #include <Windows.h>
        com_exception(HRESULT hr) noexcept : result(hr) {}
        HRESULT result;

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:4,41-42
    #include <SpriteBatch.h>
        virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
            const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:113-116
    Platform-specific code
    lives only in the backend subfolders (`render/d3d11/`, `input/xinput/`),
    behind engine-owned interfaces, so a second platform is an addition, not
    a rewrite.

**Why it matters:** Five headers in `render/` include a D3D11/DXGI or DirectXTK header at the
top level of the module rather than from a `d3d11/` subfolder — `device_resources.h:7-10`,
`render_resources.h:5-7`, `drawer.h:3`, `sprite_sheet.h:7`, `viewport_manager.h:8` — and
`core` — the module the table says depends only on `math`,
and the one every other module leans on — puts the Win32 thread-pool types and `HRESULT` in
*public member declarations*, not behind a pimpl. So `windows.h` is compiled by anything that
includes `engine/core/thread_pool.h`, which `engine/app/application.h:8` and
`game/objects/level.h:18` both do. The `core → DirectX::SpriteBatch*` edge at
`i_game_object.h:41` is the known-open renderer seam; the module-graph fact worth adding is
that it makes the table's most load-bearing row — `core | math` — false, and drags DirectXTK
into `ui/widget.h` (`ui → core`) and therefore into the entire widget set. A second platform is
not an addition here; it is an edit to `core`.

**Remedy:** Create `render/d3d11/` and move `device_resources` and the SpriteBatch-touching
implementations into it; make `ThreadPool`'s Win32 handles private implementation state behind
an opaque pointer so `core`'s headers stop naming them.

#### Stop rapidjson escaping the assets module into every client

- **File:** `engine/assets/json_loader.h:3,12`, `engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49`, `game/CMakeLists.txt:64-66`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules ("rapidjson reaches assets and stops there")

**What:** `assets` returns a `rapidjson::Document` from a public engine header and the engine
exports `external/rapidjson/include` as a `PUBLIC` include directory, so the parser is part of
the engine's published API and the game declares its own direct edge to `external/`.

**Evidence:**

    engine/assets/json_loader.h:3,12
    #include <rapidjson/document.h>
    ...
        rapidjson::Document read_json_file(const char* path);

    engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49
    target_include_directories(ArtAttackEngine PUBLIC
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/rapidjson/include"
    )

    game/CMakeLists.txt:64-66
    target_include_directories(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/rapidjson/include"
    )

    game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4,30-31,38
    #include "rapidjson/document.h"
    ...
        const rapidjson::Value& collision_objects_json() const;
        const rapidjson::Value& non_collision_objects_json() const;
    ...
        rapidjson::Document json_doc_;

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:146-151
    Nothing points back at `assets`, ... No type on the draw path reads a file, so
    `rapidjson` reaches `assets` and stops there — drawing a sprite does not
    compile a JSON parser.

**Why it matters:** Inside the engine the claim holds — I checked every includer of
`json_loader.h` and all three are in `assets/`. It fails at the target boundary. The
ARCHITECTURE target graph has exactly one arrow into rapidjson, `engine --> rapidjson`; the
build now has two, because `game/CMakeLists.txt:65` declares its own. Four game headers depend
on it, one of them (`level_loaded_info.h:38`) storing a `Document` by value and two
(`level_object_builder.h:18,22,32,36`) taking `const rapidjson::Value&` as parameters, so the
game's object-building API *is* rapidjson. `level_loaded_info.h` is reached from `game_data.h`,
which is reached from `menu_data.h` and thence most of `states/`, so the parser is compiled by
the majority of game TUs. The `PUBLIC` on `engine/CMakeLists.txt:48` also means any future
client inherits this without asking.

**Remedy:** Make the rapidjson include directory `PRIVATE` on `ArtAttackEngine`, and have
`assets` expose parsed results (`AssetManifest`-style structs) rather than
`rapidjson::Document`/`Value` — then the game's dependency dissolves rather than being declared.

#### The collision module contains no collision code

- **File:** `engine/collision/partitioner.h:1-18`, `engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:5-28`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree (`collision/` — broad phase, narrow phase, manifolds, resolution)

**What:** `engine/collision/` holds exactly one type, a generic integer range splitter with no
geometric content, while the actual collision code lives in `engine/math/` and the collision
interface lives in `game/objects/`.

**Evidence:**

    engine/collision/partitioner.h:1-18
    #pragma once

    #include <vector>

    namespace artattack
    {
        class Partitioner
        {
        public:

                partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const;

    engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:8-9
        int elements_per_partition = num_elements / num_partitions;
        int remainder = num_elements % num_partitions;

    engine/math/collision_tools.h:6-8
    namespace mattmath
    {
        class CollisionTools

**Why it matters:** This is new, specific information for outstanding finding `#13`. The split
did not fix the collision interface carrying a game enum; it moved the whole subject out of the
engine. Today the engine ships *no* collision mechanism: `CollisionTools` and `Shape` are in
`MattMath` (and therefore in the target that is supposed to depend on nothing), and
`ICollisionGameObject` — the interface ARCHITECTURE names as one of the three seam types — is
at `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h`, which includes
`game/objects/collision_object_type.h`. So `#13` cannot be fixed by editing an engine file,
because the file is not in the engine. Meanwhile `Partitioner` is a work-splitting utility used
by the thread-pool fan-out (`engine/app/application.h:5,122,157`) and has nothing to do with
collision; it is in the wrong module, which makes the folder look occupied when it is not.

**Remedy:** Move `Partitioner` to `core/` (it is a scheduling helper), move `collision_tools`
and `Shape` out of `math` into `collision/`, and re-file `#13` as "the engine has no collision
module" rather than "the interface has a game enum".

#### The input module is one enum; the input API is a raw DirectXTK GamePad

- **File:** `engine/input/connection_state.h:1-10`, `engine/app/application.h:17,123,158`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`input` — XInput inside `xinput/` only)

**What:** `engine/input/` contains a single enum that no engine file includes, and the actual
input mechanism is `DirectX::GamePad`, owned by `app` and handed to clients raw.

**Evidence:**

    engine/input/connection_state.h:1-10  (the entire module)
    #pragma once

    namespace artattack
    {
        enum class ConnectionState
        {
            connected,
            disconnected
        };
    }

    engine/app/application.h:17,123,158
    #include <GamePad.h>
    ...
        DirectX::GamePad* gamepad() const;
    ...
        std::unique_ptr<DirectX::GamePad> gamepad_ = nullptr;

    game/objects/player_input.h:34,45
        explicit PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad);
        DirectX::GamePad* gamepad_ = nullptr;

    samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:44
        const GamePad::State pad = this->app_->gamepad()->GetState(0);

**Why it matters:** No engine `.cpp` includes `connection_state.h` — its only two includers are
`game/objects/player_input_data.h:3` and `game/states/menu_input.h:5` — and `engine/input/`
contributes no source file to `engine/CMakeLists.txt`. So the module exists on disk and not in
the graph. The table's "input | core, math — XInput inside `xinput/` only" describes nothing
that exists; XInput enters at `app/application.h:17` and leaves through a public accessor, so
*both* clients (`game/objects/player_input.cpp:21`, `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:44`)
call `GamePad::GetState` themselves. There is no action mapping and no device abstraction, which
means "Input devices and action mapping" in ARCHITECTURE's engine/game table is currently
supplied by the game. A second input backend is a change to every client, not an addition.

**Remedy:** Either build the input module (device abstraction plus action mapping, XInput behind
`input/xinput/`) or delete `engine/input/` and move `ConnectionState` to the game until it is
built — an empty folder that names a module the engine does not have misleads a reader.

#### Make the assets test link the engine instead of recompiling two of its translation units

- **File:** `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-11`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout ("Tests link libraries, never `#include` implementation files")

**What:** `AssetsTests` adds two engine `.cpp` files to its own source list rather than linking
`ArtAttackEngine`, so the code under test is a second, separately built copy that the engine
target's own dependencies never validate.

**Evidence:**

    tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-11
    # The manifest loader reads a file and parses JSON, and that is all it does -
    # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units
    # directly rather than linking the engine and everything the engine drags in.
    add_executable(AssetsTests
        asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp
        test_main.cpp
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/json_loader.cpp"
    )

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:273
    Tests link libraries, never `#include` implementation files.

**Why it matters:** The rule's purpose is that the tested artefact is the shipped artefact. Here
it is not: the objects in `AssetsTests` are compiled from a different target with a different
link line, and the manual source list must be edited by hand the first time
`asset_manifest_loader.cpp` calls into a third engine TU — at which point the failure is an
unresolved-symbol error in a test, not a compile error where the dependency was added. More
importantly it is *evidence*, written down in the file's own comment, that the module walls do
not survive contact: the author had to bypass the library because `assets` drags DirectXTK
(finding 5). Fix that finding and this workaround becomes unnecessary.

**Remedy:** Link `ArtAttackEngine`; if the drag is genuinely intolerable, promote `assets` (or a
dependency-free subset of it) to its own static library, which ARCHITECTURE:124-126 already
names as the sanctioned escalation.

#### Fix inverted include order and quoted external includes across engine headers

- **File:** `engine/audio/sound_bank.h:3-7`, `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-4`, `engine/render/drawer.h:3-6`, `engine/render/resolution_manager.h:3-5`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (include order; include paths from the repository root)

**What:** Several engine headers put external and standard-library includes before engine
includes, and external headers are included with quotes in some files and angle brackets in
others.

**Evidence:**

    engine/audio/sound_bank.h:3-7
    #include <Audio.h>
    #include <memory>
    #include <string>
    #include "engine/core/registry.h"
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"

    engine/render/resolution_manager.h:3-5
    #include <string>
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"
    #include "engine/render/screen_resolution.h"

    engine/render/drawer.h:3-6
    #include "SpriteBatch.h"
    #include "engine/render/render_resources.h"
    #include "engine/render/rotation_origin.h"
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"

    engine/math/matt_math.h:3-4
    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"

    docs/design/CONVENTIONS.md:114-115
    - Include order: own header first — proving every header compiles on its
      own — then engine headers, then external, then standard library.

**Why it matters:** The engine's *only* mechanism for enforcing module direction is a human
reading include blocks (ARCHITECTURE:120-123). A consistent order is what makes a foreign
`#include` visible at a glance; interleaved blocks make it invisible. The quote form is a small
real trap on top: `#include "SpriteBatch.h"` searches the including file's own directory first,
so a first-party `engine/render/sprite_batch.h` — a plausible name for the renderer seam — would
silently shadow DirectXTK's for `drawer.h`, `sprite_sheet.h:7` and `viewport_manager.h:8` but
not for `i_game_object.h:4` or `application.h:18`, which use `<SpriteBatch.h>`. The same
inconsistency exists for rapidjson: `<rapidjson/document.h>` in `engine/assets/json_loader.h:3`
and `game/save.h:6`, `"rapidjson/document.h"` in `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4`,
`level_builder.h:13` and `level_object_builder.h:5`.

**Remedy:** One ordering everywhere — own header, engine, external, standard — and angle
brackets for every non-first-party header.

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:53-56`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 / PHILOSOPHY/The boundary ("Engine headers contain no game nouns")

**What:** The documented contract of the engine's root object interface refers the reader to
`ICollisionGameObject`, a type that lives in `game/objects/` and does not exist in the engine.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:53-56

        // and "which pairs overlap each other" are one query against one

**Why it matters:** It is not a compile dependency, but PHILOSOPHY (The public face) says "a

- **File:** `docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:105`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree

**What:** The authoritative tree says `external/` contains rapidjson and DirectXTK; it contains
only rapidjson, because DirectXTK now arrives through vcpkg — which the same document's build
section already says.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:105
    ├── external/               third-party source: rapidjson, DirectXTK

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:60-62
    - The bought edge (T9) is declared, not clicked: `vcpkg.json` (manifest

      rapidjson stays vendored in `external/`.

    $ ls external
    rapidjson

**Why it matters:** The document names itself "the authoritative roster of modules and folders",

<a id="g-sweep-game-nouns-in-engine"></a>

## sweep-game-nouns-in-engine — Game vocabulary inside engine headers

*Group `sweep-game-nouns-in-engine` · 7 findings (2 high, 4 medium, 1 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-game-nouns-in-engine.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I grepped every file under `engine/` (headers and `.cpp` alike) for the paint-shooter's
vocabulary — team, paint, weapon, splat, player, match, round, score, level, menu, ink, plus the
specific asset, weapon and state names the game uses — then opened every hit and decided whether
it was a real breach or a general concept sharing a word. Most of the engine is genuinely clean:
`engine/core/`, `engine/assets/`, `engine/audio/`, `engine/app/` and `engine/math/matt_math.*`
contain no game nouns at all, and the asset-kind registry (`ResourceLoader::register_kind`, with
the game adding `"level"` from `game/main.cpp:60`) is a textbook T1 mechanism — the engine ships
four kinds, the game teaches it a fifth, and no engine header learns the word "level". The
breaches cluster almost entirely in `engine/render/`, and they are not scattered nouns: they are
three places where a *policy* was moved into the engine and dragged its vocabulary along with it.
Two of them are load-bearing for the paint-shooter and would fail outright for a stranger:
`ViewportManager` publishes the game's texture-atlas and frame names as engine constants, and
`ScreenLayout`/`calculate_viewport` hardcodes the split-screen composition — where I found a live
off-by-one that mis-draws the fourth panel in every three-player match. The surprise was
`engine/math/colour.h`, the lowest layer in the whole build, the one ARCHITECTURE says "depends on
nothing": it ends with five constants named `TEAM_BLUE` through `TEAM_GREEN`, which is the exact
noun PHILOSOPHY names first when it says engine headers contain none. The second surprise was how
often the engine's *documentation* reaches down into the game — `engine/core/i_game_object.h`
explains its own contract in terms of `Level`, `Player` and `ICollisionGameObject`, none of which
the engine ships or can include.

### Themes

- The vocabulary leak always follows a policy leak: every genuine breach is a case where the
  engine decided *what* rather than *how*, and the game noun is just the visible symptom.
- `engine/render/` holds all of it. `core`, `assets`, `audio`, `app` and `matt_math` are clean,
  which suggests the recent extraction work was done with the boundary in mind and that render was
  the module lifted wholesale from the pre-split tree.
- Baked-in policy comes as a closed enum plus a switch: `ScreenLayout` and `ScreenResolution` both
  enumerate the paint-shooter's four options and make anything else unrepresentable, so a
  stranger's first change to the engine is editing an enum in two files.
- The sample game does not exercise the breached APIs — `samples/minimal` uses no
  `ViewportManager`, no `CameraTools` and no `ScreenLayout` — so the "second client keeps the
  boundary honest" mechanism is not actually catching any of this yet.
- Where the engine publishes a game asset name, it also publishes a game *style* decision
  (the divider colour, the camera scroll margins in pixels), so the fix is not a rename but a
  parameter.
- Engine header comments document engine contracts in terms of game classes, which inverts the
  dependency direction in the one place ARCHITECTURE cannot enforce — prose.
- Several breaches are `static inline const std::string` / SCREAMING constants in headers, which
  is separately a CONVENTIONS/Never breach; I have not filed that here since it is a conventions
  sweep, but it co-locates exactly with the game nouns.

---

#### Delete the paint-shooter's asset names from the ViewportManager header

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:15-21`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (PHILOSOPHY/The boundary: "no ... asset name")

**What:** An engine header publishes two of the paint-shooter's content names — the sprite sheet
`"sprite_sheet_1"` and the frame `"pixel"` — plus a hardcoded colour, as the documented way to
fill viewport dividers.

**Evidence:**

    // How a split-screen divider is drawn. They live on the class that shapes
    // the dividers rather than in a `consts` namespace of strays (CONVENTIONS,
    // Constants and enumerators); a game asks for the rectangles and then for
    // these to fill them.
    static inline const std::string DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1";
    static inline const std::string DIVIDER_FRAME_NAME = "pixel";
    static inline const mattmath::Colour DIVIDER_COLOUR = colour_consts::BLACK;

**Why it matters:** These are not general names. `sprite_sheet_1` is declared only in
`game/content/manifest.json`, and the sole consumer is `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:223-227`,
which builds a `Visual` from all three. `samples/minimal/content/manifest.json` declares one font
and nothing else, so a second client that follows the header's own instruction ("a game asks for
the rectangles and then for these to fill them") calls `RenderResources::resolve_sprite_sheet`
with a name nothing has loaded and gets the documented `std::out_of_range` at load. The comment
defends the *location* of the constants while missing that the engine should not know either
string: divider styling is "what is drawn", which the boundary table assigns to the game.

**Remedy:** Delete all three from the engine and move them to
`game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp`; `viewport_dividers()` already returns rectangles, which is
the whole mechanism the engine owes.

---

#### Move split-screen composition out of ViewportManager — the three-player case is wrong

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:86-91`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** `all_viewports()` encodes the paint-shooter's rule "a three-player match still shows four
panels" inside the engine, and asks for viewport index 4 when it means index 3, so the fourth
entry is the full-screen viewport rather than the bottom-right quadrant.

**Evidence:**

    // Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
    if (player_count == 3)
    {
        result.push_back(this->player_viewport(4));
    }

`calculate_viewport` (same file, 143-234) has no `case` for `player_num == 4`, and its inner
switches `break` into the next layout's block:

    case ScreenLayout::three_player:
        switch (player_num)
        {
        ...
        default:
            break;
        }
    case ScreenLayout::four_player:
        switch (player_num)
        {
        ...
        default:
            break;
        }
    default: //1P screen
        result.x = 0.0f;
        result.y = 0.0f;
        result.width = screen_size.x;
        result.height = screen_size.y;
        return result;

So `player_viewport(4)` under `three_player` falls through both inner defaults and returns the
full screen.

**Why it matters:** Reachable in the shipped game. `game/states/main_menu.cpp:911` selects
`ScreenLayout::three_player`; `game/states/game_states.cpp:134` applies it before the level is
built; pausing calls `game/states/pause_menu.cpp:222` → `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` →
`game/states/menu_page.cpp:105` `all_viewports()`. The loop at `menu_page.cpp:108-117` then calls
`apply_player_viewport(3)` — which *does* correctly return the bottom-right quadrant, because
index 3 falls through into `case four_player`'s `case 3:` — while drawing the widget with
`viewports[3]`, the full-screen rect. `MObject::draw(sprite_batch, viewport)` converts that to
`Camera(viewport)` (`engine/ui/widget.cpp:19-22`), and `Camera::Camera(const Viewport&)`
(`engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4093-4098`) takes the translation from `viewport.x/y`. The fourth
panel is therefore drawn with translation `(0, 0)` inside a quadrant whose origin is
`(width/2, height/2)`, i.e. shifted half a screen down and right and effectively off its own
panel. Underneath the bug is the boundary problem: "three players still get four panels" is the
paint-shooter's screen composition, not a rendering mechanism.

**Remedy:** Have the engine return exactly the viewports its layout defines and let the game ask
for the spare panel it wants; if the fourth panel stays, the index is 3, not 4, and the fallthrough
in `calculate_viewport` should be replaced by explicit returns.

#### Move the team palette out of MattMath

- **File:** `engine/math/colour.h:308-312`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (PHILOSOPHY/The boundary: "no team")

**What:** The math library — the one ARCHITECTURE says depends on nothing — ships the
paint-shooter's five team colours.

**Evidence:**

    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_BLUE = { 6, 52, 204, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_YELLOW = { 255, 255, 0, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_ORANGE = { 255, 127, 0, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_PINK = { 255, 0, 127, 255 };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_GREEN = { 0, 255, 0, 255 };

**Why it matters:** "Team" is the first noun PHILOSOPHY names when it says engine headers contain
none, and this is the deepest layer in the build — every target in the repo transitively includes
it. The named HTML colours above (lines 9-156, 159-306) are a general facility; these five are a design decision from
one game, and every consumer is game code: `game/objects/team_colour.h:8-9,28-29,33-34,38-39`,
`game/states/main_menu.h:28`, `game/states/end_menu.h:21`, `game/states/pause_menu.h:17`. A
stranger's engine-supplied palette should not contain the colours of somebody else's match.

**Remedy:** Delete the five constants from `engine/math/colour.h` and declare them in
`game/objects/team_colour.h`, which already owns the team-to-colour mapping.

#### ScreenLayout names viewports after players and closes the set at four

- **File:** `engine/render/screen_layout.h:5-11`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** The engine's only description of a screen layout is an enum of four player counts, and
every viewport accessor is spelled "player".

**Evidence:**

    enum class ScreenLayout
    {
        one_player,
        two_player,
        three_player,
        four_player
    };

with, in `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:34-45`:

    void apply_player_viewport(int player_num,
        ID3D11DeviceContext* context,
        DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch) const;
    ...
    mattmath::Viewport player_viewport(int player_num) const;
    ...
    mattmath::RectangleF camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect(
        int player_num, const mattmath::Camera& camera) const;

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY/Structural types says there is no engine `Player` and that "the
engine-worthy parts of 'player' already exist as input slots and *views*" — this API is the views,
named after the thing the engine is not supposed to have. Beyond vocabulary it is a closed policy:
the four arrangements are hardcoded in `calculate_viewport` (`viewport_manager.cpp:143-234`), so a
game wanting a picture-in-picture minimap, a vertical two-way split, or six panels must edit two
engine files. The litmus test fails outright.

**Remedy:** Express a layout as a count plus an arrangement the game supplies (or a vector of
normalised rects), and rename the accessors to `view` — `view_count()`, `view(int index)`.

#### CameraTools follows a "player" and bakes the paint-shooter's camera feel

- **File:** `engine/render/camera_tools.h:11-15`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy), T7 (data over code)

**What:** The engine's camera helper names its subject `player_center` and hardcodes the scroll
margins, in pixels, that give this one game its feel.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/camera_tools.h:11-15`:

    mattmath::Camera calculate_camera(
        const mattmath::Vector2F& player_center,
        const mattmath::Vector2F& viewport_size,
        const mattmath::Camera& prev_camera,
        const mattmath::RectangleF& camera_bounds) const;

`engine/render/camera_tools.cpp:14-22`:

    constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_LEFT = 0.4f;
    constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_TOP = 0.2f;
    constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_RIGHT = 0.4f;
    constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_BOTTOM = 0.4f;

    constexpr float MIN_BORDER_LEFT = 400.0f;
    constexpr float MIN_BORDER_TOP = 250.0f;
    constexpr float MIN_BORDER_RIGHT = 400.0f;
    constexpr float MIN_BORDER_BOTTOM = 250.0f;

**Why it matters:** The function is pure geometry — it chases a point inside a dead zone and clamps
to bounds — so nothing about it needs the word player; a stranger's camera might follow a ball, a
cursor or the midpoint of two things. Worse, the dead-zone shape is not a parameter: the asymmetric
0.2 top / 0.4 bottom ratio and the 400×250 pixel floors are one game's tuning, and CONVENTIONS
(Constants and enumerators) says a block of numeric constants like this is tuning data in the wrong
place. The only caller is `game/objects/level.cpp:81,210`, which cannot change any of it. The
in-file comment ("these tune how the camera chases a player and configure nothing else") defends
the location and concedes the coupling.

**Remedy:** Rename the parameter to `target` (or `focus`) and take the dead-zone ratios and floors
as an options struct the caller supplies, defaulted or loaded from data.

#### ScreenResolution is a closed list of four, and anything else is silently snapped to 720p

- **File:** `engine/render/screen_resolution.h:5-12`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy), T6 (loud failure)

**What:** The engine can only represent four 16:9 resolutions, and every conversion from a real
size to that enum falls back to 1280×720 without saying so.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/screen_resolution.h:5-12`:

    enum class ScreenResolution
    {
        s_1280_720,
        s_1920_1080,
        s_2560_1440,
        s_3840_2160,
        max = s_3840_2160
    };

`engine/render/resolution_manager.cpp:147-150` (the tail of `convert_vec_to_resolution`; the
string and ivec conversions at 118-121 and 172-175 are identical):

    else
    {
        return ScreenResolution::s_1280_720;
    }

**Why it matters:** Not vocabulary, but the same litmus test, and it fails it plainly: a stranger's
game targeting 1366×768, an ultrawide, or the user's actual desktop size must edit
`engine/render/screen_resolution.h` and three `switch`/`if` chains in
`engine/render/resolution_manager.cpp`. The silent fallback compounds it — `set_resolution(vec)` on
an unlisted size reports success and leaves the manager claiming 1280×720, which every viewport and
widget position is then computed from (`ViewportManager::calculate_viewport` reads
`resolution_manager_->resolution_vec()` at `viewport_manager.cpp:47,56,76,115`). Under T6 an
unrepresentable resolution is a broken contract that should name the size, not a quiet substitution.

**Remedy:** Store the resolution as a `Vector2I` and keep the enum, if it stays at all, as a
convenience list of presets the game may ignore.

#### Stop documenting engine contracts in terms of game classes

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:8`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The boundary

**What:** Public engine headers explain their contracts by naming types that live in `game/` and
that no engine file can include.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:8`:

    // Anything the level can update and draw.

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:37` and `:55`:

    // time it was deleted Player's copy of it had silently drifted - it had
    ...
    // structure. ICollisionGameObject::shape() stays the fine half of that

`engine/render/texture_object.h:60`:

    // Level::draw_active_level runs draw() on the SAME object from every render

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY/The public face says "a stranger starts from the headers". The first
line of the engine's central interface tells that stranger the answer is "anything the level can
update and draw" — but there is no engine `Level` (PHILOSOPHY/Structural types says so explicitly),
`Player` is `game/objects/player.h`, `Level::draw_active_level` is `game/objects/level.cpp:393`,
and `ICollisionGameObject` is `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:7` — a type the engine
documents but does not ship, which is the residue of outstanding finding #13 now visible from the
engine side: `engine/collision/` contains only `Partitioner`. Each of these reads as an engine
concept the reader then cannot find. The comments are otherwise excellent — they explain *why*,
which is rare — so the fix is a word each, not a deletion.

**Remedy:** Replace `level` with `scene`, `Player` with "one implementer", and `Level::draw_active_level`
with "the per-view fan-out"; keep `ICollisionGameObject` only once the collision interface is an
engine type.

<a id="g-sweep-mechanism-vs-policy"></a>

## sweep-mechanism-vs-policy

*Group `sweep-mechanism-vs-policy` · 15 findings (3 critical, 8 high, 4 medium) · source `review2/raw/sweep-mechanism-vs-policy.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read PHILOSOPHY/CONVENTIONS/ARCHITECTURE, then walked every `.h`/`.cpp` under `engine/`,
`game/`, `samples/`, `tests/` and every `CMakeLists.txt`, looking for two things: general
machinery sitting in `game/` that the engine owes every client, and specific-game decisions
welded into `engine/`. The split has moved the *files*, but it has almost entirely failed to
move the *responsibilities*. `engine/` is now a library of drawable types, a resource loader,
a window shell and a maths pack — and nothing that holds, iterates, culls, collides or renders
a world. Everything above the level of "a single sprite knows how to blit itself" is in
`game/objects/level.cpp` and `game/states/`. In the other direction the leaks are smaller but
sharper: `MattMath` ships the paint-shooter's team palette, `ViewportManager` names the
paint-shooter's sprite sheet and frame, `CameraTools` hardcodes one game's camera feel (and
the numbers are already wrong for the engine's own split-screen at 1280x720), and
`ScreenResolution` is a closed list of four sizes a stranger cannot extend.

The sharpest single datum is `samples/minimal`. It is described in its own build file as the
thing that "keeps the engine/game boundary honest", and its 24-line `draw()` contains
`ID3D11DeviceContext`, `FinishCommandList`, `ExecuteCommandList` and a manual COM `Release`.
That is the honest measurement of where the boundary currently is: a new project on this
engine starts by writing D3D11. The second sharpest is arithmetic: two independent copies of
the "partition N, dispatch to the pool, record command lists, execute them on the immediate
context" protocol exist in `game/`, and they have already diverged on the
`FinishCommandList`/`ExecuteCommandList` restore flag.

What surprised me: the *newest* code is the best code. `Registry`, `ResourceLoader`,
`AssetManifest` and `game/main.cpp` are genuinely well-shaped mechanism with the policy pushed
out — `ResourceLoader::register_kind` is exactly the pattern PHILOSOPHY asks for, and
`main.cpp` teaches it the word "level" from the game side without the engine ever learning it.
The machinery for the migration below already exists in the codebase; it just has not been
applied to scenes, collision, input or UI.

### Themes

- The engine has no scene: object ownership, iteration, culling, collision dispatch, deletion
  and per-view render fan-out are all methods of the game's `Level` class, so a stranger's
  game inherits an interface (`IGameObject`) and nothing that holds one.
- Modules named in ARCHITECTURE exist as folders but not as content — `engine/collision/`
  holds a thread-range splitter, `engine/input/` holds a two-value enum, and there is no
  `engine/render/d3d11/` at all.
- The renderer seam is absent rather than deferred: every `SpriteBatch::Begin`/`End` pair in
  the repository is in `game/` or `samples/`, so drawing orchestration is a client
  responsibility today, including in the new-project template.
- Where the engine does contain policy it is spelt as a closed C++ enum or a `constexpr`
  block — team colours, four resolutions, four screen layouts, camera scroll borders — none of
  which a game can extend without editing engine source, which is PHILOSOPHY's own litmus
  test for game code.
- Duplication that has already diverged: two copies of pad-polling plus edge detection
  (`PlayerInput`, `MenuInput`), two copies of the parallel-render protocol
  (`Level::draw_active_level`, `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports`).
- The good pattern is present and unexploited: `Registry` + `ResourceLoader::register_kind`
  is the exact `map<string, factory>` shape PHILOSOPHY prescribes for the object builder, and
  the object builder does not use it.
- The build already tells the truth the code denies: `tests/assets` compiles engine `.cpp`
  files into the test binary rather than linking `ArtAttackEngine`, because linking the engine
  drags in D3D11 — the headless-testability claim is currently false at the link line.

#### Move the scene out of `Level` and into the engine

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:181-340`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1 (PHILOSOPHY/Structural types: "a **concrete class** … the `Scene` (registration, update/draw orchestration, culling, collision dispatch, cameras and views, spawn groups)")

**What:** Every responsibility PHILOSOPHY assigns to the engine's `Scene` is a private method
of the game's `Level`, and `grep -r "Scene" engine/` returns nothing.

**Evidence:**

    // level.cpp:233-261 — collision dispatch, O(n·m), no broad phase
    	// check player collisions
    	for (auto& player : *this->player_objects_)
    	{
    		bool player_colliding_with_structure = false;
    		for (auto& other_object : *this->collision_objects_)
    		{
    			if (other_object->for_deletion()) { continue; }
    			if (player->is_colliding(other_object.get()))
    			{
    				player->on_collision(other_object.get());
    				other_object->on_collision(player.get());

    // level.cpp:289-304 — the O(n²) half
    		for (auto& object_2 : *this->collision_objects_)
    		{
    			if (object->for_deletion() || object_2->for_deletion()) { continue; }
    			if (object == object_2) { continue; }
    			if (object->is_colliding(object_2.get()))

    // level.cpp:320-329 — swap-and-pop retirement of dead objects
    	for (size_t i = 0; i < this->collision_objects_->size(); i++)
    	{
    		if (this->collision_objects_->at(i)->for_deletion())
    		{
    			this->collision_objects_->at(i) = std::move(
    				this->collision_objects_->back());
    			this->collision_objects_->pop_back();
    			i--;

    // level.cpp:534-540 — culling
    		for (auto& object : *this->non_collision_objects_)
    		{
    			if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))
    			{
    				object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);

**Why it matters:** A stranger writing a game gets `IGameObject` (update/draw/bounds) and
`Application` (window, device, services, one state) and nothing in between. To draw two
objects they must write the container, the update loop, the cull test, the collision pair
loop, the deletion pass and the per-view fan-out themselves — which is what `samples/minimal`
demonstrably does, badly, in `HelloState::draw`. `IGameObject::bounds()` was introduced
specifically so "the caller build an index once and query it" (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:49-51`);
there is no caller in the engine to build that index, so the comment describes an intent no
engine code holds.

**Remedy:** Add `engine/core/scene.h` owning the object list, the cull query, the pair
dispatch and the deletion pass, and make `Level` a game class that owns a `Scene` and adds the
paint-battle rules — the shape PHILOSOPHY/Structural types already specifies.

#### `engine/collision/` contains no collision

- **File:** `engine/collision/partitioner.h:1-18`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The tree (`collision/  broad phase, narrow phase, manifolds, resolution`)

**What:** The only file in the engine's collision module is a thread-range splitter with no
collision concept in it, while the collision *interface* lives in `game/`, the collision
*maths* lives in `engine/math/`, and the collision *dispatch* lives in `game/objects/level.cpp`.

**Evidence:**

    // engine/collision/partitioner.h — the entire module
    	class Partitioner
    	{
    	public:
    		Partitioner() = default;
    		std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>
    			partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const;
    		std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>
    			partition(size_t num_elements, int num_partitions) const;
    	};

    // game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:7-21 — the interface PHILOSOPHY names as the
    // engine's, defined in the game, in the global namespace
    class ICollisionGameObject : public artattack::IGameObject
    {
    public:
    	virtual bool is_colliding(const ICollisionGameObject* other) const = 0;
    	virtual void on_collision(const ICollisionGameObject* other) = 0;
    	virtual CollisionObjectType collision_object_type() const = 0;
    	virtual const mattmath::Shape* shape() const = 0;
    	virtual bool for_deletion() const = 0;

**Why it matters:** This is new information beyond outstanding finding #13. #13 says the
collision interface carries a game enum; the post-split state is worse — the interface is not
in the engine *at all*, so there is no engine type for #13's enum to be removed *from*. Two
concrete consequences: (a) `samples/minimal` cannot use collision, because
`ICollisionGameObject` is in `game/` and the sample links only `ArtAttackEngine`, so the
"permanent second client" cannot exercise the engine's flagship subsystem without including
`game/` headers, which its own build file forbids in as many words ("It links ArtAttackEngine
and nothing from game/", `samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:16`); (b) the broad phase
PHILOSOPHY/Collision promises has nowhere to live, which is why `Level` runs an all-pairs loop.
Also note `Partitioner` is a thread-work concern filed under `collision/`, which mislabels the
one file that is there.

**Remedy:** Create `engine/collision/collision_object.h` with `shape()`, layer/mask and an
opaque game tag, move `Partitioner` to `engine/core/` beside `ThreadPool`, and let the enum
question (#13) be answered by the tag rather than by a type that does not exist yet.

#### The new-project template makes the game author write D3D11

- **File:** `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:62-85`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T10 ("Not a licence for: an expert-only API"); PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering ("Objects draw through a renderer interface")

**What:** The sample that ARCHITECTURE calls "the template a new project copies" opens a
deferred context, records a command list, executes it on the immediate context and releases a
COM object by hand — eight lines of graphics-backend code in the smallest possible game.

**Evidence:**

    	artattack::DeviceResources* device = this->app_->device_resources();
    	ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred = device->deferred_context(0);
    	SpriteBatch* sprite_batch = this->app_->sprite_batches()->at(0);

    	sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred);
    	this->greeting_->draw(sprite_batch);
    	this->hint_->draw(sprite_batch);
    	sprite_batch->End();

    	ID3D11CommandList* commands = nullptr;
    	if (FAILED(deferred->FinishCommandList(FALSE, &commands)))
    	{
    		throw std::runtime_error("HelloState::draw - FinishCommandList failed");
    	}

    	device->GetD3DDeviceContext()->ExecuteCommandList(commands, FALSE);
    	commands->Release();

**Why it matters:** Every `SpriteBatch::Begin`/`End` in the repository is in `game/` or
`samples/` — I grepped; the engine never opens a batch. So "drawing" is not a service the
engine provides, it is a protocol every client must reimplement, and the two existing
implementations have already diverged: `game/objects/level.cpp:606` and `:670` pass
`FinishCommandList(TRUE, …)` while `game/states/menu_page.cpp:120` passes `FALSE`, and
`game/states/game_states.cpp:337` passes `ExecuteCommandList(…, TRUE)` while
`game/states/menu_page.cpp:164` passes `FALSE`. This also nails the second-platform door shut:
ARCHITECTURE says backend code lives only in `render/d3d11/`, and there is no such folder —
the backend has instead escaped into two applications and a sample. A copy-paste new project
inherits a raw-COM leak on any early return added later.

**Remedy:** Give the engine the render-frame mechanism (`Scene`/`Renderer` opens the batches,
records the lists and submits them) so a state's `draw()` names what to draw and nothing about
how it reaches the GPU; the sample should then contain no `ID3D11*` identifier at all.

#### `ViewportManager` names the paint-shooter's sprite sheet and frame in an engine header

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:15-21`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1; PHILOSOPHY/The boundary ("Engine headers contain no game nouns — no team, weapon, paint, menu or **asset name**")

**What:** Two of the paint-shooter's content identifiers, and its divider colour, are public
static members of an engine class.

**Evidence:**

    		// How a split-screen divider is drawn. They live on the class that shapes
    		// the dividers rather than in a `consts` namespace of strays (CONVENTIONS,
    		// Constants and enumerators); a game asks for the rectangles and then for
    		// these to fill them.
    		static inline const std::string DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1";
    		static inline const std::string DIVIDER_FRAME_NAME = "pixel";
    		static inline const mattmath::Colour DIVIDER_COLOUR = colour_consts::BLACK;

    // game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:222-227 — the only consumer

    			ViewportManager::DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME,
    			ViewportManager::DIVIDER_FRAME_NAME,
    			rectangle,
    			this->render_resources_,
    			ViewportManager::DIVIDER_COLOUR));

**Why it matters:** `"sprite_sheet_1"` and `"pixel"` are entries in
`game/content/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json`. A stranger's game that does not ship a sheet by
that name gets a load-time throw from `RenderResources::resolve_texture` the moment it draws
split-screen dividers, and its only fix is to edit an engine header — which is exactly the
litmus test PHILOSOPHY gives for "this is game code". The comment defending their placement
argues the wrong point: the issue is not `consts`-namespace hygiene, it is that the engine has
learned two of this game's asset names.

**Remedy:** Delete all three; `viewport_dividers()` already returns rectangles, so the game
decides what fills them.

#### There is no state stack, so the game builds one out of four `StateContext`s

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.h:8-18`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Structural types ("the application shell — window, device, services, main loop, **the state stack**")

**What:** `StateContext` holds exactly one `State` with no push/pop, so a game that wants a
pause menu over a running level hand-rolls the nesting: `GameLevel` owns four separate
`StateContext`s plus an enum to route `update()`/`draw()` between them.

**Evidence:**

    // engine/core/state_context.h — the whole state machinery
    	class StateContext
    	{
    	public:
    		void update() const;
    		void draw() const;
    		void transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state);
    	private:
    		std::unique_ptr<State> state_ = nullptr;
    	};

    // game/states/game_states.h:59-69
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> pause_menu_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuAction> pause_menu_action_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuData> pause_menu_data_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<MenuInput> menu_input_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> results_menu_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuAction> results_menu_action_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuData> results_menu_data_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::StateContext> end_menu_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<EndMenuAction> end_menu_action_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<EndMenuData> end_menu_data_ = nullptr;
        GameLevelState state_ = GameLevelState::first_update;

**Why it matters:** "Modal state over a suspended state" is the flow every menu-having game
needs, and it is machinery, not policy. Because the engine does not provide it, the game
carries three parallel triples of (context, action-out-param, data) and a six-value enum whose
only job is to decide which of the four contexts `update()` and `draw()` forward to
(`game_states.cpp:141-354`). Each action is heap-allocated as a `unique_ptr<enum>` purely so a
child state can write a result back through a pointer — an out-param protocol the engine could
have made a return value. `GameMenu` repeats the shape at `game_states.h:24`.

**Remedy:** Make `StateContext` a stack — `push`/`pop` alongside `transition_to`, with
`update()`/`draw()` reaching the top — and let a popped state return a result.

#### `transition_to()` destroys the state that is calling it

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("Construction and destruction order are designed. If an ordering is load-bearing, it is either designed away or stated where it lives.")

**What:** `transition_to` assigns over `state_`, which deletes the currently-running `State` —
and its only callers call it from inside that state's own `update()`, so `this` is dangling
for the rest of the calling frame. Nothing in the header says so.

**Evidence:**

    	void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
    	{
    		this->state_ = std::move(state);   // deletes the running state
    		this->state_->set_context(this);
    		this->state_->init();
    	}

    // game/states/game_states.cpp:80-85 — called from GameMenu::update()
    void GameMenu::order_level_creation()
    {
        this->context()->transition_to(
            std::make_unique<GameLevel>(this->game_data_,
                *this->menu_data_->level_settings()));
    }

**Why it matters:** The reachable path is `Application::update()` →
`StateContext::update()` (`state_context.cpp:11`) → `GameMenu::update()`
(`game_states.cpp:72-79`) → `order_level_creation()` → `transition_to` → `~GameMenu`. Today
this is *not* UB, because every call site I opened either `return`s
immediately or touches no member afterwards (`game_states.cpp:82`, `:221`, `:262`, `:272`,
`:282`, `:299`; `main_menu.cpp:148`, `:157`, `:165`). But that is a property of the callers,
not of the API, and it is undocumented — the first person who adds a line after a
`transition_to` gets a use-after-free with no compiler help. `GameLevel` even calls
`this->level_->stop_music()` *before* each `transition_to` for exactly this reason, without
saying why.

**Remedy:** Defer the swap — record the pending state and apply it after `update()` returns —
and say so in the header.

#### `engine/input/` is a two-value enum; device polling and edge detection are duplicated in the game

- **File:** `engine/input/connection_state.h:1-10`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** T1; PHILOSOPHY/The boundary ("The engine provides: Input devices and action mapping | The game provides: Which actions exist and their bindings")

**What:** The engine's entire input module is `enum class ConnectionState { connected,
disconnected }`; `Application` hands out a raw `DirectX::GamePad*`, and both device polling and
press/release edge detection are written twice in `game/`.

**Evidence:**

    // engine/input/connection_state.h — the whole module
    namespace artattack
    {
        enum class ConnectionState { connected, disconnected };
    }

    // engine/app/application.h:123 — the mechanism the engine actually offers
    		DirectX::GamePad* gamepad() const;

    // game/objects/player_input.cpp:18-27 and game/states/menu_input.cpp:18-27 — same code
    	const auto pad = this->gamepad_->GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_NONE);
        if (pad.IsConnected())
        {
            result.left_analog_stick = Vector2F(pad.thumbSticks.leftX,
                -pad.thumbSticks.leftY);

**Why it matters:** `PlayerInput` and `MenuInput` are structurally identical — same
`RawXInput` struct shape, same `prev_inputs_[MAX_PAD_COUNT]` ring, same
`update_and_get_*()` loop with the same "one entry per pad slot, never compacted" invariant
re-documented in both (`player_input.cpp:128-134`, `menu_input.cpp:141-143`). Both define
their own `MAX_PAD_COUNT = 4` (`player_input.h:15`, aliased at `menu_input.h:14`). A stranger's
game gets none of this: it gets the DirectXTK object and writes deadzones and edge detection
from scratch, which also means the engine cannot ever grow a keyboard or a second backend
behind a seam (`input/xinput/` in ARCHITECTURE does not exist). The `ConnectionState` enum in
the engine while the polling is in the game is the split at its most inverted: the engine kept
the vocabulary and gave away the machinery.

**Remedy:** Move device polling, deadzones and edge detection into `engine/input/` behind a
`Device`/`ActionState` pair; leave `PlayerInputData`'s field list (jump, shoot, debug) in the
game, where the bindings belong.

#### The engine's camera-follow tuning is one game's policy, and it is already wrong for the engine's own split-screen

- **File:** `engine/render/camera_tools.cpp:14-22`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1; T7 ("data says *which* and *how much*")

**What:** `CameraTools` hardcodes a scroll-border model with pixel minimums tuned for a
full-screen 1280x720 viewport, with no parameter and no data path; at 1280x720 those minimums
invert the dead zone for every split-screen layout the same engine provides.

**Evidence:**

    		constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_LEFT = 0.4f;
    		constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_TOP = 0.2f;
    		constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_RIGHT = 0.4f;
    		constexpr float DEFAULT_BORDER_RATIO_BOTTOM = 0.4f;

    		constexpr float MIN_BORDER_LEFT = 400.0f;
    		constexpr float MIN_BORDER_TOP = 250.0f;
    		constexpr float MIN_BORDER_RIGHT = 400.0f;
    		constexpr float MIN_BORDER_BOTTOM = 250.0f;

    // camera_tools.cpp:102-105 — clamped against half the viewport…
    		clamp_ref(result.left, MIN_BORDER_LEFT, viewport_size.x / 2.0f);
    		clamp_ref(result.right, MIN_BORDER_RIGHT, viewport_size.x / 2.0f);
    		clamp_ref(result.top, MIN_BORDER_TOP, viewport_size.y / 2.0f);
    		clamp_ref(result.bottom, MIN_BORDER_BOTTOM, viewport_size.y / 2.0f);

    // engine/math/matt_math.cpp:50-60 — …but min wins when min > max
    	void mattmath::clamp_ref(float& value, float min, float max)
    	{
    		if (value < min) { value = min; }
    		else if (value > max) { value = max; }
    	}

**Why it matters:** At `ScreenResolution::s_1280_720` — the `ApplicationOptions` default
(`application.h:37`) and what `samples/minimal/main.cpp:29` selects —
`ViewportManager::calculate_viewport` gives a four-player viewport of 640x360
(`viewport_manager.cpp:197-223`). Borders then compute to left/right = 400 (from 256, floored
by `MIN_BORDER_LEFT` even though the max is 320) and top/bottom = 250 (from 72 and 144, max
180). `calculate_camera` builds `left_edge = tx+400`, `right_edge = tx+640-400 = tx+240`, so
`left_edge > right_edge`: a player at the viewport centre satisfies `player_center.x <
left_edge` and the camera translates -80; next frame the player is past `right_edge` and it
translates +160; and so on, every frame, forever. The same inversion hits the vertical axis in
two-player at 720p (360-tall viewport, 250 top and bottom). `camera_bounds` in all three
shipped levels is ~6100x5350 (`game/content/levels/*.json`), so the bounds clamp does not
absorb it away from the level edges. Separately, the parameter is named `player_center`
(`camera_tools.h:12`) — a game noun in an engine signature.

**Remedy:** Take the border ratios and minimums as a parameter struct the game supplies
(loaded from its own tuning data), and clamp the minimums against the maximums before applying
them.

#### `ScreenResolution` is a closed list of four sizes, and a window resize never reaches it

- **File:** `engine/render/resolution_manager.cpp:153-176`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1; T6 ("Quiet failure is the most expensive kind")

**What:** The engine models "resolution" as an enum of four 16:9 sizes and silently snaps
anything else to 1280x720 — and `Application` never tells `ResolutionManager` about a
user-driven window resize, so after one the whole engine lays out against a stale size.

**Evidence:**

    // resolution_manager.cpp:153-176
        ScreenResolution ResolutionManager::convert_ivec_to_resolution(
            const Vector2I& vec) const
        {
            if (vec.x == 1280 && vec.y == 720) { return ScreenResolution::s_1280_720; }
            …
            else
            {
        		return ScreenResolution::s_1280_720;
        	}
        }

    // engine/app/application.cpp:359-362 — the resize path
    	void Application::on_window_size_changed(int width, int height)
    	{
    		std::ignore = this->device_resources_->WindowSizeChanged(width, height);
    	}

**Why it matters:** The window is created `WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW` (`application.cpp:112-116`) with a
320x200 minimum (`application.h:50-51`), so dragging its edge is a supported action. That path
resizes the swap chain and leaves `resolution_manager_` reporting whatever the game last
selected. Everything downstream reads the manager, not the backbuffer:
`ViewportManager::player_viewport` (`viewport_manager.cpp:73-77`),
`Level::update` for the countdown position (`level.cpp:91`), every menu via
`MenuPage::float_resolution` (`menu_page.cpp:195-198`). So after any drag-resize the viewports
and all UI layout are computed against a size the backbuffer no longer has. The enum itself is
policy: which resolutions a game offers is a game's decision, and a stranger wanting 1366x768
or a borderless desktop-native size cannot express it — `ApplicationOptions::resolution` is
typed as the enum, so the door is closed at the API.

**Remedy:** Make the manager hold a `Vector2I` and update it from `on_window_size_changed`;
keep `ScreenResolution` as a game-side convenience list that maps to sizes.

#### The object builder is a hardcoded `if`-chain, not the factory registry the engine already knows how to build

- **File:** `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:16-166`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T7 ("The object builder is a `map<string, factory>` the game registers into; unknown types fail naming the type and file")

**What:** Spawning a level object from JSON is a chain of `if (type == "...")` over three
hardcoded type names inside one 150-line function, and adding a fourth object type is a
recompile of the builder — while `ResourceLoader::register_kind` in the same repository is
exactly the registry PHILOSOPHY asks for.

**Evidence:**

    	std::string type = json["type"].GetString();
    	if (type == "Structure")
    	…
    	if (type == "StructurePaintable")
    	…
    	if (type == "StructureRamp")
    	…
    	throw std::exception("Invalid collision object type");

    // engine/assets/resource_loader.h:60 — the pattern that already exists
    		void register_kind(const std::string& kind, AssetKind asset_kind);

**Why it matters:** Three concrete costs. (1) The rectangle-parsing block is copy-pasted
verbatim between the `Structure` and `StructurePaintable` branches
(`level_object_builder.cpp:38-57` and `:81-100`) — 20 duplicated lines that will diverge. (2)
The failure is `std::exception("Invalid collision object type")` with no type name and no file
name, which is precisely the T6 contract PHILOSOPHY writes for this function and precisely what
`ResourceLoader::load_manifest` already does correctly. (3) The keys are `PascalCase`
(`"Structure"`) and the collision-type values are `SCREAMING_SNAKE` (`"STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH"`),
both against CONVENTIONS/Data, which says JSON keys and names are `snake_case`.

**Remedy:** Give the engine a `Registry<std::function<…>>`-shaped object factory the game
registers into, the way `register_kind` works, and have the miss throw naming the type and the
file.
