#### Delete the `interface` macro from `engine/render/device_resources.h`

- **File:** `engine/render/device_resources.h:17`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12 (the language over a dialect)

**What:** A public engine type is declared with `interface`, which is not C++ but a Windows SDK
macro (`combaseapi.h` defines it as `struct`), reaching this file only because
`<Windows.h>` is included ten lines above.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/device_resources.h:7
    #include <Windows.h>
    ...
    engine/render/device_resources.h:16
        // Provides an interface for an application that owns DeviceResources to be notified of the device being lost or created.
        interface IDeviceNotify
        {
            virtual void OnDeviceLost() = 0;
            virtual void OnDeviceRestored() = 0;

**Why it matters:** T12 names exactly this: "no macro that reads like a keyword… the line is
that a macro may not invent syntax". `IDeviceNotify` is not private — `engine/app/application.h:71`
reads `class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext`, so it is on the engine's
public inheritance surface and a reader of `application.h` who follows the base class arrives
at a declaration whose first token is not C++. It is also fragile in the direction the project
is heading: the day `<Windows.h>` stops being included by that header (a second platform, or
just tidying), the file stops compiling for a reason that has nothing to do with what changed.
This is the only occurrence in the repository — I grepped.

**Remedy:** Write `class IDeviceNotify` (or `struct`), and rename it in the same pass as the
other `I`-prefixed types.

#### Mark the three Microsoft template files as vendored, or rewrite them

- **File:** `engine/core/step_timer.h:1-190`, `engine/render/device_resources.h:1-147`, `engine/render/device_resources.cpp:1-777`, `engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:1-34`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never (`m_`, `get_` on accessors, PascalCase functions), ARCHITECTURE/The tree (`external/` is where third-party source lives)

**What:** Four files inside `engine/` are the Microsoft Direct3D 11 game template verbatim, and
are indistinguishable from hand-written engine code except by their naming: 212 `m_`-prefixed
members between them, PascalCase methods, `Get`-prefixed accessors, `c_`/`s_` prefixes, and
banner comments naming filenames that no longer exist.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/step_timer.h:1
    //
    // StepTimer.h - A simple timer that provides elapsed time information
    //
    ...
    engine/core/step_timer.h:44
            uint64_t GetElapsedTicks() const noexcept { return m_elapsedTicks; }
            double GetElapsedSeconds() const noexcept { return TicksToSeconds(m_elapsedTicks); }

    engine/render/device_resources.h:2
    // DeviceResources.h - A wrapper for the Direct3D 11 device and swapchain
    ...
    engine/render/device_resources.h:30
            static constexpr unsigned int c_FlipPresent  = 0x1;

    engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:10
        class com_exception : public std::exception
    ...
    engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:27
        inline void ThrowIfFailed(HRESULT hr)

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS is explicit that `m_` is never used ("the trailing underscore
already does that job"), that accessors are the bare noun, and that functions are snake_case.
`StepTimer` is a member of `Application` (`engine/app/application.h:149`) and
`ThrowIfFailed`/`com_exception` are reachable from every game translation unit through
`game/pch.h:79`, so a stranger learning the engine's conventions from its own source meets two
contradictory schemes with nothing telling them which is the engine's. The banner comments make
it worse rather than better: a reader who greps for `DeviceResources.h` after reading line 2
finds nothing, because the conventions pass renamed the file and left the comment. This is not
"the existing pattern" — it is unattributed third-party code that the naming rules were never
applied to, and the tree already has a home for third-party source.

**Remedy:** Either move them under `external/` (or a clearly-marked `engine/**/vendor/`) with
the upstream attribution the template asks for, or adopt them properly and rename members and
methods to the engine's scheme; the banner comments should go either way.

- **File:** `engine/ui/widget.h:9,33,59,76,114,140`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (one primary type per header; named for the primary type they hold)

**What:** The engine's entire UI surface is one 168-line header holding six unrelated public
classes, under a filename that names none of them.

**Evidence:**

    engine/ui/widget.h:9

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE promises `ui/` will hold "widgets, focus, controller
navigation" — a growing module — and it starts as one file whose name matches no type in it, so
there is no obvious place for the next widget to go, and no smaller unit than "all of the UI"

#### `tests/assets` compiles engine sources instead of linking the engine, with different defines

- **File:** `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-11`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout ("Tests link libraries, never `#include` implementation files")

**What:** `AssetsTests` adds two `ArtAttackEngine` source files directly to its own target
rather than linking the library, and the generated build shows those objects compiled with a
different set of preprocessor definitions than the objects that ship.

**Evidence:**

    tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3
    # The manifest loader reads a file and parses JSON, and that is all it does -
    # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units
    # directly rather than linking the engine and everything the engine drags in.
    add_executable(AssetsTests
        asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp
        test_main.cpp
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/json_loader.cpp"
    )

    out/build/x64-debug/build.ninja:105 (ArtAttackEngine's copy of asset_manifest_loader.cpp)
      DEFINES = -DDIRECTX_TOOLKIT_IMPORT -DNOMINMAX -DUNICODE -DUSING_XAUDIO2_REDIST -DUSING_XINPUT -DWIN32 -DWIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN -D_UNICODE -D_WINDOWS

    out/build/x64-debug/build.ninja:1361 (AssetsTests' copy of the same file)
      DEFINES = -DNOMINMAX -DUNICODE -DWIN32 -DWIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN -D_UNICODE -D_WINDOWS

**Why it matters:** The object the test exercises is not the object that ships:
`DIRECTX_TOOLKIT_IMPORT`, `USING_XAUDIO2_REDIST` and `USING_XINPUT` are absent from the test
build because it does not link `Microsoft::DirectXTK`. Today neither loader includes a DirectXTK
header so the two builds agree, but nothing enforces that, and the first asset loader that does
will either fail to compile in the test target or — worse — compile differently there. The
stated reason ("everything the engine drags in") is also not how a static library links: the
linker only pulls objects that are referenced, so linking `ArtAttackEngine` would not have
brought in the device. Related: no test target in the repository links `ArtAttackEngine` at all
(`tests/core` links nothing, `tests/math` links `MattMath`), so the claim that the engine is
linkable headlessly is not currently exercised by `ctest`.

**Remedy:** Link `ArtAttackEngine` from `AssetsTests` and delete the two source entries; if a
runtime DLL dependency is what actually blocks it, say so in the comment and fix that instead.

#### Publish rapidjson through the engine's public API, or stop exposing it

- **File:** `engine/assets/json_loader.h:3,12`, `engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules ("`rapidjson` reaches `assets` and stops there"), T9

**What:** A public engine header returns `rapidjson::Document` by value, which forces
`ArtAttackEngine` to export rapidjson's include directory as **PUBLIC**, so every consumer of
the engine — and every module of the engine — compiles with a vendored third-party parser on
its include path.

**Evidence:**

    engine/assets/json_loader.h:1
    #pragma once

    #include <rapidjson/document.h>

    namespace artattack
    {
    ...
    engine/assets/json_loader.h:12
    	rapidjson::Document read_json_file(const char* path);

    engine/CMakeLists.txt:46
    target_include_directories(ArtAttackEngine PUBLIC
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/rapidjson/include"
    )

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE's stated invariant is that "no type on the draw path reads a
file, so `rapidjson` reaches `assets` and stops there — drawing a sprite does not compile a JSON
parser". As declared, rapidjson reaches everything: it is on the include path of every
`ArtAttackEngine` translation unit and of every downstream target, and the engine's public API
surface now contains a third-party DOM type a stranger did not choose. It also means any game
extending the loader (which `ResourceLoader::register_kind` invites) is writing against
rapidjson's API with the engine's blessing but no versioning promise. It is inconsistent in the
source too: `json_loader.h` and `game/save.h:6` spell it `<rapidjson/document.h>` while
`game/objects/level_builder.h:13`, `level_loaded_info.h:4` and `level_object_builder.h:5` spell
it `"rapidjson/document.h"`.

**Remedy:** Either make the dependency explicit and supported (keep it PUBLIC, and say so in
ARCHITECTURE), or return an opaque engine document type from `json_loader.h` and make the
rapidjson include directory PRIVATE.

#### Eleven headers put the standard library and external dependencies before project includes

- **File:** `engine/audio/sound_bank.h:3-6`, `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-4`, `engine/render/drawer.h:3-4`, `engine/render/resolution_manager.h:3-4`, `game/objects/level_builder.h:13-14`, `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:3-8`, `game/objects/level_object_builder.h:4-6`, `game/objects/player_input.h:3-4`, `game/save.h:3-7`, `game/states/menu_input.h:3-4`, `game/states/menu_level_settings.h:3-5`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (include order: own header, engine, external, standard library)

**What:** Eleven headers list a standard-library or external include ahead of a project include,
inverting the documented order; two of them interleave all three categories.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:3
    #include <cstdio>
    #include "rapidjson/document.h"
    #include <string>
    #include <vector>
    #include <map>
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"

    game/save.h:3
    #include <iostream>
    #include <chrono>
    #include "game/directory_consts.h"
    #include <rapidjson/document.h>
    #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"
    #include "engine/render/screen_resolution.h"

    engine/audio/sound_bank.h:3
    #include <Audio.h>
    #include <memory>
    #include <string>
    #include "engine/core/registry.h"

**Why it matters:** The order is not decoration: putting project headers first is what makes a
missing include in a project header show up as an error rather than being papered over by a
standard header that a later line would have supplied. `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h` is
the clearest case — `<string>`, `<vector>` and `<map>` are pulled in above `matt_math.h`, and
`matt_math.h` itself includes all three, so nothing in that file tells a reader which of them
the header genuinely needs. These eleven are the complete list across `engine/`, `game/`,
`samples/` and `tests/`; every `.cpp` in the repository is already correct.

**Remedy:** Reorder the eleven into own-header / project / external / standard-library groups
separated by a blank line, and treat the grouping as reviewable.

- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Constants ("Enumerations are `enum class`"), CONVENTIONS/Never (SCREAMING constants)

**What:** The one enum the conventions pass missed is unscoped, snake_case-typed and

nothing else". This is the only surviving unscoped enum in the repository (I grepped all 208
sources), so it is a single-file fix, but its blast radius is not single-file: `projectile.h`
is included by `projectile_ball/jet/mist/rolling/spray.h`, `projectile_builder.h`,
`weapon_details.h` and thence `weapon.h` and `player.h`, so five bare uppercase names are
visible almost everywhere in `game/`. `weapon_consts.h:27,49,83,99,127` already needs the
comment `//projectile_type` beside each bare `SPRAY`/`JET`/`ROLLING`/`MIST` to say what the
value means — which is exactly the readability the scoped form gives for free.

**Remedy:** `enum class ProjectileType { spray, jet, rolling, mist, ball };` and update the
fourteen use sites.

#### `tests/math/math_tests.cpp` is named for its folder and holds two subjects

- **File:** `tests/math/math_tests.cpp:1-1013` (suites at 20 and 209)
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files ("Tests are named for their subject: `vector2_tests.cpp`")

**What:** One 1013-line file in `tests/math/` is called `math_tests.cpp` and contains two
doctest suites covering two different translation units, `ericson_math.cpp` and `matt_math.cpp`.

**Evidence:**

    tests/math/math_tests.cpp:20
    	TEST_SUITE("EricsonMathTests")
    ...
    tests/math/math_tests.cpp:209
    	TEST_SUITE("MattMathTests")

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS names the intended granularity with an example —
`vector2_tests.cpp` — and this is the opposite: a file named for the folder it sits in,
holding 36 test cases across intersection tests for rectangles, circles, triangles, quads,
segments and rotated rectangles, plus Ericson's closest-point and segment routines. Adding a
test for `Vector2F` has no obvious home other than "the end", which is how a 1013-line test file
becomes a 2000-line one. `collision_tools_tests.cpp` in the same folder shows the right shape.

**Remedy:** Split into `ericson_math_tests.cpp` and per-subject files as `matt_math.h` itself is

#### The build copies the game's authoring tools and dead content into every output directory

- **File:** `game/CMakeLists.txt:91-98`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (files and directories are snake_case), ARCHITECTURE/The build

**What:** The content mirror copies whole directories, and those directories contain three
committed third-party executables, a GIMP source file, 8.3 MB of superseded textures, 2.4 MB of
unused fonts and 295 MB of audio that is not in the repository at all — into every build
directory, for every configuration.

**Evidence:**

    game/CMakeLists.txt:91
    foreach(content_dir textures levels fonts sounds)
        add_custom_command(TARGET artattack_content POST_BUILD
            COMMAND "${CMAKE_COMMAND}" -E copy_directory_if_different
                "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/content/${content_dir}"
                "$<TARGET_FILE_DIR:ArtAttackGame>/${content_dir}"
            VERBATIM
        )
    endforeach()

    tracked under those directories:
      game/content/textures/texconv.exe              (922 KB)
      game/content/fonts/MakeSpriteFont.exe          (40 KB)
      game/content/sounds/sound_bank_1/XWBTool.exe   (108 KB)
      game/content/textures/sprite_sheet_1.xcf       (176 KB)
      game/content/textures/old textures/            (84 files, 8.3 MB)
      game/content/fonts/unuseed fonts/              (25 files, 2.4 MB)
      game/content/levels/unused/                    (4 files)
      game/content/levels/player_movement_notes.txt, close_quarters.pub, turebulence.pub

**Why it matters:** The manifest (`game/content/manifest.json`) names 7 fonts, 1 sprite sheet,
3 levels and 1 sound bank — everything else in those four directories is copied for nothing, and
`content/sounds` alone is 295 MB on disk. Three of the copied files are executables that land
beside the shipped game. The directory names also break the file convention twice over: two of
them contain spaces (`old textures`, `unuseed fonts`, `new player textures`) and one contains a
typo, as does `turebulence.pub`. This extends, rather than repeats, README.md's known
repo-hygiene finding: the CMake conversion turned committed clutter into build output.
(The audio being gitignored — `.gitignore:366-368` vs `resource_loader.cpp:167`'s
`directory + name + ".xwb"` — remains outstanding from the previous review and still means a
fresh clone cannot start a level; `samples/minimal` is unaffected, its manifest names only a
font.)

**Remedy:** Copy only what the manifest names (the loader already knows), and move the tools and
superseded assets out of `content/` into a non-copied `tools/`/`archive/` directory with
snake_case names.

#### Spell third-party includes one way

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:3`, `engine/render/drawer.h:3`, `engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:7`, `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:8`, `game/objects/level_builder.h:13`, `game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4`, `game/objects/level_object_builder.h:5`, `game/save.cpp:7-8`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files (include paths), T4

**What:** DirectXTK and rapidjson headers are included with quotes in eight places and with
angle brackets everywhere else, so the same dependency is spelled two ways in one tree.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/drawer.h:3
    #include "SpriteBatch.h"

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:4
    #include <SpriteBatch.h>

    game/objects/level_loaded_info.h:4
    #include "rapidjson/document.h"

    engine/assets/json_loader.h:3
    #include <rapidjson/document.h>

**Why it matters:** The quoted form searches the including file's own directory first, so
`engine/render/drawer.h`'s `"SpriteBatch.h"` would silently prefer an `engine/render/SpriteBatch.h`
if one ever appeared — the failure mode the all-lowercase filename rule was introduced to delete,
in a different guise. It also removes the at-a-glance signal that separates "mine" from "bought"
(T9), which is the whole point of the quote/bracket distinction in a codebase where project
includes are always quoted and always start with a module name.

**Remedy:** Angle brackets for everything outside the repository; quotes only for
repository-root-relative project paths.

#### Settle on one indentation style and commit a `.clang-format`

- **File:** repository-wide; worst cases `game/objects/player.cpp` (332 tab-indented lines, 284 space-indented), `game/objects/weapon.cpp`, `game/states/game_states.cpp`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness)

**What:** 156 source files are tab-indented, 32 are space-indented and 16 mix both within a
single file; there is no `.clang-format` or `.editorconfig` in the repository.

**Evidence:** counted over all 208 tracked `.h`/`.cpp` files outside `external/` (four contain
no indented lines and fall into no bucket):

    tab-indented only:    156
    space-indented only:   32   (incl. engine/core/thread_pool.{h,cpp}, engine/math/collision_tools.{h,cpp},
                                 engine/render/device_resources.{h,cpp}, engine/render/resolution_manager.{h,cpp})
    mixed within a file:   16   (game/objects/player.cpp 332/284, game/objects/weapon.cpp 83/191,
                                 game/objects/projectile_builder.cpp 168/4, game/save.cpp 12/84, ...)

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS opens by saying the scheme has to be "learnable in one sitting"
and boring everywhere; a contributor's first diff currently depends on which file they opened.
Mixed indentation inside one function body is also the thing that makes a whitespace-only diff
land in the middle of a real change. A committed `.clang-format` costs one file and removes the
question permanently — and it is the kind of wall PHILOSOPHY prefers: boring, mechanical, not
review's job.

**Remedy:** Add a `.clang-format` recording the chosen style and reformat once in a
whitespace-only commit.

#### The `*_consts.h` headers are named for no type and collect strays

- **File:** `game/directory_consts.h:8-12`, `game/objects/player_consts.h:1-121`, `game/objects/weapon_consts.h:1-172`, `game/objects/projectile_consts.h:1-106`, `game/states/main_menu.h:13-88`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Constants ("Constants that stay in code live next to the one thing they configure, not in a `consts` namespace collecting strays"), CONVENTIONS/Never (SCREAMING constants), T7

**What:** Five headers exist to hold namespace-scope SCREAMING constants and declare no type at
all, which is both the naming rule CONVENTIONS calls out by name and the file-naming rule
("named for the primary type they hold").

**Evidence:**

    game/directory_consts.h:8
    namespace directory_consts
    {
    	const static std::string MANIFEST_PATH = "./manifest.json";
    	const static std::string SAVE_FILE_PATH = "./save/save_data.json";
    }

    game/objects/weapon_consts.h:27
            SPRAY,         //projectile_type

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS anticipates this exactly: "A header full of numeric constants is
usually tuning data in the wrong place — *which* and *how much* belong in JSON (T7)."
`weapon_consts.h` (172 lines) and `projectile_consts.h` (106 lines) are the paint-shooter's
weapon and projectile tuning tables compiled into the binary, so changing a fire rate is a
rebuild — the thing T7 exists to prevent, in a project that already has a manifest and a JSON
loader for exactly this. `const static` at namespace scope in a header also means internal
linkage and a per-TU copy, and the SCREAMING spelling collides with the rule that a screaming
name always signals a macro.

**Remedy:** Move the tuning tables into the content JSON the registries already load, and put
whatever must stay in code next to the type it configures.

<a id="g-sweep-dialect"></a>

## sweep-dialect — T12: the language over a dialect

*Group `sweep-dialect` · 17 findings (4 high, 9 medium, 4 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-dialect.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I swept every first-party file in `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/`, `tests/`, `cmake/` and the
root build files for macros, generated code, and vocabulary that shadows the language's own.
The macro clause of T12 comes out almost clean: there are exactly twelve `#define`s in
first-party code — nine in `game/pch.h` configuring `<Windows.h>` and three
`DOCTEST_CONFIG_IMPLEMENT_WITH_MAIN` lines in the test mains — and not one of them invents
syntax, hides control flow, or renames anything. There is no code generator, no reflection
macro, no `TArray`. Every header carries `#pragma once`; no header contains `using namespace`.
The content JSON is clean too: I read all six level/manifest/sheet/bank files and there is not
one expression, conditional or loop in them — nothing a T10 reader would call a DSL.

The dialect is real, but it is not made of macros. It is made of everything that reads *like*
a macro or a foreign language and is not one. SCREAMING_SNAKE is the codebase's default
constant style — roughly 300 declarations, `colour_consts::WHITE`, `Vector2F::ZERO`,
`player_consts::MAX_VELOCITY`, and two SCREAMING `typedef`s (`AABB`, `OBB`) that are types —
so the one signal CONVENTIONS deliberately reserves ("a screaming name always signals
preprocessor danger and nothing else ever does") now means the opposite of danger in every
place it appears. Types wear `I` and `M` prefixes in the engine's most-touched headers. One
public engine header declares a type with the Windows SDK's `interface` macro, which is a
macro that reads exactly like a keyword. And two DirectXTK-lineage files were pulled inside
`namespace artattack` without being translated, so a reader crossing from `handle.h` into
`step_timer.h` changes language mid-library.

What surprised me most was the build: `artattack_settings` carries `NOMINMAX` and
`WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN`, and it is linked `PRIVATE` into both libraries — so the definitions that
stop `<Windows.h>` from redefining `min` and `max` do not reach anyone who links
`ArtAttackEngine` from outside this tree, while `engine/app/application.h` includes
`<Windows.h>` unconditionally. The engine's own public header hands a stranger the single most
famous name-stealing macro in C++. Second surprise: `engine/core/step_timer.h` uses
`LARGE_INTEGER` and `QueryPerformanceCounter` while including only `<cmath>`, `<cstdint>` and
`<exception>` — it compiles today only because its one includer happens to pull Windows in
first.

### Themes

- The preprocessor is used correctly and sparingly, but the *reservation* CONVENTIONS makes
  for it — SCREAMING means macro — has been spent on ~300 ordinary constants, so the warning
  signal is gone.
- Foreign vocabulary entered the engine by adoption, not by writing: `interface`, `IDeviceNotify`,
  `m_` members and PascalCase methods came in with DirectXTK sample code that was wrapped in
  `namespace artattack` and then left in its own language.
- The type-prefix rule CONVENTIONS lists under "Never" is broken by exactly the two examples
  the document names (`IGameObject`) plus an unexplained `M` family, and the prefixes have been
  carried into filenames, so they will cost a rename of files as well as types.
- Compile-time contracts that the engine's headers *require* are declared `PRIVATE` in CMake,
  so they hold inside this repository and evaporate for the stranger the engine is being built
  for.
- The engine's vocabulary is not yet free of the game's: three separate engine files name the
  paint-shooter's teams, sprite sheet and icon resource.
- Data files are clean of logic, but their *identifiers* speak three dialects at once —
  PascalCase C++ class names, SCREAMING enum names and snake_case asset names — one of which
  welds the content format to C++ class spellings.
- Header self-sufficiency is asserted by CONVENTIONS and proven nowhere: all 46 game `.cpp`
  files open with the PCH rather than their own header, and at least one engine header does not
  compile alone.

---

#### Stop declaring a type with the Windows SDK's `interface` macro

- **File:** `engine/render/device_resources.h:16-24`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12

**What:** A public engine header declares `IDeviceNotify` with `interface`, which is not a C++
keyword but a Windows SDK object-like macro — the exact shape T12 forbids.

**Evidence:**

    // Provides an interface for an application that owns DeviceResources to be notified of the device being lost or created.
    interface IDeviceNotify
    {
        virtual void OnDeviceLost() = 0;
        virtual void OnDeviceRestored() = 0;

    protected:
        ~IDeviceNotify() = default;
    };

`interface` is defined in the Windows SDK, `Include/10.0.26100.0/shared/basetyps.h`:

    161 #define interface __STRUCT__
    ...
    179 #define interface               struct

**Why it matters:** T12's line is "a macro may not invent syntax". This one invents a
class-key. A reader who greps the repository for `interface` finds no definition, because it
comes from a header three levels deep in the `<d3d11_1.h>` chain; a reader who assumes it means
something stronger than `struct` (MSVC's `__interface`, or C++/CX's `interface class`, both of
which impose real restrictions) is wrong. It is also the only declaration in the engine whose
default member access is decided by a third party's preprocessor. `Application` publicly
derives from it (`engine/app/application.h:71`), so this is on the inheritance path of the type
every game constructs.

**Remedy:** Write `class DeviceNotify` (or `struct`), and drop the prefix while touching it.

---

#### Remove the `I` and `M` type prefixes from the engine's public types

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:23`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never, T12

**What:** The interface a game implements is named `IGameObject`, the widget set is named
`MObject`/`MContainer`/`MWidget`/`MTexture`/`MText`/`MTextDropShadow`, and the prefixes are
carried into filenames — all against a rule CONVENTIONS states with `IGameObject` as its own
worked example.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:23`

    class IGameObject

`engine/ui/widget.h:9,33,59,76,114,140`

    class MObject : public IGameObject
    class MContainer final : public MObject
    class MWidget : public MObject
    class MTexture final : public MWidget, public TextureObject
    class MText final : public MWidget, public Text
    class MTextDropShadow final : public MWidget, public TextDropShadow

`engine/render/device_resources.h:17`, `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:7`,
`game/objects/i_paintable_game_object.h:9`

    interface IDeviceNotify
    class ICollisionGameObject : public artattack::IGameObject
    class IPaintableGameObject

CONVENTIONS, Types: "**No prefixes, ever.** Interfaces are just types — `GameObject`, not
`IGameObject`". CONVENTIONS, Never: "`I`, `C`, `F`, `U` or any other type prefix." T12 names the
same thing: "the prefix on every type name … exists to tell you which dialect you are currently
in."

**Why it matters:** `IGameObject` is the first type a stranger meets and the only one they must
implement; ARCHITECTURE's boundary diagram already calls it `GameObject`, so the document and
the header disagree on the name of the central abstraction. `M` is worse than `I` because it
stands for nothing a reader can recover — six public types share a prefix with no expansion
anywhere in the repository. The cost of fixing this rises every commit: the prefixes are in
three filenames (`i_game_object.h`, `i_collision_game_object.h`, `i_paintable_game_object.h`)
and in 76 `namespace artattack` blocks' worth of use sites.

**Remedy:** Rename to `GameObject`, `CollisionObject`, `PaintableObject`, `DeviceNotify`, and
give the widget family real nouns (`Widget`, `Container`, `Image`, `Label`, `ShadowLabel`),
renaming the headers with them.

#### Stop spelling non-macro constants in SCREAMING_SNAKE

- **File:** `engine/math/colour.h:9-312`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Constants, T12

**What:** Roughly 300 ordinary constants — and two `typedef`s, which are types — are spelled
SCREAMING_SNAKE, the form CONVENTIONS reserves for macros alone so that a screaming name always
means preprocessor; since the codebase contains no first-party macros, the signal now means
exactly the opposite of what it was reserved for.

**Evidence:**

`engine/math/colour.h:9,16,303,308-312` (148 in `html::`, 153 beside it)

        const std::string ALICE_BLUE = "f0f8ff";
        const std::string BLACK = "000000";
    const mattmath::Colour WHITE = { html::WHITE };
    const mattmath::Colour TEAM_BLUE = { 6, 52, 204, 255 };

`engine/math/matt_math.h:46-47,295,496-505,1057` — engine values:

    constexpr float PI_OVER_2 = PI / 2.0f;
    constexpr float EPSILON = 0.0001f;
        static const RectangleF ZERO;
        static const Vector2F DIRECTION_UP_RIGHT;
        static const Camera DEFAULT_CAMERA;

`engine/math/matt_math.h:298,1149` — SCREAMING **types**, and `typedef` rather than `using`:

    typedef mattmath::RectangleF AABB;
    typedef RectangleRotated OBB;

`engine/render/viewport_manager.h:19-21,52`, `game/objects/player_consts.h:19-25`,
`game/objects/weapon_consts.h:8-15`, `game/directory_consts.h:10-11`,
`tests/math/math_tests.cpp:11-13` all follow the same style.

CONVENTIONS, Constants: "SCREAMING_SNAKE is reserved for macros alone, so that a screaming name
always signals preprocessor danger and nothing else ever does." CONVENTIONS, Never: "SCREAMING
constants — screaming means macro, nothing else."

**Why it matters:** This is the largest single divergence between the code and the naming
document, and it is self-reinforcing: because every constant screams, a genuine macro
introduced tomorrow (the assertion macro T12 explicitly permits) will be invisible in a diff.
`AABB` and `OBB` are the sharpest case — they are types wearing macro clothing, and they are a
second name for `RectangleF` and `RectangleRotated`, appearing 71 and 13 times across the tree, so a
reader has to learn that `AABB` and `RectangleF` are the same thing before they can read
`collision_tools.h`.

**Remedy:** Rename to value casing (`Colour::white`, `Vector2F::zero`, `epsilon`,
`max_velocity`), and replace the `typedef`s either with `using Aabb = RectangleF;` or, better,
delete them so each shape has one name.

#### Propagate NOMINMAX and the language standard to consumers, not just to the library

- **File:** `engine/CMakeLists.txt:50-53`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** T12

**What:** `artattack_settings` — which carries `NOMINMAX`, `WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN`, `UNICODE` and
`cxx_std_20` — is linked `PRIVATE` into both libraries, while `engine/app/application.h`
includes `<Windows.h>` unconditionally, so anyone linking `ArtAttackEngine` from outside this
repository gets the `min`/`max` macros in every translation unit that includes the engine's
entry header.

**Evidence:**

`engine/CMakeLists.txt:50-53`

    target_link_libraries(ArtAttackEngine
        PUBLIC MattMath Microsoft::DirectXTK d3d11 dxgi dxguid
        PRIVATE artattack_settings
    )

`engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:15-18` does the same. `cmake/settings.cmake:7,16-21`

    target_compile_features(artattack_settings INTERFACE cxx_std_20)
    ...
    target_compile_definitions(artattack_settings INTERFACE
        UNICODE _UNICODE
        WIN32 _WINDOWS
        NOMINMAX             # std::min/max, never the Windows.h macros
        WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN
    )

`engine/app/application.h:19` and `engine/core/thread_pool.h:3`, `engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:3`,
`engine/render/device_resources.h:7`

    #include <Windows.h>

**Why it matters:** T12's line is that a macro may not "change the meaning of a name that
already had one", and `min`/`max` are the canonical instance. The path is short: a stranger
writes `#include "engine/app/application.h"` in their `main.cpp`, links `ArtAttackEngine`
(ARCHITECTURE, A game project: "an ordinary C++ application that links two static libraries"),
and then `std::max(a, b)` in their own file fails to compile with an error naming neither
`max` nor Windows. In-tree this is invisible because `game/`, `samples/minimal/` and all three
test targets each link `artattack_settings` explicitly, which is exactly why it will not be
found until the first outside user. The same `PRIVATE` also means the C++20 requirement is not
propagated, so a consumer can compile the engine's headers under a different standard than the
library was built with.

**Remedy:** Split the settings target: keep `/W4 /WX /permissive- /sdl` private, and move
`cxx_std_20`, `NOMINMAX`, `WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN` and `UNICODE` to a target the libraries link
`PUBLIC` (or set them as `PUBLIC` compile definitions on the libraries themselves).

#### Translate the two DirectXTK-lineage files, or move them back out of `namespace artattack`

- **File:** `engine/core/step_timer.h:15-189`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12

**What:** `StepTimer` and `DeviceResources` were wrapped in `namespace artattack` and adopted as
first-party, but keep the Microsoft sample dialect — `m_` members and PascalCase methods —
so the engine's own library speaks two naming languages depending on which header you open.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/step_timer.h:44,58,88-89,171-172,187`

        uint64_t GetElapsedTicks() const noexcept { return m_elapsedTicks; }
        void SetFixedTimeStep(bool isFixedTimestep) noexcept { m_isFixedTimeStep = isFixedTimestep; }
        template<typename TUpdate>
        void Tick(const TUpdate& update)
        ...
        LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcFrequency;
        LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcLastTime;
        bool m_isFixedTimeStep;

`engine/render/device_resources.h:47-52,107-109`

        void CreateDeviceResources();
        void CreateWindowSizeDependentResources();
        void SetWindow(HWND window, int width, int height) noexcept;
        ...
        Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<IDXGIFactory2>               m_dxgiFactory;

CONVENTIONS, Never: "`m_` — the trailing underscore already does that job." Functions:
"Actions are verbs: `update`…". `DeviceResources` has already been half-converted — lines
97-100 and 143-145 of the same header are `create_deferred_contexts()`,
`deferred_contexts_owned_`, `deferred_context_count_` — so one class now carries both dialects
in one member list.

**Why it matters:** These are not third-party files any more; they are in `namespace artattack`,
they are listed in `ArtAttackEngine`'s sources, and `Application` exposes `DeviceResources*` and
holds a `StepTimer` by value, so both appear in the engine's public surface. A stranger reading
`handle.h` then `step_timer.h` has to work out which convention is load-bearing, which is
precisely the "which dialect am I in" tax T12 exists to refuse. The half-converted
`DeviceResources` is the strongest evidence that the file is now owned rather than vendored: an
upstream update can no longer be applied to it, so keeping the upstream naming buys nothing.

**Remedy:** Finish the conversion in one pass (`elapsed_ticks()`, `set_fixed_time_step()`,
`tick()`, trailing-underscore members), and note in the header that the algorithm is derived
from the DirectX Tool Kit sample.

#### `step_timer.h` uses Win32 types it does not include

- **File:** `engine/core/step_timer.h:7-9`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** The header uses `LARGE_INTEGER`, `QueryPerformanceFrequency` and
`QueryPerformanceCounter` while including only `<cmath>`, `<cstdint>` and `<exception>`, so it
compiles only when something else has already pulled `<Windows.h>` in.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/step_timer.h:7-9`

    #include <cmath>
    #include <cstdint>
    #include <exception>

`engine/core/step_timer.h:29,92,171-172`

            if (!QueryPerformanceFrequency(&m_qpcFrequency))
            ...
                LARGE_INTEGER currentTime;
            ...
            LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcFrequency;
            LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcLastTime;

Its only includer is `engine/app/application.h:7`, which sits after `resource_loader.h`,
`audio_resources.h`, `partitioner.h` and `state_context.h` — the Windows declarations arrive
transitively through one of those, not from anything `step_timer.h` asked for.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS, Files states the rule that would have caught this — "own header
first — proving every header compiles on its own" — and nothing in the build enforces it, so
the guarantee is asserted and untested. A translation unit that opens with
`#include "engine/core/step_timer.h"` fails to compile today, which is the first thing a test
for the fixed-step timing would do; reordering the includes in `application.h` would also break
the build with an error pointing at the wrong file.

**Remedy:** Add `#include <Windows.h>` to `step_timer.h`, and add a target that compiles each
public engine header alone so the rule is checked rather than stated.

#### `throw_if_failed.h` names the function like a type and the type like a function

- **File:** `engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:10-33`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Types

**What:** In the engine's only error helper, the class is `com_exception` (snake_case) and the
free function is `ThrowIfFailed` (PascalCase) — the naming rule applied exactly backwards, in
`namespace artattack`.

**Evidence:**

    class com_exception : public std::exception
    {
    public:
        com_exception(HRESULT hr) noexcept : result(hr) {}
    ...

    inline void ThrowIfFailed(HRESULT hr)

Also note `HRESULT result;` at line 23 — a private member with no trailing underscore, and a
non-`explicit` single-argument constructor.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS opens with one rule — "PascalCase names a type. snake_case names
everything else" — and this file inverts it in both directions in twenty lines. It is a header
a game includes when it calls D3D directly, and it is the only exception type in the engine
carrying diagnostic information, so it is read more often than its size suggests. The file was
moved out of `pch.h` into `engine/core/` during the split without being renamed, so the
inversion is now part of the engine library's public surface rather than a game-private detail.

**Remedy:** `class ComException` with `result_`, and `throw_if_failed()` matching the filename;
mark the constructor `explicit` while renaming.

`engine/math/matt_math.cpp:2206-2208,2354-2361` — the constructor is not constant-evaluable:

#### No game translation unit includes its own header first

- **File:** `game/pch.h:59-77`

- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** All 46 `.cpp` files in `game/` open with `#include "game/pch.h"` — which CMake already
force-includes via `target_precompile_headers`, making the line redundant — so no game header is
ever compiled first in its own TU, and the PCH force-feeds every one of them at least ten
DirectXTK headers nothing in the repository uses.

**Evidence:**

`game/CMakeLists.txt:72`

    target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)

First line of every game source, e.g. `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:1`,
`game/states/main_menu.cpp:1`, `game/main.cpp:1`:

    #include "game/pch.h"

`game/pch.h:59-77` lists 19 DirectXTK headers. Grepping their entry-point names across

ten of them: `BufferHelpers.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `GraphicsMemory.h`, `Keyboard.h`,
`Model.h`, `Mouse.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h`, `VertexTypes.h`,
`WICTextureLoader.h`.

#### The content format's type keys are C++ class names in three casings

- **File:** `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:20-21`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Data, T7

**What:** Level JSON identifies object types with the exact spelling of C++ class names
(`"Structure"`, `"StructurePaintable"`, `"StructureRamp"`, `"Visual"`), collision types with
SCREAMING enum names, and colours with SCREAMING palette names, against CONVENTIONS' rule that
every name in data is snake_case.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:20-21,68,130,172`

    std::string type = json["type"].GetString();
    if (type == "Structure")
    ...
    if (type == "StructurePaintable")
    ...
    if (type == "StructureRamp")
    ...
    if (type == "Visual")

`game/content/levels/close_quarters.json:86,96-97`

            "type": "Structure",
    ...
            "collision_type": "STRUCTURE",
            "colour": "SADDLE_BROWN"

The complete set of identifier-shaped values across the three shipped levels is
`"Structure"`, `"StructurePaintable"`, `"StructureRamp"`, `"Visual"`, `"STRUCTURE"`,
`"STRUCTURE_JUMP_THROUGH"`, `"STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE"`, `"STRUCTURE_RAMP_RIGHT"`, plus seven
SCREAMING colour names — everything else (asset names, object names, music names) is snake_case.
`game/content/sounds/sound_bank_1.json:4-27` adds a fourth casing: `"BowlingBallRoll"`,
`"UI_Clicks01"`, `"Top_Of_The_Morning"` beside `"holly_dolly"`.

as code-side variables, so a definition reads continuously from file to loader."

meaningful and which is accidental. Note this is a naming defect only — I read all three level
files, the manifest, the sprite-sheet table and the sound bank end to end, and there is no

<a id="g-sweep-value-semantics"></a>

## sweep-value-semantics — T11: the stack over the heap

*Group `sweep-value-semantics` · 16 findings (7 high, 9 medium) · source `review2/raw/sweep-value-semantics.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read PHILOSOPHY/CONVENTIONS/ARCHITECTURE and IMPLEMENTED.md, then swept every
`new` / `make_unique` / `make_shared` / `shared_ptr` / `virtual` / `vector<unique_ptr<…>>`
in `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/`, `tests/`, `cmake/` and the root build files, and opened
every candidate. The good news first, because it is real and it is new: `Handle`, `Registry`,
`NameTable`, `SpriteSheet` and `SoundBank` are exactly the shape T11 describes — values,
contiguous storage, indices instead of pointers, one owner — and there is not one
`shared_ptr` in first-party code. The bad news is that this island of value semantics sits
inside a codebase whose *default* modelling grammar is still inheritance and heap. The shape
of the problem is that T11 is being violated at three different altitudes at once, and each
one causes the next. At the bottom, `mattmath::Shape` makes every geometry primitive
polymorphic, so `RectangleF` — the type `IGameObject::bounds()` returns by value on the
culling path — carries a vtable, is not trivially copyable, cannot be `constexpr`, and has to
be heap-cloned to be copied through its own interface. In the middle, `DrawObject` and
`MovingObject` declare 36 virtual accessors between them for which the whole repository
contains two overrides, one of which just calls the base; drawing a single sprite therefore
costs six virtual dispatches to read six members of the object doing the drawing. At the top,
`Level`, the menu pages and `GameLevel` are a pointer-linked object web: `unique_ptr` to a
`vector` of `unique_ptr`, sixty `unique_ptr` widget members whose lifetime is exactly their
page's, and — the purest instance I found — four heap-allocated scalars (`bool`,
`PauseMenuAction`, `ResultsMenuAction`, `EndMenuAction`) plus `Application`'s
`unique_ptr<float>`, each allocated solely so a child object can hold its address and write
through it.

What surprised me most was how much of this is in code the recent work *created or blessed*.
`samples/minimal` is the file a stranger copies to start a project, and it models two labels
as `unique_ptr<Text>` and comments that "dt is a pointer because the objects reading it
outlive any one frame" — teaching heap-first modelling and a design the engine has already
moved away from (`update(float dt)`). `engine/ui/widget.h` is the engine's own widget set and
it is built on a container of borrowed raw pointers keyed by string. And `GameData::dt()`
carries a `const_cast` justified by a comment claiming "the game's older signatures still take
a `float*`" — there are three call sites left and all three dereference immediately, so the
cast is dead and the justification is false. The second surprise was `StateContext::transition_to`:
it destroys the state that is calling it, mid-`update()`, and the entire game is currently safe
only because every call site happens to touch nothing afterwards.

### Themes

- Inheritance is the default modelling grammar, not a last resort: `DrawObject`, `MovingObject`, `Drawer`, `MObject`/`MWidget` and `Shape` are all base classes that exist to hold data and hand out accessors, and their virtual accessors are almost never overridden.
- Value types have been made non-values by inheriting something polymorphic — `RectangleF`, `Circle`, `Triangle`, `Quad` and `RectangleRotated` are none of them trivially copyable, none `constexpr`-constructible, and all of them sliceable through `Shape&`'s implicit copy assignment.
- The heap is used to give a value a stable address so someone else can hold a pointer to it: `unique_ptr<float>`, `make_unique<bool>`, three `make_unique<SomeEnum>`, and `unique_ptr<vector<unique_ptr<T>>>`.
- Stateless helper types (`Partitioner`, `CameraTools`, `TeamColourTools`, `ProjectileBuilder`) are heap-allocated and held by `unique_ptr` when a plain member would be a zero-byte subobject.
- Fixed-size geometry is returned and stored in `std::vector`: `edges()` allocates four segments per call on the collision path, and `RectangleRotated` keeps its four corners in a heap vector.
- Per-frame heap allocation is routine on the exact paths PHILOSOPHY promises are allocation-free: task submission, partitioning, per-page draw lists, and projectile spawning.
- The engine's teaching artefacts — `samples/minimal` and the widget set — model the pointer web rather than the value style, so the first thing a stranger copies is the thing T11 forbids.

---

#### Stop making every geometry primitive polymorphic

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:69-90, 185-207`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap)

**What:** `Shape` is an abstract base with a virtual destructor and a `clone()` returning `unique_ptr<Shape>`, and `RectangleF`, `Circle`, `Triangle`, `Quad` and `RectangleRotated` all derive from it, so the engine's most value-like types are heap-cloned, non-trivially-copyable, non-`constexpr` polymorphic objects.

**Evidence:**

    struct Shape
    {
        virtual ~Shape() = default;
        virtual RectangleF bounding_box() const = 0;
        virtual ShapeType shape_type() const = 0;
        virtual bool intersects(const RectangleF& rect) const = 0;
        ...
        virtual void offset(const Vector2F& amount) = 0;
        virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;
        virtual Point2F center() const = 0;
        virtual std::vector<Segment> edges() const = 0;
        virtual void inflate(float amount) = 0;
    };

    struct RectangleF : public Shape
    {
        float x = 0.0f;
        float y = 0.0f;
        float width = 0.0f;
        float height = 0.0f;

**Why it matters:** `RectangleF` is 24 bytes instead of 16 (vptr plus padding); `std::is_trivially_copyable_v<RectangleF>` is `false`, so a `vector<RectangleF>` cannot be relocated with `memcpy` and the type can never be a POD the way a rect should be. `IGameObject::bounds()` returns one **by value** on the culling path (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:61`), and `Shape::AABB_intersects` (`matt_math.cpp:144-147`) constructs two of them per broad-phase test. Copying one through the interface requires a heap allocation (`clone()`), which `CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth` does on every diagonal player collision. `Shape` also has a public implicitly-declared copy assignment operator, so `Shape& a = …; a = b;` silently slices — nothing does that today, but nothing prevents it either. And because no constructor is `constexpr`, `RectangleF::ZERO`, `player_consts::DEFAULT_BOUNDS` and every other geometry constant is a dynamically-initialised object rather than a compile-time value (T5). Dispatch is not even virtual in the end: `Shape::intersects(const Shape*)` (`matt_math.cpp:120-137`) switches on `shape_type()` and then `dynamic_cast`s, so a collision test costs a virtual call plus RTTI.

**Remedy:** Make the primitives plain structs and move the polymorphism out of them — a `ShapeType` tag plus a `std::variant<RectangleF, Circle, Triangle, Quad, RectangleRotated>` (or free overloaded `intersects` functions) gives the same dispatch with no vptr, no `clone()`, and `constexpr` constants.

#### Document or remove `transition_to`'s destruction of its own caller

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T11 / PHILOSOPHY "Services and lifetimes" ("If an ordering is load-bearing, it is either designed away or stated where it lives")

**What:** `StateContext::transition_to` assigns over the `unique_ptr` that owns the currently running state, so the state is destroyed synchronously from inside its own `update()`, and every caller is one added line away from a use-after-free.

**Evidence:**

    void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
    {
        this->state_ = std::move(state);
        this->state_->set_context(this);
        this->state_->init();
    }

and the reachable call, from inside `PauseMenuInitial::update()` (`game/states/pause_menu.cpp:84-97`):

    else if (highlighted_element == "restart")
    {
        this->play_wave(this->confirm_sound_);
        this->context()->transition_to(std::make_unique<
            PauseMenuConfirmation>(this->pause_menu_data(),
                ConfirmationType::restart));
    }

**Why it matters:** At the `transition_to` call the `PauseMenuInitial` object — its `MTextDropShadow` widgets, its sound handles, its base `MenuPage` — is freed while `PauseMenuInitial::update()` is still executing, and then `PauseMenuConfirmation::init()` runs and allocates over that memory. I traced every one of the ~25 `context()->transition_to` sites in `game/states/`: all of them either `return;` immediately (`main_menu.cpp:63, 150, 160, …`) or `break;` out of a switch with no further member access (`game_states.cpp:221-225, 262-264, 272-274`), so **there is no crash on any path today**. But this contract is written nowhere — not in `state.h`, not in `state_context.h`, not in the sample — and it is the engine's public flow API. A stranger writing `context()->transition_to(next); this->play_sound();` gets a use-after-free with no diagnostic. `pause_menu.cpp:84-97` is already the shape that would break: it is the only site that neither returns nor is the last statement of its function.

**Remedy:** Defer the swap — queue the pending state and install it after `update()` returns, in `StateContext::update()` — or, at minimum, state on `transition_to` that it destroys the calling state and that the caller must return immediately.

#### Delete the `unique_ptr` wrapper around `Level`'s object vectors

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:57-60, 92-102`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap)

**What:** `Level` owns its four object lists as `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>>>` — a heap allocation whose only content is a `vector` that already owns heap storage, adding an extra indirection and a null state to every access.

**Evidence:**

    Level(std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<artattack::IGameObject>>> non_collision_objects,
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<ICollisionGameObject>>> collision_objects,
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Player>>> player_objects,
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<artattack::IGameObject>>> viewport_dividers,

    private:
        std::unique_ptr<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<artattack::IGameObject>>>
            non_collision_objects_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** Three levels of indirection to reach a game object, on the paths that run every frame for every object: `update_level_logic` dereferences them 8 times (`level.cpp:185, 191, 228, 234, 239, 264, 271, 289`) and `draw_player_view_level` again per view. The outer `unique_ptr` buys nothing — a `vector` is already movable and already owns its storage — and it costs a null state that no code checks: `Level() = default;` (`level.h:56`) leaves all four null, and `Level::update` would null-dereference on such an instance. It propagates: `LevelObjectBuilder::build_collision_objects` and its two siblings (`level_object_builder.cpp:188-231`) all return `unique_ptr<vector<unique_ptr<…>>>`, so the shape is baked into three builder signatures too.

**Remedy:** Make them plain `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>>` members and return plain vectors from the builders; the move is free and the null state disappears.

#### Stop heap-allocating scalars so other objects can point at them

- **File:** `game/states/game_states.h:28, 60, 64, 67`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap — "designs that lean on shared object webs … must be rethought")

**What:** Four scalars — a `bool` and three enums — are heap-allocated with `make_unique` purely so their addresses can be handed to child objects as raw mutable back-pointers, which is the pointer-linked object web T11 exists to forbid, in miniature.

**Evidence:**

`game/states/game_states.h`:

        std::unique_ptr<bool> is_ready_to_load_level_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuAction> pause_menu_action_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuAction> results_menu_action_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<EndMenuAction> end_menu_action_ = nullptr;

`game/states/game_states.cpp:24, 160-167`:

        this->is_ready_to_load_level_ = std::make_unique<bool>(false);
        ...
        this->pause_menu_action_ = std::make_unique<PauseMenuAction>(
            PauseMenuAction::none);
        this->pause_menu_data_ = std::make_unique<PauseMenuData>(
            this->data(), this->menu_input_.get(),
            pause_menu_player, this->pause_menu_action_.get());

and the receiving end, `game/states/main_menu_data.h:20` and `game/states/pause_menu_data.h:18`:

        bool* is_ready_to_load_level_ = nullptr;
        PauseMenuAction* action_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** The written protocol between a page and its owner is "write `true` through this `bool*`" (`pause_menu.cpp:74`: `*this->pause_menu_data()->action() = PauseMenuAction::resume;`). Every one of these has the same lifetime as the object that owns it — a plain `bool` / `PauseMenuAction` member has an equally stable address — so the allocation buys nothing and the raw pointer buys nothing except an unchecked aliasing relationship the compiler cannot see. It is also the pattern that made the pre-review device-loss bugs fatal: a heap scalar reachable by raw pointer from eleven places is exactly what finding #9 (`OnDeviceRestored` reallocates the shared frame-time float) was.

**Remedy:** Make them value members and pass a reference — or better, have the page return its action from `update()` instead of writing into its parent.

#### Devirtualise `DrawObject`: eleven virtual accessors, one override, six dispatches per sprite

- **File:** `engine/render/draw_object.h:20-32`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T11 / T8 (performance over customisability — "indirection must pay for itself")

**What:** `DrawObject` declares eleven virtual accessors and setters over six plain members; the entire repository contains exactly one override of any of them, and reading those six members to draw one sprite costs six virtual dispatches on the hot draw path.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/draw_object.h`:

    protected:
        virtual RenderResources* render_resources() const;
        virtual const mattmath::Colour& colour() const;
        virtual float draw_rotation() const;
        virtual const mattmath::Vector2F& origin() const;
        virtual DirectX::SpriteEffects effects() const;
        virtual float layer_depth() const;

        virtual void set_colour(const mattmath::Colour& colour);
        ...

`engine/render/texture_object.cpp:42-55` — the draw:

    void TextureObject::draw(SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
        const RectangleI& destination_rectangle) const
    {
        SpriteSheet* sprite_sheet = SpriteSheetObject::sprite_sheet();

        sprite_sheet->draw(sprite_batch,
                            this->frame_,
                            destination_rectangle,
                            this->colour(),
                            this->draw_rotation(),
                            this->origin(),
                            this->effects(),
                            this->layer_depth());
    }

`engine/render/sprite_sheet_object.cpp:22-25` — a sixth, inside the first line:

    SpriteSheet* SpriteSheetObject::sprite_sheet() const
    {
        return this->render_resources()->sprite_sheet(this->sheet_);
    }

**Why it matters:** Five of those six calls are unqualified virtual calls, and the sixth (`render_resources()`) is virtual inside `sprite_sheet()`. That is six indirect calls to read six members of `*this`, per drawable, per view, per frame — on the exact path PHILOSOPHY/Performance names as the measure. The only override in the codebase is `Weapon::render_resources()` (`weapon.h:141`, `weapon.cpp:518-521`), which is declared `protected` exactly like the base it overrides and returns `this->render_resources_` — a *duplicate* copy of the same pointer `Weapon` already passed to `TextureObject`'s constructor (`weapon.cpp:22-25`). So the entire virtual mechanism exists to return the identical value, and it also poisons `SpriteSheetObject`'s constructor path, which must call the non-virtual `render_resources` behaviour during base construction.

**Remedy:** Make all eleven non-virtual and delete `Weapon::render_resources_` and its override; `Weapon` already has the pointer through its base.

#### Devirtualise `MovingObject`: twenty-five virtual accessors, one forwarding override

- **File:** `engine/core/moving_object.h:17-52`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (inheritance and virtual dispatch are tools of last resort)

**What:** `MovingObject` is a three-member struct — two `Vector2F` and a `float` — wrapped in twenty-five virtual accessors, of which the whole repository overrides one, and that override does nothing but call the base.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/moving_object.h`:

    protected:
        virtual const mattmath::Vector2F& velocity() const;
        virtual float velocity_x() const;
        virtual float velocity_y() const;
        virtual void set_velocity(const mattmath::Vector2F& velocity);
        ...
        virtual float rotation() const;
        virtual void set_rotation(float rotation);
        virtual void alter_rotation(float rotation);

    private:
        mattmath::Vector2F velocity_ = mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO;
        mattmath::Vector2F dx_ = mattmath::Vector2F::ZERO;
        float rotation_ = 0.0f;

The single override, `game/objects/player.cpp:970-973`:

    const Vector2F& Player::velocity() const
    {
        return MovingObject::velocity();
    }

**Why it matters:** Twenty bytes of data carry a vtable pointer and twenty-five vtable slots for one override whose only effect is to change access from `protected` (`moving_object.h:17`) to `public` (`player.h:104`) — a `using MovingObject::velocity;` declaration does that with no runtime cost at all. `MovingObject` is a base of `Player` and of every `Projectile`, and the tax lands on both sides: `Player` calls the accessors unqualified, so `set_velocity_y`, `velocity()` and friends dispatch indirectly at seventeen sites in `player.cpp` alone (`297, 317, 326, 335, 344, 357, 364, 374, 395, 594, 601, 636, 654, 943, 945, 1044, 1069`), several of them every tick, while `Projectile::update_movement` writes `MovingObject::` in front of every single call (`projectile.cpp:230-269`, eighteen qualifications in forty lines) to avoid the same. It is also the reason `Player` and `Projectile` are forced into multiple inheritance rather than composition: there is nothing here that a `Motion` *member* would not do better.

**Remedy:** Make `MovingObject` a plain struct with non-virtual accessors and hold it by composition; replace `Player::velocity()` with `using MovingObject::velocity;`.

#### Replace the widget pointer web with owned, indexed storage

- **File:** `engine/ui/widget.h:33-57`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (the stack over the heap) / PHILOSOPHY "UI"

**What:** The engine's widget set is a pointer-linked object web: `MContainer` holds non-owning `MObject*` keyed by a `std::string` copy, while the actual owners are dozens of individual `unique_ptr` members on the game's pages — so the ownership graph and the traversal graph are two different structures kept in step by hand.

**Evidence:**

`engine/ui/widget.h`:

    class MContainer final : public MObject
    {
    public:
        void add_child(MObject* child);
        void remove_child(const std::string& name);
        ...
    private:
        std::vector<std::pair<std::string, MObject*>> children_;
    };

`engine/ui/widget.cpp:41-44`:

    void MContainer::add_child(MObject* child)
    {
        this->children_.push_back(std::make_pair(child->name(), child));
    }

and the owning side, one page out of ten in `game/states/main_menu.h:141-146`:

        std::unique_ptr<artattack::MContainer> texture_container_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::MContainer> text_container_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::MTexture> background_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::MTextDropShadow> title_ = nullptr;
        std::unique_ptr<artattack::MTextDropShadow> start_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** `main_menu.h` alone declares 63 `std::unique_ptr<artattack::M…>` widget members, two of them inside per-player structs held as `vector<unique_ptr<Struct-of-four-unique_ptr>>` (`main_menu.h:257, 291`); every one of them has a lifetime identical to the page that declares it, so every one of those allocations and indirections is pure ceremony. The dangerous half is the borrowed pointers: `MContainer` stores raw `MObject*` and a *copy of the child's name*, so a container outliving its children — or a page destroying a widget without calling `remove_child` — leaves a dangling pointer that `MContainer::update`/`draw` walks blind (`widget.cpp:93-107`). Nothing in the API states that the container borrows. This is the engine's own `ui/` module and PHILOSOPHY commits to shipping it as a public widget set, so this shape is what a stranger will meet.

**Remedy:** Have the container own its children (`std::vector<std::unique_ptr<MWidget>>`, or a per-type vector plus indices) and hand back handles, so ownership and traversal are the same structure; make the pages' widgets value members where they stay members.

#### Remove the per-frame allocations from the parallel-draw submission path

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:397-417`, `engine/core/thread_pool.cpp:39-55`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8 / PHILOSOPHY "Performance" ("Per-frame code performs no heap allocation")

**What:** Submitting the render tasks allocates at least four times per task per frame: the partition vector, a copy of that vector into every lambda, the `std::function` that erases the lambda, and a `make_unique<task_item>` inside `add_task`.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp`:

    auto partitioned_players =
        this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);

    // draw player objects
    for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
    {
        this->thread_pool_->add_task([this, i, partitioned_players,
            deferred_contexts, command_lists, sprite_batches]()
            {

`engine/core/thread_pool.cpp`:

    void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)
    {
        auto item = std::make_unique<task_item>(task_item{ std::move(task), this });

        PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback, item.get(),
            &callback_environment_);

**Why it matters:** `partitioned_players` is captured **by value**, so each task copies a `vector<pair<int,int>>` — one heap allocation per task. The capture list is 3 pointers + an `int` + a `vector` (24 bytes on MSVC) + `this`, far past any small-object buffer, so constructing the `std::function` allocates again, and `add_task` then allocates the `task_item`. `Partitioner::partition` (`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:5-23`) `push_back`s into a fresh vector with no `reserve`, so it reallocates as it grows. At 60 Hz with `max_threads = 16` that is on the order of 4000 allocations per second before a single sprite is drawn, and `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (`game/states/menu_page.cpp:130-153`) repeats the same shape for menus. The `Partitioner` result is also the same every frame unless the player count changes.

**Remedy:** Cache the partition in the caller, capture it by reference (the pool is joined before the frame ends), and give `ThreadPool` an `add_task` overload taking a callable plus a caller-owned storage slot instead of `std::function` + `make_unique`.

#### Stop heap-cloning a shape to measure collision depth

- **File:** `engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:281-292`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T11 / T8

**What:** `calculate_object_collision_depth` allocates a polymorphic copy of the collider on the heap on every call, purely to have something mutable to push around, on a path reached from four player-collision handlers every frame.

**Evidence:**

    Vector2F CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth(
        const Shape* collider,
        const Shape* collidee,
        const Vector2F& collision_direction)
    {
        std::unique_ptr<Shape> collider_copy = collider->clone();
        Vector2F amount;

        resolve_object_collision(collider_copy.get(), collidee, collision_direction, amount);

        return amount;
    }

reached from `game/objects/player.cpp:608, 622, 640, 658`, e.g.:

    void Player::on_top_left_collision(const ICollisionGameObject* other)
    {
        Vector2F amount = CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth(
            this->shape(), other->shape(), Vector2F::DIRECTION_UP_LEFT);

**Why it matters:** A player standing on a corner hits `on_top_left_collision` / `on_bottom_right_collision` every tick, and each one is a `make_unique` plus a virtual destructor call. Worse, the copy is then run through `bracket_object_collision_generic`, which loops `BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40` times calling the virtual `intersects` and `bounding_box` (`collision_tools.cpp:66-80`) — so the allocation is the cheap part, but it is the part that is trivially avoidable: a `RectangleF` copy on the stack is 24 bytes. The allocation exists only because `Shape` cannot be copied by value through its own interface (see the first finding).

**Remedy:** Once shapes are values, take the collider by value; until then, add a stack-based overload for the rectangle-vs-rectangle case, which is what `Player` always is.

- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY "Performance" ("fixed-size geometry returns fixed-size containers")

**What:** `Shape::edges()` returns a heap-allocated `std::vector<Segment>` even though every shape's edge count is a compile-time constant, and `RectangleRotated` stores its four corners in a `std::vector<Point2F>` that allocates on every default construction and every setter.

**Evidence:**

`engine/math/matt_math.cpp`:

    std::vector<Segment> RectangleF::edges() const
    {
        std::vector<Segment> edges =
        {
            this->top_edge(),
            this->bottom_edge(),
            this->left_edge(),
            this->right_edge()
        };
        return edges;
    }

`engine/math/matt_math.h`:

        std::vector<Point2F> points_ = { Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO,
                    Point2F::ZERO, Point2F::ZERO };

**Why it matters:** `edges()` is called from the intersection routines, two at a time — `matt_math.cpp:394-395` (`triangles_intersect`), `647-648` (`quads_intersect`), `220`, `289`, `370`, `436`, `481`, `600` — so a single triangle-vs-triangle test costs two allocations and two frees, and `quad_rectangle_rotated_intersect` reaches several of these transitively. `RectangleRotated`'s member is worse in kind: the default member initialiser means `RectangleRotated x;` allocates, the copy constructor allocates, and `calculate_points()` returns another vector on every setter (`matt_math.h:1135-1142`). #### Make `colour_consts` compile-time values instead of 301 per-TU dynamic objects

- **File:** `engine/math/colour.h:9-312, 314-465`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T11 (constants are values) / T5 (compile-time over run-time) / CONVENTIONS "Constants and enumerators"

**What:** `colour.h` defines 148 `const std::string` and 153 `const mattmath::Colour` objects at namespace scope in a header — internal linkage, so a fresh copy of all 301 is constructed at startup in every translation unit — and then an `inline` function with external linkage reads them, which is an ODR violation.

**Evidence:**

    namespace colour_consts
    {
        namespace html
        {
            const std::string ALICE_BLUE = "f0f8ff";
            ...
        }

        const mattmath::Colour ALICE_BLUE = { html::ALICE_BLUE };
        ...

        inline mattmath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)
        {
            if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;
            ... (148 branches)
            return colour_consts::WHITE;
        }
    }

**Why it matters:** Two consequences, one certain and one formal. Certain: `colour.h` is pulled in by `draw_object.h`, which every drawable header includes, so 34 first-party files include it directly or one hop away and effectively every TU in the engine and the game gets 148 `std::string` constructions and 153 `Colour` constructions — each parsing a hex string through `Colour(const std::string&)` — before `main` runs, plus roughly 7 KB of duplicated static data per TU. None of it can be `constexpr`, because `Colour` has no `constexpr` constructor (`matt_math.h:601-608`). Formal: `colour_from_name` is `inline`, therefore external linkage, defined in every TU that includes the header, and each definition names *different entities* (`colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE` is a distinct object per TU) — that is an ODR violation under [basic.def.odr], ill-formed with no diagnostic required. It happens to be harmless because all copies hold equal values, but the linker keeps one definition and the other TUs' 301 objects are constructed at startup for nothing.

**Remedy:** Give `Colour` `constexpr` constructors and declare the constants `inline constexpr` (one entity, zero startup cost, usable in constant expressions); drop the parallel `html::` string table, which exists only to feed the hex constructor. The 148-branch name lookup is load-time-only and belongs in a `.cpp` behind a sorted table.
