        // frame; the shell rewrites the value behind it every fixed step.
        const float dt = *this->app_->dt();

**Why it matters:** The stated reason for the `unique_ptr` — deferred construction until after `load_manifest` — does not need one: `Text` is default-constructible (`engine/render/text.h:10`) and copy-assignable, so `Text greeting_;` plus `greeting_ = Text(...)` in `init()` is the same program with two fewer allocations. This is the single most-read file the engine will have, and it models the heap as the default for a value with a lexical lifetime, which is precisely what T11 forbids in "everything it ships". The `dt` comment compounds it: `IGameObject::update(float dt)` was changed *specifically* to stop objects holding a `const float*` (see the note in `engine/core/i_game_object.h:27-33`), and the sample now teaches the pattern that change removed.

**Remedy:** Make both labels value members and reword the `dt` comment to say the shell keeps the value and the sample is reading it, not that a pointer is the intended design.

---

#### Take the collision shape by value, not by pointer-then-clone

- **File:** `game/objects/structure.h:13, 38`, `game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:59-63`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T11 / T4 (clarity over cleverness)

**What:** `Structure` accepts its collision shape as `const Shape*` and immediately heap-clones it, so every caller has to take the address of a local it is about to discard — an API that reads like a borrow and behaves like a copy.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/structure.h`:

        const mattmath::Shape* collision_shape,
        ...
        std::unique_ptr<mattmath::Shape> collision_shape_ = nullptr;

`game/objects/structure.cpp:23`:

        collision_shape_(collision_shape->clone())

`game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:59-63` — the caller:

        return std::make_unique<Structure>(
            json["sheet_name"].GetString(),
            json["frame_name"].GetString(),
            rectangle,
            &rectangle,

**Why it matters:** `&rectangle` is the address of a `RectangleF` local declared 20 lines earlier at `level_object_builder.cpp:38`, passed alongside the same object by const reference. Nothing at the call site says whether `Structure` keeps the pointer or copies through it; this exact ambiguity is what produced the old critical finding #20 ("`StructurePaintable` stores a reference to a builder local"), and the fix was to clone rather than to change the signature — so the trap is still there for the next caller, and it is unenforced (`collision_shape->clone()` null-dereferences if anyone passes `nullptr`). The clone also means each `Structure` costs a heap allocation and a virtual destructor for what is 16 bytes of rectangle in every level file shipped.

**Remedy:** Take the shape by value once it is a value type, or by `const Shape&` in the meantime, so the signature cannot be read as a borrow.

---

#### Compose the sprite and the animation instead of inheriting `DrawObject` twice

- **File:** `game/objects/player.h:63-64`, `game/objects/player.cpp:91-101`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 (inheritance as a last resort)

**What:** `Player` derives from both `AnimationObject` and `TextureObject`, each of which derives from `SpriteSheetObject`/`DrawObject`, so it carries two independent copies of `render_resources_`, `colour_`, `draw_rotation_`, `origin_`, `effects_` and `layer_depth_` that must be kept in step by hand.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/player.h`:

    class Player final : public artattack::MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject,
                         public artattack::AnimationObject, public artattack::TextureObject

`game/objects/player.cpp` — every base access has to name which copy:

        // Every base call is explicitly qualified: Player inherits DrawObject
        // twice, once through TextureObject and once through AnimationObject, and
        // the two subobjects carry independent colour/origin/rotation.
        TextureObject::draw_with(sprite_batch, this->rectangle_, camera,
            this->TextureObject::frame(),
            this->TextureObject::colour(),
            this->TextureObject::origin(), effects,
            this->TextureObject::draw_rotation());

        AnimationObject::draw_with(sprite_batch, this->rectangle_, camera,
            this->AnimationObject::colour(), effects);

**Why it matters:** Four base classes, two of them duplicated three levels deep, means every unqualified call to `colour()`, `origin()`, `render_resources()` or `set_colour()` inside `Player` is ambiguous and a compile error — which is why the code is littered with `this->TextureObject::` — and the six duplicated members can silently diverge: the constructor already gives them different colours (`player.cpp:28-32` passes `DEFAULT_PLAYER_COLOUR` to one and `team_colour` to the other), which is deliberate here but is exactly the divergence a reader cannot see from the class declaration. `Player` is also the class PHILOSOPHY names as starter code the sample should hand over for users to copy, so this shape gets copied.

**Remedy:** Hold a `TextureObject` and an `AnimationObject` as *members* — `Player` needs their behaviour, not their identity — and implement `IGameObject` on `Player` alone.

---

#### Delete the dead `const_cast` in `GameData::dt()` and the `unique_ptr<float>` behind it

- **File:** `game/game_data.cpp:62-69`, `engine/app/application.h:159`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T11 / T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** `GameData::dt()` casts away the `const` the shell deliberately applies, justified by a comment that says older game signatures still take a `float*` — no such signature exists any more — and the value it points at is a heap-allocated single `float`.

**Evidence:**

`game/game_data.cpp`:

    float* GameData::dt() const
    {
        // The shell hands out a const float* because nothing downstream should be
        // writing the frame's own timestep. The game's older signatures still take
        // a float*, so the cast lives here, in one place, rather than at each of
        // the several dozen call sites - and goes when those signatures do.
        return const_cast<float*>(this->application_->dt());
    }

`engine/app/application.h:159` and `application.cpp:149`:

        std::unique_ptr<float> dt_ = nullptr;
        this->dt_ = std::make_unique<float>(0.0f);

**Why it matters:** There are exactly three remaining reads of `dt()` in first-party code, and every one dereferences into a `const float` or passes by value: `game/states/results_menu.cpp:34` (`const float dt = *this->data()->dt();`), `game/states/game_states.cpp:196` (`this->level_->update(player_inputs, *this->game_data_->dt());`) and `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:55`, which does not go through `GameData` at all. The comment's "several dozen call sites" and "older signatures" are both false, so a reader is told a cast is load-bearing when it is dead — and a live `float*` into the shell's own timestep is exactly the aliasing the `const` was added to stop. The `unique_ptr<float>` is the last survivor of the pattern the `update(float dt)` change was made to kill.

**Remedy:** Change `GameData::dt()` to return `float` by value (or delete it, since two of the three callers could take `dt` as a parameter like `IGameObject` does) and make `Application::dt_` a plain `float` member.

<a id="g-sweep-memory-safety"></a>

## sweep-memory-safety — T2: memory safety and undefined behaviour

*Group `sweep-memory-safety` · 11 findings (5 high, 4 medium, 2 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-memory-safety.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read every first-party `.h`/`.cpp` under `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/` and `tests/` that
could plausibly hold a lifetime, aliasing or indexing hazard, plus the CMake files, and
spot-checked the vendored rapidjson only to confirm what the project's *consumption* of it
does. The reassuring news first: the classic hits from the previous review really are gone.
Every draw path I traced is a pure `const` read, `Registry`/`NameTable`/`Handle` bounds-check
before they index, the four JSON loaders no longer read through 1-byte buffers, the thread
pool has an exception barrier and owns its task payload with a `unique_ptr`, and the
declaration-order comment in `application.h` correctly keeps `AudioEngine` alive past its
`WaveBank`s. I found no live data race and no reachable heap corruption.

The shape of what is left is different, and it is almost all **destruction and transfer
order rather than indexing**. Three of the five highest findings are the same defect wearing
different clothes: an object is torn down while something that still refers to it is alive,
and the code only survives because nothing currently dereferences in the window. The single
most surprising thing is structural — `Application` inherits `StateContext`, and C++ destroys
base-class subobjects *after* members, so the running state is destroyed after every service
the shell owns, which is the exact opposite of what `application.h` promises three lines
above the member list. The second surprise is that the engine's own asset loaders are the
*least* validated code in the repo: `asset_manifest_loader.cpp` carries a paragraph
explaining why unchecked rapidjson access is undefined behaviour in a release build, and then
`sprite_sheet_loader.cpp` and `sound_bank_loader.cpp`, sitting in the same folder, do exactly
that. I also could not find any signed/unsigned or narrowing hazard worth reporting — `/W4
/WX` is genuinely doing its job — so nothing in that category is filed here.

**Themes**

- Destruction order is the dominant hazard class: base-after-member, teardown-body-before-members, and self-destruction inside a member function are three separate instances of the same unexamined question, and PHILOSOPHY's "Construction and destruction order are designed" is not yet true.
- Several contracts are load-bearing but stated nowhere the compiler or a stranger can see them: `transition_to` requires the caller to touch nothing afterwards, `deferred_contexts()` hands out a pointer whose identity changes, and neither header says so.
- Validation quality is inverted relative to the boundary: the file a person hand-edits most (the manifest) is fully checked, while sprite-sheet and sound-bank definitions — also hand-edited, also engine-parsed — are not checked at all.
- The engine survives on "no current caller does the dangerous thing" rather than on structure, which is exactly the property that breaks the first time a stranger writes a destructor or caches a pointer.
- Fall-through and off-by-one in `ViewportManager` combine so that an out-of-range viewport index returns a plausible-looking wrong answer instead of failing loudly (T6).
- Polymorphic value types in MattMath (`Shape` and its descendants) have one un-overridden `clone()`, which silently slices; the same trap is waiting for the first user-written `Shape`.
- Unchecked divisors appear wherever a count is derived from data or from options — thread count, tile count — with no guard and no documented precondition.

---

#### Destroy the running state before the services it borrows, not after

- **File:** `engine/app/application.h:71,113-114,144-166`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T2 (PHILOSOPHY, Services and lifetimes)

**What:** `Application` inherits `StateContext`, and C++ destroys base-class subobjects after
data members, so the running `State` — and everything it owns — is destroyed *after* every
service the header promises will outlive it.

**Evidence:**

    engine/app/application.h:71
        class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext

    engine/app/application.h:113-114
            // Borrowed, every one: the Application owns them and outlives the states
            // it runs.

    engine/app/application.h:144-163
            std::unique_ptr<DirectX::AudioEngine> audio_engine_ = nullptr;
            ...
            std::unique_ptr<AudioResources> audio_resources_ = nullptr;
            std::unique_ptr<RenderResources> render_resources_ = nullptr;
            ...
            std::unique_ptr<DirectX::CommonStates> common_states_ = nullptr;
            std::vector<std::unique_ptr<DirectX::SpriteBatch>> sprite_batches_;

    engine/core/state_context.h:17
            std::unique_ptr<State> state_ = nullptr;

**Why it matters:** `[class.dtor]` orders teardown as body → non-static members (reverse
declaration) → direct base classes (reverse declaration). `StateContext` is a base, so
`state_` is released last — after `audio_resources_`, `render_resources_`, `common_states_`
and `sprite_batches_` are already gone. Today nothing crashes only because no `State` or game
object in the tree has a destructor body at all (I grepped: the only user-written destructors
in `engine/`, `game/` and `samples/` are `~Application` and `~ThreadPool`). The moment a
stranger writes the obvious `~MyState() { audio_->stop_music(); }` — which the sample
invites, since `HelloState` holds an `Application*` — they get a use-after-free on a normal
window close, with a header three lines away telling them it is safe.

**Remedy:** make the state stack a member rather than a base — hold a `StateContext` (or the
`unique_ptr<State>` itself) as the *first* member so it dies first — or add an explicit
`this->transition_to(nullptr)`-equivalent teardown at the top of `~Application`.

---

#### Release the COM objects before calling CoUninitialize, not after

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:21-31`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T2

**What:** `~Application` calls `CoUninitialize()` from its destructor *body*, which runs
before every member is destroyed, so the XAudio2, D3D11 and DXGI interfaces the shell owns
are all released after COM has been closed on that thread.

**Evidence:**

    engine/app/application.cpp:21-31
        Application::~Application()
        {
            if (this->audio_engine_)
            {
                this->audio_engine_->Suspend();
            }
            if (this->com_initialized_)
            {
                CoUninitialize();
            }
        }

    engine/app/application.h:144-165
            std::unique_ptr<DirectX::AudioEngine> audio_engine_ = nullptr;
            ...
            std::unique_ptr<DeviceResources> device_resources_ = nullptr;
            std::unique_ptr<AudioResources> audio_resources_ = nullptr;
            std::unique_ptr<RenderResources> render_resources_ = nullptr;
            ...
            bool com_initialized_ = false;

**Why it matters:** the destructor body runs first, so the order on every clean exit is:
`CoUninitialize()` → `sprite_batches_` → `common_states_` → `render_resources_` (which owns
`ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView>` per `engine/render/render_resources.h:87-88`) →
`audio_resources_` (SoundBanks → `WaveBank`s and `SoundEffectInstance`s, all XAudio2 COM
voices) → `device_resources_` (device, swap chain, deferred contexts, all `ComPtr`) →
`audio_engine_` (`IXAudio2`). `CoUninitialize`'s documented contract is that all interface
pointers are released first; XAudio2 in particular is a COM API that the shell explicitly
`CoInitializeEx`es for (`application.cpp:41-46`). I have not observed a crash — D3D11 usually
tolerates it — so this is filed as a contract violation on a path taken every run, not as an
observed fault. Note the intent was clearly the opposite: `com_initialized_` is declared at
line 165, i.e. destroyed *early*, which is what someone reasoning about member order would
have wanted.

**Remedy:** replace the flag plus destructor-body call with a tiny RAII guard declared as the
*first* member of `Application` (before `audio_engine_`), so COM closes last.

---

#### State the "return immediately" contract on transition_to, or stop destroying the caller

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** T2, T4

**What:** `transition_to` destroys the outgoing state at the assignment on line 23, and the
outgoing state is almost always the object whose member function is currently on the stack —
so every one of the ~40 call sites is running inside a destroyed object when the call
returns, and nothing in the header says so.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26
        void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
        {
            this->state_ = std::move(state);
            this->state_->set_context(this);
            this->state_->init();
        }

    engine/core/state_context.h:15
            void transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state);

    game/states/pause_menu.cpp:84-97   (a call site with no `return` after it)
            else if (highlighted_element == "restart")
            {
                this->play_wave(this->confirm_sound_);
                this->context()->transition_to(std::make_unique<
                    PauseMenuConfirmation>(this->pause_menu_data(),
                        ConfirmationType::restart));
            }
            else if (highlighted_element == "quit")

**Why it matters:** `this->state_ = std::move(state)` runs `~State` on the old state before
`transition_to`'s body continues, so control returns into a member function of freed memory.
I checked all forty-odd call sites in `game/states/`: every one either `return`s straight away
or, as at `pause_menu.cpp:84-97` and `game_states.cpp:216-225`, falls out of the enclosing
blocks touching only stack locals — so there is no reachable use-after-free today. That is
luck held in place by review, not by structure, and the contract is undiscoverable: the header
comment is absent, the sample game never transitions, and the natural thing to write after a
transition (`this->play_wave(...)`, `this->reset()`, a loop that continues) is a
use-after-free. It is also the single API a stranger writing game flow touches most.

**Remedy:** either document the precondition on `transition_to` in the header ("the calling
state may be destroyed by this call; return immediately and touch no member"), or defer the
swap — record the pending state and apply it at the top of the next `update()`.

#### Check the sprite-sheet and sound-bank JSON the way the manifest loader already does

- **File:** `engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.cpp:11-56`, `engine/assets/sound_bank_loader.cpp:14-67`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2, T6

**What:** both engine loaders read hand-edited JSON through rapidjson's asserting accessors,
so in a release build a missing or mistyped key yields a null `Value` whose `GetString()`
returns `nullptr`, which is then handed straight to `std::string`.

**Evidence:**

    engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp:12-16   (the rule, stated in this repo)
            // rapidjson's operator[] asserts on a missing member and GetArray() asserts
            // on the wrong type - a crash in debug and undefined behaviour in release.
            // The manifest is the one file a person edits by hand to add an asset, so
            // every read below goes through these instead and a typo comes back as a
            // sentence naming the file and the group it was in (T6).

    engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.cpp:14-23   (the rule, broken)
                for (auto& frame : json.GetArray())
                {
                    std::string name = frame["name"].GetString();
                    Vector2F origin = Vector2F::ZERO;
                    bool rotated = false;
                    RectangleI source_rectangle(
                        frame["position"]["x"].GetInt(),

    engine/assets/sound_bank_loader.cpp:51-54
                for (auto& effect : instances_json.GetArray())
                {
                    std::string name = effect["name"].GetString();
                    std::string wave = effect["wave"].GetString();

**Why it matters:** with `NDEBUG` (the Release preset), `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT` is a no-op, so
`operator[]` on a missing member returns the thread-local placement-new'd null
`GenericValue` (`external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/document.h:1226-1238`). Its
`GetString()` skips the assert and reaches
`DataString(data_)` (`document.h:2107-2109`), which for `kNullFlag` takes the
non-inline branch and returns `data_.s.str` — nullptr, because `GenericValue()`
value-initialises the union (`document.h:690`). `std::string name = nullptr` is undefined
behaviour. The reachable path is ordinary content authoring: `Application::load_manifest`
→ `ResourceLoader::load_sprite_sheet` (`resource_loader.cpp:143-153`) →
`read_sprite_sheet("…/sprite_sheet_1.json")` on a file where someone renamed `name` to
`frame_name`. Debug builds abort in an assert dialog with no file name; release builds
access-violate inside `strlen`. Both are worse than the sentence the manifest loader
would have produced.

**Remedy:** lift the `require_member` / `require_array` / `require_string` helpers out of
`asset_manifest_loader.cpp`'s anonymous namespace into a shared header and route these two
loaders (and the equivalent `GetInt`/`GetFloat`/`GetBool` reads) through them.

#### Break out of every layout case in calculate_viewport

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:143-234`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2, T6

**What:** each layout case ends its inner `switch` with `default: break;` and then falls
through into the next layout's case, so an out-of-range `player_num` silently gets a viewport
from a different layout instead of failing.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:155-175
            case ScreenLayout::two_player:
                switch (player_num)
                {
                case 0:
                    ...
                    return result;
                case 1:
                    ...
                    return result;
                default:
                    break;
                }
            case ScreenLayout::three_player:
                switch (player_num)
                {
                case 0:

**Why it matters:** `two_player` with `player_num == 2` returns the *three-player* bottom-left
quadrant; `player_num == 3` falls through twice and returns the four-player bottom-right
quadrant; anything higher reaches the outer `default:` and returns the whole screen. That is
what turns the off-by-one above into a plausible-looking wrong picture rather than a throw
naming the index (T6). MSVC does not warn on implicit fall-through at `/W4`, so `/WX` did not
catch it, and every case's `return` makes the fall-through invisible on a skim.

**Remedy:** replace each `default: break;` with a `throw std::out_of_range` naming the layout
and the index, so a bad index is loud, and the fall-through disappears with it.

#### Give TriangleRightAxisAligned its own clone(), or the base slices it

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3452-3455`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2

**What:** `Shape::clone()` is virtual but `TriangleRightAxisAligned` does not override it, so
cloning one through a `const Shape*` produces a plain `Triangle` — the derived type is
silently sliced away.

**Evidence:**

    engine/math/matt_math.cpp:3452-3455
        std::unique_ptr<Shape> Triangle::clone() const
        {
            return std::make_unique<Triangle>(*this);
        }

    engine/math/matt_math.h:908-927   (no clone() among the overrides)
        struct TriangleRightAxisAligned : public Triangle
        {
            ...
            Segment hypotenuse() const;
            float hypotenuse_gradient() const;

    game/objects/level_object_builder.cpp:147-162   (the reachable caller)

            return std::make_unique<Structure>(

                &triangle,

    game/objects/structure.cpp:23

**Why it matters:** every ramp in every level file goes down this path, so no ramp `Structure`
in the game actually stores a `TriangleRightAxisAligned` — it stores a `Triangle`. Nothing
currently calls `hypotenuse()` or `hypotenuse_gradient()` through the stored shape, so the
loss is invisible today; the moment ramp response wants the hypotenuse gradient (which is
plainly why the subclass exists) it will `dynamic_cast` to null or read the base's generic
gradient. The same trap is loaded for the first user-defined `Shape`: `clone()` is the one
virtual whose omission compiles cleanly and corrupts the type.

**Remedy:** override `clone()` in `TriangleRightAxisAligned` (and in any future `Shape`), or
make `clone()` non-virtual and implement it once via a CRTP intermediate so forgetting is
impossible.
