#### Loop the mist spread angles instead of pasting the block five times

- **File:** `game/objects/projectile_builder.cpp:125-190`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4

**What:** `build_mist_projectiles` repeats the same twelve-line `push_back` five times, differing only in the rotation applied to the velocity.

**Evidence:** `game/objects/projectile_builder.cpp:126-189` — the five blocks differ only
at the velocity argument:

    			velocity,                                                  // :130
    			Vector2F::rotate_vector(velocity, mattmath::PI / 12.0f),    // :142
    			Vector2F::rotate_vector(velocity, -mattmath::PI / 12.0f),   // :155
    			Vector2F::rotate_vector(velocity, mattmath::PI / 6.0f),     // :168
    			Vector2F::rotate_vector(velocity, -mattmath::PI / 6.0f),    // :181

**Why it matters:** The spread pattern — how many particles, at what angles — is tuning
data that PHILOSOPHY T7 places in JSON; hardcoding it as five pasted blocks means changing
the mister's spread is a code edit in five places that must stay symmetric. The signature
also still carries a `projectile_type` parameter it ignores (`:118`,
`projectile_type /*type*/,	// always MIST here`), which is the residue of the copy.

**Remedy:** Iterate a `constexpr` array of offsets and drop the unused parameter.

<a id="g-sweep-frame-loop-cost"></a>

## sweep-frame-loop-cost — T7/T8: what the frame loop actually does

*Group `sweep-frame-loop-cost` · 15 findings (3 high, 10 medium, 2 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-frame-loop-cost.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I traced the real per-frame call graph twice: the gameplay path
(`Application::run` → `tick` → `StepTimer::Tick` → `Application::update` →
`StateContext::update` → `GameLevel::update` → `Level::update` →
`update_level_logic` → every object's `update(dt)`, then `Application::render` →
`clear` → `StateContext::draw` → `GameLevel::draw` → `Level::draw` →
`draw_active_level` → thread pool → `draw_player_view_level` → every object's
`draw`), and the menu path (`MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` →
`draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` → `draw_mobject_in_viewports`). I then
read every drawable, `Registry`, `NameTable`, `Handle`, `SoundBank`,
`ViewportManager`, `Partitioner`, `ThreadPool` and `CollisionTools`, and
computed the actual object counts from the shipped level JSON.

The handle work is real and it did what it says on the *draw* path: `Registry`
and `NameTable` are honest names-in/handles-out tables, and every drawable I
opened stores a `Handle`, not a name. Two places still descend a
`std::map<std::string,int>` inside the loop, and both are on the *update* side,
which the handle work did not sweep: `Player::update_animation_state` resolves
four names on every animation transition, and `TextObject::set_text` remeasures.
So the answer to "did the handle work remove the string lookups or only move
them" is: removed from draw, moved to update.

The frame's dominant cost is not a string lookup, though. It is that the engine
gives a batch object no way to cull. `Level` computes a view rectangle, uses it
for one `bounds()` test per registered object, and then discards it —
`IGameObject::draw` takes only a `Camera`. `StructurePaintable` is one
registered object holding thousands of `PaintTile`s (4,116 in
`king_of_the_hill.json`, 5,230 in `turbulence.json`), and once its bounding box
touches the view every tile it owns is drawn, per viewport, forever. PHILOSOPHY
calls interface granularity "the user's performance dial"; the dial has no
handle on it.

The second theme is that the engine's own per-frame APIs return owning
containers. `Partitioner::partition`, `ViewportManager::all_viewports`,
`PlayerInput::update_and_get_player_inputs` and
`MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs` all return a `std::vector` whose element
count is fixed and tiny (≤4 in every case), so a stranger writing a game against
this engine cannot reach zero allocations per frame no matter how carefully they
write their own code.

What surprised me: `max_threads` defaults to 16 and the *frame* pays for it, not
just startup — `Application::clear()` re-binds a render target and a viewport on
all sixteen deferred contexts every frame, and `GameLevel::draw` builds a
sixteen-slot command-list vector, to service at most four recorders. And the one
piece of performance instrumentation in the whole project — the debug overlay's
`dt`/`fps` line — is arithmetically incapable of ever showing anything but the
target rate, because `StepTimer` in fixed-step mode reports `dt` as a constant.
The recent dt refactor added a `Level` member, a `DebugText` parameter and a
six-line comment to carry that constant.

### Themes

- The scene knows the cull rectangle and the draw interface cannot receive it, so an object that stands for N things must draw all N or none.
- Engine APIs called every frame return owning `std::vector`s whose size is fixed and small, which makes per-frame allocation a property of the engine rather than of the client.
- `max_threads = 16` is spent per frame, not just at startup: contexts, command-list slots and state binds are sized by the pool's width instead of by the work.
- The string lookups the handle work removed from `draw()` are still present on the `update()` side, where nothing swept for them.
- The same D3D operation is performed two different ways in two places, and the gameplay path consistently picked the more expensive flag.
- Work that exists only for a debug overlay (`count_projectiles`, nineteen `std::string`s, `player_move_state_string`) runs inside the parallel render workers at per-view frequency.
- Load-time-shaped work — resolving names, cloning shapes, measuring strings — reappears inside the loop wherever an object changes state.

#### Give `draw()` the view rectangle, or batch objects can never cull

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:41-61`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T8 (and PHILOSOPHY/The object model, "Interface granularity is the user's performance dial")

**What:** The scene computes a per-view cull rectangle and throws it away before calling `draw()`, so an object that represents thousands of sub-items has no information with which to skip any of them.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/i_game_object.h:41-42` — the only draw entry point:

        virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
            const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;

`game/objects/level.cpp:527-549` — the rectangle exists and is used once per registered object, then dropped:

        const RectangleF camera_view =
            this->viewport_manager_->camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect(
                player_num, camera);
        ...
        // draw collision objects
        for (auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
        {
            if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))
            {
                object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);
            }
        }

`game/objects/structure_paintable.cpp:44-51` — what one of those objects then does:

        void StructurePaintable::draw(SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const Camera& camera) const
        {
            Structure::draw(sprite_batch, camera);
            for (const auto& paint_tile : this->paint_tiles_)
            {
                paint_tile.draw(sprite_batch, camera);
            }
        }

**Why it matters:** `Structure::bounds()` (`game/objects/structure.cpp:36-39`) returns the whole sprite rectangle. `king_of_the_hill.json`'s `boundary_floor` is 6000×1000 and paintable on its top face; at `paint_tile_consts::WIDTH == 4.0f` that is 1,500 tiles in one registered object whose bounds intersect every camera in the level. Summing all `StructurePaintable` entries with their `paintable_faces` gives 4,116 tiles for `king_of_the_hill`, 5,230 for `turbulence`, 1,898 for `close_quarters`. Every painted tile issues two sprite submissions (`game/objects/paint_tile.cpp:49-53`), once per viewport, per frame — up to ~41,800 submissions per frame on a fully-painted four-player `turbulence`, with no way for the tile loop to know that 90% of it is off-screen. A `Camera` carries translation and scale but not a viewport size, so the callee cannot reconstruct the rectangle either. This is the shape `Scene` will inherit.

**Remedy:** Pass the view rectangle alongside the camera (`draw(sprite_batch, camera, const RectangleF& view)`), so a batch object can do internally exactly what the scene does externally.

#### `all_viewports()` asks for viewport index 4 and gets the full screen

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:87-91`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** -

**What:** The "fill the empty quadrant" branch passes `4` where the highest valid player index is `3`, and `calculate_viewport`'s switch falls through to the one-player default, so the fourth viewport of a three-player layout is the entire screen.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:87-91`:

        // Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
        if (player_count == 3)
        {
            result.push_back(this->player_viewport(4));
        }

`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:173-232` — `case ScreenLayout::three_player:` with `player_num == 4` matches no inner case, hits `default: break;` (194-195), falls through into `case ScreenLayout::four_player:` (197), matches no inner case there either (`default: break;` 224-225), and lands on:

        default: //1P screen
            result.x = 0.0f;
            result.y = 0.0f;
            result.width = screen_size.x;
            result.height = screen_size.y;
            return result;

**Why it matters:** `all_viewports()` has exactly one caller, `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (`game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-118`), which draws each widget once per returned viewport. `layout_` is only ever written from `GameLevel::build_and_enter_level` (`game/states/game_states.cpp:133-134`) and never reset when a state returns to the menu, so after any three-player match every menu widget is drawn a fourth time stretched across the whole screen, on top of the split-screen copies. `player_viewport(3)` would have produced the bottom-right quadrant the comment is asking for, because the same fall-through reaches `case ScreenLayout::four_player:`'s `case 3:`.

**Remedy:** Pass `3`, and terminate every `case` in `calculate_viewport` so an out-of-range player index throws instead of silently becoming a full-screen viewport (T6).

#### Frame time is still shared mutable state behind a raw pointer, and the sample teaches it

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:149`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("Frame time is a parameter — `update(float dt)` — not shared state")

**What:** `dt` moved into `IGameObject::update(float)` but stopped there: the shell still owns a heap-allocated `float`, publishes a `const float*` service, and `State::update()` takes no parameters, so every state — including the sample that is the new-project template — reads frame time through the pointer.

**Evidence:**

`engine/app/application.cpp:149`, inside `create_services()`:

        this->dt_ = std::make_unique<float>(0.0f);

`engine/app/application.cpp:259` and `engine/app/application.cpp:433-436`:

        *this->dt_ = static_cast<float>(this->timer_.GetElapsedSeconds());
        ...
        const float* Application::dt() const
        {
            return this->dt_.get();
        }

`engine/core/state.h:12-13` — no `dt` anywhere in the interface the engine calls into:

        virtual void update() = 0;
        virtual void draw() = 0;

`samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:53-57` — the template hands the pattern to every new project:

        // dt is a pointer because the objects reading it outlive any one
        // frame; the shell rewrites the value behind it every fixed step.
        const float dt = *this->app_->dt();

**Why it matters:** `IGameObject`'s own comment (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:26-33`) records that the `const float*` "put that pointer in eleven classes" and "made the object outlive-the-pointer question real". The same pointer is still the only way a `State` gets frame time — `GameLevel::update` dereferences it at `game/states/game_states.cpp:195-197` — so the lifetime question was moved up a layer rather than closed, and the sample documents it as the intended API. Fixing it after strangers have written states against `State::update()` is a breaking change to the one interface every game implements.

**Remedy:** Change `State::update()` to `State::update(float dt)` and have `StateContext::update(float dt)` forward the value; delete `Application::dt()` and the `unique_ptr<float>`.

#### The per-frame draw dispatch heap-allocates four times per task, in engine code

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:397-417`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8 (PHILOSOPHY/Performance: "Per-frame code performs no heap allocation")

**What:** Submitting the per-view draw tasks allocates the partition vector, a full copy of it per task, a `std::function` control block per task, a `task_item` per task, and a Win32 pool work object per task — every frame, entirely inside engine-provided API shapes.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp:400-414`:

        auto partitioned_players =
            this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);

        // draw player objects
        for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
        {
            this->thread_pool_->add_task([this, i, partitioned_players,
                deferred_contexts, command_lists, sprite_batches]()

`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:7-22` — an owning vector, built by unreserved `push_back`:

        std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> result;
        ...
            result.push_back(std::make_pair(start, end));

`engine/core/thread_pool.cpp:41-50`:

        auto item = std::make_unique<task_item>(task_item{ std::move(task), this });

        PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback, item.get(),
            &callback_environment_);

**Why it matters:** `partitioned_players` is captured **by value**, so each task copies the vector — one guaranteed heap allocation per task per frame. The closure is 64 bytes (`this` 8, `i` 4+4 pad, `std::vector` 24, three pointers 24), larger than MSVC's 56-byte `std::function` small-object buffer, so type erasure allocates again. `add_task` then allocates a `task_item`, and `CreateThreadpoolWork`/`CloseThreadpoolWork` create and destroy a pool work object per submission (`engine/core/thread_pool.cpp:59-63`). With four players that is ~16 allocations plus 4 pool objects per frame, before `GameLevel::draw` adds a sixteen-element `command_lists` vector (`game/states/game_states.cpp:322`) and `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` repeats the identical shape (`game/states/menu_page.cpp:130-152`). Note also that `Partitioner` — a generic index-range splitter used only by the renderer — is the sole occupant of `engine/collision/`, the folder ARCHITECTURE reserves for "broad phase, narrow phase, manifolds, resolution".

**Remedy:** Have `partition` fill a caller-owned `std::array`/span, give `ThreadPool` a fixed set of pre-created `PTP_WORK` objects reused across frames, and take the task as a template parameter or a non-owning callable reference so nothing is type-erased per frame.

#### Fixed-size input results are returned as heap-allocated vectors, once per frame each

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.cpp:135-145`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8 (PHILOSOPHY/Performance: "fixed-size geometry returns fixed-size containers")

**What:** Both input readers return exactly `MAX_PAD_COUNT` entries — a compile-time constant of 4 — as a `std::vector`, so every frame in every state pays a heap allocation for a result whose size can never vary.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/player_input.cpp:135-145`:

        std::vector<PlayerInputData> result(MAX_PAD_COUNT);
        for (int i = 0; i < MAX_PAD_COUNT; i++)
        {
            ...
        }
        return result;

`game/objects/player_input.h:36-39` — the contract is already stated as fixed:

        // Returns exactly player_input_consts::MAX_PAD_COUNT entries, indexed by
        // XInput pad slot.
        std::vector<PlayerInputData> update_and_get_player_inputs();

`game/states/menu_input.cpp:144-153` is the same function for menus, and is called through `MenuPage::menu_inputs()` (`game/states/menu_page.cpp:190-193`), which returns the vector **by value again**.

**Why it matters:** `GameLevel::update` calls this every gameplay frame (`game/states/game_states.cpp:151-152`); every menu page calls `menu_inputs()` every menu frame (e.g. `game/states/main_menu.cpp:55`), and `MenuPage::menu_inputs` copies the vector on the way out, doubling it. `std::array<PlayerInputData, MAX_PAD_COUNT>` is a drop-in for every call site I read — all of them index or range-for — and costs nothing.

**Remedy:** Return `std::array<PlayerInputData, player_input_consts::MAX_PAD_COUNT>` from both, and return it by value from `MenuPage::menu_inputs()`.

#### `all_viewports()` allocates a vector per widget, per frame, on a render worker

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:79-93`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** An engine accessor that returns at most four values builds an unreserved `std::vector` on every call, and its only caller calls it once per widget per frame from inside a thread-pool task.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:79-86`:

        std::vector<Viewport> ViewportManager::all_viewports() const
        {
            std::vector<Viewport> result;
            int player_count = this->player_count_from_layout(this->layout_);
            for (int i = 0; i < player_count; i++)
            {
                result.push_back(this->player_viewport(i));
            }

`game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-108` — the call site, inside `draw_mobject_in_viewports`, which `draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` runs per widget on a worker thread:

        std::vector<Viewport> viewports =
            this->viewport_manager()->all_viewports();

        size_t num_viewports = viewports.size();

**Why it matters:** With an unreserved `push_back` loop, four viewports cost four reallocations under MSVC's 1.5× growth. `MainMenuTitle::draw` submits two widgets; other pages submit more. Every one of them allocates and frees this vector every frame, on a worker thread, for data that is a pure function of `layout_` and the resolution and changes only when one of those changes. `player_count_from_layout` already bounds it at 4.

**Remedy:** Return a fixed-capacity result (`std::array<Viewport,4>` plus a count, or a small inline vector), or cache the layout's viewports and invalidate in `set_layout`/on resolution change.

#### The handle work did not reach `update()`: an animation transition still descends four string maps

- **File:** `game/objects/player.cpp:62-67`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T7/T8 (PHILOSOPHY/Content and assets: "Names resolve to handles once, at load")

**What:** Changing a player's animation state re-resolves the sheet, the frame, the sheet again and the strip by `std::string` through `std::map`, on the update path, at frame time.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/player.cpp:62-67`, reached from `Player::update` (`game/objects/player.cpp:734`):

        this->animation_state_ = new_animation_state;

        const PlayerAnimationInfo& info = this->animation_info(new_animation_state);
        TextureObject::set_frame(info.sprite_sheet, info.uniform_texture);

        set_animation_strip_and_reset(info.sprite_sheet, info.animation);

`engine/render/texture_object.cpp:30-35` and `engine/render/animation_object.cpp:162-170` — each of those two calls resolves twice:

        void TextureObject::set_frame(const std::string& sheet_name,
            const std::string& frame_name)
        {
            this->set_sprite_sheet(sheet_name);
            this->frame_ = this->sprite_sheet()->resolve_sprite_frame(frame_name);
        }

`engine/core/registry.h:84-93` — what `resolve` costs:

        const auto it = this->indices_.find(name);

with `std::map<std::string, int> indices_;` at `engine/core/registry.h:156`.

**Why it matters:** `PlayerAnimationInfo` holds three `std::string`s (`game/objects/player_consts.h:7-15`), so the names survive to run time by construction. `calculate_animation_state` switches between `walking` and `running` at `|velocity_x| > 600.0f` (`game/objects/player.cpp:1049`), which a player accelerating or decelerating crosses repeatedly, and `jumping`↔`falling` flips at every jump apex — so this is a per-frame-class event, not a load-time one. `RenderResources`' own header (`engine/render/render_resources.h:35-37`) states the rule this breaks: "a name costs a `std::map` descent and a string compare per node".

**Remedy:** Make `PlayerAnimationInfo` hold `SpriteSheetHandle` / `frame_handle` / `strip_handle` resolved once in `Player`'s constructor, and add handle-taking overloads of `set_frame` / `set_animation_strip_and_reset` beside the name-taking ones.

#### The gameplay path saves and restores context state per command list; the menu path does not

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:606`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** `FinishCommandList` and `ExecuteCommandList` are called with the state-restore flag set on the gameplay path and clear on the menu path, and on the gameplay path the saved state is overwritten by `Application::clear()` at the top of the next frame anyway.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp:606` (per view, per frame) and `game/objects/level.cpp:670`:

        HRESULT hr = deferred_contexts->at(i)->FinishCommandList(TRUE, &command_lists->at(i));

`game/states/game_states.cpp:337`:

        immediate_context->ExecuteCommandList(command_lists[i], TRUE);

`game/states/menu_page.cpp:120` and `game/states/menu_page.cpp:164` — the same two calls, opposite flags:

        HRESULT hr = deferred_context->FinishCommandList(FALSE, &command_list);
        ...
        immediate_context->ExecuteCommandList(command_lists[i], FALSE);

**Why it matters:** `TRUE` asks the runtime to snapshot and restore the whole pipeline state around each call — D3D11 documents this as the slow option and recommends `FALSE`. On the gameplay path the restore buys nothing: `Application::clear()` (`engine/app/application.cpp:298-302`) unconditionally re-binds the render target and viewport on every deferred context at the start of every frame, and `Level::draw_player_view_level` re-applies the per-player viewport at `game/objects/level.cpp:523-524`, so the restored state is discarded before it is read. Two code paths doing the same D3D operation with opposite flags also means nobody can tell which is the intended contract.

**Remedy:** Pass `FALSE` in both places on the gameplay path, matching the menu path, since the next frame re-establishes the state explicitly.

#### `clear()` re-binds render target and viewport on all sixteen deferred contexts every frame

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:296-302`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** The frame's clear step walks the full deferred-context array — sized by `max_threads`, default 16 — issuing two D3D calls each, though at most four of them ever record a command list.

**Evidence:**

`engine/app/application.cpp:296-302`:

        // Every worker draws into its own deferred context, so each needs the
        // same target and viewport bound before the frame fans out.
        for (auto& deferred_context : *deferred_contexts)
        {
            deferred_context->OMSetRenderTargets(1, &render_target, nullptr);
            deferred_context->RSSetViewports(1, &viewport);
        }

`engine/app/application.h:43-46` — what sizes that array:

        // The render thread pool. max_threads also sizes the deferred contexts and
        // sprite batches, so it is the widest the renderer can ever go.
        int min_threads = 1;
        int max_threads = 16;

**Why it matters:** `Partitioner::partition` caps its output at `num_elements` (`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:11`), and it partitions `player_objects_->size()`, which is at most 4. So contexts 4–15 are bound twice per frame and never record anything, and `GameLevel::draw` allocates a matching sixteen-slot `command_lists` vector (`game/states/game_states.cpp:322`) of which twelve entries are always null. The per-frame cost scales with the pool's declared width instead of with the frame's actual parallelism, which is the wrong axis for a value a game is invited to raise.

**Remedy:** Bind only the contexts the frame will use — pass the recorder count down, or have the recorder bind its own context in `draw_player_view_level` where it already sets the viewport.

#### Painted tiles draw a finished, paused splash animation forever

- **File:** `game/objects/paint_tile.cpp:43-53`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** `PaintTile::draw` submits the splash sprite unconditionally, and the splash strip is non-looping, so once its 0.25 s animation ends every painted tile keeps drawing the strip's last frame for the rest of the match — two sprites per painted tile instead of one.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/paint_tile.cpp:43-53`:

        if (this->team_ == PlayerTeam::none)
        {
            return;
        }
        const Colour tint = this->team_colours_.team_colour(this->team_);

        this->splash_.draw_with_colour(sprite_batch, camera, tint);

        this->TextureObject::draw_with(sprite_batch, this->rectangle_, camera,
            this->frame(), tint, this->origin(),
            this->effects(), this->draw_rotation());

`engine/render/animation_object.cpp:111-121` — how a non-looping strip ends:

                    if (animation_strip.looping())
                    {
                        this->frame_index_ = 0;
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        this->frame_index_--;
                        this->paused_ = true;
                    }

`game/content/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json`, strip `splash_1`: `"frame_count": 5, "frame_time": 0.05, "looping": false`.

**Why it matters:** `paused_` stops the *animation*, not the *draw*. `AnimationObject::source_rectangle()` keeps returning frame 4, so a tile painted at t=10 s is still submitting its splash quad at t=240 s. Combined with the culling finding above this doubles the largest sprite count in the game: on `turbulence` (5,230 tiles), a fully-painted four-player match submits ~41,800 sprites per frame where ~20,900 would do. `AnimationObject::is_paused()` already exists and is `protected`.

**Remedy:** Skip the splash draw once the animation has finished (expose `is_paused()` on `PaintTileSplash` and test it), unless the last frame is deliberately the settled-paint look — in which case say so and fold it into the tile's own frame.

#### A corner collision heap-allocates a virtual clone of the collider to measure penetration

- **File:** `engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:281-292`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T11 (and T8)

**What:** `calculate_object_collision_depth` clones the collider onto the heap through a virtual `clone()` and runs a full collision resolution on the copy, purely to read back how far it moved.

**Evidence:**

`engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:281-292`:

        Vector2F CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth(
            const Shape* collider,
            const Shape* collidee,
            const Vector2F& collision_direction)
        {
            std::unique_ptr<Shape> collider_copy = collider->clone();
            Vector2F amount;

            resolve_object_collision(collider_copy.get(), collidee, collision_direction, amount);

            return amount;
        }

Four call sites, all in `Player`'s corner-contact handlers — `game/objects/player.cpp:608`, `:622`, `:640`, `:658`:

            Vector2F amount = CollisionTools::calculate_object_collision_depth(
                this->shape(), other->shape(), Vector2F::DIRECTION_DOWN_LEFT);

**Why it matters:** `on_bottom_left_collision` / `on_bottom_right_collision` are the ordinary case of a player resting on or walking over a platform edge, reached from `Player::on_structure_collision` (`game/objects/player.cpp:545-552`) every frame the contact persists. Each one allocates, virtual-dispatches a clone, and — for anything that is not two rectangles — runs the 40-iteration bisection in `bracket_object_collision_generic` (`engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:66-80`) on the copy. For two AABBs the answer is `RectangleF::intersection`'s width and height, which `resolve_object_AABB_collision` already computes at `engine/math/collision_tools.cpp:225-228`.

**Remedy:** Add a non-mutating `penetration_depth(const Shape*, const Vector2F&)` that returns the intersection extents for the rect/rect case and never copies the collider.

#### The debug overlay builds nineteen strings and a vector per player per frame, inside a render worker

- **File:** `game/objects/debug_text.cpp:44-102`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** `draw_debug_info` constructs a `std::vector<std::string>` and nineteen concatenated strings on every call, and it is called once per viewport per frame from a thread-pool task.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/debug_text.cpp:44-48`:

        std::vector<std::string> lines;

        lines.push_back("rect: " + std::to_string(rect.x) + ", " +
            std::to_string(rect.y) + ", " + std::to_string(rect.width) + ", " +
            std::to_string(rect.height));

`game/objects/debug_text.cpp:87-88` adds another allocation via `Player::player_move_state_string()` (`game/objects/player.cpp:1251-1271`), which returns `std::string` by value:

        std::string move_state_string = "move_state: ";
        move_state_string += player->player_move_state_string();

Call site, `game/objects/level.cpp:590-596`, inside `draw_player_view_level`:

            if (this->player_objects_->at(i)->showing_debug())
            {
                int num_projectiles = this->count_projectiles();

                this->debug_text_->draw_debug_info(sprite_batches->at(i),

**Why it matters:** Each `"rect: " + std::to_string(...) + ", " + ...` chain builds and discards several intermediate strings, most exceeding SSO once floats are formatted (`std::to_string(float)` produces 6 decimal places). The `lines` vector grows unreserved to 19 elements — roughly 6 reallocations. With four players holding Back this is on the order of a few hundred allocations per frame, on the worker threads, in the exact configuration a developer is in when they are trying to measure performance.

**Remedy:** Format into a reused `char` buffer with `std::format_to_n`/`snprintf` and draw each line as it is formatted; the overlay needs no container at all.

#### `count_projectiles()` rescans every collision object once per viewport, for one debug line

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:682-706`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** A linear scan of the whole collision-object list, doing up to ten enum comparisons per object, runs once per player view per frame inside the parallel draw, to produce a single number for the debug overlay.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp:682-700`:

        int Level::count_projectiles() const
        {
            int count = 0;
            for (const auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
            {
                CollisionObjectType type = object->collision_object_type();

                bool is_projectile =
                    type == CollisionObjectType::projectile_spray_team_a ||
                    ...
                    type == CollisionObjectType::projectile_mist_team_b;

Called at `game/objects/level.cpp:592`, inside the per-view loop of `draw_player_view_level`.

**Why it matters:** `collision_object_type()` is a virtual call, and it is invoked once per object per call. `weapon_consts::DETAILS_SPRAYER` has `shoot_interval == 0.0f` (`game/objects/weapon_consts.h:44`) and `projectile_consts::DETAILS_SPRAY` has `delete_timer == 5.0f` (`game/objects/projectile_consts.h:31`), so a firing sprayer adds one projectile per frame and each lives five seconds — the list reaches several hundred entries in normal play. Four views then perform four full scans of it per frame, each computing the same answer. The `||` chain also re-encodes, for the third time in this file, the "is this a projectile" predicate that `CollisionObjectType` already fails to express (see the outstanding #13).

**Remedy:** Compute the count once in `update()` and store it, or hoist it above the view loop in `draw_active_level`.

#### The one performance readout in the project cannot show anything but the target rate

- **File:** `game/objects/debug_text.cpp:81-82`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Performance ("A throughput regression is a defect, not a curiosity")

**What:** Under fixed timestep `StepTimer` reports `GetElapsedSeconds()` as exactly the target step, so the overlay's `dt` and `fps` lines are constants; the real frame rate is measured, exposed, and never read.

**Evidence:**

`engine/core/step_timer.h:134-142` — fixed-step mode assigns the target, never the measured delta:

                while (m_leftOverTicks >= m_targetElapsedTicks)
                {
                    m_elapsedTicks = m_targetElapsedTicks;

`engine/app/application.cpp:73-75` turns that mode on; `engine/app/application.cpp:259` copies the constant into `dt_`; `game/objects/level.cpp:67` copies it into `frame_dt_`; `game/objects/debug_text.cpp:81-82` prints it:

            lines.push_back("dt: " + std::to_string(dt));
            lines.push_back("fps: " + std::to_string(1.0f / dt));

`engine/core/step_timer.h:55` computes the genuine presented rate and has no callers anywhere in the tree:

            uint32_t GetFramesPerSecond() const noexcept { return m_framesPerSecond; }

**Why it matters:** The overlay reads `60.000000` whether the game is running at 60 Hz or 6 Hz. The recent dt work added `Level::frame_dt_`, a six-line comment justifying it (`game/objects/level.h:114-120`), and a fourth parameter to `DebugText::draw_debug_info` specifically to carry this value to the render workers — machinery built to transport a compile-time constant. Anyone profiling this engine from inside it is being lied to.

**Remedy:** Print `StepTimer::GetFramesPerSecond()` for `fps` and the measured wall-clock delta for the readout; keep the fixed step for the simulation.

#### `draw_timer` formats the same integer into a `std::string` twice per player per frame

- **File:** `game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:159-175`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** T8

**What:** The HUD countdown converts the same float to text twice per call — once for the shadow and once for the text — on the draw path, per viewport, per frame.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:159-175`:

            sprite_font->DrawString(
                sprite_batch,
                std::to_string(static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))).c_str(),
                (pos + (TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET * scale)).xm_vector(),
        ...
            sprite_font->DrawString(
                sprite_batch,
                std::to_string(static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))).c_str(),
                pos.xm_vector(),

**Why it matters:** `draw_gameplay_interface` is called once per player view per frame (`game/objects/level.cpp:578-587`), so this is eight `std::to_string` calls per frame in a four-player match where two would do — and each result is discarded at the end of the full expression. Short values fit SSO so this is arithmetic and formatting rather than allocation, but it is formatting done twice inside the render worker for a value that changes once per second. `draw_respawn_timer` two functions below already gets this right (`game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:189`).

**Remedy:** Hoist the conversion into a local, as `draw_respawn_timer` does.

<a id="g-sweep-testability"></a>

## sweep-testability — Headless testability

*Group `sweep-testability` · 15 findings (6 high, 7 medium, 2 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-testability.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read the three design documents, all three `tests/` targets and their `CMakeLists.txt`, the root and per-target build files, every engine header outside `engine/math/`, the engine `.cpp` files behind the types those headers expose, `samples/minimal/` in full, and the game call sites needed to establish reachability. For each engine module I worked out by construction what a test executable would have to build before it could call anything, and where it stops.

The shape of the problem is narrower than "there is no renderer interface", and worse. PHILOSOPHY says everything below the platform edge is testable headlessly "because the boundary (targets) and the seams (renderer interface, parameterised draw) make it linkable and constructible without a window". The boundary half landed — `ArtAttackEngine` is a real static library now. The seam half did not exist at any point: `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` **is** the renderer interface, and `DirectX::SpriteBatch`'s only constructor takes an `ID3D11DeviceContext*` which it immediately dereferences. So the claim in the document is currently false, and the document does not know it.

The number that surprised me is not the seam, though: **`ArtAttackEngine` has 32 translation units and not one test executable links it.** `MattMathTests` links `MattMath`; `CoreTests` links nothing and includes two headers directly; `AssetsTests` recompiles two engine `.cpp` files into itself. Thirty of the thirty-two engine TUs have no coverage of any kind. That is not a seam problem — nine of those thirty need a `ResolutionManager` and nothing else, or two ints, or no arguments at all. `Partitioner`, the single-method class that slices work for every render fan-out in the game, is nineteen lines long, needs nothing to construct, has no tests, and divides by its second argument without checking it. `ViewportManager` needs only a `ResolutionManager` to exercise (its `DeviceResources*` member is never read by any member function), has no tests, and contains a live off-by-one that hands the fourth pane of a three-player split screen a full-screen viewport rectangle.

So the ranked answer to "which single change unblocks the most" is: replacing `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` in `IGameObject::draw` with an engine-owned renderer interface unblocks 14 engine types and gates 9 of the 32 TUs — but it is not the change that would buy the most coverage *today*, because roughly a third of the engine is already reachable and simply has no tests written against it.

### Themes

- The renderer seam does not exist: `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` appears in the member signatures of 14 engine types, and DirectXTK's `SpriteBatch::Impl` calls `deviceContext->GetDevice(...)` in its constructor, so none of those 14 can be driven by a fake.
- The `dt`-as-parameter and `draw`-takes-parameters conversions stopped at `IGameObject`: `State::update()` and `State::draw()` still take nothing and reach back through `Application` for the frame time, the device and the sprite batches, so no state — the unit a game is actually made of — can be driven headlessly.
- A large amount of engine machinery is *already* headlessly testable and simply untested; the barrier is not the seam, it is that nobody has written the file.
- Where a class does hold pure, testable logic, that logic is routinely `protected` or `private` while the only public door takes a platform object, so exercising it requires a probe subclass.
- Two sibling loaders written in the same folder as the tested one have neither shape validation nor tests, and one of them is testable today with the exact temp-file harness that already exists in `tests/assets/`.
- Headers are not self-contained in two places, and one of them (`game/objects/player_input.h`) compiles only because a force-included precompiled header supplies `GamePad.h` — which means no game source can be pulled into a test target without replicating `game/pch.h`.
- The gaps line up with a bug each time: every place my "what would a test build here" walk found something free-to-test-and-untested, opening the file found a defect in it.

---

#### Replace `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` in `IGameObject::draw` with an engine-owned renderer interface

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:4,41-42`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain, PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering

**What:** The engine's central drawing interface names a DirectXTK concrete class that cannot be constructed without a live D3D11 device context, so no drawable in the engine can be exercised by a test.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/i_game_object.h
      4: #include <SpriteBatch.h>
     41:		virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
     42:			const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;

DirectXTK's only public constructor, and what it does with the argument:

    vcpkg_installed/x64-windows/include/directxtk/SpriteBatch.h:69
        explicit SpriteBatch(_In_ ID3D11DeviceContext* deviceContext);

    directxtk/Src/SpriteBatch.cpp:35,39
        inline ComPtr<ID3D11Device> GetDevice(_In_ ID3D11DeviceContext* deviceContext)
            deviceContext->GetDevice(&device);
    directxtk/Src/SpriteBatch.cpp:377,390
        SpriteBatch::Impl::Impl(_In_ ID3D11DeviceContext* deviceContext)
            mDeviceResources = deviceResourcesPool.DemandCreate(GetDevice(deviceContext).Get());

Passing `nullptr` is an immediate null dereference, so there is no null-object trick available.

**Why it matters:** Fourteen engine types name `DirectX::SpriteBatch` in a member signature — `IGameObject` (`core/i_game_object.h:41`), `AnimationObject` (`render/animation_object.h:42,44,46,49,52,58`), `SpriteSheet` (`render/sprite_sheet.h:48,59,69,80`), `TextureObject` (`render/texture_object.h:42-65`), `TextObject` (`render/text_object.h:29,31,37`), `TextDropShadow` (`render/text_drop_shadow.h:29,31`), `ViewportManager` (`render/viewport_manager.h:36`), `Visual` (`render/visual.h:34`), and the six widget types `MObject`, `MContainer`, `MWidget`, `MTexture`, `MText`, `MTextDropShadow` (`ui/widget.h:16,25,52,69,95,134,163`). Four more — `Text`, `SpriteSheetObject`, `DrawObject`, `Drawer` — sit on the same path without naming it. A test can construct most of them (a `SpriteSheet` accepts a null `ID3D11ShaderResourceView*`, so `RenderResources::add_sprite_sheet` seeds fine), but the moment it calls `draw` it needs a real device context, and even with a WARP device it can only assert "did not throw", because a `SpriteBatch` exposes nothing a test can read back. PHILOSOPHY names the fix — `draw_sprite(texture, src, dst, tint, rotation, origin, depth)` — and calls this seam the thing that "serves headless testing today"; it does not exist. It is also the single change that unblocks the most: nine of the 32 engine TUs (`animation_object`, `sprite_sheet`, `sprite_sheet_object`, `texture_object`, `visual`, `widget`, `viewport_manager`, `text_object`, `text_drop_shadow`) are gated on it alone.

**Remedy:** Introduce `artattack::Renderer` with the `draw_sprite` / `draw_text` calls PHILOSOPHY already specifies, take `Renderer&` in `IGameObject::draw`, and put the DirectXTK `SpriteBatch` behind one implementation in `engine/render/d3d11/`; a recording fake in `tests/` then makes every drawable assertable.

---

#### No test executable links `ArtAttackEngine`; 30 of its 32 translation units have no coverage

- **File:** `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:6-19`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout ("Tests link libraries, never `#include` implementation files")

**What:** The engine library is never linked by a test; the one test that touches engine code recompiles two engine `.cpp` files into its own target, and the other two link `MattMath` or nothing at all.

**Evidence:**

    tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt
      3: # The manifest loader reads a file and parses JSON, and that is all it does -
      4: # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units
      5: # directly rather than linking the engine and everything the engine drags in.
      6: add_executable(AssetsTests
      7:     asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp
      8:     test_main.cpp
      9:     "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp"
     10:     "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/json_loader.cpp"
     11: )

    tests/core/CMakeLists.txt
      3: # Registry and NameTable are header-only and depend on nothing but the
      4: # standard library, so this target links neither the engine nor D3D - it
      5: # includes the two headers directly.
     12: target_link_libraries(CoreTests PRIVATE
     13:     doctest::doctest
     14:     artattack_settings
     15: )

`engine/CMakeLists.txt:12-45` lists 32 sources. `AssetsTests` reaches 2 of them by recompilation. `MattMathTests` links `MattMath` (a different target). No `CMakeLists.txt` under `tests/` mentions `ArtAttackEngine`.

**Why it matters:** Two consequences, both concrete. First, the stated reason is a cost a static library does not actually impose — the linker pulls only the objects whose symbols are referenced, so linking `ArtAttackEngine` from `AssetsTests` would drag in `asset_manifest_loader.obj` and `json_loader.obj` and stop there. Second, the recompiled copy is a second build recipe that will diverge: the day `asset_manifest_loader.cpp` gains an include of anything in `engine/render/`, `AssetsTests` fails to build for a reason that has nothing to do with the test. Meanwhile the headline number is that thirty engine TUs — the whole of `render/`, `ui/`, `collision/`, `audio/`, `app/`, and all of `core/` except the two header-only types — are never compiled into anything a test runs. Old review finding #2 ("`ConfigurationType=Application`, so nothing can link it") is recorded as done; the library links, and nothing links it.

**Remedy:** Have each test target `target_link_libraries(... ArtAttackEngine)` and delete the duplicated source entries, so a test's dependency on engine code is the linker's problem and not a hand-maintained list.

#### `all_viewports()` returns a full-screen rectangle as the fourth pane of a three-player split screen

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:86-91,170-173,194-197,224-227`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** For `ScreenLayout::three_player`, `all_viewports()` asks for viewport index 4 — which does not exist — and three stacked `switch` fallthroughs turn that into the full-screen viewport rather than the fourth quadrant.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp
     86:         }
     87:         // Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
     88:         if (player_count == 3)
     89:         {
     90:             result.push_back(this->player_viewport(4));
     91:         }

`calculate_viewport(three_player, 4)` walks the inner `three_player` switch to `default: break;`, and every case block falls through because none of them ends in `break` or `return` on that path:

    170:             default:
    171:                 break;
    172:             }
    173:         case ScreenLayout::three_player:
    ...
    194:             default:
    195:                 break;
    196:             }
    197:         case ScreenLayout::four_player:
    ...
    224:             default:
    225:                 break;
    226:             }
    227:         default: //1P screen
    228:             result.x = 0.0f;
    229:             result.y = 0.0f;
    230:             result.width = screen_size.x;
    231:             result.height = screen_size.y;

Slots are 0-based (`all_viewports` pushed 0, 1, 2 in the loop at :83-85), so the intended fourth pane is index **3**, not 4. MSVC does not diagnose implicit switch fallthrough at `/W4`, so `/WX` never saw it.

**Why it matters:** Reachable from the shipped game. `game/states/main_menu.cpp:905-911` sets `ScreenLayout::three_player` when the player picks 3 players; `game/states/game_states.cpp:132-134` applies it to the `ViewportManager` before the level is built; `game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-118` — the base of `PauseMenuPage`, `ResultsMenuPage` and `EndMenuPage` — then does:

    104:		std::vector<Viewport> viewports =
    105:		 	this->viewport_manager()->all_viewports();
    ...
    110:			this->viewport_manager()->apply_player_viewport(
    111:				static_cast<int>(i), deferred_context, sprite_batch);
    ...
    115:			widget->draw(sprite_batch, viewports[i]);

For `i == 3` the D3D viewport applied is the bottom-right quarter (that call path *does* reach the `four_player` case 3 and returns the quadrant) while the `Viewport` the widget lays itself out against is the full screen. Pausing a three-player match therefore draws the fourth pane's menu content positioned for a 1280x720 screen inside a 640x360 scissor. This is the finding that most directly makes the case for the sweep: `ViewportManager` needs a `ResolutionManager` and nothing else to test (see the next finding), so a dozen lines of doctest would have caught it.

**Remedy:** Change `player_viewport(4)` to `player_viewport(3)` and terminate every `case` in `calculate_viewport` with an explicit `return` for the out-of-range `player_num`, then pin the four layouts with a table-driven test.

#### `ViewportManager` holds a `DeviceResources*` no member function reads

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:23-24,55`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** The constructor demands a `DeviceResources*` that is stored and never used, so the split-screen geometry — pure arithmetic over a resolution — cannot be constructed in a test without a live device, and every includer of the header compiles `<Windows.h>`, `<d3d11_1.h>` and `<dxgi1_6.h>`.

**Evidence:**

    engine/render/viewport_manager.h
      5: #include "engine/render/device_resources.h"
     23:		ViewportManager(ResolutionManager* resolution_manager,
     24:			DeviceResources* device_resources);
     55:		DeviceResources* device_resources_ = nullptr;

The member's only appearance in the implementation is the initialiser:

    engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:8-13
        ViewportManager::ViewportManager(ResolutionManager* resolution_manager,
            DeviceResources* device_resources) :
            resolution_manager_(resolution_manager),
            device_resources_(device_resources)
        {
        }

`grep -n device_resources_ engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp` returns exactly that one line.

**Why it matters:** Seven public queries — `player_viewport`, `all_viewports`, `viewport_dividers`, `camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect`, `layout`, `set_layout`, `fullscreen_d3d11_viewport` — are functions of `ScreenLayout` and a `Vector2F` resolution, and they are where the split-screen behaviour PHILOSOPHY lists as engine mechanism actually lives. The unused parameter is the only reason a test writer would conclude this type needs a device; in practice they would have to pass `nullptr` and hope, which no comment sanctions. It is also a documented-loan violation: PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes says "a non-owning pointer is a documented loan: the member declaration says who owns the object and why it outlives the holder", and this one has no comment and no reason.

**Remedy:** Delete the parameter and the member, and drop `#include "engine/render/device_resources.h"` from the header.

#### `State::update()` and `State::draw()` take no parameters, so no game state can be driven headlessly

- **File:** `engine/core/state.h:12-14`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes ("Frame time is a parameter — `update(float dt)` — not shared state")

**What:** The state interface — the unit PHILOSOPHY says a game *is* to the engine — passes nothing, so every state reaches back through a borrowed `Application*` for the frame time, the device, the deferred contexts and the sprite batches.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/state.h
     12:		virtual void update() = 0;
     13:		virtual void draw() = 0;
     14:		virtual void init() = 0;

The engine's own sample shows what that forces on a game author:

    samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp
     55:		const float dt = *this->app_->dt();
    ...
     68:	artattack::DeviceResources* device = this->app_->device_resources();
     69:	ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred = device->deferred_context(0);
     70:	SpriteBatch* sprite_batch = this->app_->sprite_batches()->at(0);
     71:
     72:	sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred);
     73:	this->greeting_->draw(sprite_batch);
     74:	this->hint_->draw(sprite_batch);
     75:	sprite_batch->End();
     76:
     77:	ID3D11CommandList* commands = nullptr;
     78:	if (FAILED(deferred->FinishCommandList(FALSE, &commands)))

**Why it matters:** `IGameObject::update` was converted to take `dt` (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:27-34` documents the reasoning at length) and `IGameObject::draw` was made `const` and given a camera parameter; `State` got neither. The consequence for testing is total: to construct any state you need an `Application*`, and `Application::initialize` opens a Win32 window and creates a D3D11 device (`engine/app/application.cpp:104-125,154-169`). All 44 game states and the sample's one state are therefore unreachable from a test, and a stranger writing their first state on this engine has to learn `FinishCommandList` and `ExecuteCommandList` to draw two strings. The `const float*` returned by `Application::dt()` is the shared-state form PHILOSOPHY explicitly rules out, still live because `State::update()` has nowhere to put a parameter.

**Remedy:** Give `State` `update(float dt)` and `draw(Renderer&)` (the same seam as the previous finding), and let `StateContext` pass both down from the shell.

                slot.name + "' has been released.");
        }

**Why it matters:** `Text` is the only thing `samples/minimal` — the new-project template — draws, so the engine's own showcase drawable is the one with the hardest construction barrier. A test can only get there by hand-assembling `DirectX::SpriteFont::Glyph` records and calling DirectXTK's third, rarely-used constructor (`SpriteFont(ID3D11ShaderResourceView*, Glyph const*, size_t, float)`, `directxtk/SpriteFont.h:53-56`) with a null texture — which works, but requires the test to know DirectXTK's internals rather than the engine's API. Contrast `TextureObject`, which is fully constructible today because `SpriteSheet` accepts a null `ID3D11ShaderResourceView*` (`engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:23,92`). Text measurement is also the one piece of the draw path with an assertable return value, so this is the coverage the engine is furthest from and would benefit most from.

**Remedy:** Put font metrics behind an engine-owned type (a `Font` holding a glyph table, with `measure(text)`), so `RenderResources` stores an engine type and a test can seat a two-glyph fake.

#### `Partitioner::partition` divides by its argument without checking it, and has no tests

- **File:** `engine/collision/partitioner.cpp:5-23`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T9 ("a standing obligation that built code meet library standard — contracts, tests, documentation")

**What:** `num_partitions` is used as a divisor on the first line of the function with no precondition check and no documented contract, and the value comes from a public field of `ApplicationOptions`.

**Evidence:**

    engine/collision/partitioner.cpp
      5:	std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> Partitioner::partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const
      6:	{
      7:		std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> result;
      8:		int elements_per_partition = num_elements / num_partitions;
      9:		int remainder = num_elements % num_partitions;

The header documents nothing:

    engine/collision/partitioner.h:12-16
        std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>
            partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const;

The value's provenance:

    engine/app/application.h:46      int max_threads = 16;
    game/objects/level.cpp:397       int num_threads = this->thread_pool_->max_num_threads();
    game/objects/level.cpp:400-401   auto partitioned_players =
                                         this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);
    game/states/menu_page.cpp:133-138 int num_threads = this->data()->thread_pool()->max_num_threads();
                                      partitioner->partition(mobjects->size(), num_threads);

`ThreadPool::max_num_threads()` returns `options.max_threads` unmodified (`engine/core/thread_pool.cpp:6-7,108-111`).

**Why it matters:** A game that sets `options.max_threads = 0` — a public field on the struct the engine tells a game to fill in, with no validation anywhere between it and this line — gets integer division by zero and a hardware exception on the first frame it draws, not a message naming the problem (T6). `num_partitions` negative is silently wrong instead. This is the whole of `engine/collision/` — nineteen lines, a default constructor, no dependencies at all beyond `<vector>` — and it has no test file. It is the cheapest possible demonstration that the gap is not the renderer seam.

**Remedy:** Throw `std::invalid_argument` naming the value for `num_partitions <= 0` (or validate `ApplicationOptions` at `Application::initialize`), state the precondition in the header, and add `tests/collision/partitioner_tests.cpp`.

#### `engine/core/step_timer.h` does not compile on its own, and fixed-step timing has no injectable clock

- **File:** `engine/core/step_timer.h:7-9,29-37,92-101,171-173`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files ("Include order: own header first — proving every header compiles on its own")

**What:** The header uses `LARGE_INTEGER`, `QueryPerformanceFrequency` and `QueryPerformanceCounter` without including any Windows header, so it compiles only when something upstream has already pulled `<Windows.h>` in.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/step_timer.h
      7: #include <cmath>
      8: #include <cstdint>
      9: #include <exception>
    ...
     29:            if (!QueryPerformanceFrequency(&m_qpcFrequency))
    ...
     92:            LARGE_INTEGER currentTime;
    ...
     94:            if (!QueryPerformanceCounter(&currentTime))
    ...
    171:        LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcFrequency;
    172:        LARGE_INTEGER m_qpcLastTime;

`step_timer.h` has exactly one includer in the tree, and it sits below other engine headers that reach the Windows SDK first:

    engine/app/application.h:3-19
      3: #include "engine/assets/resource_loader.h"     // -> <Audio.h>, <d3d11_1.h>
      4: #include "engine/audio/audio_resources.h"
      5: #include "engine/collision/partitioner.h"
      6: #include "engine/core/state_context.h"
      7: #include "engine/core/step_timer.h"
     ...
     19: #include <Windows.h>

So the build only works because of include order in a file `step_timer.h` knows nothing about, and `<Windows.h>` at line 19 arrives twelve lines too late to be the reason.

**Why it matters:** A test TU that opens with `#include "engine/core/step_timer.h"` — the exact thing CONVENTIONS says must work — does not compile. Beyond that, `StepTimer` is where PHILOSOPHY's "game loop, fixed-step timing" mechanism lives, and it reads `QueryPerformanceCounter` directly in its constructor and in `Tick()`, so its catch-up loop, its 1/10-second delta clamp and its 1/4-millisecond snapping (lines 105-142) cannot be driven to a known state by a test. This is one of very few engine types that needs no device at all and is still untestable.

**Remedy:** Add `#include <Windows.h>` to the header, and take the tick source as a template parameter or a `uint64_t` argument so the fixed-step logic can be stepped deterministically.

#### `game/objects/player_input.h` compiles only under the force-included precompiled header

- **File:** `game/objects/player_input.h:1-6,34`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** The header declares a constructor taking `DirectX::GamePad*` without including `GamePad.h` or anything that provides it; it builds only because `game/pch.h` is force-included into every `ArtAttackGame` translation unit.

**Evidence:**

    game/objects/player_input.h
      1: #pragma once
      2:
      3: #include <vector>
      4: #include "game/objects/player_input_data.h"
      5: #include "engine/math/matt_math.h"
    ...
     34:		explicit PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad);

Neither include reaches `GamePad.h`: `player_input_data.h:3-4` pulls `engine/input/connection_state.h` and `engine/math/matt_math.h`, and `matt_math.h:3-5` pulls `SimpleMath.h`, `shape_type.h` and `<d3d11.h>`. The supplier is:

    game/CMakeLists.txt:72   target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackGame PRIVATE pch.h)
    game/pch.h:64            #include "GamePad.h"

`game/states/menu_input.h:7` includes `player_input.h`, so it inherits the same defect.

**Why it matters:** No source file from `game/` can be added to a test executable without also replicating `game/pch.h`'s 30-line Windows/DirectXTK prologue — which is why there is no game test target at all. It also means the include graph is not what the source says it is: `game/pch.h` force-includes `BufferHelpers.h`, `Effects.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `Model.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `ScreenGrab.h` and `WICTextureLoader.h` into every game TU, none of which any game file uses, and PHILOSOPHY makes compile time an engine responsibility ("a build-time regression is a defect"). The immediate victim is `PlayerInput::calculate_player_input` (`player_input.h:43-44`) — a `static` pure function over two `RawPlayerInput` values implementing the deadzone, trigger threshold and press-edge logic — which is both `private` and, because of this header, unreachable from a test target.

**Remedy:** Add `#include <GamePad.h>` to `player_input.h` (and audit the rest of `game/` the same way), then reduce `pch.h` to headers the game actually uses.

#### `read_sprite_sheet` and `read_sound_bank` have neither shape validation nor tests, unlike their sibling in the same folder

- **File:** `engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.cpp:11-67`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** The sprite-sheet decoder indexes and type-converts rapidjson values with no `IsObject`/`HasMember`/`IsArray` guard, and its header says so; the manifest loader beside it was hardened against exactly this and has 17 assertions covering it.

**Evidence:**

    engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.h:14-15
        // Throws std::runtime_error naming the path if the file cannot be read or
        // parsed, and whatever rapidjson throws if the document is the wrong shape.

    engine/assets/sprite_sheet_loader.cpp
     14:			for (auto& frame : json.GetArray())
     15:			{
     16:				std::string name = frame["name"].GetString();
     ...
     19:				RectangleI source_rectangle(
     20:					frame["position"]["x"].GetInt(),
     ...
     62:		const Document doc = read_json_file(json_path);
     63:
     64:		return std::make_unique<SpriteSheet>(texture,
     65:			decode_sprite_frames(doc["sprite_frames"]),
     66:			decode_animation_strips(doc["animation_strips"]));

rapidjson's only guard is `#define RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(x) assert(x)` (`external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/rapidjson.h:437`), which the project does not override. The project's own test file names the consequence:

    tests/assets/asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp:138-140
        // Each of these reaches a rapidjson call that asserts on the wrong
        // shape - a crash in debug, undefined behaviour in release - if the
        // loader does not check first.

**Why it matters:** `read_sprite_sheet` takes an `ID3D11ShaderResourceView*` that it only forwards to `SpriteSheet`'s constructor, which stores it unexamined (`engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:92`), so `read_sprite_sheet("temp.json", nullptr)` is testable **today** with the exact `TempManifest` harness already sitting in `tests/assets/asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp:14-48`. `game/content/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json` is a hand-edited 14 KB file; a mistyped `"size"` key in it is a debug abort and a release read against a wrongly-typed union, not the named error T6 promises. `read_sound_bank` (`engine/assets/sound_bank_loader.cpp:73-78`, same unguarded `doc["waves"]` / `doc["sound_effect_instances"]` / `.GetBool()`) has the same defect and is *not* testable, because its second parameter is a `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::WaveBank>` that needs a live `AudioEngine` and a real `.xwb`.

**Remedy:** Reuse whatever guarded-access helper `asset_manifest_loader.cpp` uses in both siblings, and add `tests/assets/sprite_sheet_loader_tests.cpp` modelled on the manifest tests.

#### Engine machinery that needs nothing to construct has no tests at all

- **File:** `engine/collision/partitioner.h:7-17`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain ("A new public primitive ships with behavioural tests in the same commit")

**What:** At least seven engine types are fully constructible and callable with no device, no window, no file and no fake, and none of them has a single test.

**Evidence:** Each of these is reachable from a bare doctest TU today —

    engine/collision/partitioner.h:10-16   Partitioner() = default;  partition(int, int) const;
    engine/render/resolution_manager.h:12  ResolutionManager() = default;   (+ 8 conversion methods)
    engine/render/camera_tools.h:11-15     mattmath::Camera calculate_camera(...) const;   [public, pure]
    engine/core/state_context.h:11-15      StateContext() = default;  update/draw/transition_to
    engine/core/thread_pool.h:14           ThreadPool(int min_num_threads, int max_num_threads);
    engine/render/sprite_frame.h:10-20     SpriteFrame() = default;  three ctors, source_rectangle()
    engine/render/animation_strip.h:10-17  AnimationStrip(const RectangleI&, int, float, bool);

`tests/` contains exactly three subdirectories — `assets/`, `core/`, `math/` — and `tests/core/` contains only `name_table_tests.cpp` and `registry_tests.cpp`.

**Why it matters:** `ThreadPool` publishes a contract in its own header — "Blocks until every submitted task has finished. If any task threw, the first such exception is rethrown here, on the calling thread" (`engine/core/thread_pool.h:22-26`) — implemented across a Win32 callback, a mutex and an `exception_ptr` (`thread_pool.cpp:57-101`), on a Win32 thread pool that needs no window whatsoever. Nothing verifies that exceptions propagate, that a second throw is discarded, or that `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` clears state for the next frame. `CameraTools::calculate_camera` is the entire camera-framing and scroll-border model, public and pure. `ResolutionManager` round-trips a resolution through four representations including a string. These are the primitives PHILOSOPHY says ship with tests in the same commit; the two that *do* have tests (`Registry`, `NameTable`) show what that looks like and how cheap it is.

**Remedy:** Add `tests/collision/`, `tests/render/` and the missing `tests/core/` files; none needs anything the build does not already have.

#### Pure, testable logic is hidden behind `protected` and `private` while the public door takes a platform object

- **File:** `engine/render/drawer.h:15-31`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness), PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain

**What:** In several engine types the only computation worth asserting is non-public, so exercising it requires writing a probe subclass in the test — a pattern that repeats often enough to be a design habit rather than an accident.

**Evidence:** `Drawer`'s three helpers are documented as pure functions of their arguments and are `protected`:

    engine/render/drawer.h
     15:	protected:
     16:		RenderResources* render_resources() const;
     17:		// const because they are on the draw path and are pure functions of
     18:		// their arguments - none of the three reads a member.
     22:		mattmath::RectangleI calculate_draw_rectangle(
    ...
     29:		mattmath::Vector2F calculate_sprite_origin(
     30:			const mattmath::Vector2F& size,
     31:			RotationOrigin origin) const;

`MovingObject` has no public members at all beyond its constructors — 26 velocity/dx/rotation accessors, all `protected`:

    engine/core/moving_object.h:17-52
     17:	protected:
     18:		virtual const mattmath::Vector2F& velocity() const;
    ...
     52:		virtual void alter_rotation(float rotation);

The animation frame-advance — accumulator, looping and frame wrap — is `protected` too:

    engine/render/animation_object.h:25-26
     25:	protected:
     26:		virtual void update(float dt);

Same shape at `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:59-66` (`calculate_viewport`, `player_count_from_layout`) and `game/objects/player_input.h:43-44` (`calculate_player_input`, `private static`).

**Why it matters:** Each of these is the piece a test would actually want to pin, and each forces the test to declare a subclass whose only job is to widen access — which means the test is coupled to the inheritance shape rather than the behaviour, and a later refactor to composition breaks tests that were testing arithmetic. `Drawer::calculate_sprite_origin` and `calculate_draw_rectangle` in particular sit on the camera transform for every drawable, and `MovingObject`'s twenty-six accessors are the base of `Player`, `Projectile` and everything else that moves. The engine's own comment on `Drawer` argues the functions are pure; if they are pure they can be free functions in `artattack::` and testable directly.

**Remedy:** Move genuinely pure helpers to free functions in their module's header (`calculate_draw_rectangle`, `calculate_sprite_origin`, `calculate_viewport`, `calculate_player_input`), and make `MovingObject`'s reads public.

#### `StateContext::transition_to` dereferences the incoming state while `update()` and `draw()` guard against null

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** The same class null-checks its state in two methods and dereferences it unchecked in the third, with no documented precondition on the parameter.

**Evidence:**

    engine/core/state_context.cpp
      5:	void StateContext::update() const
      7:		if (this->state_ == nullptr)
      9:			return;
    ...
     13:	void StateContext::draw() const
     15:		if (this->state_ == nullptr)
     17:			return;
    ...
     21:	void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
     22:	{
     23:		this->state_ = std::move(state);
     24:		this->state_->set_context(this);
     25:		this->state_->init();
     26:	}

The header says nothing about the argument:

    engine/core/state_context.h:15
        void transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state);

**Why it matters:** All 45 call sites in the tree pass `std::make_unique<...>` (`engine/app/application.cpp:189` and 44 in `game/states/`), so **this path is not reachable today** — I checked every one. It is graded on what it is: a public engine API, in a class that is one of the handful testable with no dependencies at all, whose only failure mode is a silent null dereference in a build with no assertions. The internal inconsistency is the tell — a reader who sees the guards in `update`/`draw` will reasonably conclude `nullptr` is an accepted way to clear the state, and it is not. `StateContext` has no test file, which is why nobody has had to write down which behaviour is intended.

**Remedy:** Either throw naming the caller for a null state, or accept null as "clear the state" and guard it; state the choice in the header and pin it with a test.

against the nine modules the same file rosters at lines 79-93 (`math`, `core`, `render`, `collision`, `input`, `audio`, `ui`, `assets`, `app`) and:

#### `MattMath`'s public header includes `<d3d11.h>`, so the one tested library compiles the graphics SDK

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout (`MattMath` — "Depends on: nothing")

**What:** The math library's public header pulls in DirectXTK's `SimpleMath.h` and `<d3d11.h>`, and its `CMakeLists.txt` links `Microsoft::DirectXTK` publicly, so the target the philosophy says depends on nothing depends on the graphics stack.

**Evidence:**

    engine/math/matt_math.h
      3: #include "SimpleMath.h"
      4: #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"
      5: #include <d3d11.h>

    engine/math/CMakeLists.txt
      1: # MattMath — the math static library. Depends on nothing but the
      2: # DirectXTK headers it currently wraps (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md).
    ...
     15: target_link_libraries(MattMath
     16:     PUBLIC Microsoft::DirectXTK

The `<d3d11.h>` dependency is one method — `mattmath::Viewport::d3d_viewport()` returning `D3D11_VIEWPORT` (used at `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:24,65`) — plus `RECT` conversions at `matt_math.h:200,228,534,548`. `SpriteFrame` and `AnimationStrip` in `engine/render/` store `RECT` rather than `mattmath::RectangleI` (`sprite_frame.h:22`, `animation_strip.h:20`), which is what keeps the Win32 type on the frame table the comments describe as "device-independent".

**Why it matters:** `MattMathTests` is the only test target with a meaningful body of coverage, and configuring it requires `find_package(directxtk CONFIG REQUIRED)` plus the Windows SDK. That is fine on this machine and is the wrong shape for the library PHILOSOPHY singles out as the one with no dependencies — it is also the first thing that would have to be unpicked for the second platform the same document plans for. The build file already admits the gap in a comment rather than filing it.

**Remedy:** Move `d3d_viewport()` and the `RECT` conversions to a small adapter header in `engine/render/`, and give `SpriteFrame`/`AnimationStrip` `mattmath::RectangleI` frame tables.

<a id="g-sweep-build"></a>

## sweep-build — The build

*Group `sweep-build` · 18 findings (4 high, 7 medium, 7 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-build.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read the root `CMakeLists.txt`, `cmake/settings.cmake`, `cmake/seed_save.cmake`, the five
target `CMakeLists.txt` files, the three `tests/*/CMakeLists.txt`, `CMakePresets.json`,
`vcpkg.json`, `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes`; then cross-checked them against the tree
(`git ls-files`, 430 tracked files), against the deleted `ArtAttack.vcxproj` recovered from
`6a15785^`, and against the configured build trees under `out/`. Several of the old review's
build findings are genuinely gone: there is a real engine static library, no `.sln`/`.vcxproj`
is committed, `.vs/` is untracked and ignored, `enable_testing()` plus three `add_test()` calls
mean a plain `ctest` runs everything, builds are out-of-source, and `/W4 /WX /permissive-` now
reaches all six targets including the tests through one `INTERFACE` library. That part of
ARCHITECTURE/The build has landed.

The shape of what is left is that the build files were converted faithfully but the *repository*
was not. Three problems dominate. First, the content pipeline: `game/content/` is 320 MB
containing raw `.wav` sources, GIMP `.xcf` files, Microsoft Publisher `.pub` files and three
committed Windows toolchain `.exe`s, all of it mirrored into every preset's output directory and
byte-compared on every single build — and the one file the game actually needs from it,
`sound_bank_1.xwb`, is gitignored, so a fresh clone builds a game that dies at startup and
cannot be repaired because the `.wav` inputs are gitignored too. Second, `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}`
appears in ten places across five build files, which is exactly the variable that stops working
the moment this repo becomes the submodule the roadmap says it will be. Third, the compile-time
engine/game wall that both CONVENTIONS and ARCHITECTURE promise as "fails to compile — that is
the feature (T5)" does not exist: the engine's own include path is the repository root, so
`#include "game/objects/player.h"` from engine code compiles today. No engine file does it, so
the wall is currently held by discipline alone — which is precisely what T5 says a wall must not
be.

What surprised me: the `settings.cmake` comment says "values carried over from the solution this
build replaced", and two of them were not — `/fp:fast` and `/Zc:__cplusplus` were in all four
configurations of the old `.vcxproj` and are in none of the new ones. Dropping `/fp:fast` is
almost certainly right (the previous review argued for it in five separate findings), but it
happened silently under a comment asserting the opposite.

### Themes

- The build files are honest CMake; the repository they build is not — content, toolchain
  binaries, design sources and generated artefacts all live in the same `content/` tree, and the
  build ships all of it.
- `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}` is used as if this repo will always be the top-level project, which
  contradicts the stated plan to consume the engine as a submodule.
- Claims about compile-time enforcement (T5) outrun what the build actually enforces: the
  engine/game include wall, MattMath's independence, and the engine's C++20 requirement are all
  asserted in documentation and absent from the build.
- The `find_package(xaudio2redist)` / `find_package(directxtk)` workaround is copy-pasted
  verbatim into four build files, including the one that is meant to be the new-project template
  a stranger copies.
- Per-build cost is treated as free: ~320 MB of content is content-compared before every relink,
  on a project whose own philosophy says a build-time regression is a defect (T10).
- The stock Visual Studio `.gitignore`/`.gitattributes` boilerplate survived the CMake
  conversion unpruned, and one of its rules — `*.wav`/`*.xwb` — is now load-bearing in the worst
  way.
