#### `interface` is a Windows macro used as a keyword in a public engine header

- **File:** `engine/render/device_resources.h:17`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** T12

**What:** `IDeviceNotify` is declared with the `interface` macro (`#define interface struct`,
reached through `<Windows.h>` at line 7), i.e. a macro that reads like a keyword, in the
header that declares the base class of `Application`.

**Evidence:**

`engine/render/device_resources.h:7` and `:16-24`

    #include <Windows.h>
    ...
        // Provides an interface for an application that owns DeviceResources to be notified of the device being lost or created.
        interface IDeviceNotify
        {
            virtual void OnDeviceLost() = 0;
            virtual void OnDeviceRestored() = 0;

        protected:
            ~IDeviceNotify() = default;
        };

`engine/app/application.h:71` puts it in the engine's most-read declaration:

        class Application : public IDeviceNotify, public StateContext

**Why it matters:** T12 was added this week and its rule is explicit — "the line is that a
macro may not invent syntax, hide control flow, or change the meaning of a name that already
had one." `interface` does the first and the third: it is not C++, it depends on
`<Windows.h>` having been included first, and a reader who greps for `class IDeviceNotify` or
`struct IDeviceNotify` finds nothing. It is also the exact thing PHILOSOPHY names Unreal for.
Separately it is a portability landmine for the "second platform is an addition, not a
rewrite" goal: this declaration does not compile without the Windows SDK.

**Remedy:** `class IDeviceNotify` (and drop the `I` while touching it — CONVENTIONS/Never).

#### The widget set is undocumented, `M`-prefixed, and owns nothing it holds

- **File:** `engine/ui/widget.h:9-57`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Never; PHILOSOPHY/UI

**What:** `engine/ui/widget.h` declares six public types with zero documentation, all carrying
a type prefix, storing children as bare non-owning pointers with no ownership statement, and
none of them implements the focus or navigation PHILOSOPHY says the widget set exists to solve.

**Evidence:**

`engine/ui/widget.h:9`, `:33`, `:59`, `:76`, `:114`, `:140` — the six types, in a file named
for one:

        class MObject : public IGameObject
        class MContainer final : public MObject
        class MWidget : public MObject
        class MTexture final : public MWidget, public TextureObject
        class MText final : public MWidget, public Text
        class MTextDropShadow final : public MWidget, public TextDropShadow

`:38-43` and `:56` — the ownership question, unanswered and then handed out publicly:

        void add_child(MObject* child);
        void remove_child(const std::string& name);
        void remove_child(const MObject* child);
        void remove_all_children();
        size_t child_count() const;
        std::vector<std::pair<std::string, MObject*>> children();
    ...
        std::vector<std::pair<std::string, MObject*>> children_;

`engine/ui/widget.cpp:41-43` confirms the pointer is stored raw; callers pass
`unique_ptr::get()` (`game/states/end_menu.cpp:217-226`). `grep -in "focus\|navigat" engine/ui/`
returns nothing.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Never bans `I`, `C`, `F`, `U` "or any other type prefix", and
these are six of them in one file (the `M` is a survivor of the pre-split `Mh.h` naming).
PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes requires "A non-owning pointer is a documented loan: the
member declaration says who owns the object and why it outlives the holder" — line 56 says
nothing, and `children()` hands the loans out to arbitrary callers. PHILOSOPHY/UI promises
"the two things every controller game needs solved once: focus, and navigation between
widgets"; neither exists, so a stranger reading `widget.h` cold learns neither what the widget
set is for nor who deletes their buttons. `MTexture` and `MText` additionally inherit from two
bases each, so the type a game writes against is a multiple-inheritance lattice — a T10
acceptance-test failure on its own.

**Remedy:** Rename to `Widget`/`Container`/`Label`/`Image`, document the ownership of
`children_` (or take ownership), and either ship focus/navigation or amend PHILOSOPHY/UI.

**What:** Both `SpriteFrame` constructors take `origin` and `rotated`, store them in members

`engine/render/sprite_frame.h:11-32`

`engine/render/sprite_frame.cpp:12-13` writes them and nothing reads them; a repository-wide

#### The "permanent second client" exercises four of the engine's public types

- **File:** `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.h:1-35`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** T1; PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** `samples/minimal/` is named as the mechanism that keeps the engine/game boundary
honest, but it touches only `Application`, `State`, `Text` and `DeviceResources`, so every
other engine type is still validated by one client only.

**Evidence:** `grep -roh "artattack::[A-Za-z_]*" samples/` returns, in full:

    artattack::Application
    artattack::DeviceResources
    artattack::State
    artattack::Text

`samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:12-16` states the claim:

    # It is a permanent target rather than a documentation snippet because a
    # second client is the only thing that keeps the engine/game boundary honest
    # (PHILOSOPHY T1). It links ArtAttackEngine and nothing from game/, so if a
    # mechanism ever drifts back into the paint-shooter, this stops building.

**Why it matters:** The link-time guarantee is real but narrow: it fails only if something the
sample uses moves into `game/`. `IGameObject`, `Visual`, the whole of `engine/ui/`,
`CollisionTools`, `AudioResources`, `SoundBankObject`, `ThreadPool`, `Partitioner`,
`ViewportManager`, `SpriteSheet` and `AnimationObject` are exercised by exactly one client —
the paint-shooter — so the boundary breaches in this report (divider asset names, `TEAM_*`
colours) are precisely the kind the sample was supposed to catch and structurally cannot. It

#### New code spells the same concept two ways: `Registry::handle` beside `TextureHandle`

- **File:** `engine/core/registry.h:53`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Types

**What:** The recently-added core headers use snake_case for nested type names in some places
and PascalCase in others, sometimes for the same concept, against the one rule the conventions
document says everything falls out of.

**Evidence:** snake_case types —

    engine/core/registry.h:53         using handle = Handle<Resource>;
    engine/core/registry.h:149        struct entry
    engine/core/thread_pool.h:34      struct task_item
    engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:10  class com_exception : public std::exception
    engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:18   using frame_handle = Handle<SpriteFrame>;
    engine/render/sprite_sheet.h:19   using strip_handle = Handle<AnimationStrip>;

PascalCase types for the identical concept, in headers from the same wave —

    engine/render/render_resources.h:38  using TextureHandle = Handle<ID3D11ShaderResourceView>;
    engine/render/render_resources.h:39  using FontHandle = Handle<DirectX::SpriteFont>;
    engine/render/render_resources.h:40  using SpriteSheetHandle = Handle<SpriteSheet>;
    engine/audio/audio_resources.h:17    using SoundBankHandle = Handle<SoundBank>;
    engine/assets/resource_loader.h:39   struct AssetKind

`engine/core/throw_if_failed.h:27` also carries a PascalCase *function*, `ThrowIfFailed`, and
`com_exception::result` (`:23`) a member with no trailing underscore.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS opens with "PascalCase names a type. snake_case names
everything else", lists aliases explicitly as types, and says the scheme must be "learnable in
one sitting". A reader who learns `RenderResources::TextureHandle` and then writes
`SpriteSheet::FrameHandle` gets a compile error. This is not legacy: `registry.h`,
`handle.h`, `name_table.h` and `sprite_sheet.h`'s handle aliases are all new work, so the
conventions passes have not converged and the divergence is inside a single feature.

**Remedy:** `Handle`, `Entry`, `TaskItem`, `ComException`, `FrameHandle`, `StripHandle`,
`throw_if_failed`.

#### The assets test recompiles engine sources instead of linking the engine

- **File:** `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:6-11`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout

**What:** `AssetsTests` compiles two engine translation units into the test executable rather
than linking `ArtAttackEngine`, so the code it validates is not the code the library ships.

**Evidence:**

    # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units

    add_executable(AssetsTests

`tests/core/CMakeLists.txt:4-6` does the same in spirit, by design, for header-only types;
`tests/math/CMakeLists.txt:8-11` links `MattMath` properly.

implementation files", and the old review named this exact pattern as the visible cost of

- **File:** `engine/assets/json_loader.h:3-12`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules

**What:** `ArtAttackEngine` publishes the vendored rapidjson include directory as `PUBLIC` and
one public engine header returns a rapidjson type by value, so every consumer of the engine
compiles against a third-party DOM library it was told it would not see.

`engine/CMakeLists.txt:46-49`

        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/external/rapidjson/include"

    #include <rapidjson/document.h>
    ...

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE.md/Modules states the intent precisely — "`rapidjson` reaches

directory is the opposite of stopping there, and `read_json_file`'s return type puts rapidjson

#### `matt_math.h` is twenty public types in one 1150-line header

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:32-43`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** conventions
- **Tenet:** CONVENTIONS/Files

**What:** The header every engine signature drags in declares twenty types and three
`typedef` aliases in 1150 lines, of which four functions are documented, and two of the
aliases are not distinct types.

**Evidence:** `grep -n "^\s*\(class\|struct\|using\|typedef\)\s" engine/math/matt_math.h` gives
`Shape`, `RectangleF`, `Matrix`, `Vector`, `Vector2I`, `Vector2F`, `Vector3F`, `Vector4F`,
`RectangleI`, `Colour`, `MatrixF`, `Matrix3x3F`, `Viewport`, `Circle`, `Triangle`,
`TriangleRightAxisAligned`, `Quad`, `Segment`, `Camera`, `RectangleRotated`, plus

    34:     typedef Vector2F Point2F;
    298:    typedef mattmath::RectangleF AABB;
    1149:   typedef RectangleRotated OBB;

Thirty-two of its comment lines are commented-out declarations (`grep -cE
'^[[:space:]]*//[[:space:]]*[A-Za-z_~#].*[;{}]$'`), e.g. `:248-251`:

        //void set_left(float left);
        //void set_top(float top);
        //void set_right(float right);
        //void set_bottom(float bottom);

`engine/math/ericson_math.h` is worse in proportion: lines 12-72, 97-98 and 104-106 — 62 of
139 — are commented-out code, and the file credits a book (`:3-5` "Real-Time Collision
Detection / Christer Ericson / 2005") with no licence statement, inside the library T9 calls
hand-rolled.

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS/Files says "One primary type per header" and, as of the most
recent commit, "No huge files… A file is too big when a reader can no longer hold what it does
in their head." This is the first header a stranger opens, because `Vector2F` and `Colour`
appear in every engine signature, and finding `Colour` means scrolling past `MatrixF` and
`Matrix3x3F`. PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain makes compile speed a maintained property —
"light headers, disciplined includes" — and this header is included, transitively, by nearly

            s_1280_720,
            s_1920_1080,
            s_2560_1440,
            s_3840_2160,
            max = s_3840_2160
        };

`engine/render/screen_layout.h:5-11`

        enum class ScreenLayout
        {
            one_player,
            two_player,
            three_player,
            four_player
        };

`engine/app/application.h:37` and `:99` make the first the only way in:

        ScreenResolution resolution = ScreenResolution::s_1280_720;
    ...
        void set_resolution(ScreenResolution resolution);

**Why it matters:** T1's litmus test — "if a game built on the engine would need to edit it, it
is game code" — is met exactly: a stranger shipping at 1366×768, 1600×900 or ultrawide, or
building a five-player shared-screen game, must edit an engine header and rebuild the library.
The whole list is this game's options menu, hardened into a type. `ResolutionManager` already
has `set_resolution(const mattmath::Vector2F&)` (`resolution_manager.h:19`), so the mechanism
for arbitrary sizes exists and the enum is the only thing narrowing it. `max = s_3840_2160` is
additionally a sentinel enumerator with no documented meaning in an otherwise-undocumented
header.

**Remedy:** Take a `Vector2I` at the boundary and keep the enum, if it is wanted at all, as a
game-side convenience; make `ScreenLayout` a player count.

#### The engine's render API speaks "player", which PHILOSOPHY reserves for the game

- **File:** `engine/render/viewport_manager.h:34-45`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** boundary
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Structural types

**What:** Twelve public identifiers across three engine render headers name a "player", the
noun PHILOSOPHY says the engine does not have.

**Evidence:** `grep -rn "player" --include=*.h engine/ | grep -v ^engine/math` —

    engine/render/camera_tools.h:12       const mattmath::Vector2F& player_center,
    engine/render/screen_layout.h:7-10    one_player, two_player, three_player, four_player
    engine/render/viewport_manager.h:34   void apply_player_viewport(int player_num,
    engine/render/viewport_manager.h:40   mattmath::Viewport player_viewport(int player_num) const;
    engine/render/viewport_manager.h:44   mattmath::RectangleF camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect(

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY/Structural types is explicit — "there is no engine `Player`,
`Level`, `Match` or `Team`. The engine-worthy parts of 'player' already exist as input slots
and views" — and ARCHITECTURE.md closes with "the boundary is not just where the code splits,
it is where the vocabulary splits." The mechanism here is correct and general (it is view
management); only the naming asserts a policy the engine does not implement, which is why this
is low rather than a design defect. A stranger building a two-viewport spectator mode reads
`apply_player_viewport(1)` and reasonably assumes player identity is engine state.

**Remedy:** Rename to `view`/`view_index`/`view_count` and let the game map players onto views.

<a id="g-sweep-docs-accuracy"></a>

## sweep-docs-accuracy — The documents against the code

*Group `sweep-docs-accuracy` · 20 findings (8 high, 8 medium, 4 low) · source `review2/raw/sweep-docs-accuracy.md`, cross-cutting sweep — no separate verifier, reported as written.*

I read PHILOSOPHY.md, CONVENTIONS.md and ARCHITECTURE.md end to end, then walked the real
tree folder by folder against ARCHITECTURE's tree diagram and module table, read all five
first-party `CMakeLists.txt` files plus `cmake/settings.cmake`, `CMakePresets.json` and
`vcpkg.json`, computed every cross-module include edge inside `engine/`, and spot-checked
nine findings that `docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md` marks Fixed. The remediation itself held up
well: `#4` (`closest_pt_point_OBB` now loops 2 axes), `#24` (`delete_timer()` now returns
`details().delete_timer`), `#25`/`#26`/`#27`/`#28`/`#29` (one `read_json_file` that checks
`fopen_s` and `HasParseError`), `#31` (`RenderResources` forwards to `Registry`), `#33` (the
`try`/`catch` barrier in `work_callback`), `#35`/`#36` (`stop_sounds` returns on an
unresolved handle) and `#5` (deferred contexts are recreated in `HandleDeviceLost`) are all
genuinely fixed and survived the restructure intact. Nothing I spot-checked regressed.

The problem is the documents, not the fixes. Three distinct failures show up. First, the
design documents describe a build and a tree that partially do not exist: four of nine
`engine/` module folders hold something other than what ARCHITECTURE says they hold, three
rows of the module dependency table are false, and two subfolders the tree names
(`render/d3d11/`, `input/xinput/`) have never been created. Second, PHILOSOPHY carries at
least four statements that are not aspirational at all but factual and wrong — the worst
being the justification for parallel rendering, which the engine's own header comment and
IMPLEMENTED.md both explicitly contradict. Third, `docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md` is dated today
and still reports the two largest structural findings as Outstanding after they landed. What
surprised me most is how good the in-code documentation is where it exists —
`i_game_object.h` and `application.h` explain their contracts better than the design docs do —
and how completely absent it is elsewhere: 21 of 50 engine headers contain not one comment
line, `State` among them, and there is no README anywhere in the repository telling a stranger
how to configure, build or run any of this.

### Themes

- The design documents declare themselves "the destination" and then make factual present-tense
  claims about today's code, so a reader cannot tell which sentences to trust.
- ARCHITECTURE's tree and module table are presented as "the authoritative roster of modules and
  folders", which makes their inaccuracies actively misleading to a contributor deciding where a
  file goes.
- The recorded remediation is real and survived the CMake conversion and the engine/game split;
  the status documents that describe it have not kept pace with it.
- Everything that would let a second developer actually use this — a README, build instructions,
  a documented update order, a how-to for adding content — is missing, and the sample that the
  documents nominate as the answer requires the reader to write raw D3D11.
- Two adopted Microsoft template files live inside `engine/` under the engine's namespace while
  breaking every naming rule CONVENTIONS states, and no document acknowledges the category
  exists.
- Where the code and the documents disagree, the code comment is usually the correct one —
  PHILOSOPHY has not been amended in the same PR as the change that fought it, which is the one
  process promise the document makes about itself.

---

#### Correct PHILOSOPHY's justification for parallel rendering, which is the opposite of what the renderer does

- **File:** `docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:371-372`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** PHILOSOPHY states that parallel rendering is safe because render workers own disjoint
slices of the scene, when the parallelism axis is views and every worker draws every object.

**Evidence:**

    PHILOSOPHY.md:371-372
    - Parallel rendering is sound because drawing is a pure read; render workers
      own disjoint slices of the scene.

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15
        // draw() is const, and that is the whole contract that makes parallel
        // rendering sound. The render workers do not own disjoint slices of the
        // object list - the parallelism axis is *views*, so every worker enters
        // draw() on the SAME object at the same time. Under that fan-out the only
        // safe draw is a pure read, and const is how the compiler holds a new
        // object to it instead of a comment nobody reads.

    game/objects/level.cpp:400-415
        auto partitioned_players =
            this->partitioner_->partition(this->player_objects_->size(), num_threads);
        for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
        {
            this->thread_pool_->add_task([this, i, partitioned_players, ...]()
                {
                    this->draw_player_view_level(partitioned_players[i].first, ...);

**Why it matters:** The document that is meant to be the tie-breaker for design decisions states
a safety argument that would make a non-`const` `draw()` acceptable ("my worker owns this
object"), which is exactly the data race findings `#16`, `#23` and `#34` were about. Whoever
writes `Scene` reads PHILOSOPHY first; `partition()` splits *players*, not objects, so slices
have never been disjoint and there is no plan for them to become so. `docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md:89-93`
already records this ("PHILOSOPHY's tenet still says workers own disjoint slices, which does not
describe this renderer") and the amendment promised at PHILOSOPHY.md:27-29 was never made.

**Remedy:** Rewrite the bullet to say the parallelism axis is views, so every worker enters
`draw()` on the same object and the pure-read contract is the only thing making it sound —
i.e. copy the sentence already written at `i_game_object.h:11-13`.

#### Fix ARCHITECTURE's tree: four of nine engine folders hold something other than what it says

- **File:** `docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:82-91`

**What:** The tree diagram that ARCHITECTURE calls the authoritative roster of folders
misdescribes `collision/`, `input/`, `render/` and `ui/`, and names two subfolders that do not
exist.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:82-91

    │   ├── core/               game loop, fixed-step timing, Scene, states, services, registries
    │   ├── render/             renderer interface, cameras, viewports
    │   │   └── d3d11/          the D3D11/DirectXTK backend, behind the interface
    │   ├── collision/          broad phase, narrow phase, manifolds, resolution
    │   ├── input/              devices, action mapping

      engine/input/      connection_state.h                    <- one two-value enum

        std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>
            partition(int num_elements, int num_partitions) const;

**Why it matters:** ARCHITECTURE.md:7-8 says it "is the authoritative roster of modules and
folders" and :112 says "Every file picks its home the day it is created", so this diagram is what
a contributor consults to place a new file. It points collision work at a folder holding a
thread partitioner, while the actual collision code (`collision_tools.cpp`, `ericson_math.cpp`)
sits in `engine/math/`. `engine/collision/partitioner.h` is not collision code at all — it splits

DXGI factory calls).

`partitioner.h` to `core/` and mark the empty folders explicitly as placeholders.

#### Fix the module dependency table: math, core and render all depend on DirectXTK directly

- **File:** `docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:130-133`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules

**What:** The table says `math` depends on nothing, `core` on math, and `render` on core+math
with DirectXTK confined to `d3d11/`; all three rows are false, and PHILOSOPHY's target table
repeats the first.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:130-133
    | `math` | nothing |
    | `core` | math |
    | `collision` | core, math |
    | `render` | core, math — D3D11/DirectXTK inside `d3d11/` only |

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:264
    | `MattMath` | static library | `engine/math/` | nothing |

    engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5
    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"
    #include <d3d11.h>

    engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:15-18
    target_link_libraries(MattMath
        PUBLIC Microsoft::DirectXTK
        PRIVATE artattack_settings
    )

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:4
    #include <SpriteBatch.h>

    engine/render/{drawer.h:3, sprite_sheet.h:7, viewport_manager.h:8}
    #include "SpriteBatch.h"

**Why it matters:** "MattMath depends on nothing" is the load-bearing claim behind MattMath being
a separate target, behind `MattMathTests` being cheap, and behind the 2D math library being
portable. It is not true: MattMath pulls in `d3d11.h` and links DirectXTK publicly, so every
consumer of the math library also compiles the Direct3D headers. `core` is worse, because
`IGameObject` — the root interface every game object implements — names `DirectX::SpriteBatch`
in its pure-virtual `draw()`, so no game object can be declared without DirectXTK. `engine/math/CMakeLists.txt:1-2`
even cites ARCHITECTURE as authority for a dependency that ARCHITECTURE forbids.

**Remedy:** Either amend the three rows to state the DirectXTK dependency and why it is
tolerated for now, or record it as the debt it is with a named owner — but do not leave the
table asserting a property the build contradicts.

- **File:** `docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:277-279, 367-370`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** PHILOSOPHY, which states at :11-13 that it "deliberately says nothing about the current
codebase", makes two claims about "today" — that the D3D11 backend sits behind seams and that
the renderer seam serves headless testing today — and both are false.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:11-13

    the current codebase — no findings, no history; [docs/review/](../review/)
    holds all of that.

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:277-279
    ... Cross-platform is an eventual
    goal, not a current work item: today there is one backend (D3D11/DirectXTK,
    XInput), kept behind seams that don't presume it is the only one.

      (`draw_sprite(texture, src, dst, tint, rotation, origin, depth)`). The
      D3D11/DirectXTK backend is one implementation behind it — the same seam

    engine/core/i_game_object.h:41-42
        virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch,
            const mattmath::Camera& camera) const = 0;

**Why it matters:** There is no `draw_sprite` anywhere in the tree and no renderer interface; the

#### Fix or document the on-ramp: the sample the docs nominate as the template writes raw D3D11

- **File:** `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:62-85`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T10 (one language over a scripting layer)

**What:** PHILOSOPHY nominates `samples/minimal/` as the answer to "how do I start a project" and
sets an acceptance test that the game-facing API be explicable in an introductory C++ series;
drawing two strings in that sample requires deferred contexts, command lists and manual COM
release.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:431-438
    - A minimal sample game lives beside the paint-shooter. It is the standing
      answer to "how do I start a project on this engine" ...
    - An "Introduction to C++" video series accompanies the engine (T10) ... The
      game-facing API is the series' subject matter — and its acceptance test:
      a feature that can't be explained in an introductory series has an API
      that is too hard.

    samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp:62-85
    void HelloState::draw()
    {
        artattack::DeviceResources* device = this->app_->device_resources();
        ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred = device->deferred_context(0);
        SpriteBatch* sprite_batch = this->app_->sprite_batches()->at(0);
        sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred);
        this->greeting_->draw(sprite_batch);
        this->hint_->draw(sprite_batch);
        sprite_batch->End();
        ID3D11CommandList* commands = nullptr;
        if (FAILED(deferred->FinishCommandList(FALSE, &commands)))
        {
            throw std::runtime_error("HelloState::draw - FinishCommandList failed");
        }
        device->GetD3DDeviceContext()->ExecuteCommandList(commands, FALSE);
        commands->Release();
    }

**Why it matters:** This is the file a new project starts from — `main.cpp:1-3` says so. A
beginner copying it must understand `SpriteSortMode_Deferred`, immediate versus deferred
contexts, `FinishCommandList`'s `FALSE` argument, and that `ID3D11CommandList` is refcounted and
must be `Release()`d exactly once. That is not the simple subset of the language, and it is the
same "no renderer interface" defect as the previous finding seen from the user's side. It also
means the sample cannot keep the boundary honest in the way `samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:12-16`
claims: it does not exercise an engine drawing API, because there is not one.

**Remedy:** Give the shell a `begin_frame()/end_frame()` pair or a one-call draw list so
`HelloState::draw` is three lines, and until then say in the sample header that the D3D11
plumbing is temporary and will move behind the shell.

**Why it matters:** The document that decides where a file goes gives two answers for the two

there is no rule in the document that says which is right. The `app` paragraph is the accurate

#### Honour or qualify the "zero suppressions" promise made in two documents

- **File:** `engine/render/device_resources.cpp:26`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time)

**What:** PHILOSOPHY and CONVENTIONS both state that warnings are errors with zero suppressions;
there is exactly one warning suppression in first-party code, and it is unscoped.

**Evidence:**

    docs/design/PHILOSOPHY.md:449
    - Warnings are errors with zero suppressions; the language standard is

    docs/design/CONVENTIONS.md:105-107
      threshold crisp enough to enforce mechanically would be wrong often
      enough to need suppressing — and zero suppressions is a promise kept
      elsewhere (Tests and toolchain, PHILOSOPHY.md).

    engine/render/device_resources.cpp:21-26
    #ifdef __clang__
    #pragma clang diagnostic ignored "-Wcovered-switch-default"
    #pragma clang diagnostic ignored "-Wswitch-enum"
    #endif

    #pragma warning(disable : 4061)

**Why it matters:** CONVENTIONS explicitly leans on "zero suppressions is a promise kept
elsewhere" as the reason not to enforce a file-size limit mechanically — so the promise is load-
bearing for a second rule. The suppression has no `push`/`pop`, so C4061 (unhandled enumerator in
a `switch` on an enum) is disabled for the remaining 750 lines of the file, and any future
`switch` added there loses the diagnostic silently. One suppression is a defensible exception;
two documents claiming there are none is not.

# Gap analyses

<a id="g-gap-coverage"></a>

## gap-coverage — unread code and unasked questions

*Group `gap-coverage` · 7 findings (4 medium, 3 low) · source `review2/verified/gap-coverage.md`, verified report.*

I enumerated all 430 tracked files, filtered to the 259 first-party sources, and diffed
that list against every path cited in the 84 prior reports. **File coverage is close to
complete**: only 24 first-party sources are cited nowhere, and 21 of those are the
forwarding-constructor leaves (`weapon_mister.cpp`, `weapon_sprayer.cpp`,
`projectile_jet.cpp`, four `*_action.h` enums, four `*_data.cpp` accessor files,
`confirmation_state.h`, `menu_player_settings.h`) that the weapon/projectile/menu groups
already characterised as a class. I read all 24 anyway; the only thing in them worth
reporting is `MainMenuData`'s half-built constructor. The three `tests/*/test_main.cpp`
files are two identical doctest lines each and are fine.

So the gap is not unread files — it is unasked questions. I went after the categories the
brief named and checked each against the reports before opening code. **DPI, `/utf-8`,
byte-wise path widening, shutdown ordering, resolution-change-mid-match, fixed-step
catch-up, the 4-player-with-one-pad stall and the gitignored wave bank are all already
covered, several of them better than I would have.** Four categories are genuinely absent
from all 84 reports: continuous integration (zero mentions, in a repo whose ARCHITECTURE
names CI by name), precompiled-header and compile-cost hygiene (zero mentions, against a
PHILOSOPHY clause that calls a build-time regression a defect), multi-window/second-
`Application` state, and the runtime consequence of XInput slot instability. I also used
the configured build tree at `out/build/x64-debug` as evidence rather than guessing —
which is how I killed my own best-looking finding (`for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); i++)`
under `/W4 /WX` at `game_states.cpp:330`: the object file is newer than the source, so it
compiles clean; game-main-menu reached the same conclusion independently).

The shape of what remains: the *code* has been read hard, and the *repository* has not.
Everything I found sits in the layer between the source files and the person cloning
them — what the build carries, what runs on a push, what the shell assumes about being
the only one of itself, and what a controller does when it moves.

### Themes

- Four whole question categories are absent from 84 reports, and all four live outside
  the `.cpp` files: CI, compile-cost/PCH hygiene, second-`Application` state, and
  input-device identity across a replug.
- The repository's non-source files — `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes`, and the absent
  `.github/`, `.editorconfig`, `.clang-format` — are unmodified third-party templates or
  simply missing, and they are what a stranger meets before any header.
- ARCHITECTURE and PHILOSOPHY each make a checkable infrastructure promise (CI runs
  `ctest`; build time is a maintained property) that no file in the repository keeps, and
  no prior reviewer checked either.
- Where the prior review did read a file, it read it well: every behavioural edge I
  probed in `application.cpp`, `state_context.cpp`, `registry.h` and `resource_loader.cpp`
  turned out to be either correct or already filed, including three I expected to be bugs.
- The uncited files are uncited because they are empty of content, not because they were
  skipped — which is itself the finding the weapon and projectile groups already made.
- The build tree on disk is a legitimate, read-only evidence source that nobody used, and
  it settles questions (does this warn? does the content copy work? do the tests pass?)
  that were otherwise argued from first principles.

- **Severity:** medium

- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/The build

**What:** The design document states that `ctest` runs "on a contributor's machine or in
CI", and the repository contains no CI configuration of any kind.

**Evidence:**

`docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:63-65`:

    - Tests use a portable test framework and register with CTest: `ctest`
      runs everything, on a contributor's machine or in CI, with no IDE
      present.

The repository root, in full (`ls -a`), contains no `.github`, no `.gitlab-ci.yml`, no

`grep -rin "github actions\|\.github\|appveyor\|workflow"` across all 84 prior reports

#### Drop the thirteen unused DirectXTK headers from the game PCH, and give the engine one

- **File:** `game/pch.h:59-77`, `engine/CMakeLists.txt:12-45`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** performance
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Tests and toolchain ("Build time is iteration time... a build-time regression is a defect", `:452-454`)

**What:** The game's precompiled header force-includes nineteen DirectXTK headers into all
46 game translation units, thirteen of which nothing in `engine/`, `game/` or `samples/`
uses — including the three 3D ones, in a project whose non-goals name 3D as a design
constant — while the engine's 32 translation units have no precompiled header at all.

**Evidence:**

`game/pch.h:59-77`:

    #include "BufferHelpers.h"
    #include "CommonStates.h"
    #include "DDSTextureLoader.h"
    #include "DirectXHelpers.h"
    #include "Effects.h"
    #include "GamePad.h"
    #include "GeometricPrimitive.h"
    #include "GraphicsMemory.h"
    #include "Keyboard.h"
    #include "Model.h"
    #include "Mouse.h"
    #include "PostProcess.h"
    #include "PrimitiveBatch.h"
    #include "ScreenGrab.h"
    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "SpriteBatch.h"
    #include "SpriteFont.h"
    #include "VertexTypes.h"
    #include "WICTextureLoader.h"

Grepping `engine/ game/ samples/` (excluding `pch.h` itself) for the distinctive type each
header exists to provide returns zero hits for thirteen of them:

    BasicEffect|IEffect|EffectFactory|AlphaTestEffect|DualTextureEffect => 0
    GeometricPrimitive => 0
    Model\b => 0
    PostProcess|BasicPostProcess => 0
    SaveDDSTextureToFile|SaveWICTextureToFile => 0
    Keyboard => 0
    Mouse => 0
    PrimitiveBatch => 0
    GraphicsMemory => 0
    ConstantBuffer|CreateStaticBuffer => 0
    VertexPosition|VertexType => 0
    CreateWICTextureFromFile => 0
    CreateInputLayoutFromEffect|SetDebugObjectName|MapGuard => 0

(`DDSTextureLoader.h` has one user, `engine/assets/resource_loader.cpp`, which includes it
directly — so it too is dead weight in the *game's* PCH.) `Model.h`, `Effects.h` and
`GeometricPrimitive.h` are DirectXTK's 3D model/effect pipeline; `PHILOSOPHY.md:469` reads
"**3D.** MattMath is a 2D library; the dimension is a design constant, not a parameter."

`engine/CMakeLists.txt` has no `target_precompile_headers` line anywhere; the only one in
the repository is `game/CMakeLists.txt:72`.

**Why it matters:** PHILOSOPHY makes compile speed a maintained property and calls a
regression in it a defect, and this is the largest single lever on it that nobody has
pulled. Every game TU parses the 3D model pipeline it will never call, and the 32 engine
TUs — the ones a stranger will actually be editing — each re-parse `<windows.h>`,
`<d3d11_1.h>`, `<dxgi1_6.h>` and the DirectXTK headers from scratch, because the PCH was
inherited from the game's old project file and never extended to the library that was
extracted out of it.

**Remedy:** Delete the thirteen unused includes from `game/pch.h`, and add
`target_precompile_headers(ArtAttackEngine PRIVATE ...)` over the platform headers the
engine actually uses.

#### Move `window_proc`'s three `static bool`s into the Application

- **File:** `engine/app/application.cpp:441-517`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** The engine's window procedure keeps `in_sizemove`, `in_suspend` and `minimized`
in function-local statics, so every `Application` in a process shares one copy of the
window state each of them owns — in a class whose own header documents opening a second
window as a supported thing to do.

**Evidence:**

`engine/app/application.cpp:441-447`:

    LRESULT CALLBACK Application::window_proc(HWND window, UINT message,
        WPARAM w_param, LPARAM l_param)
    {
        static bool in_sizemove = false;
        static bool in_suspend = false;
        static bool minimized = false;

`engine/app/application.cpp:491-517`, the branch that reads them:

    case WM_SIZE:
        if (w_param == SIZE_MINIMIZED)
        {
            if (!minimized)
            {
                minimized = true;
                if (!in_suspend && app) { app->on_suspending(); }
                in_suspend = true;
            }
        }
        else if (minimized)
        {
            minimized = false;
            if (in_suspend && app) { app->on_resuming(); }
            in_suspend = false;
        }
        else if (!in_sizemove && app)
        {
            app->on_window_size_changed(LOWORD(l_param), HIWORD(l_param));
        }
        break;

`engine/app/application.h:32-34`:

    // The window class name has to be unique per process, so a game that ever
    // opens two windows needs two of these.
    std::wstring window_class_name = L"ArtAttackWindowClass";

**Why it matters:** With two Applications A and B: minimising A sets the shared
`minimized`/`in_suspend` and suspends A's audio and gamepad. The next ordinary resize of
**B** takes the `else if (minimized)` arm, calls **B**'s `on_resuming()` — resetting B's
step timer and resuming B's audio, neither of which was suspended — clears the shared
flags, and swallows B's resize so B's swap chain keeps the old size. A is then never
resumed for the life of the process, because the flag that would have resumed it is gone.
The path is **currently unreachable**: `main.cpp` constructs exactly one `Application`.
This is a design defect in the one class a stranger instantiates, not a live bug, and it
is a three-line fix now versus a debugging session for whoever first takes the header at
its word.

**Remedy:** Make the three flags private members of `Application` and read them through
the `app` pointer the handler already recovers from `GWLP_USERDATA`.

#### A player is welded to an XInput slot, so a replug hands them another player's character

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:191-207`, `game/objects/player_input.h:13-15`, `engine/input/connection_state.h:1-10`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation)

**What:** Player *N* reads input from XInput slot *N* for the whole match, and XInput user
indices are not stable across an unplug and replug, so a controller that comes back in a
different slot silently drives a different character — or nothing — with no notification,
because the `ConnectionState` that would carry one is written and never read.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp:191-207`:

    for (const auto& object : *this->player_objects_)
    {
        // Index by the player's own pad slot, not by position in this loop.
        // player_inputs is one entry per pad slot; a running counter only
        // happened to agree while every pad stayed connected.
        const int player_index = object->player_num();

        if (player_index >= 0 &&
            static_cast<size_t>(player_index) < player_inputs.size())
        {
            object->set_player_input(player_inputs[player_index]);
        }
        else
        {
            object->set_player_input(PlayerInputData());
        }

`game/objects/player_input.h:13-15`:

    // XInput slots. An index into the vector returned by
    // update_and_get_player_inputs() is a pad slot, never an ordinal.
    constexpr int MAX_PAD_COUNT = 4;

`game/objects/player_input.cpp:136-144` writes the neutral value for an absent pad, and
`:112` writes `ConnectionState::connected` for a present one. `grep -rn "connection"`
across `engine/ game/ samples/` finds it assigned in two files and read in none.

**Why it matters:** Two reachable outcomes in a live match. (1) Player 2's pad is
unplugged: their character receives `PlayerInputData()` forever — it stands still,
survives, and continues to count toward the level's paint area and its end condition —
and nothing on screen says why. (2) The same pad is replugged and Windows assigns it slot
0 (the common case when slot 0 is free): its owner now drives Player 1's character while
Player 1's pad, if it moved to slot 1, drives Player 2. This is not the same finding as
"`ConnectionState` has no engine mechanism"; that one says the enum is dead. This one says
what the deadness costs at runtime, and that the fixed slot↔player binding is the
mechanism that makes it cost that.

**Remedy:** Have the engine surface a per-slot connect/disconnect edge (the enum already
exists), and give the level a defined response — pause and prompt "Player 2, reconnect
your controller" — rather than treating an absent pad as a player who chose to stand still.

#### Give the sample the manifest and icon resource the engine unconditionally asks for

- **File:** `samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:17-25`, `engine/app/application.cpp:85-89`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/The public face ("A minimal sample game... the standing answer to 'how do I start a project on this engine'")

**What:** `Application::create_window` unconditionally loads a resource named `IDI_ICON`
and the game supplies one through `resource.rc` plus an OS-compatibility
`settings.manifest`; the sample — the file a stranger copies to start a project — ships
neither, and nothing in it says they are needed.

**Evidence:**

`engine/app/application.cpp:85-89`:

    window_class.hIcon = LoadIconW(instance, L"IDI_ICON");
    window_class.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW);
    window_class.hbrBackground = reinterpret_cast<HBRUSH>(COLOR_WINDOW + 1);
    window_class.lpszClassName = this->options_.window_class_name.c_str();
    window_class.hIconSm = LoadIconW(instance, L"IDI_ICON");

`game/CMakeLists.txt:61-62` supplies both:

        resource.rc
        settings.manifest

`samples/minimal/CMakeLists.txt:17-20`, the whole source list:

    add_executable(ArtAttackSample WIN32
        main.cpp
        states/hello_state.cpp
    )

`git ls-files samples/` confirms there is no `.rc` and no `.manifest` under `samples/`.

**Why it matters:** The sample builds and runs, so this is not a failure — it is a silent
divergence in exactly the file that exists to be copied. `LoadIconW` returns null and the
sample gets the default application icon; more consequentially, with no application
manifest the sample's process declares no `supportedOS`, so Windows applies legacy
compatibility behaviour that the game, which does ship one, does not get. A stranger who
starts from `samples/minimal` inherits both differences and has nothing to read that
explains them.

**Remedy:** Either add a minimal `.rc` and `.manifest` to the sample (the honest template),
or move the icon to an `ApplicationOptions` field so `create_window` stops naming a
resource the engine cannot guarantee.

#### Delete `MainMenuData`'s callerless one-argument constructor

- **File:** `game/states/main_menu_data.cpp:5-9`, `game/states/main_menu_data.h:10,19-20`, `game/states/game_states.cpp:5-10,65-71`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `MainMenuData` has a constructor that leaves both of its borrowed pointers null
and no caller uses it as intended: `GameMenu` calls it and then patches the object into
validity with three public setters a frame's worth of construction later.

**Evidence:**

`game/states/main_menu_data.cpp:5-9`:

    MainMenuData::MainMenuData(GameData* game_data) :
        MenuData(game_data)
    {

    }

`game/states/main_menu_data.h:19-20`:

    MenuLevelSettings* menu_level_settings_ = nullptr;
    bool* is_ready_to_load_level_ = nullptr;

`game/states/game_states.cpp:5-10` then `:65-71`:

    GameMenu::GameMenu(GameData* game_data) :
        game_data_(game_data),
        menu_data_(std::make_unique<MainMenuData>(game_data))
    ...
    void GameMenu::set_main_menu_data_ptrs()
    {
        this->menu_data_->set_level_settings(this->menu_level_settings_.get());
        this->menu_data_->set_input(this->menu_input_.get());
        this->menu_data_->set_is_ready_to_load_level(
            this->is_ready_to_load_level_.get());
    }

**Why it matters:** No live null dereference exists — `GameMenu::init()` always calls

`GameMenu::order_level_creation` dereferences `level_settings()` only afterwards. What
exists is the same two-phase-construction shape already filed against `GameData`,
re-instantiated in `MenuData` and `MainMenuData`: a type whose invariant is "these three
are never null", a constructor that builds it invalid, and public setters that let anyone

**Remedy:** Delete the one-argument constructors on `MenuData` and `MainMenuData` and the

#### Replace the vendored `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` templates with rules for this project

- **File:** `.gitignore:1-370`, `.gitattributes:1-63`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** Both files that decide what a clone receives are unmodified Visual Studio
C#/.NET templates — Xamarin, BizTalk, NuGet, Paket, F#, Azure — with six project-specific
lines bolted onto the end of one and every rule in the other commented out.

**Evidence:**

`.gitignore:365-370`, the entire project-specific content of a 370-line file:

    # Audio files
    *.wav
    *.xwb
    *.mp3
    # CMake out-of-source build tree
    out/

`.gitattributes:4` is the only uncommented line in 63:

    * text=auto

Everything else in `.gitattributes` is a commented-out rule for `*.csproj`, `*.vbproj`,
`*.wixproj`, `*.jpg`, `*.doc` and `*.pdf`.

`git status --ignored -- game` shows what those four audio globs currently exclude: 30+
`.wav` sources plus `game/content/sounds/sound_bank_1.xwb`, the file the shipped manifest
names.

**Why it matters:** The blanket `*.wav`/`*.xwb` globs — not a path rule, not scoped to a
source directory — are why a fresh clone cannot start the game, which is filed elsewhere;
what is not filed is that they were written as an afterthought on a file that has never
been read for this project. The 350 lines above them describe a toolchain that is not in
use, and `.gitattributes` leaves `.dds`, `.spritefont`, `.xcf`, `.ico` and three committed
`.exe` tools to git's content heuristic rather than declaring them binary. Both files are
part of the front door a stranger meets before any header.

**Remedy:** Cut `.gitignore` to the handful of patterns this repository needs (`out/`,
`.vs/`, and a *path*-scoped audio rule with an exception for the shipped wave bank), and
either declare the binary content types in `.gitattributes` or delete the file.

<a id="g-gap-structure"></a>

## gap-structure — what only the whole path shows

*Group `gap-structure` · 6 findings (1 high, 3 medium, 2 low) · source `review2/verified/gap-structure.md`, verified report.*

I traced four slices end to end and, where the slice ran through content, I ran the shipped
JSON through the code's own arithmetic rather than reasoning about it. Slice 1 (keypress →
projectile → paint → score) and slice 3 (device lost → restored frame) came back clean:
every candidate I opened — the pad-slot/ordinal split, the asymmetric `is_colliding`
double-dispatch, `PaintTile::on_collision`'s throw, `Registry`'s slot-preserving reload,
the `ComPtr` storage specialisation, `SpriteSheet::set_texture` re-seating, the sprite-batch
recreation order — is either correct or already filed, and the whole content graph is
internally consistent (every `frame_name`, `icon_frame`, font and sound name in every level
file and every C++ constant resolves against `sprite_sheet_1.json`, `manifest.json` and
`sound_bank_1.json`; I checked all of them mechanically). What did not come back clean is
slice 2 (level JSON → drawn frame) and slice 4 (gameplay → pause/results → back), and the
defects there are all of one kind: **a quantity crosses a module boundary and the two sides
hold different, unwritten beliefs about what it means.** The end-of-match overview camera is
handed a rectangle whose height the engine never reads and whose width no one ever compared
to the level, so the shot that decides the match frames 64% of the arena. Three coordinate
spaces meet in one function — world-plus-camera, screen-space-via-`Camera(Viewport)`, and
raw viewport-local — and nothing in the tree names any of them; one of the three is
delivered by an *implicit* conversion. Pausing stops the simulation and nothing else,
because "pause" is a game-state word and the engine's `pause_effect`/`resume_effect` pair —
written for exactly this — has never had a caller. What surprised me most was how often the
mechanism turned out to be right and the *number* wrong: the split-screen screen-space
overlay convention genuinely does reassemble a glyph across four viewports, and I killed my
own best-looking finding by parsing `gill_sans_mt_bold_144.spritefont` and measuring the
digit instead of guessing at it.

### Themes

- Every defect I found is a value crossing a seam with two different meanings on the two
  sides, and in each case both sides read correctly on their own — which is precisely why
  eighty-four module reviews did not produce them.
- Content is validated for *presence* everywhere and for *sense* nowhere: the three level
  files parse, resolve and load perfectly and still describe a camera that cannot see the
  level, because nothing relates one field of the file to another or to the geometry beside it.
- Where the engine grew a mechanism during the recent passes, the game did not pick it up:
  `TextObject::measured_size_` exists and the one hand-guessed text size in the game still
  guesses; `SoundBank::pause_effect` exists and the pause path still does not pause.
- Culling is a property of one draw path, not of the renderer: `draw_player_view_level` culls
  on `bounds()` and `draw_zoom_out_level_component` twenty lines below does not, and the
  uncullled one is the path that runs for the whole post-match menu flow.
- The half-dozen `LevelEndInfo` accessors nobody calls are the shape the group reviews kept
  finding in MattMath, reproduced in game code: a score API where the used half is guarded
  against division by zero and the unused half is not.
- Running the shipped data through the shipped arithmetic is cheap and settles questions that
  cannot be settled by reading either one: it produced two of these six findings and disproved
  three more I would otherwise have filed.

#### The end-of-match overview never shows the half of the level team B painted

- **File:** `game/content/levels/turbulence.json:74-80` (identical in `king_of_the_hill.json`, `close_quarters.json`), `game/objects/level.cpp:151-160`, `engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4149-4162`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T6 (loud failure over graceful degradation), T7 (data over code)

**What:** the zoom-out camera that ends every match is built from `zoom_out_finish_bounds`,
whose width is 3840 in all three shipped levels, while the arena is 6000 wide — so the shot
that shows who won frames the left two-thirds of the level and cuts off all four of team B's
spawns.

**Evidence:**

`game/content/levels/turbulence.json:74-80`:

        "zoom_out_finish_bounds":
        {
            "x": 0.0,
            "y": 4000.0,
            "width": 3840.0,
            "height": 2160.0
        }

`game/objects/level.cpp:155-160`:

        Camera finish_camera = Camera::calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle(
            this->zoom_out_finish_bounds_,
            RectangleF(Vector2F::ZERO, this->resolution_manager_->resolution_vec()));

        this->zoom_out_camera_ = Camera::calculate_intermediate_camera(
            start_camera, finish_camera, this->zoom_out_camera_ratio());

`engine/math/matt_math.cpp:4158-4160`:

        return Camera(view_rectangle.x - world_rectangle.x,
            view_rectangle.y - world_rectangle.y,
            world_rectangle.width / view_rectangle.width);

**Why it matters:** the camera that results is `translation = (0, 4000)`, `scale =
resolution.x / 3840`. `Camera::calculate_view_position` maps world to screen as
`(p - translation) * scale`, so the visible world rectangle is exactly
`x ∈ [0, 3840]`, `y ∈ [4000, 4000 + 2160]` at any 16:9 resolution — the height field in the
file is never read, so the vertical extent is derived from the width and the aspect. The
arena is `x ∈ [-100, 6100]` (the two wall structures at `x = -100` and `x = 6000`, each 7000
tall) with team B's four spawns at `x ∈ [5752, 5938]` and team A's at `x ∈ [10, 196]`. So at
the moment the match ends, the camera pans out to a view that contains every team A spawn and
no team B spawn. Measuring the paintable structures against that rectangle: `close_quarters`
has 82% of its paintable area on screen, `king_of_the_hill` 13%, `turbulence` 14%, and each of
the latter two has one paintable structure entirely off screen (`turbulence`'s at
`x ∈ [4060, 4660]`, off the right edge). `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` draws every
object unconditionally, so the missing third is drawn and then clipped — there is no error, no
warning and nothing in the file that could have been checked. `close_quarters` differs only
because its geometry happens to sit further left; all three files carry the same
`zoom_out_start_bounds`/`zoom_out_finish_bounds` block, so the number was copied twice without
being re-derived. Note that `math-impl-c` already filed the height-ignoring API as a defect in
`calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle`; this is its shipped consequence, which is separate —
fixing the API alone leaves the three files wrong, and fixing the three files alone leaves the
next author's `height` silently discarded.

**Remedy:** derive the zoom-out bounds from the level's own extents (or validate at load that
they contain `camera_bounds`), and make `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle` fit both axes so
the rectangle in the file means the rectangle on screen.

#### Three viewport coordinate conventions meet in one function and none of them is named

- **File:** `game/objects/level.cpp:561-587`, `game/states/menu_page.cpp:104-118`, `engine/math/matt_math.h:1029`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness), PHILOSOPHY/The public face

**What:** within twenty lines of `draw_player_view_level`, drawables are positioned in three
different spaces — world-with-camera, full-screen-space corrected by a `Camera` built from the
viewport, and raw viewport-local — and no header, comment or type distinguishes them; the
middle one arrives through an implicit `Viewport` → `Camera` conversion.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.cpp:543-587`, in order, in one function:

        // world space, culled against the camera's view rectangle
        for (auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
        {
            if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))
            {
                object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);
            }
        }
        ...
        // full-screen space: the camera's only job is to subtract the viewport origin
        const Camera viewport_camera = Camera(player_vp);
        for (auto& divider : *this->viewport_dividers_)
        {
            divider->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), viewport_camera);
        }
        ...
        // viewport-local: laid out against the viewport's own size, no camera at all
        Vector2F viewport_size = player_vp.size();
        this->interface_gameplay_->draw_gameplay_interface(
            sprite_batches->at(i),
            viewport_size,
            ...

and `game/states/menu_page.cpp:110-115`, where the second convention is invoked without the
word `Camera` appearing at all:

            this->viewport_manager()->apply_player_viewport(
                static_cast<int>(i), deferred_context, sprite_batch);

            sprite_batch->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, sampler_state);

            widget->draw(sprite_batch, viewports[i]);

`engine/math/matt_math.h:1029` is what makes that last line compile:

        Camera(const mattmath::Viewport& viewport, float scale = 1.0f);

**Why it matters:** the convention is load-bearing and correct — `SpriteBatch::SetViewport`
makes sprite coordinates viewport-local, so a full-screen-space element drawn once per view
with the viewport origin subtracted reassembles across the split screen, which is exactly why
the two-player divider joins up and why the pause-menu box spans all four quadrants. But
nothing states it. `ViewportManager::player_viewport` returns a `Viewport` with no
documentation of what its origin means to a drawable; `IGameObject::draw`'s fifteen lines of
contract (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:35-42`) say a camera is always passed and say nothing
about which space the position is in; and `widget->draw(sprite_batch, viewports[i])` reads as
"draw into this viewport" when it means "translate by this viewport's origin". A stranger
adding a HUD element has to choose between two conventions used four lines apart in the same
function, and a wrong guess produces an element that is silently mispositioned only in
split-screen — the configuration hardest to notice in a single-player test. This is also the
one call site in the tree where the implicit `Viewport` → `Camera` conversion actually fires,
which is the concrete instance behind `sweep-compile-time-guardrails`' general complaint.

**Remedy:** make the space explicit in the type or the name — a `Camera::for_viewport(vp)`
named constructor with `explicit` on the converting one, and a sentence on
`player_viewport()` and on `IGameObject::draw` saying which space a position is in.

#### Pausing pauses the simulation and nothing else; the engine's pause API has never had a caller

- **File:** `game/states/game_states.cpp:149-226`, `game/objects/weapon.cpp:242-260`, `engine/audio/sound_bank.h:54-55`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T1 (mechanism over policy)

**What:** entering the pause menu stops calling `Level::update`, which is the only thing that
ever tells a weapon's looping voice to stop, so the level music and any weapon that was firing
at that instant play on for the whole pause — and `SoundBank::pause_effect` /
`resume_effect`, the pair written for this, have zero callers anywhere.

**Evidence:**

`game/states/game_states.cpp:200-203` — the pause branch drives only the menu:

        case GameLevelState::pause_menu:
        {
            this->pause_menu_->update();

`game/objects/weapon.cpp:242-259` — the loop is started and stopped only from the update path:

        void Weapon::handle_shoot_sound(bool shooting_this_update, bool holding_shoot)
        {
            ...
            if (holding_shoot || shooting_this_update)
            {
                this->sound_bank_->play_effect(
                    this->loop_sound_,
                    true,
                    this->details_.shoot_sound_volume);
            }
            else
            {
                this->sound_bank_->stop_effect(this->loop_sound_, true);
            }
        }

`engine/audio/sound_bank.h:54-55`, and the whole of their reach:

        void pause_effect(EffectHandle effect) const;
        void resume_effect(EffectHandle effect) const;

`grep -rn "pause_effect\|resume_effect"` over `engine/`, `game/`, `samples/` returns six
lines: the two declarations, the two definitions in `sound_bank.cpp:66-73`, and the two
forwarding wrappers in `sound_bank_object.cpp:46-53`. Nothing calls them.

**Why it matters:** every pause in the shipped game is audibly wrong. The level's music
(`level.cpp:74`, `play_effect(music_, true, music_volume_)`) keeps playing at full volume under
the pause menu's own UI sounds, and a player who pauses mid-burst leaves a looping weapon
voice running until the level resumes — the voice is per `(weapon, team, player_num)`, so it
is a single sustained tone for the duration. The same freeze is why `Application::on_suspending`
(minimise) does the right thing and pausing does not: the engine has one audio suspend at the
platform edge and one per-voice pause in `SoundBank`, and the game state that most obviously
needs the second uses neither. T1 says the engine supplies *how* — it does, twice — and the
game decides *what*; the game has not decided.

**Remedy:** give `Level` a `pause()`/`resume()` that walks its music handle and its players'
weapon handles through `pause_effect`/`resume_effect`, and call them from the two
`GameLevelState` transitions in `game_states.cpp`.

- **Category:** performance

**What:** `draw_zoom_out_level_component` draws every object in the level with no `bounds()`
test, on the calling thread, and `GameLevel::draw` keeps calling it every frame throughout the
results and end-menu states — so the full scene is re-recorded behind an opaque menu box for

`game/objects/level.cpp:652-661` — the same loops as `draw_player_view_level`, minus the

        // draw collision objects
        for (const auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
        {
            object->draw(sprite_batch, camera);

against `game/objects/level.cpp:543-549`, the culled path:

        for (auto& object : *this->collision_objects_)
        {
            if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))
            {
                object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);

and `game/states/game_states.cpp:314-326`, which gates only the first two frames:

        if (this->state_ == GameLevelState::first_update ||
            this->state_ == GameLevelState::second_update)
        {
            return;
        }
        ...
        this->level_->draw(this->data()->device_resources()->deferred_contexts(),

**Why it matters:** `Level::draw` routes `zoom_out`, `overview` *and* `finished` to this path
(`level.cpp:383-390`), and `GameLevelState::results` and `end_menu` never stop calling

their whole tile vector: 5230 `PaintTile::draw` calls per frame (4116 for
`king_of_the_hill`, 1898 for `close_quarters`), single-threaded, entirely behind the results
box. The two frames that *are* skipped are skipped by an ad-hoc enum; the thousands that are
wasted are not skipped at all. The philosophy makes culling the scene's job and names it as
the reason `bounds()` replaced `is_visible_in_viewport`; this path is the one that never got
the replacement's benefit.

**Remedy:** cull this path against the zoom-out camera's view rectangle like the per-player
path does, and stop drawing the level once a full-screen menu owns the frame.

#### The countdown is centred against a guessed text size, so it sits off-centre and jumps on "GO!"

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:40-41`, `game/objects/level.cpp:91-105`, `engine/render/text_object.cpp:112-119`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T4 (clarity over cleverness)

**What:** the start countdown is positioned by subtracting a hardcoded 400 × 600 "text box"
from the screen centre, while the actual rendered text is 212 × 445 for a digit and 752 × 445
for `"GO!"` — so the countdown is never centred and shifts 270 px right when it changes to
`"GO!"`; `TextObject` has measured the real size since the handle pass and nothing reads it.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level.h:40-41`:

        constexpr float COUNTDOWN_TEXT_WIDTH = 400.0f;
        constexpr float COUNTDOWN_TEXT_HEIGHT = 600.0f;

`game/objects/level.cpp:91-94`:

            Vector2F resolution = this->resolution_manager_->resolution_vec();
            Vector2F position = resolution / 2.0f;
            position = position - Vector2F(COUNTDOWN_TEXT_WIDTH / 2.0f,
                                COUNTDOWN_TEXT_HEIGHT / 2.0f);

`engine/render/text_object.cpp:112-119`, the measurement that already exists:

        void TextObject::remeasure()
        {
            const SpriteFont* sprite_font =
                this->render_resources()->sprite_font(this->font_);
            const XMVECTOR size = sprite_font->MeasureString(this->text_.c_str());
            this->measured_size_ =
                Vector2F(XMVectorGetX(size), XMVectorGetY(size));
        }

Parsing `game/content/fonts/gill_sans_mt_bold_144.spritefont` (DXTKfont, 95 glyphs) gives a
line spacing of 222.66 and per-glyph advances that make `MeasureString("3")` ≈ 106 × 223 and
`MeasureString("GO!")` ≈ 376 × 223; `COUNTDOWN_SCALE` is 2.0 (`level.h:38`), so the drawn text
is 212 × 445 and 752 × 445 respectively. `TextObject::draw` places `position` as the top-left
(`origin` is `Vector2F::ZERO`), so at 1280×720 a digit occupies x ∈ [440, 652] against a screen
centre of 640, and `"GO!"` occupies x ∈ [440, 1192].

**Why it matters:** a digit is drawn 94 px left of centre and `"GO!"` 176 px right of it, so the
countdown visibly jumps sideways on its final beat, every match, at every resolution (the
offset is absolute because the glyph size does not scale with the window). The two constants
are a guess at a quantity the engine now computes exactly — and the reason the game guesses is
worth noting: `TextObject::text_bounds()` is non-virtual and, as `render-text` filed, wrong for
`TextDropShadow`, which is the type `countdown_text_` actually is. So the mechanism exists, is
one call away, and is not yet trustworthy for the caller that needs it.

**Remedy:** position the countdown from `text_bounds()` after each `set_text`, and fix
`text_bounds()` for `TextDropShadow` first so the answer is right for the type that asks.

---

#### Six of `LevelEndInfo`'s fourteen accessors have no caller, and the unused half divides by zero

- **File:** `game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:80-128`
- **Severity:** low
- **Category:** correctness
- **Tenet:** T2 (correctness over speed)

**What:** `winning_score`, `losing_score`, `winning_ratio`, `losing_ratio`,
`winning_percentage` and `losing_percentage` are called from nowhere, and unlike the two
accessors that *are* used they carry no zero guard — `winning_ratio()` divides by
`losing_score()`, which is `0.0f` in the ordinary case where one team painted nothing.

**Evidence:**

`game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:114-121`:

        float LevelEndInfo::winning_ratio() const
        {
            return this->winning_score() / this->losing_score();
        }
        float LevelEndInfo::losing_ratio() const
        {
            return this->losing_score() / this->winning_score();
        }

against the two that are used, `game/objects/level_end_info.cpp:19-26`:

        float LevelEndInfo::team_a_ratio() const
        {
            if (this->team_a_area == 0.0f && this->team_b_area == 0.0f)
            {
                return 0.5f;
            }
            return this->team_a_area / (this->team_a_area + this->team_b_area);
        }

`grep -rn "winning_ratio\|losing_ratio\|winning_percentage\|losing_percentage\|winning_score\|losing_score" game/` outside `level_end_info.*` returns nothing; the results screen uses
`team_a_ratio`/`team_b_ratio` (`results_menu.cpp:231, 244`) and the two percentage strings
(`results_menu.cpp:134, 145`).

**Why it matters:** this is the score, the one number the match produces, and half its API is
dead surface written to a lower standard than the half that ships — exactly the pattern the
MattMath reviews found (the dead half is the broken half), reproduced in game code that
post-dates it. `losing_score()` returns `team_b_area` whenever team A leads, and a shut-out is
a completely ordinary result of a short or one-sided match, so the first caller of
`winning_ratio()` gets `inf` and `winning_percentage()` gets `inf`, with `losing_percentage()`
then returning `-inf`. There is no test on any of it (`tests/` links only MattMath).

**Remedy:** delete the six, or guard them the way `team_a_ratio` is guarded and pin them with
a test in the same commit.

<a id="g-gap-roadmap"></a>

## gap-roadmap — the order of operations

*Group `gap-roadmap` · 13 findings (1 critical, 4 high, 6 medium, 2 low) · source `review2/verified/gap-roadmap.md`, verified report.*

I read the three design documents, the triage headline and its fifty duplicate clusters, the
verified reports for `game-level`, `core-objects`, `render-primitives` and `game-states-flow`,
and the raw sweeps for mechanism-vs-policy, module-graph and testability. Then I opened the
pivot files myself and checked every line I lean on below: `engine/core/i_game_object.h`,
`state.h`, `state_context.cpp`, `engine/CMakeLists.txt` and the three `tests/*/CMakeLists.txt`,
`engine/math/matt_math.h`, `engine/ui/widget.h`, `engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp`,
`engine/collision/partitioner.cpp`, `game/objects/level.{h,cpp}`,
`game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h`, `game/objects/interface_gameplay.{h,cpp}`,
`game/states/game_states.cpp` and `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp`, plus DirectXTK's
`Src/SpriteFont.cpp` in the build tree. The shape of the problem is not that the findings
disagree about what to do — they are unanimous — it is that they are all written as if they
were independent, and about a third of them are not. Two facts decide the whole order. First,
every method the `game-level` report lists as "becomes engine `Scene`" carries
`std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>*`, `std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>*` and
`std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>*` in its own signature (`game/objects/level.h:164-183`), so
extracting `Scene` before the renderer seam writes the backend into `engine/core/scene.h` and
guarantees the largest new engine file gets written twice. Second, the seam and the `Scene` view
list are one design and not two: the parallelism axis is *views*
(`engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15`), the view count/viewport/camera today all come off
`Player` (`level.cpp:401,521-529`), and the D3D11 unit of a view — a deferred context, a sprite
batch, a command list — is exactly what the seam has to own. What surprised me is how much is
genuinely unblocked and simply unwritten: `ViewportManager`, `ResolutionManager`, `CameraTools`,
`Partitioner`, `StateContext` and all of widget *focus and navigation* need no renderer and no
device, and none of them has a test or an engine home.

### Themes

- The seam is not merely the highest-value item, it is a hard prerequisite: three of the four
  outstanding structural findings (#13, #18, and both halves of "no headless tests") have their
  fix site inside it, and doing any of them first produces code the seam deletes.
- The interface-signature edits are one pass, not four: the `I` prefix, `SpriteBatch*` →
  `Renderer&`, `SpriteEffects` → an engine enum, and `State::update(float dt)` /
  `State::draw(Renderer&) const` all rewrite the same declarations in the same files, and each
  one done separately is a second sweep of 20 overrides across 13 headers plus 45 state classes.
- A large block of work is genuinely parallel and nobody has said so: the state stack, widget
  focus/navigation, and the input module touch files the seam and `Scene` never open, and the
  state stack alone closes two bugs that are live in the shipped game.
- The refactor has no regression net and the stated reason for that is false: linking
  `ArtAttackEngine` from a test pulls only the objects whose symbols are referenced, so the
  comment at `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-5` is describing a cost a static library does not
  impose.
- Roughly a dozen reported findings are scheduled to delete themselves, and fixing them directly
  is the cheapest way to waste a week — including three whose *remedies as written* are throwaway.
- Both open questions are already answered by the evidence: the seam's requirements are fully
  determined by six findings taken together, and every candidate for an event system in 84
  reports resolves to a returned value, a contact manifest, or the state stack.

### The order of operations

Sizes are rough: **S** ≈ a day, **M** ≈ a few days, **L** ≈ a week or more. Cluster numbers are
the indices in `meta/triage.md`.

| # | Item | Files | Size | Resolves |

#### Cut the renderer seam before extracting `Scene` — every method that becomes `Scene` carries D3D11 in its own signature

- **File:** `game/objects/level.h:164-183`
- **Severity:** critical
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1 (also PHILOSOPHY/Structural types, ARCHITECTURE/Modules)

**What:** All five private draw methods the `game-level` report assigns to the engine's future
`Scene` take three raw pointers to vectors of D3D11/DirectXTK objects, so extracting `Scene`
before the renderer seam exists writes `ID3D11DeviceContext`, `ID3D11CommandList` and
`DirectX::SpriteBatch` into `engine/core/scene.h` and guarantees the file is written twice.

**Evidence:**

    // game/objects/level.h:164-183 — the whole set, verbatim
    	void draw_active_level(std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
    		std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
    		std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

    	void draw_zoom_out_level(std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
    		std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
    		std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

    	float zoom_out_camera_ratio() const;

    	void stop_player_sounds() const;

    	void draw_player_view_level(int start, int end,
    		std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
    		std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
    		std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

    	void draw_zoom_out_level_component(std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* deferred_contexts,
    		std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>* command_lists,
    		std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>* sprite_batches) const;

The cull, which is the one part of that body that is unambiguously `Scene`'s, is interleaved with
the backend three lines away — `game/objects/level.cpp:531-540`:

    		sprite_batches->at(i)->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, this->sampler_state_);

    		// draw non-collision objects
    		for (auto& object : *this->non_collision_objects_)
    		{
    			if (object->bounds().intersects(camera_view))
    			{
    				object->draw(sprite_batches->at(i), camera);

**Why it matters:** The two claims that decide this order are checkable. (1) The engine's stated
module rule gives `core` exactly one dependency; today the breach is one include
(`engine/core/i_game_object.h:4`, `#include <SpriteBatch.h>`). A `Scene` extracted now makes it
three types in a parameter list, one of them an *output* parameter whose caller must pre-size the
vector, pre-fill it with `nullptr` and `Release` every non-null entry — three obligations stated
nowhere. That is strictly worse than the hole it would sit next to, in the file a stranger reads
second. (2) The seam and `Scene`'s view list are the same design, not two: the parallelism axis is
views (`engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15`), and `Scene` cannot be built at all until it owns an
explicit view list because the number of render tasks (`level.cpp:401`), each view's viewport
(`level.cpp:523`) and each view's camera (`level.cpp:526`) are all read off `Player`. Whoever
designs the view list is designing the seam's unit of work. Doing them separately means designing
the same thing twice and reconciling the two answers.

**Remedy:** Design the per-view draw target and `Scene`'s view list as one interface, implement
the seam first so `Scene`'s draw path can be written in engine vocabulary, and only then move the
eleven members and nine methods out of `Level`.
