#### Link `ArtAttackEngine` from the tests before the refactor, not after — the stated reason not to is false

- **File:** `tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-11`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** testing
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Targets and layout ("Tests link libraries, never `#include` implementation files")

**What:** The one change that would give the seam, `Scene` and the state stack any automated
regression net at all is three lines in three build files, and it is being avoided for a cost a
static library does not impose.

**Evidence:**

    # tests/assets/CMakeLists.txt:3-11
    # The manifest loader reads a file and parses JSON, and that is all it does -
    # no device, no DirectXTK - so this target compiles the two translation units
    # directly rather than linking the engine and everything the engine drags in.
    add_executable(AssetsTests
        asset_manifest_loader_tests.cpp
        test_main.cpp
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.cpp"
        "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/assets/json_loader.cpp"
    )

The two translation units are self-contained — `asset_manifest_loader.cpp:1-4` and
`json_loader.cpp:1-8` between them include only their own headers, `<rapidjson/...>` and the
standard library:

    #include "engine/assets/asset_manifest_loader.h"
    #include "engine/assets/json_loader.h"
    #include <stdexcept>
    #include <string>

so linking `ArtAttackEngine` (`engine/CMakeLists.txt:12`, `add_library(... STATIC ...)`) pulls
`asset_manifest_loader.obj` and `json_loader.obj` and stops. What actually arrives beyond that is
`Microsoft::DirectXTK`'s import library on the *link line*, transitively via
`engine/CMakeLists.txt:50-53` — a name for the linker, not thirty translation units of object code.

**Why it matters:** P1 is a rewrite of every draw signature in the engine, P2 moves eleven members
and nine methods out of a 780-line class, P3 rewrites `game/states/`. Today the total automated
coverage of `ArtAttackEngine` is zero translation units, and `ctest` will stay green through any
of them. This is the cheapest possible thing to do first and the only one that makes the next
three items falsifiable. It is also the item most likely to be deferred, because it looks like
tidying rather than enablement. Note the second-order effect: once `AssetsTests` links the
library, the `${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/engine/...` entries in a test's source list stop being a pattern
anyone copies for `tests/render/` and `tests/collision/`.

**Remedy:** Add `ArtAttackEngine` to `target_link_libraries` in `tests/assets` and `tests/core`
and delete the copied source entries and the include directory they needed.

#### Land the deferred `transition_to` alone and first — P3 rewrites all ten sites that are currently correct by luck

- **File:** `engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** lifetime
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Services and lifetimes

**What:** `transition_to` destroys the state whose `update()` is on the stack, and the ten call
sites that do this are safe only because none of them touches a member afterwards — which is
exactly the property a state-stack rewrite of `game/states/` will be moving around.

**Evidence:**

    // engine/core/state_context.cpp:21-26 — the whole function
    	void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
    	{
    		this->state_ = std::move(state);
    		this->state_->set_context(this);
    		this->state_->init();
    	}

    // engine/core/state_context.h has no comment on any of its 19 lines

The hazard is invisible from the call site — `game/states/game_states.cpp:131-137` shows the
shape a rewrite will be editing, one function away from a `transition_to`:

    void GameLevel::build_and_enter_level()
    {
        this->data()->viewport_manager()->
            set_layout(this->settings_.screen_layout());

        this->level_ = this->level_builder_->build_level(this->settings_);
    }

**Why it matters:** The verified reports agree the ten sites are latent, not live, and both graded
it medium on that basis. That grading is right for the code as it stands and wrong for the code as
it is about to be. P3 deletes `GameLevelState`, three nested `StateContext`s and three
`unique_ptr<enum>` out-parameters, which means rewriting every branch that currently ends in a
`transition_to`; the person doing that will be moving statements across a call whose danger is
recorded nowhere. The fix is about five lines — park the incoming state in a `pending_` member and
swap it in inside `StateContext::update()` after `state_->update()` returns — and it converts a
property of forty-two call sites into a property of one function. It is also the natural first
test in `tests/core/`, which the previous item has just made linkable.

**Remedy:** Make the transition a request applied after `update()` returns, and pin the ordering
(`set_context` then `init()`, outgoing destroyed before incoming initialised) with the first
`StateContext` test.

#### The seam's specification is already fully determined — six requirements, and `DeviceResources` is far narrower than it looks

- **File:** `engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15,41-42`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** api
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/Simulation and rendering

**What:** The first of the author's two open questions can be closed from the evidence already
collected: six separate findings each constrain the seam in a way that is not obvious from
PHILOSOPHY's one-line `draw_sprite(...)` sketch, and a seam that misses any of them has to be cut
twice.

**Evidence:** The six, each with its source line.

*(1) The unit is a view, not an object.* `engine/core/i_game_object.h:10-15`:

    	// draw() is const, and that is the whole contract that makes parallel
    	// rendering sound. The render workers do not own disjoint slices of the
    	// object list - the parallelism axis is *views*, so every worker enters
    	// draw() on the SAME object at the same time.

*(2) Depth must be per draw.* `engine/render/texture_object.cpp:110` reads it off the shared
object inside the one function built so callers could pass everything as locals — and the same
sprite drawn into two viewports at different sort depths cannot be expressed at all:

    		this->layer_depth());     // a per-draw member, read from the object

*(3) Sampler state must be inside the seam.* `game/objects/level.cpp:531`:

    		sprite_batches->at(i)->Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, this->sampler_state_);

*(4) Command-list lifetime must be RAII and inside the seam.* `game/objects/level.cpp:606-610`:

    		HRESULT hr = deferred_contexts->at(i)->FinishCommandList(TRUE, &command_lists->at(i));
    		if (FAILED(hr))
    		{
    			throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list");
    		}

*(5) Font metrics must be an engine type.* `engine/render/text_object.cpp:112-118` — the
*constructor* measures, so text is unconstructible headlessly, not merely undrawable:

    	void TextObject::remeasure()
    	{
    		const SpriteFont* sprite_font =
    			this->render_resources()->sprite_font(this->font_);
    		const XMVECTOR size = sprite_font->MeasureString(this->text_.c_str());

*(6) The text entry point must be wide.* `game/objects/interface_gameplay.cpp:156-161` and
DirectXTK `Src/SpriteFont.cpp:365-391`, where the `const char*` overload writes and may
reallocate a buffer owned by the shared font:

    	const wchar_t* SpriteFont::Impl::ConvertUTF8(_In_z_ const char *text) noexcept(false)
    	{
    	    if (!utfBuffer)
    	    {
    	        utfBufferSize = 1024;
    	        utfBuffer.reset(new wchar_t[1024]);

**Why it matters:** Each of these is reported somewhere as its own defect; together they are a
specification, and none of them is derivable from "replace `SpriteBatch*` with `Renderer&`". The
countervailing fact, which makes the job smaller than it reads: the `render-device` group found
that twelve of `DeviceResources`' seventeen graphics accessors have no caller anywhere, and
`ViewportManager` is already split down the middle — `camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect`
(`viewport_manager.cpp:27-45`) is pure arithmetic that survives untouched, while
`apply_player_viewport` (`:43-58`) is three lines of `RSSetViewports`/`SetViewport` that are
purely backend. The seam is a narrow cut through wide-looking classes.

**Remedy:** Write the six constraints down as the interface's contract before the first line of
`engine/render/d3d11/` is written, and let `samples/minimal/states/hello_state.cpp` containing no
`ID3D11*` identifier be the acceptance test.

#### The state stack is parallel with `Scene`, closes two live bugs, and should not queue behind it

- **File:** `game/states/game_states.cpp:131-137`
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T1; ARCHITECTURE/`app` ("owns the state stack")

**What:** P2 (`Scene` out of `Level`) and P3 (a real `StateContext` stack) share no files and can
run concurrently once the seam lands, and P3 is the smaller of the two while fixing two defects
that are reproducible in the shipped game today.

**Evidence:** The file sets are disjoint. P2 opens `game/objects/level.{h,cpp}`,
`level_builder.*` and the new `engine/core/scene.*`; P3 opens `engine/core/state_context.*` and
`game/states/*`. The single point of contact is `GameLevel::draw()` calling `level_->draw(...)`.

The two live bugs P3 closes, both verified in `game-states-flow`. `game/states/game_states.cpp:131-137`

so every exit from a level leaves split-screen applied and the main menu is then drawn once per

            if (pause_menu_player != -1)

**Why it matters:** The obvious reading of "the next steps are the split and a `Scene`" puts every

main menu drawn four times into quarter-screens after a four-player match, and a spray loop that
plays under the pause menu — are fixed by a push/pop pair and a `Scene::pause`-shaped hook, and
neither needs `Scene` to exist. A stack also gives the level an obvious place to hang "quiet down

#### Do not unpick MattMath's D3D dependency first — it is not what blocks headless testing, and its conversions need the backend to land in

- **File:** `engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** build
- **Tenet:** ARCHITECTURE/Modules (`math` | nothing)

**What:** "`MattMath` depends on nothing" is the most-cited violation in the whole review (cluster
3, seven findings) and reads like a prerequisite for the seam; it is neither a prerequisite nor
independently fixable, and attempting it first produces an adapter the seam then re-homes.

**Evidence:**

    // engine/math/matt_math.h:3-5
    #include "SimpleMath.h"
    #include "engine/math/shape_type.h"
    #include <d3d11.h>

The live consumers of exactly the thing that forces line 5 —
`engine/render/viewport_manager.cpp:22-26` and `:65`:

        D3D11_VIEWPORT ViewportManager::fullscreen_d3d11_viewport() const
        {
            Viewport vp = this->fullscreen_viewport();
            return vp.d3d_viewport();
        }

and `:43-58`, which is the other half of the same class and pure backend:

        void ViewportManager::apply_player_viewport(int player_num,
            ID3D11DeviceContext* context) const
        ...
            context->RSSetViewports(1, &vp);

**Why it matters:** The reasoning that makes this look urgent is that headless tests need `math`
to be dependency-free. That is false, and the distinction is worth being exact about: nothing in
this repository fails to *compile* or *link* because of `<d3d11.h>` — the SDK is present and
`Microsoft::DirectXTK` resolves. What blocks a headless test is that `DirectX::SpriteBatch`'s only
constructor dereferences its `ID3D11DeviceContext*`, so a drawable cannot be *driven*. `MattMath`'s
D3D dependency is a compile-time and portability cost, not a testability one. And it cannot be
removed before the seam: `Viewport::d3d_viewport()` has two live callers that only a D3D11 backend
folder can absorb, so doing it first means inventing a temporary adapter home for a conversion that
belongs in `engine/render/d3d11/` — a folder P1 creates.

**Remedy:** Keep it in P5, after `engine/render/d3d11/` exists, and move the `D3D11_VIEWPORT`,
`SimpleMath` and `RECT` conversions there in one step rather than twice.

#### Event-based logic: nothing in eighty-four reports requires one, and each candidate resolves to a value

- **File:** `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:11-15`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** T11 ("designs that lean on shared object webs — observers, self-reference, polymorphic bags — must be rethought as indices, variants or per-type storage")

**What:** The author's second open question can be answered from the same evidence: the three
places in this codebase that look like they want a publish/subscribe mechanism are each answered
by something already on the plan — a returned value, a contact manifest, or the state stack — and
no finding anywhere requires an event bus.

**Evidence:** *Candidate 1 — collision response.* `game/objects/i_collision_game_object.h:11-15`:

    	virtual bool is_colliding(const ICollisionGameObject* other) const = 0;
    	virtual void on_collision(const ICollisionGameObject* other) = 0;
    	virtual CollisionObjectType collision_object_type() const = 0;
    	virtual const mattmath::Shape* shape() const = 0;
    	virtual bool for_deletion() const = 0;

The dispatch already fires both responders off one participant's predicate
(`game/objects/level.cpp:245-248` and `:280-284`), so the callback pairing is broken *before* any
event machinery is added. PHILOSOPHY/Collision names the replacement and it is data, not an event:
"the narrow phase produces a contact manifold — normal and penetration depth — and resolution is
analytic (MTV)". A manifest of contacts the game iterates after `Scene::resolve()` is a value.

*Candidate 2 — a child state reporting a result.* `game/states/game_states.h:60,64,67`, three
`unique_ptr<enum>` used as out-parameters. This is the one place the codebase actually reached for
indirection, and what it wanted was a return value; P3 supplies it.

*Candidate 3 — "something happened to the level".* `game/objects/level.h:89`, `void stop_music()
const;`, called by hand at seven `GameLevel` exits, plus the weapon loop that keeps playing under
the pause menu. Both want a lifetime and a suspend hook, which P3 also supplies.

**Why it matters:** The question is worth closing rather than leaving open, because an undecided
event system is a standing invitation to answer each of these three with a subscription, and T11
names that shape as "the single loudest thing this engine is *not*". The stronger form of the
argument is the absence: across 84 group reports and 178 clustered findings I found no case where
the fix requires a sender that does not know its receivers. Split-screen local multiplayer with a
fixed step and one scene is precisely the domain where direct calls and per-frame value lists are
sufficient. The falsifiable version: if a genuine case exists it will appear after P2 and P3 land,
and it will be specific enough to answer with a narrow mechanism rather than a bus.

**Remedy:** Record the decision as "no event machinery; results are returned, contacts are a list,
suspend/resume is the stack" in PHILOSOPHY, and revisit only against a named case.

#### Two engine modules are unblocked by everything on the critical path and neither is scheduled

- **File:** `engine/ui/widget.h:59-74`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Category:** design
- **Tenet:** PHILOSOPHY/UI; ARCHITECTURE/Modules

**What:** Widget focus and navigation, and the input module, are pure logic over `bounds()` and
pad state; both can be built today, in parallel with P1–P3, and both are currently scheduled
nowhere because they are filed under modules everyone assumes are seam-blocked.

**Evidence:** `engine/ui/widget.h:59-74` — the widget base already exposes everything a focus ring
and a directional walk need, and nothing about focus:

    	class MWidget : public MObject
    	{

Focus is a `MWidget*` per viewport; navigation is a nearest-neighbour walk over `bounds()`; a

`Scene`, so they are the right work for whatever capacity exists beside P1.

**Remedy:** Schedule focus/navigation/`Button` and the input module as P4, explicitly parallel,
and do not let either wait on the seam.

<a id="g-gap-adversary"></a>

## gap-adversary — the review reviewed

*Group `gap-adversary` · 12 findings (3 high, 6 medium, 3 low) · source `review2/verified/gap-adversary.md`, verified report.*

I read the three design documents, `docs/review/IMPLEMENTED.md`, `meta/triage.md`, and then
worked the corpus mechanically: I parsed all 52 reports into a table of 863 findings (file,
line, severity, category, tenet, title), diffed `raw/` against `verified/`, cross-checked every
finding's cited file against `git ls-files`, and machine-audited 307 sweep citations by probing
whether the quoted evidence appears near the cited line. Then I opened the source behind the
claims that carry the most weight: `engine/render/camera_tools.cpp`, `viewport_manager.cpp`,
`text_object.cpp`, `state.h`/`state_context.h`, `matt_math.cpp:2473`, `sprite_sheet_loader.cpp`,
every `CMakeLists.txt`, `CMakePresets.json`, `.gitignore`, `game/pch.h`, and — because a
critical finding rests on it — DirectXTK's own `Src/SpriteFont.cpp` in the vcpkg build tree.

The technical work is good. The `SpriteFont::Impl::ConvertUTF8` race is real (`utfBuffer` is a
per-font member mutated from a `const` method, `SpriteFont.cpp:365-391`); the camera judder
traces exactly as `render-viewports` says; `player_viewport(4)` and the fall-through switch are
where they are claimed; `MatrixF(int,int)` really never sizes `elements_`; the only warning
suppression in the tree really is inert. Of 242 tracked source/build/content files, only 11 are
never named by any report, and the eleven are dead JSON and forwarding headers. Citation
accuracy is high: my automated audit surfaced no case where quoted evidence was absent from the
cited file.

The failure is not in the findings. It is in the corpus as a document. Half the review — the 20
cross-cutting sweeps, 308 findings — never went through the verification pass that visibly
corrected the other half, and that unverified half is where seven of the twelve criticals and
88 of the 166 highs live. The triage's one dedupe mechanism references a numbered list that
exists in no file. The math groups were partitioned by file rather than by concern, so nine
defects are filed twice and three of them carry contradictory severities with no adjudication.
And one convention breach is graded high, medium and low by six different agents. What surprised
me most was the size of the review's own self-correction — 284 rejected claims, 59 findings added
by verifiers, 88 re-gradings — and that none of it is reported to the author anywhere.

### Themes

- The review has two halves with two different standards of evidence, and nothing on the page
  tells the author which half a finding came from — yet the unverified half grades
  critical-or-high at 31% against the verified half's 15%.
- Duplication was created by the group partition, not by the code: splitting one 5,700-line type
  across a header agent and three implementation agents guaranteed that the same member would be
  reported twice, and the triage's cluster list catches almost none of it.
- Severity is not a property of a defect in this corpus; it is a property of which agent found it.
  The same SCREAMING-constants breach is graded high, medium and low in six places, and the same
  wrong-answer function is graded medium and high.
- Tenet citation is sometimes doing rhetorical rather than logical work: T11 is cited 20 times
  against `game/` code, where T11's own "Not a licence for" clause hands game code its own
  grammar, and no report states which reading of the document it adopted.
- The review enforces the documents' obligations selectively: it audits the test suite in 20
  findings and never once mentions the benchmark suite that PHILOSOPHY/Performance makes an equal
  obligation, while asserting per-frame cost in ~30 findings with no measurement.
- The record-keeping obligations the review imposes on the codebase (name the file, name the
  value, say what is provisional) are not met by the review itself: no finding carries a
  "previously reported" field, and half the reports never opened the 13,029-line prior appendix.

#### Verify the twenty sweep reports, or mark every grading in them provisional

- **File:** `scratchpad/review2/raw/sweep-*.md` (20 files, 308 findings) vs `scratchpad/review2/verified/` (32 files, 555 findings)
- **Severity:** high
- **Category:** docs
- **Tenet:** T5 (compile-time over run-time — "the build is the cheapest reviewer"; here the verification pass is)

**What:** Every module report has a verified counterpart; not one sweep report does, so the half
of the corpus that supplies most of the structural narrative and 7 of the 12 criticals has never
been checked by a second reader.

**Evidence:**

    $ ls verified/ | wc -l          # 32 - all module groups
    $ ls raw/sweep-*.md | wc -l     # 20 - none has a verified counterpart

Timestamps show the verification pass ran 12:54–13:25 and touched module reports only; the
sweeps were written 12:29–12:56 and never revisited. The pass demonstrably changes conclusions:

    verified/render-device.md:20-21
    I re-graded four findings down. The `#pragma warning(disable : 4061)` is real and is the only one
    in the tree, but C4061 is off by default and `/W4` does not enable it, so the line is inert

    verified/math-impl-a.md  — "- **Origin:** added-by-verifier"   (59 such findings corpus-wide)

Across the 32 verified reports the pass produced 284 rejected or corrected claims, 88 explicit
re-gradings, and 59 new findings.

**Why it matters:** the two halves grade differently by a factor of two. Verified: 5 critical,
78 high out of 555 (15% critical-or-high). Unverified: 7 critical, 88 high out of 308 (31%).
That gap is the size of the correction the sweeps did not receive. The author's first action
will be the critical list, and 7 of its 12 entries — including `engine/collision/ contains no
collision`, `Move the scene out of Level`, and `no README` — come from the unchecked half.

**Remedy:** run the same verification pass over the 20 sweeps before the criticals are actioned;

### What this review has not established

Stated plainly, because the corpus does not say it anywhere:

1. **That the tree builds.** Nothing was configured, built or run — correctly, per the brief.
   Every "this compiles / this is green" statement is inherited from `IMPLEMENTED.md:20-23`
   ("Debug|x64 and Release|x64 build clean … 38/38 unit tests pass"), which describes the
   *pre-CMake* solution. Individual reviewers did compile probe files with `cl` (the scratchpad
   holds `warncheck*.cpp`, `probe*.cpp` and their `.obj`s), so specific compiler behaviours were
   tested; the project itself was not. Settling it costs one `cmake --build` and one `ctest`.

2. **That any runtime defect actually manifests.** The camera judder, the fullscreen fourth pane
   in three-player, the ramp pass-through, the weapon loop surviving into the main menu, the
   `SpriteFont` race — every one is a static trace. They are good traces and I re-derived the
   camera one line by line, but no one has seen the judder, and the `SpriteFont` race in
   particular needs two workers in `Level::draw_active_level` reaching the *same* `SpriteFont`
   in the same frame, which is argued from code shape rather than observed. Settling it costs
   one run per bug, plus a thread-sanitised or instrumented build for the race.

3. **That any performance claim is true in magnitude.** No allocation count, no frame time, no
   object count was measured. The corpus has no benchmark to measure against and never says so
   (finding 5). "Ten allocations per quad-vs-quad test" and "around a thousand pellets live" are
   both derived from reading, not counting.

4. **That the unverified sweeps' 308 findings hold.** My automated citation audit found no
   evidence quoted from the wrong file, which is reassuring about *accuracy*; it says nothing
   about *severity* or about consequences that were traced rather than reached, which is exactly
   what the verification pass corrected 284 times in the other half.

5. **Whether the game is currently playable at all.** `.gitignore` ends with `*.wav`, `*.xwb`,
   `*.mp3`, and `git ls-files` shows no `sound_bank_1.xwb` — only `XWBTool.exe` and a `cmd.txt`
   beside it. Two findings state that a fresh clone cannot start; no one confirmed it by cloning.

6. **Anything about the four "Outstanding" items' cost.** The brief asked for new specific
   information on `#13` and `#18`. `verified/game-level.md` and `raw/sweep-mechanism-vs-policy.md`
   give call sites for `#18`, which is the new information asked for; `#13` (the collision
   interface carrying a game enum) is restated in several places without a cost estimate or a
   list of what breaks.

What the review *has* established, and I could not shake: the corpus's factual base. Of 242
tracked files, 231 are named by some report; the numeric claims I resampled (325 `M*` references,
82 lowercase `mobject`, 135 `I*` references, ~593 SCREAMING declarations, zero `[[nodiscard]]`,
one `#pragma warning`, no `SpriteBatch::Begin` in `engine/`) all check out; and the two
structural claims the whole narrative rests on — that both libraries publish
`${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}` as a `PUBLIC` include root, and that `MattMath` links
`Microsoft::DirectXTK PUBLIC` — are visible in six lines of `engine/CMakeLists.txt` and
`engine/math/CMakeLists.txt`. The problems above are problems of the document, not of the
looking.
